overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Proximal aortic repair may replace the root, ascending aorta, or arch and requires cardiopulmonary bypass; arch work may require hypothermic circulatory arrest and a cerebral-perfusion strategy.
Priorities are to limit aortic wall stress without compromising organ perfusion, detect malperfusion promptly, and assess ventricular, valve, and aortic findings with TEE.
During circulatory arrest, cerebral protection depends on the operative strategy and close perfusion monitoring; rewarming should be gradual to reduce cerebral injury risk.

Recovery requires prompt neurologic assessment and surveillance for cardiac dysfunction, bleeding, coagulopathy, renal injury, and respiratory problems; the sources do not establish a universal extubation schedule.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Root replacement entails resection, graft replacement, and coronary-button reimplantation; the native valve may be resuspended or replaced. A composite graft with valve is a Bentall procedure; valve-sparing root replacement is also described.
Ascending-aortic repair commonly uses an interposition graft. Hemi-arch addresses proximal transverse arch; total arch replaces the transverse arch and is performed under circulatory arrest.

Cannulation and cerebral-perfusion approaches depend on anatomy and operation. Arch strategies include antegrade or retrograde cerebral perfusion, or arrest without adjunctive perfusion; no single approach is established for every case.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Acute type A dissection is a time-sensitive surgical emergency. Review imaging for dissection extent, planned repair and cannulation, aortic insufficiency, branch-vessel patency, and malperfusion; assess baseline neurologic status when feasible.

Assess ventricular and valve function, coronary involvement, peripheral pulses, and signs of malperfusion. Pulse deficits and neurologic compromise can indicate higher risk and affect monitoring priorities.

For aneurysmal disease, timing is informed by diameter, growth, symptoms, connective-tissue disorder, and operative risk. Thresholds vary by phenotype and guideline; the cited review’s examples are not a complete indication set.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate the cardiac operating room, perfusion team, and availability of blood products before an emergency case; establish invasive pressure monitoring and large-bore venous access before induction when feasible.

Use multisite arterial pressure monitoring to help detect malperfusion and interpret pressure changes during cannulation, clamping, and cerebral perfusion. The useful sites depend on the operation and cannulation plan; a low reading warrants investigation.

TEE is recommended unless contraindicated; use it to assess cardiac and valve function, dissection, and repair. NIRS, EEG, or TCD may supplement cerebral monitoring, but each has limitations. The reviewed sources specify no patient-positioning protocol.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The described airway is a single-lumen endotracheal tube. Induction should blunt sympathetic stimulation and avoid hypertension or tachycardia that increase aortic wall stress; agent choice must reflect hemodynamic stability.

In an unstable patient, probe insertion for TEE may itself cause hemodynamic compromise; defer until stability if clinically necessary. The sources do not establish a universal RSI or ventilation protocol.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring, including ECG, oxygenation assessment, and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring during general anesthesia; temperature monitoring is indicated when significant temperature change is anticipated.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Before bypass, control heart rate and pressure to reduce wall stress while preserving end-organ perfusion. The balance is especially important in dissection; excessive hypertension risks propagation or rupture, while malperfusion must be actively sought.

Closely reassess perfusion at bypass initiation, aortic clamping, distal anastomosis, and circulatory arrest. If malperfusion is detected, the review advises immediate reassessment of the flow route and cannulation strategy with the surgical team.

Cerebral protection aims to limit ischemic time and maintain oxygenated flow; the choice and temperature strategy vary. Comparative evidence on perfusion approaches is conflicting, and the sources do not support a universal safe arrest duration.
Rewarm gradually and avoid cerebral hyperthermia. After bypass, reassess ventricular function and volume status and titrate support to the observed physiology.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Major hazards include cerebral, coronary, visceral, or limb malperfusion; false-lumen pressurization; aortic rupture; stroke; and myocardial dysfunction. Interpret pressure, NIRS, ECG, TEE, and perfusion findings together rather than relying on one monitor.

Hypothermia and prolonged bypass can contribute to coagulopathy; other postoperative concerns include delirium, respiratory failure, metabolic disturbance, renal failure, and stroke. Escalate concerning perfusion or neurologic changes to the operative team promptly.

After repair, evaluate ventricular and valve function, residual insufficiency, and the visible aortic repair with TEE; investigate new hemodynamic instability or evidence of ischemia rather than assuming an uncomplicated separation from bypass.

sources.label: Recommendations for Haemodynamic and Neurological Monitoring in Repair of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection
Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Expect platelet dysfunction, depletion of coagulation factors and fibrinogen, and increased fibrinolysis after lower-temperature aortic procedures. Dissection may also be associated with preoperative coagulation derangement.

Use viscoelastic testing such as TEG or ROTEM to guide hemostatic replacement; the review describes goal-directed replacement of fibrinogen, platelets, and factor deficiencies. It does not establish a universal transfusion threshold or product protocol.
Reassess volume after bypass as temperature equilibration, vasodilation, and capillary leak shift fluid distribution. Use available TEE and hemodynamic data; no fixed fluid total is supported.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For adult cardiac surgery, the consensus report recommends multimodal nonopioid analgesia and opioid stewardship rather than routine high-dose opioid anesthesia; tailor choices to patient risks and local expertise.

Regional techniques may be considered, but the consensus recommendation is weak and systemic anticoagulation is a relevant safety consideration. The report does not define a required regimen for aortic repair.
Nausea or vomiting is common after cardiac surgery, but the source does not establish an aortic-repair-specific PONV prevention protocol.

sources.label: Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location, such as an ICU, with monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition. The reviewed aortic source does not establish extubation criteria or a fixed timing.

Assess neurologic status as soon as possible, including a brief assessment while intubated when appropriate; continue surveillance for bleeding, coagulopathy, cardiac instability, renal injury, and malperfusion.

When neuromuscular blockers have been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this applies to cases using blockade, not to every anesthetic.

sources.label: Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Anesthetic Management for Proximal Aortic Repair
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The proximal-aortic source is an open-access review, not a trial or guideline; it reports limited high-quality evidence and substantial variation in practice. Its recommendations and institutional preferences should not be treated as universal standards.

The acute-dissection monitoring source is a narrative review with little randomized evidence and no universally accepted monitoring standards. The cardiac analgesia source is a consensus report with comparatively sparse evidence for many interventions.

The basic ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade sources provide general standards, not aortic-repair-specific technique. The supplied adult cardiac anesthesia review is also broad and provides no detailed procedure-specific protocol.
Positioning, a procedure-specific analgesic regimen, and extubation criteria remain unspecified in the supplied aortic-repair evidence; this draft does not infer them.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) replaces a diseased valve through open surgery, generally using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and cardioplegia; partial sternotomy or right anterior thoracotomy may be options for selected patients.
The underlying lesion matters: SAVR treats aortic stenosis or regurgitation, while valve choice and whether to use SAVR or TAVR are individualized to the patient and clinical context.

Major perioperative concerns include arrhythmia, bleeding, stroke, and conduction disturbance that may require permanent pacing; maintain close coordination with the surgical and perfusion teams during bypass and separation from it.
Recovery requires monitored postanesthesia care, in an ICU or equivalent when appropriate; extubation timing and disposition depend on the patient's condition rather than a fixed schedule.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Anesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: SAVR removes the damaged aortic valve and sews in a replacement. The described conventional approach uses a sternotomy; partial sternotomy and right anterior thoracotomy are described as minimally invasive options when appropriate.
The operation uses a heart-lung machine to divert blood and permit cardioplegic arrest while the valve is replaced. The supplied SAVR overview does not detail the anesthetic conduct of bypass.
TAVR is a distinct transcatheter procedure, not a substitute source for routine SAVR anesthetic management. The choice between procedures is made in light of the patient's heart and overall health.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the valve lesion and overall cardiac status from the clinical assessment and available imaging. The supplied sources do not establish specific anesthetic thresholds for stenosis severity, gradients, ventricular function, or regurgitation.

Review coexisting disease and whether additional cardiac procedures are anticipated; open surgery may be favored for some patients who need CABG or other cardiac procedures, but the source does not define selection criteria.

Discuss prosthesis selection with the treating team. Mechanical valves require lifelong warfarin; the source describes biological and mechanical options but does not provide perioperative anticoagulation interruption or restart guidance.

Consider operative risk, age, and medical conditions in procedure selection. The supplied overview lists common investigations but does not provide an anesthesia-specific risk-stratification protocol.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan a cardiac operating-room environment with the surgical and perfusion teams. The supplied SAVR source establishes use of a heart-lung machine but does not specify a complete room setup or line configuration.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical condition. ASA standards require ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; additional monitoring is not specified here for SAVR.
Continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature during anesthesia, applying the standards within their stated scope and clinical exceptions.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The SAVR source describes deep general anesthesia but does not specify an airway device or a procedure-specific anesthetic technique. Do not infer a drug recipe from the supplied case fields.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify its position clinically and by identifying carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, perform continual quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis.
If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation; this recommendation does not impose blockade on every case.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The key procedural transition described for SAVR is institution of bypass and cardioplegia, followed by valve excision and replacement. Specific anesthetic targets for aortic stenosis or regurgitation are not established in the supplied evidence.

Coordinate closely with the surgeon and perfusionist throughout bypass. The general cardiac-surgery review states that bypass management and weaning follow conventional cardiac-surgery principles but does not supply AVR-specific targets.

Use echocardiographic assessment according to the operative approach and clinical need. The MICS review describes TEE as a tool for surgical and hemodynamic guidance in its scope; this does not establish a universal SAVR-specific TEE protocol.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Anesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anticipate arrhythmia, bleeding, stroke, infection, and possible need for permanent pacing. The supplied SAVR overview identifies these risks but does not provide a procedure-specific rescue algorithm.
Maintain communication among the surgeon, anesthesiologist, and perfusionist throughout cardiopulmonary bypass.

During postanesthesia care, evaluate the patient continuously, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; escalate concerns through the responsible clinical team.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Anesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: CPB is part of the described SAVR procedure. The supplied sources do not establish a universal fluid strategy, transfusion trigger, hematocrit threshold, or blood-product protocol for SAVR.
Bleeding is a recognized possible SAVR complication. Manage perfusion and blood loss in coordination with the operative and perfusion teams, individualized to the case.
The MICS review reports no specific fluid or transfusion regimen; its discussion of minimally invasive cases should not be used to impose a protocol on conventional SAVR.

sources.label: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Anesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use an individualized multimodal analgesic approach rather than routine high-dose opioid anesthesia; the adult cardiac-surgery consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesics and opioid stewardship.

Regional techniques may be considered in context, with systemic anticoagulation and patient- and procedure-specific limitations taken into account. The consensus describes the recommendation to consider regional techniques as weak.
Provide education on analgesia options and adverse effects, and plan opioid prescribing across transitions of care. The evidence does not establish a single required SAVR analgesic regimen.

sources.label: Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Base extubation readiness on clinical condition and, when neuromuscular blockers were used, quantitative confirmation of adequate recovery. The sources do not support a fixed SAVR extubation timetable.
Provide PACU or equivalent monitored care after anesthesia unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise; transport and handoff require ongoing evaluation and communication.

Continue appropriate observation for arrhythmia and other postoperative complications. Cleveland Clinic describes hospital recovery and monitoring but does not provide an anesthesia-specific ICU or extubation protocol.

sources.label: New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement — Cleveland Clinic
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The SAVR-specific source is a patient-facing clinical overview, not an anesthesia reference. It supports procedural description and general complications, but not detailed anesthetic management.

The MICS review includes minimally invasive aortic valve surgery and transcatheter interventions, but its broad discussion should not be treated as a conventional SAVR protocol. It notes limited randomized data and practice variation.

The adult cardiac-surgery consensus informs pain stewardship, while ASA standards inform general monitoring, postanesthesia care, and neuromuscular-blockade practice; none supplies a complete SAVR anesthetic plan.
Case-specific anesthetic targets and complete bypass, transfusion, and recovery protocols are not established by the supplied material.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Flexible bronchoscopy is commonly performed with sedation and topical airway anesthesia; rigid bronchoscopy is usually performed under general anesthesia, particularly for airway obstruction or therapeutic work.
The dominant anesthetic hazard is a shared, instrumented airway: obstruction, apnea, and rapid desaturation can occur, so airway access and oxygenation require active attention throughout.
Coordinate airway and ventilation technique with the bronchoscopist; rigid procedures may interrupt ventilation, and jet ventilation carries barotrauma risk.
Recovery priorities include surveillance for respiratory compromise, bleeding, and pneumothorax; when neuromuscular blockade is used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Flexible bronchoscopy provides airway visualization for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes and is commonly performed with sedation plus topical anesthesia. The supplied sources do not establish a single sedation depth or airway device for every flexible procedure.

Rigid bronchoscopy is usually performed under general anesthesia and is commonly used to diagnose or treat airway obstruction. It requires an operating-room setting according to the educational review.
Select technique with the bronchoscopist according to procedural goals, patient comorbidity, and the relative risks of flexible versus rigid access; obtain consent.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review medical and surgical history, medications, airway examination, and time since oral intake. Assess cardiopulmonary reserve and the likelihood that even brief apnea or instrumentation-related obstruction will be poorly tolerated.

Consider pulmonary function testing or arterial blood gas when needed to characterize respiratory status. The review also suggests pulmonary function testing when severe obstruction is suspected and baseline blood gas in selected patients with hypoxemia or hypercarbia.

Poor oxygen reserve or unstable cardiopulmonary disease increases concern: the review identifies pulmonary hypertension, severe COPD, poorly controlled asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, and morbid obesity among conditions warranting particular caution for routine diagnostic bronchoscopy.
For suspected airway foreign body, establish timing, location, and shape; urgent obstruction may preclude imaging before intervention.

sources.label: Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Have airway-management equipment readily available; the educational review identifies the operating room as the preferred setting for bronchoscopy, particularly rigid procedures.

The airway and working space are shared with the bronchoscopist. One review describes the patient usually supine at the table edge with the head extended; positioning is not specified by the other review, so adapt to procedural access and team requirements.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards require continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment invalidates that method. This takes precedence over the older review's observation that end-tidal monitoring is usually not done.

sources.label: Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Flexible bronchoscopy may be performed with spontaneous breathing under sedation; oxygen is typically delivered by nasal cannula, while an LMA or ETT may be used when clinically appropriate. Do not assume a natural airway is suitable for every patient or procedure.
For deeper sedation or general anesthesia, the airway may be secured with an ETT or LMA using a bronchoscope adaptor. Anticipate the need to intervene for apnea, desaturation, or obstruction.

Rigid bronchoscopy usually requires general anesthesia. Ventilation options include apnoeic oxygenation, spontaneous assisted ventilation, controlled ventilation, manual jet ventilation, and high-frequency jet ventilation. The anesthetic plan should be agreed by the bronchoscopy operator and anesthesia team, taking the technique, patient comorbidities, and procedure goals into account.
With jet ventilation, watch for abrupt oxygenation or carbon-dioxide deterioration that may indicate barotrauma, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum; escalate promptly with the procedural team.

sources.label: Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Topical anesthesia is an important adjunct, especially for flexible bronchoscopy; anesthesia beyond the glottis can blunt cough and facilitate the procedure. Maintain vigilance after pharyngeal topicalization because airway reflexes may be impaired.

Sedation can depress ventilation, and limited cardiopulmonary reserve may make brief apnea consequential. Titrate the technique to the patient and procedural conditions, with the ability to support ventilation promptly.

The scope can narrow the effective airway and impede ventilation; coordinate scope position, suctioning, and ventilation changes with the bronchoscopist while following oxygenation and ventilation continuously.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize hypoxemia, airway obstruction, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, bleeding, and pneumothorax as important complications. Hypoxemia may reflect inadequate ventilation, hemorrhage, or obstructing secretions or tissue.

For deterioration, communicate immediately with the bronchoscopist and assess airway patency, ventilation, scope position, and secretions; the review describes increasing inspired oxygen, repositioning the scope, and suctioning as responses to hypoxia.

Transbronchial biopsy and lung brushing carry pneumothorax risk. New respiratory or oxygenation deterioration after these procedures warrants prompt evaluation; the supplied sources do not establish a universal routine imaging protocol.
Pharyngeal anesthesia and altered consciousness are among aspiration risk factors. Maintain vigilance for aspiration risk and respond to respiratory compromise with prompt assessment and escalation.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No routine fluid regimen is specified for bronchoscopy. Individualize access and fluid administration to the patient's condition and procedural needs; invasive access is described only for selected, hemodynamically compromised cases.

Biopsy can cause airway bleeding, with concern heightened by vascular lesions; assess the clinical impact and coordinate hemostatic management with the bronchoscopist. The available educational review does not provide a bleeding-management or transfusion protocol.
Monitor circulation as part of standard anesthetic care; the supplied bronchoscopy sources do not define procedure-specific perfusion targets or a universal blood-loss threshold.

sources.label: Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures
Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Post-procedure discomfort is usually laryngeal and the review reports response to simple analgesics. The sources do not define a required analgesic regimen.
The supplied bronchoscopy sources do not provide a procedure-specific PONV prevention or treatment protocol; assess and manage according to the patient's needs and applicable local guidance.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Anesthetic Considerations for Bronchoscopic Procedures

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Continue observation for respiratory distress and reassess oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness in postanesthesia care; ensure a capable recovery area is available.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.
After anesthesia, transport with an anesthesia care team member who can monitor and support the patient; provide a verbal handoff and document arrival status.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The procedure-specific anesthesia review is a narrative review rather than a formal guideline or trial; its recommendations are not uniformly graded by evidence strength.
The StatPearls source is a broad educational overview, not a trial or guideline, and does not provide detailed anesthetic dosing protocols.

ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards provide general anesthesia-care requirements, not bronchoscopy-specific management; apply their monitoring and recovery provisions within their stated scope.

Available sources do not establish an adult, procedure-specific protocol for EBUS, post-biopsy imaging, or timing of oral intake after topical anesthesia; these remain local/procedural decisions rather than settled recommendations in this draft.

Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Conventional adult CABG is usually performed through median sternotomy with autologous arterial or venous conduits; the reference source focuses on on-pump surgery, not off-pump or minimally invasive approaches.

The central anesthetic priority is stable myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance while avoiding ischemia and major hemodynamic swings across induction, sternotomy, bypass, and separation from bypass.

CPB introduces perfusion, temperature, anticoagulation, and air-management hazards; coordinate closely with the perfusionist and use phase-appropriate monitoring rather than relying on a single fixed target.

Plan recovery around hemostasis, temperature, hemodynamic and respiratory stability, and neuromuscular recovery when blockade is used; ICU care and fast-track weaning are usual considerations, not fixed extubation deadlines.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: CABG restores coronary blood flow by grafting around obstructed arteries. Common conduits include internal mammary, radial, and saphenous vein grafts; most patients receive multiple grafts.
The principal approach described here is full-sternotomy, on-pump CABG with cardiac arrest and CPB. Do not assume these details apply unchanged to off-pump or minimally invasive surgery.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the surgical and cardiac assessment, including ventricular function, unstable angina or recent infarction, arrhythmias, mechanical support, extent of coronary disease, and prior cardiac surgery.

Identify comorbidities that modify perioperative risk, including diabetes, lung disease, renal dysfunction, peripheral vascular disease, and cerebrovascular disease. The source notes use of the STS risk score for risk stratification.

Individualize medication and laboratory planning with the cardiac surgical team. The available sources do not establish CABG-specific instructions for antiplatelet or antihypertensive continuation or interruption.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
Basic Standards for Preanesthesia Care

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate the cardiac operating room, perfusion team, CPB equipment, defibrillation capability, invasive pressure monitoring, and central vascular access. The specific access configuration is determined by the patient and team.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring and continuous ECG, with arterial pressure monitoring and core temperature assessment. ASA standards also require ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

TEE is associated with measurable outcome benefits in cardiac surgery. PA catheter use remains controversial and is a care-team decision; do not treat either as a universally mandated configuration based on these sources.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Endotracheal intubation with a single-lumen tube is most commonly described for conventional CABG. The sources do not establish a universal airway device or induction recipe; induction should be controlled to limit ischemia and avoid excessive hypotension.
Ventilation is usually stopped once adequate CPB flow is established and the heart stops ejecting; resume ventilation with oxygenation support during preparation for bypass termination.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring where available and confirm recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; these recommendations do not impose blockade on every patient or technique.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Anticipate variable responses to stimulation: skin preparation and draping may accompany hypotension, while incision, sternotomy, retraction, and pericardial opening may provoke hypertension or tachycardia; retraction can also produce marked bradycardia and hypotension.

Before CPB, confirm anticoagulation adequacy with ACT and coordinate cannulation and pump initiation with the perfusionist. The source describes a range as adequate; this draft does not prescribe a universal ACT target.
During CPB, monitor serial ACT and arterial blood gases, with particular attention to hematocrit, potassium, and blood glucose.
For separation from bypass, assess rhythm, cardiac function, laboratory status, temperature, and ventilation with the team; TEE is often used to assess cardiac function.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize that aortic cannulation carries dissection risk and that cerebral or coronary air emboli are hazards. Escalate concerns immediately with the surgeon and perfusionist; the source does not provide a universal rescue algorithm.
If venous return or pump flow is inadequate, promptly assess the circuit and cannula path with the perfusionist; listed causes include malposition, clamps, kinks, and air locks.

After bypass, monitor for bleeding, hemodynamic instability, arrhythmias, and protamine reactions. The source notes rare reactions and recommends checking ACT after reversal; specific reaction treatment protocols are not supplied here.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use perfusion and clinical assessment to guide fluid, vasoactive, and blood-product decisions. The CABG source lists goal-directed fluid therapy but does not specify a fluid regimen.
Anticipate CPB-associated hemodilution and postoperative bleeding/coagulopathy; coordinate antifibrinolytic use, surgical hemostasis, and anticoagulation reversal with the cardiac team.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
Small incisions still require great anesthesia: anesthesiology techniques to enhance recovery in robotic coronary bypass grafting

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use an individualized multimodal, opioid-sparing approach while preserving adequate analgesia and recovery. The adult cardiac-surgery consensus advises against routine high-dose opioid anesthesia or analgesia.

Consider regional techniques selectively, weighing anticipated benefit, expertise, and systemic anticoagulation-related risk. The consensus recommendation to consider regional techniques is weak, and it notes potential neuraxial hematoma and hypotension concerns.

NSAID use requires particular caution in CABG: the consensus notes platelet, renal, gastrointestinal, and thrombotic cardiovascular concerns, including an FDA warning related to coronary revascularization. A CABG-specific PONV regimen is not established in these sources.

sources.label: Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Many patients are transported intubated to ICU, but operating-room extubation may be considered in selected circumstances. The source describes ICU fast-track weaning and early extubation, without establishing a universal time point or eligibility rule.
Recovery assessment should include oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with appropriate handoff and monitoring in PACU or an equivalent setting such as ICU.

If neuromuscular blockers were used, verify quantitative recovery before extubation; postoperative care should also address hemostasis, hemodynamic support, rhythm, renal function, glucose, and respiratory progress.

sources.label: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The CABG-specific source is an educational summary focused on conventional on-pump surgery; it provides no evidence grading and states that off-pump and minimally invasive approaches are discussed elsewhere.

The POQI/ERAS cardiac pain report is a consensus report based on a scoping review and Delphi process; it notes sparse cardiac-surgery evidence for many interventions. It supports opioid stewardship, not a single required regimen.
The robotic CABG review describes a minimally invasive approach and practices based in part on the authors’ center or experience; those details should not be treated as routine open-CABG standards.

The available sources do not resolve specific CABG medication-management protocols, transfusion criteria, or detailed postbypass rescue algorithms. These remain institutional and patient-specific decisions, not universal evidence gaps requiring fixed targets.
The supplied CABG summary gives no specific fluid regimen and lists goal-directed fluid therapy among ERAS measures; it does not establish a transfusion threshold, fluid total, or blood-loss target.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adult PCI, mild sedation is usual; anesthesia involvement is particularly relevant when acute MI causes respiratory distress or hemodynamic instability, or sedation cannot be managed safely by the procedural team.
Do not treat PCI and transcatheter valve intervention as the same anesthetic. General anesthesia is commonly used for TAVI, while deep sedation and noninvasive ventilation have also been reported.
The catheterization laboratory is a remote, radiation-exposed environment. Priorities include room familiarity, team communication, appropriate monitoring, and radiation protection.

During recovery after anesthesia, continue condition-appropriate observation, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness. The supplied PCI evidence does not establish a specific access-site recovery protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Diagnostic catheterization and PCI are performed in the catheterization laboratory. PCI is usually conducted with mild sedation under cardiologist supervision; anesthetic choice remains dependent on the procedure and patient.

Differentiate coronary intervention from structural procedures. For TAVI, general anesthesia is commonly used in the reviewed practice, but deep sedation with noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation has also been tried; this is not a universal technique prescription.

For PCI, proper IV access and airway management are emphasized, and close communication with the cardiologist is useful. The review does not establish a single access route or anesthetic plan for all cases.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the procedure and clinical context, including whether instability or respiratory distress is present; these factors may change the need for anesthesia support and airway intervention.

Review renal impairment when contrast is anticipated. The source identifies potential worsening of renal impairment and advises adequate hydration and limiting contrast exposure; it does not provide an individualized hydration prescription.

Establish whether there has been a prior contrast reaction and communicate this to the procedural team; the review describes differences between contrast types and their reported use after prior reaction.

Anesthetic choices should be discussed with the cardiologist and matched to patient and procedure. The available sources do not give a PCI-specific risk score or a complete preprocedure assessment protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The remote laboratory requires familiarity with its equipment, personnel, access routes, and complications. Check available equipment and medications and coordinate with the procedural team; the source does not prescribe a fixed equipment list for every case.

Fluoroscopy creates occupational radiation exposure. The review describes protection through distance, minimizing exposure time, and shielding such as lead aprons and thyroid collars; this supports radiation precautions, not a claim that any one item guarantees safety.
For anesthesia care, maintain ECG display and determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes. Apply other monitoring according to the anesthetic and clinical condition.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates it. Do not infer that an arterial line is required for every catheterization.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For uncomplicated PCI, the review describes mild sedation as usual, not routine general anesthesia. Sedation can deepen, so personnel must be prepared to recognize airway and hemodynamic complications.

When PCI requires airway intervention, the review prefers endotracheal intubation over a laryngeal mask airway. This is a source-specific statement about PCI airway management, not a mandate to intubate stable patients.

If general anesthesia is used, verify airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, with continual quantitative end-tidal CO₂ monitoring from placement until extubation or transfer begins.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain close communication with the cardiologist during PCI. Acute respiratory distress or hemodynamic instability may require anesthesia involvement and a change in airway or anesthetic support.

The catheterization review identifies thrombosis as an acute PCI complication. Monitor for clinical deterioration and coordinate promptly with the procedural team; the supplied evidence does not give a universal anticoagulation target or rescue algorithm.

For TAVI, the review identifies adequate preload and afterload, sinus rhythm, and avoidance of tachycardia as hemodynamic goals. These are procedure-specific considerations and should not be imposed as fixed targets for PCI.
Fluoroscopy exposure is an ongoing occupational hazard; apply radiation-protection practices throughout the case and limit exposure consistent with the procedure.

bullets: If sedation becomes deep or airway/hemodynamic problems arise, obtain appropriate anesthesia support and manage the airway and circulation in coordination with the procedural team. Recognize thrombosis as a reported acute PCI complication and escalate with the interventional cardiologist; no source-supported universal treatment sequence is provided here.
Contrast exposure can worsen renal impairment. The review supports attention to contrast dose and hydration, but does not supply a patient-specific renal-protection regimen.

bullets: For contrast procedures, the review supports adequate hydration before and after the procedure to reduce contrast-associated renal risk, with particular concern in impaired renal function. No fixed fluid volume is established.

Limit contrast exposure where feasible in consultation with the interventional cardiologist; prolonged or multiple studies may be staged according to the review, rather than assuming a universal contrast limit.

The TAVI review describes preparation including blood availability and large-bore IV lines. This is specific to the reviewed valve-intervention context and does not establish routine crossmatching or access requirements for all PCI.

bullets: The supplied PCI-focused review does not establish a procedural analgesia or PONV regimen. Avoid importing cardiac-surgery drug options or doses as a cath-laboratory protocol.

bullets: After anesthesia care, transfer to a PACU or equivalent unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Continue appropriate evaluation and support during transport, with handoff to the receiving nurse.

In the initial recovery phase, use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry and continue condition-appropriate observation of ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open valve surgery is lesion- and anatomy-dependent. Standard surgical mitral repair usually uses cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and cardiac arrest; approaches described include sternotomy, thoracotomy, and robotic surgery.
Use intraoperative TEE to assess ventricular function and mitral repair adequacy; recognize that SAM can cause residual regurgitation and LV outflow tract obstruction.

Assess LV and RV dysfunction in heart failure; pulmonary hypertension is associated with increased perioperative morbidity and mortality. Restoring aortic valve competence can increase LV afterload and unmask or worsen LV failure.

Recovery planning should be individualized: the supplied sources do not define valve-surgery extubation criteria or an analgesic regimen. Postanesthesia care requires monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition, in a PACU or equivalent area such as an ICU.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For standard surgical mitral repair, the described approach uses CPB and usually full cardiac arrest. Median sternotomy is described particularly when concomitant CABG, ascending aortic intervention, or additional valve surgery is required; thoracotomy and robotic approaches are also described.

Aortic valve repair and valve-sparing root procedures preserve the native valve in selected anatomy. The aortic review describes root remodeling or reimplantation and notes that heavily calcified, stiff, or retracted cusps may not be amenable to repair.

Mitral repair techniques described include annuloplasty, leaflet resection, and neochordae. For mitral stenosis with substantial thickening, subvalvular fibrosis, and tethering, the review says replacement may be more appropriate; this is not a universal choice rule for all valves.

bullets: Review valve anatomy and severity, ventricular function, coronary anatomy, comorbidities, and prior cardiac or thoracic operations. The mitral review recommends a focused history, examination, diagnostic-study review, and risk assessment; it does not supply a valve-surgery anesthetic protocol.

Preoperative TEE assessment of the aortic apparatus should include the annulus, sinus, sinotubular junction, and cusps. The review emphasizes experienced clinicians and collaboration among cardiology, surgery, and anesthesia.

Pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, and marked LV dysfunction are relevant risk modifiers in the mitral review. It also identifies renal insufficiency as a reason to avoid nephrotoxic agents and optimize volume status; individual assessment remains necessary.

bullets: Standard mitral repair generally involves CPB and cardiac arrest. The mitral review describes aortic cannulation, bicaval venous cannulation, and antegrade and retrograde cardioplegia in its median-sternotomy sequence; these details are not a universal protocol for every valve operation.

For aortic repair, the source describes antegrade cardioplegia through the aortic root or directly into the coronary ostia when severe aortic insufficiency is present. It does not specify a cardioplegia dose or an anesthetic hemodynamic target.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: After mitral repair, SAM can cause residual regurgitation and LV outflow tract obstruction. If identified intraoperatively, optimize ventricular filling, use atrioventricular pacing to improve synchrony, and reduce ventricular hypercontractility.

The mitral review identifies circumflex artery injury as a procedural hazard, particularly near the anterolateral commissure. If recognized during surgery, it describes immediate surgical myocardial revascularization as generally advised; prompt recognition and escalation are important.

The aortic review lists missed prolapse, poor coaptation, cusp perforation, and injury near the base of the anterior mitral leaflet among early technical complications. It advises addressing recognized defects before concluding the operation.

bullets: The mitral review does not specify a fluid, transfusion, or hemostasis protocol. It advises optimizing volume status in renal insufficiency and describes optimizing ventricular filling as part of intraoperative SAM management; neither statement establishes a universal fluid target.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For adult cardiac surgery, the POQI/ERAS consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesia and opioid stewardship, while advising against routine high-dose opioid anesthesia or analgesia. It does not prescribe one required regimen for valve surgery.

Tailor analgesic choices to patient and procedural factors. The consensus identifies renal dysfunction and older age as relevant to gabapentinoid dosing, and significant liver dysfunction or inability to tolerate oral medication as relevant to acetaminophen use.

Opioid-related concerns include nausea and vomiting, sedation, delirium, sleep-disordered breathing, and urinary retention. The consensus gives no valve-specific PONV prevention protocol; analgesia and opioid exposure should be individualized.

After anesthesia, the patient should receive care in a PACU or equivalent setting, with monitoring appropriate to clinical condition and attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. An ICU is one example of an equivalent location.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Chest-wall resection may be performed with lung resection; reconstruction in the supplied series used titanium mesh or plates, sometimes with a muscle flap. The evidence describes varied defects and associated procedures rather than one standard operation.

General anesthesia was used in the reported reconstruction series. The airway approach varied: double-lumen intubation was used when lung resection was planned; otherwise, single-lumen intubation was used.

The available case series report postoperative bleeding, pneumothorax, wound complications, and occasional implant problems. They do not establish a chest-wall-specific physiologic target or a standardized response strategy.

Recovery planning should account for the operation performed and the patient’s condition. The supplied surgical studies do not report extubation practices; general postanesthesia standards require appropriate observation and monitoring, including oxygenation during initial recovery.

bullets: Chest-wall resection and reconstruction encompass heterogeneous defects and indications, including primary or secondary tumors, lung cancer involving the chest wall, trauma, and revision procedures. The described reconstruction materials include titanium mesh, with titanium bars used in some cases to add rigidity.

The supplied series include resections of multiple ribs and associated lung resection; some patients required a muscle flap. The reconstruction and associated procedures therefore need to be understood from the planned operative extent rather than assumed from the procedure name alone.

bullets: Clarify defect location and extent, anticipated rib or sternal work, planned lung resection, and whether soft-tissue reconstruction or other major procedures are expected. These determine the operative approach and whether lung isolation was used in the reported practice.

Pulmonary function testing was part of the evaluation for elective patients in the multicenter series. The source does not provide thresholds, predicted postoperative values, or a procedure-specific pulmonary risk model.

Coordinate the room and surgical teams with the anticipated resection, reconstruction, and any associated lung or vascular procedure. In the reported series, thoracic and plastic surgery teams performed resection and reconstruction together in one study.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pleural decortication removes pleural peel from the lung to permit re-expansion; the supplied evidence covers both empyema decortication and pleurectomy/decortication for mesothelioma.

Open thoracotomy and VATS are described approaches. For the open mesothelioma operation, lateral decubitus positioning and a dual-lumen tube with bronchoscopic confirmation are reported; these are not established as universal requirements for every decortication.

Prioritize readiness for bleeding and lung air leak, and coordinate ventilation with the surgical stage. Published P/D reports describe bleeding, respiratory complications, arrhythmias, and prolonged air leak.

Recovery priorities include adequate analgesia, respiratory assessment, and surveillance for ongoing air leak or bleeding. Extubation in the operating room and ICU care are described in the mesothelioma authors’ practice, not as universal disposition criteria.

bullets: The principal operative review concerns pleurectomy/decortication for malignant pleural mesothelioma and describes the authors’ institutional technique; it is not a dedicated anesthesia guideline for empyema decortication.
The empyema source is one case report and cannot establish comparative effectiveness, routine technique, or general safety.

The supplied general standards support monitoring and postanesthesia-care principles but do not provide decortication-specific protocols. Case-specific ventilation, blood-management, and extubation targets remain unestablished in these sources.
The cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus is outside the procedure-specific evidence base and should not be treated as a pleural-decortication analgesia protocol.
The supplied evidence does not establish cell-saver use in infected cases, routine TXA, or a universal fluid or vasopressor strategy.
The supplied procedure-specific sources do not establish a PONV prevention regimen or preferred non-neuraxial multimodal protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ECMO provides temporary cardiorespiratory support: VA-ECMO is used for refractory cardiogenic shock, while VV-ECMO supports isolated respiratory failure. Cannulation may be peripheral or central for VA support; VV access may use a single jugular catheter or separate venous drainage and return cannulas.

For VA-ECMO weaning and explantation, the central physiologic priority is whether native cardiac function can sustain perfusion as circuit support is reduced. For peripheral VA support, mixing of native and circuit blood can produce differential oxygenation; right radial sampling is preferred in the cited review.

Major hazards include bleeding, thrombosis, limb ischemia, cannula malposition and neurological events. Management priorities include monitoring circuit function and perfusion, assessing cannulation sites and limbs, and having a coordinated plan to respond to instability during weaning or decannulation.

After VA-ECMO weaning and decannulation, the described recovery is usually continued intubation with light sedation and ICU return. Extubation timing and anesthetic technique should be individualized; the available sources do not establish a universal cannulation airway or anesthetic regimen.

Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: VA-ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it through a membrane circuit and returns it to the arterial system. Central VA access returns blood to the ascending aorta; peripheral arterial return may use femoral, axillary or carotid access. The choice depends on the clinical and surgical context; the supplied evidence does not establish one preferred approach for all adults.

For VV-ECMO, one described approach uses a dual-lumen jugular catheter; another uses separate femoral drainage and jugular return cannulas. Accurate positioning is important for effective flow; imaging or echocardiography may be used where needed.

VA-ECMO explantation may be performed centrally in a cardiothoracic operating theatre; peripheral explantation may occur at bedside or in theatre. The review favors the theatre for access and sterility but does not establish a universal location for every decannulation.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients
Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For adult VA-ECMO weaning, assess the trajectory of myocardial recovery, inotropic requirements, and filling pressures. Weaning is uncommon during the first 72 hours after implantation, but this is contextual guidance rather than a fixed waiting rule.

Review rhythm and pacing dependence, ventilator settings, blood gases, chest imaging, and relevant laboratory results including blood count, coagulation, acid-base status and electrolytes. Assess vascular access and identify additional access options in anticipation of bleeding or procedural needs.

Before explantation, the multidisciplinary brief should align the indication, current circuit and echocardiographic status, anticoagulation plan, weaning strategy, abort criteria, ventilation and coagulation plans, and required equipment. Confirm goals of care and the contingency plan with the treating team.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The described setup may be ICU bedside or operating room, with the ECMO circuit, perfusionist and cannulation/explantation equipment available. The source advises team preparation and equipment planning but does not specify a universal equipment list.

The VA-ECMO explant review does not specify patient positioning. It supports standard and invasive monitoring, temperature monitoring, and serial point-of-care blood sampling; use additional monitoring in keeping with the patient’s status and local practice.

During peripheral VA-ECMO assessment, the right radial artery is preferred for blood-gas sampling because arterial mixing and native output affect upper-body oxygenation. Interpret saturation and blood gases in context; the available evidence does not establish a universal pulse-oximeter site or a single monitoring configuration for all ECMO modes.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Do not infer that every cannulation or decannulation requires general anesthesia or endotracheal intubation. The VA-ECMO explant review describes either general anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care with local anesthesia, depending on central versus peripheral ECMO; neuromuscular blockade is generally not required for explantation.

Patients receiving VV-ECMO may be ventilated through an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy. The reviewed VV practice describes low tidal-volume ventilation during support and a higher exhaled tidal volume before weaning; these values are review guidance, not a substitute for patient-specific ventilator management.

For VA-ECMO explantation, continue ventilator support as appropriate and assess gas exchange during reduced circuit support. No source here establishes a routine induction drug, RSI requirement, airway technique or extubation criterion for cannulation.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients
Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During VA-ECMO weaning, assess native cardiac performance as support is reduced, with close attention to arterial pressure and echocardiographic findings. If hemodynamics deteriorate, the review advises stopping the weaning trial and restoring support while evaluating the cause; no single weaning protocol is established here as universal.

Echocardiography during reduced support can assess ventricular function, outflow and valve function, and identify tamponade or worsening ventricular dilation. Interpret findings in light of ECMO flow and loading conditions; the review notes that reduced preload can make some right-ventricular assessments inaccurate while on support.

For VV-ECMO, assess gas exchange as sweep and circuit support are adjusted, and verify cannula position when flow or clinical findings are atypical. Coordinate changes with the perfusionist and ECMO team; the evidence does not supply a universal anesthetic or flow-adjustment protocol for all patients.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients
Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Bleeding, thrombosis and cannula-site hemorrhage are important hazards, particularly during anticoagulation. Escalate unexpected bleeding or circuit concerns with the surgical and perfusion teams; the review describes surgical hemostasis as the usual means of controlling cannulation-site bleeding.

With femoral arterial VA access, monitor distal limb perfusion for ischemia. A distal perfusion cannula or graft may be used to maintain perfusion; the source does not support treating one device as mandatory in every case.
ECMO-related concerns include low flow, cannula dislodgement or malposition, tamponade, clotting, and hemolysis.

Neurological injury, including stroke or intracranial hemorrhage, is a recognized VA-ECMO complication. Arrange neurological assessment when clinically feasible and account for anticoagulation and sedation when interpreting the examination.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients
Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Manage anticoagulation collaboratively with the ECMO and surgical teams. The VA explant review advises monitoring ACT and maintaining anticoagulation during weaning to reduce circuit thrombosis risk, but anticoagulation targets and interruption decisions must follow the applicable circuit, procedure and institutional plan.

Prepare for blood loss and coagulopathy according to the patient’s status and anticipated procedure. Review relevant blood count and coagulation results, maintain normothermia, and use surgical hemostasis; the supplied sources do not establish transfusion thresholds or a universal blood-product plan.

During reduced ECMO support, guide vasoactive therapy and volume administration by hemodynamic response. The review cautions against indiscriminate volume loading because overload can impair lung function; persistent hypotension or acidosis warrants urgent reassessment and escalation.

sources.label: Update on Anesthesia Management for Explantation of Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Adult Patients
Veno-venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: Anesthetic Considerations in Clinical Practice

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Analgesia and anesthetic depth should reflect whether the procedure is central or peripheral and the patient’s physiology. The explant review describes systemic opioids with general anesthesia for central explantation and local anesthetic at peripheral cannula sites; it does not establish a required regimen or provide ECMO-specific PONV guidance.

Adult cardiac-surgery consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesia and opioid stewardship within its scope, but it is not an ECMO-specific protocol. Select analgesia with attention to organ function, anticoagulation and the intended level of wakefulness.

Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Following VA-ECMO weaning and decannulation, the described approach is return to ICU while intubated and lightly sedated. Decisions about subsequent sedation reduction and extubation depend on respiratory and cardiac recovery; the sources do not provide universal extubation criteria.

Transfer should include monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition, with a structured handover covering the anesthetic and surgical course and expected trajectory. Continue ICU-level observation for perfusion, circuit-related issues, bleeding and neurological status as clinically indicated.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The VA-ECMO anesthesia source is a review focused on adult weaning and explantation, not a trial or a comprehensive cannulation guideline. Its authors state that many recommendations derive from expert consensus; it does not establish universal perioperative protocols.

The VV-ECMO source is a clinical-practice review with local protocol input; it notes that anticoagulation practice depends on circuit and manufacturer guidance. Its recommendations should not be generalized as universal adult ECMO targets.

The supplied sources do not establish a case-wide cannulation airway or induction plan, preferred access for every indication, universal anticoagulation target, or standardized extubation criteria. These remain decisions for the responsible ECMO, surgical and anesthesia teams.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Esophagectomy may be open or minimally invasive and include an abdominal and thoracic phase; Ivor-Lewis and McKeown approaches differ in anastomosis location. Positioning and whether one-lung ventilation is needed depend on approach and surgical exposure.

Major priorities are protective ventilation when OLV is used, avoiding fluid overload without inducing hypovolemia, and preserving adequate perfusion of the gastric conduit. Pulmonary complications and anastomotic dehiscence are important postoperative hazards.

Assess nutritional, cardiopulmonary, and treatment-related risk before surgery. Use invasive arterial-pressure monitoring as described in the procedure-specific review, alongside standard monitoring; additional monitoring should reflect risk and local practice.

Recovery planning should account for respiratory reserve, hemodynamic stability, temperature, pain control, and neuromuscular recovery when blockade is used. Extubation and postoperative destination are individualized rather than dictated by a universal pathway.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Ivor-Lewis commonly combines laparotomy and right thoracotomy with an intrathoracic anastomosis. McKeown uses a three-field approach with cervical access and a cervical anastomosis; its anastomosis location can affect access if a leak occurs.

Minimally invasive esophagectomy can use Ivor-Lewis or McKeown configurations. Technique and patient position are not standardized across centers; the review reports improved functional recovery and fewer postoperative complications than open surgery, with longer operative times.
The selected approach, planned anastomosis, and need for lung isolation are surgical-team decisions. Do not assume every minimally invasive or transhiatal case requires OLV.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess weight loss, frailty, nutritional status, and anemia; early dietician involvement is described as part of optimization. Malnutrition and cachexia may coexist with cancer-related dysphagia, but specific feeding interventions should be individualized.

Evaluate cardiac reserve and functional capacity, cardiopulmonary comorbidity, and pulmonary ability to tolerate OLV when relevant. The reviews describe CPET and functional-capacity assessment as tools, not mandatory tests for every patient.

Review prior chemotherapy and radiotherapy for potential cardiac or pulmonary effects and incorporate findings into risk assessment. The available reviews do not establish a universal FiO₂ restriction based solely on a particular prior drug exposure.
Early anesthesiologist participation in multidisciplinary evaluation is supported in the reviews; final testing and optimization depend on patient risk and the planned operation.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate room setup and repositioning with the surgical plan. Open Ivor-Lewis is traditionally performed in left lateral decubitus; thoracoscopic procedures may use lateral or prone positioning. There is no single position applicable across approaches.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring and invasive arterial-pressure monitoring as described for esophagectomy. Consider other monitoring, including cardiac-output assessment, according to patient risk and local capability; the reviews do not establish one required advanced device.
Temperature monitoring and active attention to normothermia are relevant perioperative considerations. The source describes several warming methods without making any single device mandatory.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For transthoracic surgery requiring OLV, lung separation may use a DLT or bronchial blocker. Confirm DLT position with fiber-optic bronchoscopy; a bronchial blocker is an option when airway anatomy or intubation difficulty favors it.

Use protective ventilation: control tidal volume, minimize driving pressure, optimize compliance, and use reasonable PEEP. The review cites tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight (IBW) for esophagectomy and no more than 5 mL/kg IBW during OLV to avoid volutrauma.

During OLV, hypoxemia and hypercapnia can occur from shunting and atelectasis. The review advises the lowest FiO₂ that achieves adequate oxygenation; recruitment maneuvers may be considered for intraoperative hypoxemia, but routine use is not supported.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Anticipate changing physiologic demands across abdominal and thoracic phases, including OLV when required. Coordinate ventilation and surgical exposure, particularly in prone minimally invasive cases where excessive PEEP may impair visualization.

Pay attention to systemic pressure and gastric-conduit perfusion. The conduit depends on the right gastro-epiploic artery, and poor local perfusion is identified as an important contributor to anastomotic leakage; avoid preventable hypotension while treating its cause.

Fluid strategy should balance pulmonary and tissue-edema concerns against hypovolemia and renal injury. Use clinical assessment and risk-appropriate goal-directed methods where available; avoid treating anesthesia-associated hypotension with routine fluid loading alone.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Pulmonary complications are prominent after esophagectomy; prolonged OLV, hypoxemia, fluid overload, and hemodynamic instability are among reported acute lung injury risk factors. Escalate assessment and support promptly when oxygenation or ventilation deteriorates.

Anastomotic dehiscence is a major postoperative concern. The reviews identify conduit perfusion and surgical factors as relevant, but do not provide a validated intraoperative test or a single anesthetic intervention that prevents leakage.

Maintain vigilance for evolving postoperative respiratory or hemodynamic deterioration and communicate promptly with the surgical and critical-care teams. Destination and surveillance should reflect the operation, patient risk, and local resources.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Avoid both fluid overload and excessive restriction. The review associates larger fluid exposure with postoperative pulmonary complications, while also warning that hypovolemia can contribute to renal injury; use an individualized, monitored strategy rather than a fixed total or hourly prescription.

Consider goal-directed therapy for higher-risk patients, recognizing limitations of dynamic indices during open-chest surgery and uncertainty about some monitoring methods in thoracoscopy. The evidence does not establish a universal device or fluid algorithm for this operation.
The review reports that blood loss is scarce with newer minimally invasive techniques and transfusion is now rarely needed.

Do not avoid norepinephrine solely because of the gastric conduit: the procedure-specific review describes it as justified for anesthesia-induced hypotension. The available evidence does not establish vasopressin as a preferred routine vasopressor or support a blanket prohibition of alpha-agonists.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint
Anaesthesia during oesophagectomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Thoracic epidural analgesia is described as a first-choice option in ERAS protocols, particularly for thoracotomy, with reported pulmonary and recovery benefits. Monitor for hypotension and neuraxial complications; feasibility depends on patient factors and service resources.

Paravertebral, erector spinae, transversus abdominis plane, and systemic multimodal analgesia are described alternatives or adjuncts. Tailor the technique to approach, comorbidity, anticoagulation, local expertise, and expected pain; the review does not establish one mandatory regimen.

Acetaminophen and opioids are among described systemic options. NSAIDs, including ketorolac, have raised concern about anastomotic leakage in the review; weigh potential benefit and risk rather than treating them as universally required or prohibited.

sources.label: Peri-operative approach to esophagectomy: a narrative review from the anesthesiological standpoint

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Extubation in the operating room can be feasible after an uncomplicated course when oxygenation, hemodynamics, normothermia, pain control, and neuromuscular recovery are satisfactory. The sources do not support routine postoperative intubation for every patient or routine extubation for every approach.

When neuromuscular blockade has been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies to patients receiving blockade, not to every anesthetic technique.

Select PACU-equivalent, high-dependency, or ICU care based on risk, stability, and local resources; the procedure-specific review does not prescribe a single destination. Ensure appropriate monitoring and handoff to the receiving team.

Early feeding and postoperative respiratory support are recovery considerations, but the review notes that evidence for preventive non-invasive ventilation remains incomplete. Coordinate feeding and respiratory care with the surgical team and local pathway.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The main procedure-specific source is a narrative review of perioperative care for esophagectomy in patients with esophageal cancer, not a single standardized protocol. It explicitly identifies areas where further study is needed.

The 2017 review reports that studies are often small or heterogeneous and that outcome evidence for fluid strategies and some monitoring approaches is limited. Reconcile its discussion with the later review: neither supports a universal fluid recipe or vasopressor hierarchy.
The ASA monitoring standards and neuromuscular-blockade guidance support general monitoring and reversal principles, not esophagectomy-specific airway or recovery pathways.
Case-specific targets for PONV prevention are not established in the available procedure-specific sources.
