overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Orthotopic heart transplantation is performed under general anesthesia with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): the recipient heart is removed and the donor heart implanted. Donor acceptance and operative timing are coordinated before anesthesia is induced.

The major early physiologic concern is donor right-ventricular dysfunction, particularly with elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) or prolonged ischemic time. Assess graft function and consider PVR-reducing support when indicated.

Redo dissection, pre-existing coagulation abnormalities, anticoagulant use, and CPB can contribute to bleeding. Ensure a plan for reliable access and anticipate postoperative assessment for primary graft dysfunction (PGD), rejection, and infection.

Recovery priorities include careful graft-function assessment and ongoing transplant-team surveillance. The available sources do not establish a transplant-specific extubation timetable or routine anesthetic recovery protocol.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls
Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Orthotopic transplantation is the usual approach: the recipient heart is excised, retaining atrial cuffs in the described technique, and the donor heart is implanted in the chest. Anastomoses include the atria, aorta, and pulmonary artery; the bicaval technique instead connects the venae cavae to the donor right atrium.

The operation has pre-CPB, CPB, and post-CPB phases. Native-heart and/or mechanical circulatory support (MCS) explantation and donor implantation occur during CPB; the pre-CPB anesthetic approach depends on the recipient’s condition.
Heterotopic transplantation is described as rare and retains the recipient heart while implanting the donor heart in the thoracic cavity; it is not the usual procedure described here.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls
Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm donor-heart acceptability and coordinate timing with the transplant team before induction. The source describes recipient-heart removal before the donor heart is available as a strategy to reduce ischemia time; it does not establish a universal acceptable ischemic-time limit.

Review advanced heart-failure status, end-organ dysfunction, infection, prior operations, and current MCS. In adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD), prior procedures may affect access and CPB cannulation planning; assess this in the context of the individual anatomy.

Assess PVR as part of transplant workup, recognizing that measurements may be inaccurate in ACHD. Pulmonary hypertension and prolonged ischemic time increase concern for donor RV dysfunction after CPB.
Renal and hepatic dysfunction can affect volume status, coagulation, and drug clearance; include these factors in perioperative planning rather than assuming standard responses.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls
Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare for CPB and have monitoring appropriate to the recipient and operation. The transplant review describes transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and a Swan-Ganz catheter, but does not establish a universal monitoring configuration.

For anesthesia generally, continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG is displayed continuously and blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standard.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The transplant procedure is described as being performed under general anesthesia, but the source does not specify an airway device or a detailed ventilation strategy. Do not infer a universal airway technique from the procedure description.

When general anesthesia is delivered, follow applicable basic monitoring standards, including continual evaluation of ventilation and expired carbon dioxide unless the nature of the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates it.

ACHD-specific airway considerations may apply in selected patients: suspected plastic bronchitis can complicate airway management, and the review suggests considering bronchoscopy before intubation when it is suspected. This is not a routine transplant airway requirement.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pre-CPB management is condition-dependent. In failing Fontan physiology, induction-related vasodilation can substantially reduce preload; the ACHD review describes volume administration before induction while cautioning that these patients are sensitive to volume loads. This consideration is specific to that physiology, not a general transplant fluid prescription.

After CPB, assess for donor RV dysfunction, especially with elevated PVR or prolonged ischemic time. The ACHD review identifies inhaled nitric oxide and intravenous milrinone as possible PVR-reducing interventions, not mandatory routine therapy.

During implantation and separation from bypass, de-airing is described as part of the operative sequence, followed by slow weaning from bypass. The sources do not give a transplant-specific anesthetic target set for these phases.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
Heart Transplantation — StatPearls

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) is failure of graft function within the first 24 hours after transplantation, in the absence of hyperacute rejection, pulmonary hypertension, or known surgical complications such as bleeding or tamponade.

Rejection can be cell-mediated or antibody-mediated and may range from mild findings to hemodynamic compromise. The source describes surveillance endomyocardial biopsies during the first year; follow the transplant program’s surveillance and escalation pathways.

Immunosuppression increases infection risk, with particular concern during the first post-transplant year. Postoperative care includes wound-infection prevention and ongoing transplant-team supervision.

sources.label: Heart Transplantation — StatPearls

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Reliable vascular access for resuscitation in significant bleeding is important. Extensive redo dissection, coagulation abnormalities, preoperative anticoagulant use, and CPB may contribute to bleeding.

Account for renal and hepatic dysfunction when interpreting volume status and coagulation or drug effects. The supplied sources do not provide a transplant-specific fluid, transfusion, or bleeding-management protocol.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
Heart Transplantation — StatPearls

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The transplant-specific source does not provide an analgesia regimen. For adult cardiac surgery generally, the POQI/ERAS consensus recommends avoiding routine high-dose opioid anesthesia or analgesia, using multimodal nonopioid analgesics, and considering regional techniques; these recommendations are not transplant-specific.

Tailor analgesic choices to patient-specific limitations, including renal or significant liver dysfunction, and consider anticoagulation when evaluating regional techniques. The consensus report identifies sparse cardiac-surgery evidence and does not define a single required regimen.

Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The transplant sources do not establish extubation criteria or a fixed extubation interval. Recovery planning should be coordinated with graft function and the transplant team; no fixed timetable is supported by the available evidence.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

In later anesthetics for transplant recipients, cardiac denervation can make heart rate relatively important to cardiac output and vagolytic drug effects limited. The review reports severe bradycardia or arrest with reversal agents and advises immediate availability of epinephrine; this is relevant to subsequent anesthesia, not a transplant-specific emergence protocol.

Anesthetic Management for Heart Transplantation in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The transplant anesthesia review is specifically about adults with congenital heart disease and is a narrative review; its anatomy- and physiology-specific recommendations should not be generalized to all adult transplant recipients.

The general heart-transplant review covers indications, techniques, complications, and team care, but explicitly lacks anesthesia-specific recommendations. The adult cardiac analgesia consensus and ASA standards support general perioperative principles, not a transplant-specific anesthetic protocol.

Unresolved substantive areas include transplant-specific induction and maintenance choices, donor coordination and ischemic-time management details, immunosuppression regimen, and postoperative extubation and analgesia protocols. The available sources do not establish these as universal standards.
The transplant anesthesia source does not specify patient positioning or a standard access configuration.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lobectomy removes an entire pulmonary lobe. VATS is a preferred approach for early-stage NSCLC when appropriate; open thoracotomy remains relevant for complex tumors, adhesions, or anatomy.

General anesthesia with lung isolation using a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker is the usual described approach for anatomic resection; the specific technique should suit the operation and patient.

Priorities include assessing pulmonary and cardiac reserve, maintaining safe conditions for hilar dissection, and anticipating air leak, bleeding, and cardiopulmonary complications. The supplied sources do not establish a specific one-lung ventilation protocol.
Postoperative care emphasizes pain control, pulmonary physiotherapy, chest-tube management, pulmonary hygiene, and early mobilization.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Lobectomy is complete surgical removal of one pulmonary lobe. For NSCLC, it is described as standard resection for stages I and II when negative margins and systematic lymph-node dissection are achieved; selected benign disease is also an indication.

Approach selection is surgical and patient specific. VATS avoids rib spreading; open exposure may be selected for complex disease. The source also describes robotic lobectomy but does not provide a detailed operative sequence.
The operative principle is individual dissection and division of the lobe’s vein, arteries, and bronchus. Lymph-node management for malignancy follows the applicable oncologic approach.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls
Techniques of VATS lobectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess indication, comorbidities, performance status, smoking history, imaging, bronchoscopy, cardiac risk, and pulmonary reserve. The extent of testing depends on the clinical context; the source does not establish one universal test battery.
Assess pulmonary reserve with spirometry/FEV1 and DLCO; perfusion scanning and exercise testing may be used when appropriate.

Review CT/PET imaging and bronchoscopy for tumor extent, planned resection, and bronchial anatomy that could affect the approach. Consider multidisciplinary assessment for patients with significant comorbidity or elevated operative risk.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls
Techniques of VATS lobectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning is lateral decubitus for open and VATS lobectomy. Protect pressure points and reassess access and positioning after lateral placement as part of individualized anesthetic care; the procedure source does not detail those precautions.
Plan access to lung-isolation equipment and, for VATS, the thoracoscopic system. Major-vessel injury is a recognized hazard; the source advises having vascular instruments available.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to general anesthesia, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment. An arterial line is not specified as mandatory for every lobectomy.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Lung isolation is routinely described for pulmonary resection. A double-lumen endotracheal tube or bronchial blocker are supported options; selection and placement should be coordinated with the surgical requirements.

Verify endotracheal-tube placement by clinical assessment and expired-gas carbon dioxide. After placement, continually monitor end-tidal carbon dioxide quantitatively until extubation, tube removal, or initiation of transfer.
Lung isolation is standard for anatomic lung resection; options include a double-lumen endotracheal tube or a bronchial blocker.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Lung isolation facilitates hilar dissection. The described resection requires individual management of pulmonary venous, arterial, and bronchial structures; lobar anatomy and operative sequence vary by lobe.

Vessel traction and stapler trajectory are important technical hazards. The VATS technique article advises minimal traction on pulmonary vessels and care to avoid injury to adjacent structures during stapling.

Fissure strategy depends on anatomy and surgeon technique. The sources describe fissureless approaches as a way to reduce air-leak risk in selected settings, not as a universal requirement for every lobe.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls
Techniques of VATS lobectomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Important complications include prolonged air leak, pneumonia or atelectasis, hemorrhage, and atrial fibrillation. Reported rates vary across populations and sources; do not treat any single rate as an individual prediction.

Pulmonary-artery injury can cause major bleeding. Maintain awareness of the potential need for surgical escalation and ensure appropriate vascular instruments are available; the sources do not provide an emergency conversion algorithm.

Postoperative surveillance should attend to air leak, chest-tube status, respiratory function, pain, and cardiopulmonary complications. The source notes that complications usually arise early but does not establish a lobectomy-specific monitoring schedule.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Bleeding, including major-vessel injury, is a recognized intraoperative risk. The supplied procedure sources support preparedness for vascular injury but do not establish a universal fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or fluid strategy.
Maintain perfusion using patient- and situation-specific assessment. The available lobectomy sources do not set hemodynamic targets or prescribe vasopressor-versus-fluid choices.
Before closure, confirm hemostasis. This is a procedural consideration, not evidence for a particular blood-management protocol.

sources.label: Lobectomy — StatPearls
Techniques of VATS lobectomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Effective pain control supports pulmonary physiotherapy and recovery. Analgesic planning should reflect the approach and patient factors; the sources do not establish a single required regimen.

For VATS, regional or local anesthetic adjuncts to general anesthesia have been associated with reduced hospital stay, but the source does not name a preferred technique. Thoracic epidural is common for open thoracotomy and usually omitted after thoracoscopic resection in the VATS technique article.

Techniques of VATS lobectomy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent area, with observation appropriate to the patient’s condition and attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulmonary hygiene, early mobilization, pain control, and chest-tube care are emphasized in the lobectomy sources.

bullets: The primary procedure source is an educational narrative review, not a single anesthesia protocol. It explicitly lacks specific fluid, transfusion, ventilation, monitoring-device, emergence, and extubation protocols.
The VATS source is an older operative-technique editorial, not an anesthesia guideline; it reports no ventilation settings, monitoring protocol, fluid management, or emergence/extubation practice.

No evidence-supported universal fluid total, arterial-line requirement, OLV setting, extubation threshold based on ppo-FEV1, or prophylactic atrial-fibrillation drug regimen can be derived from the supplied sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lung transplantation may be single or bilateral; the choice of approach and use of mechanical circulatory support (MCS) depend on the operation and patient needs. Lung isolation is generally used without MCS, but may not be necessary with MCS.

The dominant physiologic hazards include hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability during one-lung ventilation or pulmonary artery clamping, particularly with pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction; induction may also precipitate cardiovascular collapse.

Prioritize lung-protective ventilation, avoidance of dynamic hyperinflation, and careful management of oxygenation, pulmonary vascular resistance, and volume. Reperfusion injury and primary graft dysfunction (PGD) are central concerns.

Recovery is commonly in the ICU. Protect the allograft and pursue early extubation when graft function and hemodynamic stability permit; the supplied sources do not establish a fixed ventilation duration.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications
A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Transplantation treats chronic end-stage lung disease when nonsurgical treatment is ineffective. Single- or double-lung transplantation may be selected according to disease and patient factors; the supplied sources describe single-lung use for COPD and interstitial disease and double-lung use for infectious/suppurative disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Surgical approaches include unilateral or bilateral thoracotomies, clamshell incision, or midline sternotomy. The described operative phases include recipient dissection and resection, donor-lung anastomosis, and graft reperfusion.

MCS is not universal. VA-ECMO or CPB may be used when support is needed; the choice is shaped by hemodynamic and surgical requirements. CPB requires systemic anticoagulation and is associated with greater bleeding than ECMO in the review.

sources.label: A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation
Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiopulmonary reserve, RV function, pulmonary hypertension, comorbidities, renal function, frailty, and ability to tolerate surgery. Pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction increase concern for collapse during induction and surgical manipulation.

Identify obstructive disease and secretion burden, pulmonary hypertension, and prior thoracic surgery. Severe pleural adhesions can cause major bleeding during dissection; cystic fibrosis may require frequent suctioning.

Review pulmonary vasodilator therapy and plan continuity, since abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension. Avoid routine preoperative sedation in patients with limited reserve; minimize apnea during induction.

For high-risk patients, consider preparation for rapid MCS support with the surgical and perfusion teams immediately available; preinduction femoral access is described as an option, not a universal requirement.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications
A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare lung-isolation equipment when required; ensure adequate vascular access, including large-bore peripheral IVs, and have the surgeon and perfusionist available for emergent MCS if acute decompensation occurs at induction.

Use invasive arterial pressure monitoring and frequent arterial blood gases. A PA catheter may be used if not contraindicated; TEE assesses ventricular function and can help evaluate the graft and vascular anastomoses after reperfusion.
Include standard monitoring and consider depth-of-anesthesia monitoring and cerebral oximetry. Monitor temperature because hypothermia can worsen pulmonary hypertension and coagulation disorders.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications
A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose an airway strategy suited to the surgical approach and MCS plan. A left-sided double-lumen tube is commonly described; a single-lumen tube with bronchial blocker is an alternative. Confirm placement bronchoscopically when using a double-lumen tube.

Avoid excessive tidal volumes and inspiratory pressures. Tailor ventilation to underlying disease; in obstructive disease, prolong expiration to limit dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP. Use arterial gases because end-tidal CO₂ may not reflect arterial CO₂.

After implantation, use allograft-protective ventilation and avoid hyperoxia during reperfusion; the sources describe low tidal volumes and the lowest FiO₂ compatible with adequate oxygenation. Individualize settings to graft size and clinical gas exchange.

sources.label: A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation
Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Induction and apnea are high-risk in patients with limited reserve. Maintain systemic vascular resistance and myocardial contractility, avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia, and have a rapid escalation pathway for acute RV failure or cardiovascular collapse.

During lung isolation and PA clamping, anticipate increased shunt and RV loading, with possible hypoxemia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and hypotension. If instability persists despite appropriate ventilation and pulmonary vasodilator support, ECLS may be required.

Reperfusion can produce endothelial injury, pulmonary edema, and PGD. Reduce avoidable graft stress, maintain RV support and coronary perfusion, and correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, and hypothermia.

sources.label: A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation
Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) is a leading cause of death after lung transplantation and typically occurs within 72 hours. Treatment is supportive, including lung-protective ventilation and early postoperative MCS for severe PGD.

Acute RV failure or hemodynamic collapse may accompany PA clamping, lung isolation, or induction. Recognize deterioration early and escalate support with the transplant, surgical, and perfusion teams; no single rescue algorithm is established here.

Severe pleural adhesions can cause massive bleeding during pleural dissection and pneumonectomy. CPB requires systemic anticoagulation and is associated with more bleeding than ECMO. In obstructive disease, avoid dynamic hyperinflation; auto-PEEP may be a concern.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications
A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain euvolemia and avoid excessive fluid administration: fluid overload may worsen pulmonary edema, PGD, and RV dysfunction. The sources do not specify a universal fluid volume or replacement formula.

Minimize avoidable blood-product exposure while treating clinically important bleeding and coagulopathy. Red-cell and plasma transfusions are associated with increased PGD risk; this association does not define a transfusion threshold.

During PA clamping or anastomosis, balance RV preload, afterload, and systemic perfusion; pulmonary vasodilators and MCS may be considered according to the evolving physiology. Anticoagulation management depends on the support strategy and is not governed here by a universal target.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications
A Review of Anesthesia for Lung Transplantation

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan postoperative analgesia to support pulmonary mechanics and recovery while accounting for anticoagulation, coagulation status, and potential hypotension. Thoracic epidural is an option but has catheter-related bleeding and hemodynamic considerations.

Non-neuraxial regional options described include paravertebral, serratus anterior plane, and erector spinae plane techniques; evidence is limited and does not establish one preferred approach. Systemic analgesics may be used, with attention to opioid-related respiratory depression.

sources.label: Lung Transplantation: Anesthetic Implications

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: At case completion, the review describes exchange of the double-lumen tube for a single-lumen tube, using an exchange catheter and direct or video laryngoscopy because airway edema may occur.

Continue postoperative allograft-protective ventilation when required. Extubation may be pursued early when graft function is satisfactory and the patient is hemodynamically stable; the sources do not support a fixed duration.
Plan postoperative surveillance for PGD. Continue assessment appropriate to the patient’s condition and provide a verbal handoff to the receiving nurse.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The main transplant-specific sources are an educational anesthesia reference and a narrative review. Their recommendations are not a single validated protocol; the review reports that standardized protocols lack monitoring guidelines.
Adult scope is informed by the review's adult-transplant discussion, but it cautions that not every recommendation is established as adult-only. Procedure-specific positioning is not provided.

The available material does not establish a transplant-specific PONV approach or positioning plan. Individualized decisions should not be mistaken for evidence gaps requiring universal targets or fixed regimens.
The transplant-specific sources supplied do not specify a PONV prevention or treatment protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: LVAD implantation provides mechanical support by draining blood from the left ventricle and delivering it to the aorta. Operative access and use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) vary; the supplied sources describe both on-pump and off-pump approaches.

The dominant physiologic concern in the described implantation is right-ventricular (RV) function, particularly during CPB weaning and device optimization. TEE and pulmonary artery catheter data are used to assess ventricular function and the changing pump–heart relationship.

TEE assessment before CPB and during implantation is important for ventricular assessment, inflow alignment, aortic-valve behavior, and deairing. Aortic insufficiency, an interatrial shunt, apical thrombus, and aortic pathology may affect planning or device function.

Recovery is generally in an ICU with individualized hemodynamic support and device optimization. Extubation is described after hemodynamic stability; the sources do not establish a universal timing or readiness protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Implantation connects a ventricular inflow cannula to a pump and an outflow conduit to the aorta. Device design and outflow-graft site vary; the sources describe ascending-aortic approaches and selected alternative sites.

Approach selection is device- and patient-specific. The surgical review describes on-pump and off-pump implantation and less-invasive access, but does not establish these approaches as interchangeable or as universally preferable.
The supplied literature does not establish a routine position or a single operative approach for all LVAD implants.

sources.label: An overview of approved and investigational left ventricular assist devices

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiac and RV function, pulmonary pressures/PVR, and end-organ status. The anesthesia review highlights neurologic, hepatic, and coagulation assessment; the surgical review describes preoperative echocardiography for RV function and significant valve abnormalities.

Identify findings that may change the approach or require concomitant management, including LV apical thrombus, significant aortic insufficiency, tricuspid regurgitation, mitral stenosis, PFO, or aortic disease. The supplied surgical review gives approach preferences for some of these findings, not a universal selection rule.

Consider prior sternotomy, pulmonary disease, vascular disease, and aortic anatomy in multidisciplinary planning when selecting access and potential CPB access. These are approach-selection considerations in a single-center surgical review.
The sources do not establish a contemporary, device-specific preoperative risk score or a universal threshold for proceeding, choosing a device, or selecting on-pump versus off-pump implantation.

Minimally invasive and alternative approaches for long-term LVAD placement: the Vanderbilt strategy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The procedure requires cardiac-surgical resources appropriate to the selected approach, including CPB capability when planned or needed. A mixed-venous pulmonary artery catheter is usually placed before induction in the described anesthesia review.

TEE is described as standard for LVAD cases and is used for ventricular assessment, inflow alignment, device-flow adjustment, and deairing. The source emphasizes that the anesthesiologist should be skilled in TEE.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic, in addition to procedure-specific hemodynamic and echocardiographic assessment. ASA standards require continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature during anesthesia.
The LVAD sources do not specify routine patient positioning or a universal room-equipment list; these depend on the planned surgical approach and institutional resources.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The LVAD anesthesia review does not provide a specific airway technique or routine ventilation protocol. Airway management should therefore be determined by the planned operation and patient factors rather than inferred from this source.

Double-lumen intubation is described for a particular single-thoracotomy approach to facilitate lung retraction; it is not established as routine for LVAD implantation. The surgical review also notes that lung disease can make repeated interruption of ventilation a concern in off-pump cases.

If general anesthesia and an endotracheal tube are used, apply applicable basic monitoring standards, including continual expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring from tube placement until extubation or transfer begins.

sources.label: An overview of approved and investigational left ventricular assist devices
Minimally invasive and alternative approaches for long-term LVAD placement: the Vanderbilt strategy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Before CPB, use TEE to assess both ventricles and relevant anatomy, including the LV apex, aortic valve, atrial septum, and outflow-graft site. A PFO may become a right-to-left shunt when device activation reduces left-atrial pressure.

During CPB weaning, maintaining right-heart inflow and supporting RV function are central challenges. The cited review describes pulmonary vasodilation and RV support as important but does not establish a universally applicable drug regimen or target.

Adjust device flow in relation to RV function, LV filling, preload/afterload, and aortic-valve opening using TEE and pulmonary artery catheter data. In the described DeBakey VAD experience, excessive flow could prevent aortic-valve opening and contribute to aortic-root stasis.
Confirm deairing and appropriate inflow-cannula alignment before device activation and separation from CPB, as applicable to the device and operative approach.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: RV dysfunction/failure is a major perioperative hazard described in the LVAD anesthesia review. Assess RV function and pulmonary vascular load, recognize deterioration during weaning, and escalate support with the cardiac-surgical team; the available sources do not establish a single rescue algorithm.

Consider device-related hemodynamic consequences when aortic-valve opening is lost, including aortic-root stasis and reduced coronary flow. Evaluate pump-flow adjustment with TEE and catheter data rather than applying a universal speed target.

Bleeding and infection are prominent complications in the older device review. It attributes bleeding risk to hepatic-dysfunction-related coagulopathy, extensive surgery, and CPB/pump-related platelet dysfunction; driveline and surgical-pocket infection are also described.
TEE can identify other potential contributors to impaired oxygenation or device performance, including a right-to-left shunt through a PFO and significant aortic insufficiency.

sources.label: An overview of approved and investigational left ventricular assist devices

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The supplied LVAD review provides no fluid regimen or transfusion threshold. It notes that hepatic congestion-related coagulopathy and the extent of surgery may necessitate component therapy; guide decisions to clinical findings and the operative context.

Expect potential platelet dysfunction associated with CPB and blood-pump rheology, in addition to pre-existing coagulation abnormalities. The source does not specify a protocol for testing or correction.

The anesthesia review describes individualized adjustment of preload during recovery and management. It does not support a universal fluid target or total; balance perfusion needs against the patient’s ventricular function and device behavior.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The LVAD-specific review states that analgesics may be given as needed after extubation but gives no procedure-specific regimen. The adult cardiac-surgery consensus supports tailored multimodal nonopioid analgesia and opioid stewardship, not a single mandatory combination.

Individualize analgesic selection to patient and procedure factors, local expertise, and anticoagulation considerations when regional techniques are considered. The consensus report describes limited cardiac-surgery evidence for many interventions.

Plan for opioid-related adverse effects, including nausea and vomiting, and use opioid-sparing strategies where they preserve adequate pain control and recovery. The consensus does not provide an LVAD-specific PONV protocol.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: One anesthesia review describes transfer to the ICU sedated with propofol and extubation once hemodynamically stable. A surgical review reports that patients are typically extubated within 24 hours after surgery in the CVICU.

Postanesthesia standards require an appropriate PACU or equivalent location, such as an ICU, with condition-appropriate monitoring, handoff, and ongoing evaluation. For LVAD implantation, the sources describe ICU recovery rather than routine PACU disposition.

Continue individualized assessment of hemodynamics, RV function, device function, and bleeding during recovery. The sources do not provide a contemporary universal device-anticoagulation start or bridging protocol.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation is conditional on neuromuscular blocker use, not a requirement for cases without blockade.

bullets: The LVAD anesthesia source is a 2004 overview focused primarily on DeBakey VAD and Jarvik 2000; its device descriptions and perioperative discussion may not represent current devices or contemporary practice.

The surgical approaches source is a single-center technical review, not an anesthesia guideline; it explicitly states that larger studies are needed to clarify outcome effects. Its local techniques should not be treated as routine standards.

The general cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus and ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade sources inform their stated scopes but do not resolve LVAD-specific device management or anesthesia targets.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Cervical mediastinoscopy is the usual approach for visualizing and biopsying mediastinal lymph nodes; it is typically performed under general anesthesia, unless airway concerns alter the plan.
Prioritize identifying airway or cardiovascular compression from a mediastinal mass and the risk of major vascular injury or innominate-artery compression during scope passage.
Preserve spontaneous ventilation during airway management when evaluation indicates major airway compromise; have rigid bronchoscopy expertise and equipment available for high-risk obstruction.

Recovery priorities include surveillance for airway compromise, bleeding, pneumothorax, and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury; if neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cervical mediastinoscopy is the common approach for sampling pretracheal, paratracheal, and anterior subcarinal nodes. A parasternal/anterior mediastinotomy (Chamberlain procedure) accesses aortopulmonary nodes; the source does not establish a general rule that it is specifically for all left-sided nodes.

For the cervical approach, the described operation uses a lower-neck incision and blunt dissection along the pretracheal plane, advancing the scope into the superior mediastinum to sample nodes or masses.
Mediastinoscopy is used for diagnosis and lung-cancer nodal staging, but PET combined with EBUS-guided biopsy has replaced it for many patients; selection is procedure- and patient-specific.

sources.label: Mediastinoscopy
Mediastinal Masses: Adults, Mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review symptoms suggesting compression—particularly wheezing, dyspnea, and orthopnea, including worsening when supine—and assess imaging for mass location, airway effects, and relationships to great vessels. Supine positioning and induction can precipitate or worsen compression.

Use CT to characterize mediastinal anatomy and possible compression or deviation of vessels and airway. Consider pulmonary function testing with flow-volume loops when obstruction is suspected; routine upright-and-supine spirometry is not established as a better predictor of complications.

SVC syndrome, severe tracheal deviation, thoracic inlet obstruction, and prior chest radiation are identified as relative contraindications in one procedural review because distorted anatomy can raise airway or vascular injury risk. A separate source describes selected procedures despite an anterior mass, underscoring that this is a high-risk individualized decision, not an absolute universal rule.

With SVC involvement or syndrome, consider lower-extremity venous access because upper-extremity drainage may be impaired. Assess for collateral circulation and facial or neck swelling as part of the clinical picture.

sources.label: Mediastinoscopy
Mediastinal Masses: Adults, Mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The usual position is supine, with head extension described for the cervical approach. If a mass prevents lying flat or provokes obstruction, positioning may need to be reconsidered with the surgical and airway teams.

For large mediastinal masses, the source describes two large-bore IV lines and an arterial catheter; use lower-extremity access if SVC involvement impairs upper-body venous return. These are mass-risk recommendations, not mandatory for every case.

Monitor for innominate-artery compression using right radial pulse assessment, a right radial arterial line, or pulse-oximeter plethysmography. The available source supports these options; it does not establish mandatory bilateral pulse oximetry or bilateral blood-pressure comparison.

Prepare the anterior chest for possible sternotomy and ensure the surgical team can provide emergency thoracotomy or sternotomy if major vascular injury occurs. Rigid bronchoscopy backup is relevant when airway obstruction risk is significant.

sources.label: Mediastinoscopy
Mediastinal Masses: Adults, Mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia with tracheal intubation is typical when there are no preoperative signs or symptoms of airway obstruction. Airway management should reflect compression risk rather than assume one technique for all mediastinoscopies.

For major airway compromise, consider awake intubation with minimal sedation while maintaining spontaneous ventilation. In high-risk anterior masses, avoid muscle relaxants when airway patency may depend on spontaneous breathing; the sources do not support applying this precaution to every case.

An armored single-lumen tube may help resist tube compression in a mass-related airway-risk case. Rigid bronchoscopy and an experienced bronchoscopist should be available before airway manipulation when significant obstruction risk is present.

During general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates monitoring. These are basic anesthesia-monitoring standards, not a mediastinoscopy-specific ventilation prescription.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Airway compression may emerge with supine positioning, induction, during the procedure, at extubation, or postoperatively. Maintain a high index of suspicion for evolving obstruction in patients with a compressive mass; no specific ventilation target is established in these sources.

Scope-related innominate-artery compression can reduce cerebral blood flow. Monitor the right-sided pulse/plethysmographic signal or arterial pressure as selected, and promptly communicate a new loss or change to the surgeon for assessment of compression.

Major hemorrhage is a critical procedural hazard. Maintain communication with the surgical team and readiness for operative control; the evidence does not specify a resuscitation algorithm or hemodynamic target.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Major-vessel injury can cause significant bleeding and may require immediate sternotomy or other surgical intervention. Ensure the team and setup are prepared for rapid surgical control; the sources do not establish a detailed emergency sequence.

Innominate-artery compression can impair cerebral perfusion; airway obstruction and pneumothorax are additional recognized complications. A new pulse or plethysmographic change, ventilation difficulty, or clinical deterioration warrants immediate team communication and assessment.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury may cause hoarseness, vocal-cord paralysis, or respiratory difficulty. Pneumothorax may follow pleural entry and can require chest-tube placement; assess these complications clinically rather than assume routine imaging is specified.

Other reported hazards include tracheal or esophageal injury, air embolism, chylothorax, and infection. Their recognition and management are not detailed as a mediastinoscopy-specific anesthetic algorithm in the supplied sources.

Plan access and surgical readiness in light of the individual anatomy and operative risk; do not infer a universal crossmatch, blood-in-room requirement, or transfusion threshold from these sources.

For large mediastinal masses, the source recommends large-bore IV access and an arterial catheter; selective central venous pressure monitoring is mentioned because major hemorrhage may occur. These are risk-based considerations, not universal requirements for every case.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Extubation and recovery should account for airway status and the possibility of obstruction, especially with a mediastinal mass. The available sources do not specify a routine extubation protocol for uncomplicated mediastinoscopy.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade has been used, not to local or neuraxial techniques without blockade.

Postanesthesia care should include continual evaluation with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; quantitative oxygenation assessment is required in the initial recovery phase under the stated standard.

Assess for hoarseness or respiratory difficulty as possible signs of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. The supplied material does not establish routine post-procedure chest radiography; investigate suspected pneumothorax according to the clinical situation.

bullets: The procedure-specific evidence consists of educational clinical reviews, not a supplied trial or society guideline.
