overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A pericardial window drains fluid or clot through a subxiphoid incision or intrathoracic access, including thoracotomy or video-assisted thoracoscopy; the approach depends on the effusion and clinical situation.

The dominant anesthetic hazard is hemodynamic deterioration during induction in tamponade. Priorities are to preserve preload, heart rate and rhythm, systemic vascular resistance, and contractility while ensuring prompt access to drainage.

Do not assume every window requires general anesthesia or tracheal intubation: the sources describe local-anesthetic drainage in decompensated patients, while general anesthesia is usually used for surgical drainage. Positive-pressure ventilation can further impair venous return in tamponade.

After drainage, reassess hemodynamics and ongoing organ-support needs; critical-care observation is usually required after drainage of an acute effusion. Extubation criteria specific to a pericardial window are not established in the available sources.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The procedure creates an opening in the pericardium to drain fluid or clot. Open surgical access may be subxiphoid or intrathoracic via thoracotomy or video-assisted thoracoscopy; the review does not establish one approach as preferred for all patients.

In decompensated tamponade, a subxiphoid window may be performed under local anesthesia; general anesthesia is usually required for surgical drainage. This does not establish that every window requires an endotracheal tube or general anesthesia.

Posterior effusions, large clots, or traumatic tamponade may require a different surgical route, including sternotomy. Send fluid or tissue for culture and/or cytology according to the diagnostic indication.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the effusion’s cause and acuity, whether tamponade or other hemodynamic compromise is present, and the intended drainage approach. Consider coexisting pleural effusion and the patient’s ability to tolerate anesthesia and surgery.

Avoid preoperative volume depletion: reduced circulating volume and induction-related vasodilation can precipitate deterioration. A stable chronic or recurrent effusion without hemodynamic compromise does not, by itself, require drainage before elective surgery.

Assess comorbid disease and prior cancer treatment that may affect tolerance. Review coagulation status and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy as relevant to the planned invasive procedure; the source’s specific clotting advice is framed for pericardiocentesis, not as a universal window protocol.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For general anesthesia in tamponade, the review recommends the operating theatre with the surgeon scrubbed, drapes applied, and surgical equipment ready before induction. Emergency clinical deterioration may require drainage outside the theatre.

In tamponade, invasive arterial pressure monitoring is described as essential. Establish large-bore intravenous access and have fluids and emergency drugs available; central venous access is desirable but must not delay urgent drainage. Defibrillator pads are recommended before induction.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique: ECG, oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation are continually evaluated, with blood pressure and heart rate determined at least every five minutes. The available sources do not specify a position for the window procedure.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Select airway and anesthetic technique according to urgency, hemodynamic state, and surgical approach; do not impose intubation or general anesthesia on a local-anesthetic procedure. The review reports that a subxiphoid window may be performed under local anesthesia in decompensated patients.

If general anesthesia is used in tamponade, induction is a high-risk period because myocardial depression, vasodilation, and reduced preload can precipitate rapid deterioration. Ensure the drainage team and equipment are ready before induction.

Positive-pressure ventilation may reduce venous return. Until tamponade is relieved, avoid high PEEP and large tidal volumes and limit inspiratory pressures. A ten-patient retrospective MAC series used spontaneous breathing, but does not establish MAC as safer or superior to general anesthesia.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Pericardial Fenestration With Monitored Anesthesia Care Using Diluted Remifentanil: A Series of 10 Cases

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: In tamponade, maintain preload, sinus rhythm and heart rate, systemic vascular resistance, and contractility; avoid bradycardia and myocardial depressants. The review summarizes these physiologic priorities as “fast, full, and squeezed tight.”

The review identifies induction as a period of particular vulnerability. It describes ketamine as the authors’ practice, not a comparative trial result or mandatory regimen; no single induction drug or dose is established by the supplied evidence.

Reassess circulation as the pericardium is opened and fluid or clot evacuated: the review reports that dramatic improvement typically follows drainage. Rebound hypertension may follow chest opening and evacuation, requiring reassessment of anesthetic depth and vasopressor need.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Rapid hemodynamic deterioration at induction is a central concern in tamponade. Recognize instability promptly and escalate toward definitive drainage; the review identifies evacuation, rather than a drug regimen, as the effective intervention for hemodynamic collapse.

Cardiac arrest, chamber or vessel laceration, arrhythmias, and injury to surrounding structures are described complications of pericardiocentesis. The review does not provide open-window complication rates, so these figures and risks should not be represented as quantified window-specific outcomes.

During MAC with spontaneous breathing, airway obstruction and movement with surgical stimulation were observed in a small postoperative case series. These observations identify possible hazards, not their frequency in general practice or evidence that MAC is preferable.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Pericardial Fenestration With Monitored Anesthesia Care Using Diluted Remifentanil: A Series of 10 Cases

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Restore or maintain intravascular volume to support preload and promptly replace losses, particularly when circulating volume is depleted. The review does not prescribe a fluid type, total volume, or rate.
Do not interpret a high central venous pressure in tamponade as evidence of adequate ventricular filling: chamber compression makes it an unreliable proxy for true filling pressure.

Effusions may contain blood or clot, including after cardiac surgery. Anticipate the possibility of bleeding and reassess perfusion and ongoing blood loss; the available review supplies no universal blood-product threshold or transfusion protocol.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Tailor postoperative analgesia to incision and approach. The pericardial review describes longer-acting opioids and says an intercostal block may be appropriate for some approaches; it does not establish a required multimodal regimen.

Adult cardiac-surgery consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesia and consideration of regional techniques, but does not require one regimen. It notes that wound infiltration and intercostal nerve block are not routinely recommended in its broader cardiac-surgery context; balance this against the pericardial review’s conditional suggestion and the limited procedure-specific evidence.

Minimize avoidable opioid exposure while maintaining comfort and recovery, and consider nausea, vomiting, sedation, and other opioid-related adverse effects. The supplied sources do not establish a pericardial-window-specific PONV prevention protocol.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Base postoperative destination and monitoring on ongoing organ-support needs and hemodynamic status. Critical-care observation is usually required after drainage of an acute effusion; the sources do not define window-specific extubation criteria.

After anesthesia, provide an appropriate PACU or equivalent location, continually evaluate the patient, and monitor oxygenation during the initial recovery phase. Discharge readiness and location depend on clinical condition and local approved criteria.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is a narrative clinical review, not a trial or formal graded guideline; it reports no comparative outcome data for anesthetic techniques or drug regimens. Its described ketamine choice is explicitly the authors’ practice rather than trial evidence.

The MAC evidence is a retrospective, single-institution series of ten adults after cardiovascular surgery. It does not establish comparative safety or superiority over general anesthesia and should not define routine management.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards provide general requirements rather than pericardial-window-specific anesthetic or recovery protocols. The cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus is also broader than this procedure and identifies limits in the evidence for analgesic interventions.
Positioning, window-specific extubation criteria, and comparative complication rates for open surgical drainage are not established in the supplied sources.

sources.label: Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade
Pericardial Fenestration With Monitored Anesthesia Care Using Diluted Remifentanil: A Series of 10 Cases
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pleurodesis creates adhesions between the pleural layers to reduce recurrent fluid or air accumulation. Chemical treatment may be delivered through a chest tube or by thoracoscopic talc poudrage; mechanical pleurodesis is performed during thoracotomy or VATS.

The anesthetic approach depends on access: chemical pleurodesis may be performed under local anesthesia with moderate sedation, whereas surgical VATS or thoracotomy requires general anesthesia. The available sources do not establish a specific airway or ventilation technique for VATS.

The central procedural prerequisite is pleural apposition: a nonexpandable or trapped lung, or inadequate drainage, can cause failure. Assess whether the lung can re-expand and whether the selected approach fits the patient’s condition and goals.

Recovery priorities include adequate analgesia, respiratory assessment, and surveillance of pleural drainage. Pain and fever are recognized after pleurodesis; talc-associated ARDS is rare but documented.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Chemical pleurodesis introduces a sclerosant through a chest tube or catheter, or insufflates talc during thoracoscopy. The review describes catheter-based treatment as a less invasive option when surgery is not appropriate; approach selection remains dependent on clinical context and goals.

Mechanical pleurodesis may involve pleural abrasion during VATS or thoracotomy. VATS may also address underlying pathology, including subpleural blebs or bullae; pleurectomy is a distinct, more invasive option with substantial morbidity, not a routine substitute.

For symptomatic malignant effusion, chemical pleurodesis and tunneled pleural catheter are described as first-line options in cited guidance. In trapped lung, the review reports guidance favoring a tunneled catheter rather than pleurodesis.

sources.label: Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist
Pleurodesis – StatPearls

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the indication and clinical trajectory: malignant or other recurrent effusion, recurrent or persistent pneumothorax, and whether catheter treatment or surgery is intended. The sources describe distinct selection contexts for effusion and pneumothorax.

Assess lung expansion and drainage because pleural contact is necessary for success. Thoracentesis and assessment for trapped lung or loculations are described before treatment; an unexpandable lung increases the risk of pleurodesis failure.

For malignant disease, account for functional status, prognosis, and the patient’s preferences when considering procedural burden and alternatives. The sources describe poor performance status and limited life expectancy as relevant selection factors, but do not establish anesthetic thresholds.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Chemical pleurodesis may be a bedside or image-guided procedure rather than an operating-room general anesthetic. The source describing catheter procedures uses seated positioning for thoracostomy drainage, with supine positioning as an alternative when sitting is not tolerated; this is not a VATS positioning recommendation.

For anesthetized patients, apply basic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards require continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

The procedure sources do not specify VATS positioning, equipment configuration, or procedure-specific monitoring. Select setup with the procedural team; do not infer lateral positioning or an arterial line as universal requirements.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For chemical pleurodesis, the source supports local intrapleural anesthetic and moderate sedation as options for discomfort and anxiety. It provides no sedation regimen or airway-device recommendation; do not impose intubation or neuromuscular blockade for this approach.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify correct positioning by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. Continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis from airway-device placement until extubation or removal, or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location.

sources.label: Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The procedural mechanism is an inflammatory response leading to fibrin deposition and pleural adhesion. Adequate pleural-layer contact is essential; failure may follow trapped or inadequately expanded lung or inadequate inflammation.

During mechanical abrasion, the review identifies bleeding and lung injury as concerns. It describes inspecting for these injuries and reexpanding the lung to bring the pleural layers into contact; the sources provide no anesthetic physiologic targets.

Chemical pleurodesis is painful, and talc can provoke fever and systemic inflammation. Anticipate these effects in procedural and recovery planning; the sources do not define a specific intraoperative hemodynamic or ventilation protocol.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Respiratory complications reported include pneumothorax, hemothorax, reexpansion pulmonary edema, and ARDS. New respiratory compromise warrants prompt clinical assessment and escalation; the sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue algorithm.

Talc-associated ARDS is rare but reported, particularly with smaller particles or large doses. The reviews report substantially fewer ARDS reports with larger-particle talc; they do not establish a specific product standard in these materials.

Pleurodesis complications include chest pain and inflammation, fever, pleural infection, and empyema. Fever after talc pleurodesis is reported as likely resulting from a systemic inflammatory response.

Persistent fluid or air, or failure of pleural apposition, may indicate trapped lung or loculated effusion. The reviews describe repeat pleurodesis, an indwelling pleural catheter, or surgical options in selected cases; choice is procedural and patient specific.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Mechanical abrasion can cause bleeding or lung injury; the review advises attention to these hazards and inspection of the operative field. The source does not give a blood-management protocol.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan for pleuritic pain with chemical instillation and postoperative pain after surgical pleurodesis. The reviews describe NSAIDs or opioids for pleurodesis-related pain, but they do not establish one regimen for all patients.

The sources differ on NSAIDs after pleurodesis: one advises general avoidance because of a possible effect on inflammation, while another reports they do not reduce pleural symphysis. Avoid presenting either position as settled universal practice; weigh analgesic needs and patient-specific risks.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The pleurodesis sources do not establish extubation criteria or an airway-exchange technique. For general anesthesia, apply appropriate anesthetic recovery assessment; if neuromuscular blockers are used, ASA-derived guidance supports quantitative monitoring and confirmation of recovery before extubation.

After anesthesia, continue monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A PACU or equivalent postanesthesia care area must be available.

Obtain a chest radiograph 24 hours after pleurodesis to check for pneumothorax or fluid reaccumulation. The chest tube may be removed if the radiograph is satisfactory and there is no further fluid output. Follow-up, including chest radiography, is recommended after 4–6 weeks.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The pleurodesis sources are educational reviews, not anesthesia protocols. The principal procedure review explicitly provides limited anesthetic detail and does not specify airway, positioning, monitoring, drug regimens, ventilation, fluids, or emergence.

The second pleurodesis review likewise states it is not an anesthesia reference. ASA standards provide general monitoring and recovery requirements, not pleurodesis-specific management; adult-focused cardiac analgesia guidance is not a substitute for thoracic-procedure guidance.

The supplied sources do not define a case-specific VATS airway/ventilation plan, positioning, intraoperative targets, fluid strategy, or pleurodesis-specific PONV approach. Pleurodesis source populations are not stated to be exclusively adults; this draft is adult-focused but those details remain unresolved.
The supplied pleurodesis sources do not specify an airway device or ventilation strategy for mechanical pleurodesis under general anesthesia.
The supplied pleurodesis source does not specify blood-loss estimates, transfusion thresholds, fluid administration, or resuscitation.

sources.label: Pleurodesis – StatPearls
Treating Recurrent Pleural Disease: A Review of Indications and Technique for Chemical Pleurodesis for the Interventional Radiologist
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pneumonectomy removes an entire lung and is generally reserved for disease unsuitable for a less extensive resection. General anesthesia with lung isolation—usually a double-lumen tube (DLT)—allows operative-lung collapse; confirm placement bronchoscopically.

The dominant physiologic challenge is routing the entire pulmonary circulation through the remaining lung, with risk of right-ventricular intolerance and postoperative pulmonary oedema. Assess reserve carefully and avoid both fluid excess and hypoperfusion.

Right pneumonectomy carries greater reported mortality and higher risk of bronchopleural fistula and pulmonary oedema than left-sided resection. Maintain vigilance for haemodynamic deterioration, airway/stump complications, and arrhythmias.

Recovery priorities are effective analgesia for coughing and secretion clearance, close respiratory and haemodynamic observation, and an appropriate postoperative-care setting. Extubation and level of support depend on the patient's condition; routine postoperative intubation is not established here.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation removes the affected lung. The common indication is bronchial carcinoma not suitable for a less extensive resection; other indications include selected uncontrolled haemorrhage, chronic infection, and fungal destruction. Consider less extensive alternatives before proceeding.

Standard pneumonectomy is the focus of the principal anaesthesia review. Intrapericardial, completion, and carinal procedures may have distinct surgical and physiologic demands; extrapleural pneumonectomy (EPP) additionally removes ipsilateral pleura, hemidiaphragm, and hemipericardium with reconstruction.

Posterolateral thoracotomy is the common open approach; video-assisted thoracoscopy is an alternative. The surgical team should communicate about pulmonary-artery clamping and other critical operative steps affecting cardiac output.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess spirometry and DLCO, then estimate predicted postoperative function. NICE recommends counselling patients with ppoFEV₁ or ppoDLCO below 30% predicted about increased risk of postoperative dyspnoea and long-term oxygen therapy, and referring them for formal exercise testing. Another overview describes estimated postoperative FEV₁ or DLCO below 40% predicted as high risk warranting further functional assessment; these are distinct source thresholds, not interchangeable eligibility rules.

Use exercise capacity to refine assessment when indicated. The review describes shuttle-walk and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) measures, but notes limited evidence for using CPET to classify risk of unacceptable postoperative dyspnoea; a six-minute walk threshold is not established by these sources.

Evaluate cardiac disease and pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography is recommended for pneumonectomy candidates in the review; pulmonary hypertension is a relative contraindication, particularly for right pneumonectomy, because postoperative pulmonary vascular resistance increases.

Right-sided resection, age, cardiac comorbidity, and limited reserve modify risk. No single test determines suitability; integrate functional capacity, comorbidity, and the planned extent of resection.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Position lateral decubitus with the operative side up; protect eyes and pressure points and recheck airway-device position after turning. A table break may be used.

Provide invasive arterial-pressure monitoring and central venous access as described in the review; the need for additional advanced monitoring depends on patient condition. Temperature monitoring and a urinary catheter are specified.

Ensure postoperative-care capacity appropriate to expected risk. The review calls for availability of a level-2 postoperative bed and crossmatched red cells; this is not evidence that every case requires ICU admission or a fixed blood-preparation protocol.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Use a DLT for lung isolation in most cases; a bronchial blocker is an alternative when DLT placement is not possible, including with a difficult airway. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy confirms placement and should be repeated after position change.

For left pneumonectomy, a right-sided DLT avoids interference with the operative site; check right-upper-lobe alignment because obstruction is possible. Select and verify the device for the planned side and anatomy rather than assuming one DLT configuration fits all cases.

For one-lung ventilation, the review suggests low tidal volume, PEEP, limited airway pressures, and oxygen titration to saturation; it finds no evidence favouring pressure- over volume-control ventilation. Avoid presenting a single ventilatory recipe as mandatory.
Before bronchial stapling, ensure the DLT or suction catheter is not caught in the staple line. The review describes a saline stump test with positive pressure and no bubbling as the check for leak.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pulmonary-artery clamping redirects the full pulmonary circulation through the remaining lung and tests right-ventricular reserve. Cardiovascular collapse or a marked central venous pressure rise raises concern for inadequate RV compliance; reassess causes and decide with the surgical team whether to proceed.

Maintain normothermia and assess haemodynamic deterioration for haemorrhage, cardiac compression, or other causes. The source highlights communication during pulmonary-artery clamping but does not establish a universal haemodynamic target.

The operation leaves one functioning lung; protect its gas exchange and avoid unnecessary hyperoxia. Titrate oxygen to clinical oxygenation needs rather than use a fixed inspired-oxygen concentration.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema occurs in 2–5% of cases and is associated with reported mortality above 50%. It typically presents with respiratory distress and hypoxaemia within 72 hours. Treatment is generally supportive, with ventilatory support as required, restrictive fluids, and diuretics.

Bronchopleural fistula may present with cough, persistent air leak, a falling fluid level, or a new air-fluid level; later presentation may include empyema. Right-sided resection and prolonged ventilation are among reported risk factors. Suspected fistula requires prompt surgical and respiratory-team assessment.

Cardiac herniation is rare, particularly associated with pericardial stripping or left intrapericardial pneumonectomy. Acute hypotension, shock, or rapid collapse should prompt immediate surgical escalation; the source describes urgent repositioning and defect closure.
Atrial arrhythmias, retained secretions, contralateral-airway plugging, haemorrhage, and respiratory failure are important postoperative concerns; monitor and investigate according to presentation.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use restrictive fluid management while preserving perfusion and avoiding hypovolaemia or acute kidney injury. Excessive fluid administration is associated with pulmonary oedema and respiratory failure; no universal intraoperative fluid total is established.

For hypotension, exclude haemorrhage and consider neuraxial sympathectomy; the review favours vasoactive treatment over reflex fluid boluses for epidural-related hypotension. Individualize to the cause and perfusion state.
Anticipate operative blood loss and coordinate blood availability with the team. The sources do not provide a universal estimated blood loss, transfusion threshold, or cell-salvage requirement.
If a post-pneumonectomy drain is used, avoid suction. The review warns that prolonged unclamping can produce acute mediastinal shift and cardiovascular instability; drain strategy is variable.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Provide analgesia sufficient for coughing and secretion clearance. The pneumonectomy review describes a mid-thoracic epidural or surgeon-placed paravertebral catheter; selection depends on patient factors, contraindications, and local expertise. Neither is established here as mandatory.

Use multimodal analgesia where appropriate. A general cardiac-surgery consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesics and consideration of regional techniques, but it is not a pneumonectomy-specific protocol and does not establish a required drug combination here.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Extubate when clinically appropriate and the patient is awake, warm, and comfortable. If continued ventilation is needed, exchange the DLT for a single-lumen tube; this is not a reason for routine postoperative intubation.

Transfer to a postoperative unit with monitoring and organ support suited to the patient's condition. Continue surveillance for pulmonary oedema, airway obstruction, secretion retention, arrhythmia, and haemorrhage.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are supported by the ASA guideline overview; this does not apply to every patient independent of whether blockade was used.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is an educational review, not a trial or guideline. It states that no single test determines suitability and that evidence is limited for CPET prediction of unacceptable postoperative dyspnoea.

The second procedure overview supplies additional assessment and postoperative information but reports limited interpretation data for exercise testing and gives recommendations without formal evidence grading. Threshold differences should be interpreted in context, not collapsed into a single cutoff.

ASA monitoring and neuromuscular-blockade sources provide general standards, not pneumonectomy-specific protocols. The cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus is outside this operation's direct evidence base and is used only for broad analgesia context.

The available sources do not establish a pneumonectomy-specific PONV regimen or resolve detailed EPP-specific anesthetic choices. Individualize care with the surgical team and relevant local expertise.
No pneumonectomy-specific PONV prevention regimen is provided in the supplied sources.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Pneumonectomy — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Pain management and opioid stewardship in adult cardiac surgery: Joint consensus report of the PeriOperative Quality Initiative and the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Cardiac Society

title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Repair (TEVAR / Open Descending)
aliases: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Repair (TEVAR / Open Descending)

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TEVAR is an endovascular option for descending thoracic aneurysms with suitable anatomy; open repair is a distinct, principally thoracotomy-based approach for descending or thoracoabdominal disease. The operative approach materially changes airway, perfusion, and recovery priorities.

Major hazards include spinal-cord ischemia, renal injury, major bleeding, and cardiac or pulmonary complications; arch manipulation during TEVAR also carries embolic-stroke risk. Priorities are preserving organ perfusion and recognizing evolving neurologic or hemodynamic problems.

Open repair may require one-lung ventilation, aortic clamping, and distal perfusion adjuncts such as left heart bypass; clamp and unclamp phases can substantially alter cardiac loading and perfusion. TEVAR deployment has a different, operator-dependent hemodynamic phase.

Recovery requires close neurologic, renal, respiratory, and hemodynamic observation, commonly in an ICU for open repair. If spinal-cord ischemia is suspected, the cited TEVAR review advises prompt escalation of perfusion pressure and consideration of CSF drainage; this is not a universal protocol for every approach.

sources.label: Endovascular Repair of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms
Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair: What Should the Anaesthetist Know?

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TEVAR uses a stent graft delivered through arterial access, commonly via femoral exposure, with fluoroscopy and angiography guiding placement. Preprocedural anatomic assessment includes the aorta, branch vessels, landing zones, and iliofemoral access vessels.

Open descending/TAAA repair is principally through a left thoracotomy; extent of disease affects incision and clamp strategy. Described adjuncts include sequential clamping, distal perfusion with LHB, CSF drainage, hypothermia, and selected artery reimplantation.

Approach selection and branch-vessel coverage require case-specific anatomic and ischemia-risk assessment. The TEVAR review notes uncertainty in left-subclavian revascularization practice rather than a single universal approach.

sources.label: Endovascular Repair of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms
Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair: What Should the Anaesthetist Know?

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess symptoms, urgency, aneurysm extent and growth, cardiac and pulmonary reserve, renal function, and relevant comorbidity. Rupture or acute malperfusion changes the urgency; the supplied reviews give differing size thresholds, so this draft does not make a threshold a stand-alone indication.

For TEVAR, evaluate landing-zone anatomy and access-vessel diameter, tortuosity, stenosis, and calcification; access injury is a recognized complication. Consider spinal-cord risk modifiers, including prior abdominal aortic grafting and the length or territory of aortic coverage.

For open repair, assess respiratory reserve because exposure may require one-lung ventilation, and optimize relevant pulmonary and cardiac disease. Renal dysfunction, age, hypotension, low cardiac output, and clamp duration are described as renal-injury modifiers.

sources.label: Endovascular Repair of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms
Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair: What Should the Anaesthetist Know?

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: TEVAR requires fluoroscopic imaging and equipment/table access that accommodates the imaging angles and patient reorientation. The supplied TEVAR review does not establish a single positioning protocol.

For open repair, the review describes a right lateral decubitus position, with padding and arm positioning to protect pressure points and the brachial plexus; groin access may need to remain available for perfusion cannulation.

Open-repair monitoring described includes right radial arterial pressure, Foley urine-output assessment, TEE, and—when useful and planned—simultaneous femoral and radial pressure monitoring. Select invasive access and monitoring to the approach and perfusion strategy, not as an automatic bundle.

Basic anesthetic standards require continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG display and blood pressure/heart rate assessment at least every five minutes are specified. Procedure-specific monitoring must be added according to clinical need.

sources.label: Endovascular Repair of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms
Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair: What Should the Anaesthetist Know?
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open thoracotomy commonly uses a double-lumen tube for lung separation and one-lung ventilation to improve exposure; bronchial anatomy distorted by aneurysm may make the intended tube placement unsuitable. Confirm position supine and again after lateral positioning.

The review describes general endotracheal anesthesia with paralysis for TEVAR to limit movement and permit respiratory suspension during angiography. It does not specify a required tube type, ventilation settings, or universal apnea method.

When an endotracheal tube is used, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, perform continual quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During open aortic clamping, afterload and proximal pressure rise, increasing myocardial demand; the magnitude depends partly on clamp level and duration. Anticipate hemodynamic changes at both clamping and release and coordinate timing with the surgical and perfusion teams.

Unclamping/reperfusion can produce hypotension through central volume redistribution, vasodilation, and accumulated metabolites. The review emphasizes correcting underlying volume and metabolic problems, considering vasoactive support, and gradual release; it does not establish one universal response recipe.

For TEVAR deployment, the review reports that many operators transiently target lower MAP to reduce graft migration; this is a procedural phase-specific practice, not a general anesthetic target. Avoid unnecessary catheter or wire movement after arch deployment because of embolic risk.

Open repair spinal-cord protection is multifactorial: CSF drainage, maintaining perfusion pressure, distal perfusion, hypothermia, and selected artery reimplantation are described, but no single measure is entirely effective.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Spinal-cord ischemia may present as new postoperative lower-extremity deficit, including delayed deficit after an initially intact examination. Treat this as an urgent change requiring prompt escalation and specialist/surgical-team involvement; the TEVAR review describes raising arterial pressure and reducing CSF pressure when ischemia is suspected.

Other important complications include major vascular bleeding or access injury, stroke, cardiac and pulmonary events, renal injury, and—after relevant branch-vessel coverage—limb or vertebrobasilar ischemia. Monitor in a way that can detect approach-specific complications early.

CSF drainage has material hazards, including subdural and spinal/epidural hematoma, meningitis, and puncture headache. Drain placement, drainage, and removal therefore require a deliberate institutional and multidisciplinary approach; do not infer a universal drainage rate from this review.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Open thoracoabdominal repair can involve major blood loss, fluid shifts, hypothermia, heparin exposure, and coagulopathy. The review supports readiness for rapid infusion and blood-component availability, cell salvage, and coagulation assessment; it does not supply a universal transfusion threshold.

During open repair, preserving distal organ perfusion and avoiding prolonged clamp time are emphasized for renal and spinal-cord protection. Distal perfusion strategies may attenuate clamp-related physiology, but their selection and anticoagulation are case-specific.

For TEVAR, the review advises careful fluid balance after the procedure—adequate hydration while avoiding overload—and notes the high contrast burden. It provides no specific blood-product strategy or transfusion threshold.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Open-repair analgesia options in the TAAA review include opioid infusion or epidural infusion with local anesthetic/opioid mixtures. Choice should account for the operative approach, neurologic assessment needs, and anticoagulation or CSF-drain considerations; the source does not define a single required regimen.

The adult cardiac-surgery consensus supports multimodal nonopioid analgesia and opioid stewardship, while considering regional techniques selectively. Its evidence is not a procedure-specific analgesia protocol for aortic repair, and systemic anticoagulation is a relevant regional-technique consideration.

No case-specific PONV prevention regimen is established in the supplied procedure sources. The cardiac-surgery consensus reports opioid-related nausea and vomiting, but that evidence does not establish an aortic-repair-specific prophylaxis strategy.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After open repair, the TAAA review describes changing the DLT to a single-lumen tube when airway swelling or bleeding concerns are absent, and attempting awakening/extubation as soon as feasible to permit neurologic assessment. Clinical circumstances may require continued ventilation.

For open descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal repair, the review describes ICU monitoring, continued hemodynamic and neurologic assessment, attention to respiratory, renal, and cardiac complications, and ongoing CSF-drain management when used. It states a postoperative MAP target of 80–90 mmHg in this open-repair context; do not generalize this target to TEVAR or other contexts.

For TEVAR, postoperative care includes ICU-level monitoring in the cited review, urine-output assessment, and frequent lower-extremity vascular and neurologic checks. The source does not provide universal extubation criteria.

When neuromuscular blockers are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported by the ASA guideline overview; this applies only when NMB has been used.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The TEVAR source is a narrative review, not a dedicated anesthesia reference; it explicitly lacks detailed anesthetic, airway, positioning, analgesia, and emergence protocols. Its practice statements should not be read as a complete TEVAR anesthetic standard.

The open-repair source is a narrative review with institutional practices; it states that no single spinal-cord protection method has been proved entirely effective and that evidence and perioperative options can be evolving or conflicting.

The cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus and generic ASA monitoring standards inform limited cross-cutting issues, not aortic-repair-specific protocols. Exact approach-specific airway choices, ventilation settings, CSF-drain selection/management, and TEVAR transfusion strategy are not resolved by the supplied sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open thoracotomy provides wide pleural access when exposure requirements or the planned resection make a less invasive approach unsuitable; the operative approach varies with patient, technical, and surgeon factors.

For open thoracotomy, anticipate substantial pain and plan regional analgesia as part of multimodal care. The cited procedure-specific guidance prefers paravertebral block (PVB); thoracic epidural analgesia (TEA) is an effective alternative.

Single-lung ventilation is usually needed for surgical exposure and entails a variable shunt. Independent lung ventilation may be used for continuous desaturation but may interfere with surgery; the review does not specify general ventilation strategies or a thoracotomy-specific rescue sequence.

Recovery priorities include effective breathing and coughing, appropriate postanesthesia observation, and confirmation of adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when a neuromuscular blocker has been used.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open thoracotomy provides broader pleural-cavity exposure than VATS and may be selected when that exposure is important, including for extended resections. The approach is determined by patient-related and technical factors and surgeon preference.

The traditional posterolateral approach offers excellent access but often divides muscle and is associated with increased postoperative pain. VATS may reduce acute pain when intercostal nerve damage is avoided; these approach comparisons do not establish which is appropriate for an individual operation.

bullets: Assess the planned operation and patient-specific pulmonary reserve and comorbidity. The supplied review notes that pulmonary function testing may help predict postoperative ventilatory dependence in patients with pulmonary dysfunction, but does not provide general thoracotomy selection thresholds.

Review antithrombotic exposure, coagulopathy, and bleeding risk before selecting neuraxial or regional analgesia. TEA and PVB require a case-specific risk–benefit assessment when relevant antithrombotic or thrombolytic drugs have been used.

Incision location and pleural surgery can affect regional technique choice: the review notes SAPB is unlikely to cover a posterolateral incision and PVB spread may be unpredictable after pleurodesis or pleural resection.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: During anesthesia, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; determine and evaluate arterial blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes. The review does not describe thoracotomy-specific positioning or vascular access.

For general anesthesia, apply the basic monitoring standards: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, including quantitative oxygenation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring as specified by the standard.

An arterial pressure line is described as essential for thoracotomies in the review's specific discussion of lower-tracheal and carinal resections; the source does not establish this as a universal requirement for every open thoracotomy.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Lung isolation may be needed for surgical exposure. In the review's discussion of bronchial sleeve resection, double-lumen tubes or bronchial blockers are commonly used; this does not establish a universal device choice for all thoracotomies.

When single-lung ventilation is used, account for the variable shunt. Independent lung ventilation may be used for continuous desaturation but may interfere with surgery; the review does not provide a general ventilation strategy or physiologic targets.

In lower-tracheal or carinal procedures, the review prefers fiberoptically placed endobronchial tubes over bulky double-lumen tubes. This is specific to that airway-surgery context, not a general rule for thoracotomy.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect nociceptive input from the incision, muscle and rib retraction, pleural work, and possible intercostal nerve injury. Chest drains and residual haemothorax may also contribute to postoperative pain.

During OLV, recognize desaturation as a potential physiologic problem and coordinate assessment with the surgical team. The available evidence does not establish universal intraoperative targets or a single troubleshooting sequence.
Consider referred ipsilateral shoulder pain separately from thoracotomy-site pain; TEA and PVB do not relieve this phrenic-nerve-mediated pain.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Inadequate analgesia can impair mobility, breathing, and coughing, with associated pulmonary complications and prolonged hospitalization. Assess pain and functional breathing rather than relying on pain scores alone.

Regional techniques have distinct potential harms. The review describes neuraxial hematoma risk with relevant antithrombotic exposure and reports possible fascial-plane block complications including failure, bleeding, local-structure damage, local-anesthetic toxicity, and infection.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, residual blockade is associated with airway obstruction, reintubation, atelectasis, and pneumonia. Use quantitative monitoring rather than clinical assessment alone to assess recovery.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For open thoracotomy, the cited procedure-specific recommendations prefer PVB as first-line regional analgesia; TEA is an effective alternative when PVB cannot be placed. This evidence does not support describing TEA as mandatory or universally preferred.

For pain expected to remain moderate to severe beyond the immediate postoperative period, the review recommends a catheter-based approach; its cited open-thoracotomy guidance specifies postoperative infusion for 2–3 days. This is a source-specific recommendation, not an automatic duration for every patient.

If PVB or TEA is not possible or is contraindicated, the review describes catheter-based ESPB or intercostal nerve block as options, while noting uncertainty in open-thoracotomy fascial-plane-block evidence. Use multimodal analgesia; no specific systemic regimen is established by the supplied thoracotomy sources.

TEA has potential adverse effects including hypotension, urinary retention, pruritus, and nausea or vomiting; adding an opioid to the epidural mixture may increase respiratory-depression and urinary-retention risk. The sources do not specify a thoracotomy-specific PONV prevention regimen.

bullets: The supplied thoracotomy review does not describe an emergence or extubation protocol. Assess recovery in light of respiratory reserve, pain, and the actual perioperative course rather than applying an unsupported universal extubation rule.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Thymectomy may be performed through VATS or an open approach; for VATS, the supplied sources describe general anesthesia with either selective ventilation using a double-lumen tube or a single-lumen tube with controlled ventilation and CO₂ insufflation. The approach and intended extent of resection shape the anesthetic setup.

For VATS, CO₂ insufflation can mimic tension pneumothorax and cause respiratory and hemodynamic changes. Hypoxia and hypercarbia may occur after entry into the contralateral pleural space. Close surgeon–anesthesia communication about ventilation and plans for contralateral pleural entry is emphasized.

When myasthenia gravis (MG) is present, assess disease control, respiratory and bulbar function, and the patient’s current anticholinesterase schedule. The operative source advises minimizing or avoiding muscle relaxants and using twitch monitoring if they are needed.

Recovery planning should account for postoperative ventilation risk in MG and confirm recovery from any neuromuscular blockade before extubation. The available sources do not establish MG-specific extubation thresholds or a universal postoperative destination.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Thymectomy is used for MG and thymic pathology. The resection extent depends on indication: the VATS technical review describes extended thymectomy for MG, total thymectomy for malignant tumors, and partial thymectomy only for selected benign or early-stage tumors.

VATS may use unilateral or bilateral transpleural access; the cited technical review says bilateral access is needed for the described extended MG resection. These are procedure descriptions, not a universal approach mandate across all operations.

Tumor involvement of great vessels or chest wall may require conversion to open surgery; the VATS review states that resection of these structures is not possible by VATS. Open and robotic-specific anesthetic protocols are not established in the supplied procedure sources.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For MG, review current disease control, respiratory reserve, bulbar symptoms, medication schedule, and history relevant to postoperative ventilation. Coordinate planning with neurology and thoracic anesthesia; the source describes perioperative IVIG as considered when needed, not as routine.

The VATS article identifies five factors associated with increased postoperative intubation or ventilation risk: longer disease duration, chronic pulmonary disease, higher pyridostigmine requirement, preoperative steroid use, and previous respiratory failure. Use these as source-described risk modifiers rather than a validated standalone decision rule.

For operative planning, the VATS source describes CT with intravenous contrast, ECG, and preoperative blood work; imaging also evaluates thymoma and may reveal anatomic abnormalities. Individual workup should reflect the planned approach and patient.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For VATS, the cited positions are semi-supine with the operative side elevated or lateral decubitus. Position the ipsilateral arm to expose the axilla and keep it clear of instrument paths; protect the shoulder from overextension.

The VATS technical source emphasizes good IV access, including at least one large-bore catheter, because unexpected major-vessel bleeding may require resuscitation. It describes arterial pressure monitoring as the authors’ practice; this is not established as mandatory for every thymectomy.

Apply applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment are specified for anesthetics.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring when available and confirm recovery before extubation; the guideline specifies the adductor pollicis site. These recommendations do not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: CO₂ insufflation can produce respiratory and hemodynamic changes that resemble tension pneumothorax. The VATS authors advise slow insufflation and limiting pressure; the supplied technical sources give differing pressure limits, so no single numerical target is adopted here.

Entry into the contralateral pleural space can be accompanied by hypoxia or hypercarbia. Communicate with the surgeon about ventilation and insufflation changes; the source describes lowering insufflation pressure or adjusting ventilation as possible responses.

Phrenic nerve preservation is a key dissection concern. The technical article describes sharp dissection near the nerve and repeated identification to reduce thermal injury risk; this is operative guidance, not an anesthetic intervention.

Venous dissection and thymic-vein division are critical bleeding-risk phases. The transpleural source specifically highlights identifying the far-side left brachiocephalic vein before dividing thymic veins, particularly when energy-sealing devices are used.

bullets: Unexpected major-vessel bleeding may cause abrupt hemodynamic deterioration; ensure the team can recognize the change, communicate immediately with the surgeon, and escalate to the available resuscitation and conversion resources. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: VATS wedge resection removes a peripheral pulmonary lesion for diagnosis or treatment. The available evidence describes both double-lumen-tube anesthesia with one-lung ventilation and selected laryngeal-mask or spontaneous-breathing approaches; it does not establish one universal technique.

Key physiologic concerns in the described approaches include oxygenation changes and carbon-dioxide retention; non-intubated VATS may involve hypercapnia and acidosis, while the trial reported temporary oxygenation reductions in its double-lumen-tube group.

Priorities include continuous assessment of oxygenation and ventilation, readiness to change the airway or anesthetic approach if physiology or surgical conditions require it, and appropriate postanesthesia observation.

Postoperative recovery requires attention to pain, respiratory status, and chest drainage. Evidence describes multimodal analgesia and chest-tube management, but does not establish a single recovery or analgesic protocol for all patients.

The review's comparisons with intubated VATS and non-surgical treatment rely on cited studies whose underlying data are not provided in that article.
The cardiac-surgery review and consensus report are outside the procedure's scope and are not used here to establish VATS-specific anesthetic or analgesic recommendations.

The supplied sources do not establish a case-wide preferred airway, positioning protocol, ventilation targets, detailed fluid strategy, systemic analgesic regimen, or emergence criteria beyond the conditional neuromuscular-blockade guidance. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: APR removes the rectum, anal sphincter complex, and anus; the perineal wound is closed and the colon is brought out as a permanent end colostomy. Abdominal and perineal phases may be simultaneous or sequential.

The dominant intraoperative hazards in the available procedure review are significant presacral bleeding and injury to pelvic urinary or autonomic nerves. Maintain vigilance through both phases and ensure complications can be escalated promptly.

Choose positioning and access to support the planned abdominal and perineal work; minimally invasive approaches use steep Trendelenburg. The evidence does not establish a procedure-specific airway or anesthetic recipe.

Recovery priorities include surveillance for bleeding, urinary dysfunction, stoma and perineal-wound problems, and recovery from anesthesia. Use an opioid-sparing multimodal approach within the planned pathway; colorectal guidance supports early oral intake when appropriate.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: APR removes the rectum, mesorectum, sphincter complex, and anus, with a permanent end colostomy and closure of the perineal opening. The operation is used for selected low rectal or anal cancers when sphincter preservation is not feasible or would compromise margins or function.

The abdominal and perineal phases may be performed synchronously or sequentially. Access may be open, laparoscopic, or robotic; approach selection depends on the operative plan and available expertise.

For colorectal surgery, a minimally invasive approach is recommended when appropriate and expertise is available. The guideline describes robotic surgery as feasible but does not establish its superiority over standard laparoscopy.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess fitness for the planned major operation and review relevant preoperative imaging; the procedure review particularly emphasizes rectal MRI in cancer cases. Individual evaluation should be tailored to the patient.
Arrange stoma counseling and site marking with an enterostomal nurse therapist. Discuss practical management and psychosocial effects of a permanent colostomy.

Consider ureteral stents when injury is a significant concern, understanding that the cited review says they facilitate earlier identification and repair rather than reduce injury risk. Prior radiation, malnutrition, obesity, and diabetes are among the reported perineal-wound risk modifiers.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan the table and access for perineal exposure. Lithotomy with well-padded stirrups is described; some surgeons use prone jack-knife for the perineal phase, requiring repositioning after abdominal work.
A Foley catheter is placed in the operative description. In women, the vagina may need to be included in the operative field for uterine manipulation or palpation of the posterior vaginal wall.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards. The ASA standard calls for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; additional monitoring and vascular access are individualized rather than specified by the APR review.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure review identifies fitness for general anesthesia as a prerequisite but does not specify airway device, induction, ventilation, maintenance technique, or extubation. These choices cannot be derived as an APR-specific recipe from the available evidence.

When general anesthesia is administered, follow applicable monitoring standards, including continual evaluation of ventilation and expired carbon dioxide unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. Confirm tracheal-tube position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide when a tube is used.
Steep Trendelenburg is described for minimally invasive visualization. The provided sources do not specify an APR-specific ventilation strategy for this position.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During abdominal mobilization and total mesorectal excision, the left ureter and autonomic nerves require protection. The review identifies presacral-plane entry as a risk for significant bleeding and autonomic-nerve injury.

During perineal dissection, anterior work is performed with care to avoid the male urethra or posterior vaginal wall. The review also describes potential injury to pelvic autonomic nerves during lateral, retrorectal, and anterior dissection.

Minimally invasive surgery uses steep Trendelenburg and rectal retraction for visualization. The sources do not provide approach-specific anesthetic targets or a defined sequence for anesthetic management across the two operative phases.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Presacral bleeding is a significant operative hazard. The review identifies bleeding risk when the presacral plane is entered but does not provide a validated anesthetic rescue protocol or transfusion threshold; promptly communicate and escalate with the surgical team.

Potential complications include ureteral or urethral injury, urinary or sexual dysfunction, stoma complications, perineal wound infection or dehiscence, abscess, ileus, and small-bowel obstruction. The supplied sources do not establish a single APR-specific troubleshooting pathway.

Perineal wound risk is increased by factors including prior radiation, malnutrition, obesity, and diabetes. Large wounds or dehiscence risk may require surgical consideration of flap coverage; this is a surgical decision rather than an anesthetic intervention.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Avoid both excessive fluid administration and undue restriction. The colorectal ERAS guideline recommends tailoring fluid administration to avoid volume overload and hypovolemia, with balanced chloride-restricted crystalloids for maintenance and boluses.

Use goal-directed hemodynamic therapy for high-risk patients or when significant intravascular losses are anticipated. The guideline describes optimizing stroke volume with boluses and adding vasopressor if hypotension persists, rather than prescribing one APR-wide monitor or regimen.

The procedure review identifies potentially significant bleeding from the presacral plane. Blood-loss estimates, transfusion guidance, and an APR-specific blood-product protocol are not provided in the procedure or colorectal guideline sources.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Implement a multimodal, opioid-sparing plan. The colorectal guideline supports scheduled acetaminophen and NSAIDs as options, while emphasizing that NSAID-associated anastomotic-leak concerns may vary by drug; APR has no intestinal anastomosis.

Thoracic epidural analgesia is an option for open colorectal surgery when a dedicated acute-pain team is available; it is not recommended routinely for laparoscopic surgery. Regional blocks and wound infiltration are additional opioid-reduction approaches described by the guideline.

Use preemptive multimodal antiemetic prophylaxis tailored to risk. The guideline lists laparoscopic surgery, volatile anesthesia, prolonged operative time, and opioid analgesia among PONV risk factors; it does not mandate a single regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The APR review gives no emergence or extubation protocol. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirming train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

Provide postanesthesia care with continual assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

For elective colorectal surgery, offer a regular diet within 24 hours. After mid/lower rectal resection, urinary catheter removal is typically recommended within 24–48 hours, balancing urinary-retention risk after pelvic dissection against UTI risk; apply these recommendations to the operative and patient context.

bullets: Anal fistula surgery is selected by tract anatomy and sphincter involvement: superficial tracts may be laid open over a probe, while more complex transsphincteric disease may require staged or sphincter-preserving repair.
The dominant surgical-functional concern is continence: identify the tract accurately and avoid sphincter division when involvement makes functional preservation unlikely.

The available case-specific source does not establish a usual anesthetic technique, airway plan, position, analgesic regimen, or fluid strategy; do not infer general anesthesia or airway instrumentation from the procedure name.

Recovery should follow applicable postanesthesia standards, including appropriate observation and oxygenation assessment; quantitative neuromuscular recovery criteria apply only if neuromuscular blocking drugs were used.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Surgery addresses mechanical intestinal obstruction; the obstruction may be strangulated or not. The supplied evidence does not establish a preferred open or laparoscopic approach for adult obstruction.
Priorities are to assess and correct fluid, electrolyte, acid–base, and hemodynamic disturbances while evaluating for sepsis and threatened bowel perfusion.
Obstruction raises aspiration concern; rapid-sequence induction is commonly used, but the review does not establish it as mandatory or provide a universal airway regimen.
Recovery planning should account for the patient's physiology and operative course; postoperative ventilation and continued cardiorespiratory support are individualized.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The reference concerns operative management of intestinal obstruction. Causes described include adhesions, malignant tumors, obstructed hernia, and less common causes such as volvulus and masses.
Assess whether the obstruction is associated with mesenteric blood-flow compromise; the source treats strangulated and non-strangulated obstruction as distinct categories.
The obstruction review does not specify open versus laparoscopic selection. The colorectal review covers both approaches but does not establish an approach for an individual obstruction case.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess volume status, electrolytes, hemodynamics, and intra-abdominal hypertension; obstruction-related fluid losses may range from dehydration to septic shock.

Review available clinical and imaging information and assess end-organ dysfunction, including possible sepsis and hypovolemia. The colorectal review notes that urgent obstruction surgery may allow limited time for optimization.

Consider obstruction-associated acid–base and electrolyte abnormalities; the review describes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis in upper small-bowel obstruction and acidosis with sepsis or inflamed bowel.

Nasogastric decompression may be used to decompress the stomach, but routine tube placement in elective colorectal surgery is not recommended; that elective guidance should not be conflated with obstruction-specific decompression.

bullets: Obstruction is associated with aspiration concern. The review reports that many clinicians use RSI, while warning that an adverse event during RSI may itself cause aspiration and lung injury; it does not support a mandatory universal technique.
Gastric aspiration through a decompression tube can reduce gastric contents, but the source does not establish that it removes aspiration risk or replaces individualized airway assessment.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Abdominal opening may precipitate marked hypotension when intra-abdominal hypertension has impaired mesenteric vascular flow; anticipate this possibility and coordinate closely with the surgical team.

Reassess hemodynamics and perfusion as bowel obstruction is relieved and during bowel manipulation; the supplied review identifies these as concerns but does not prescribe a case-specific monitoring algorithm.
Maintain normothermia and monitor temperature, surgical field, and blood loss; use warming measures when indicated.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Aspiration is a central anesthetic hazard in obstruction. Keep the possibility in view during induction and recovery; the source does not establish a single technique that eliminates this risk.
Dehydration, sepsis, acidosis, and hemodynamic deterioration may coexist. Reassess physiology and escalate support when instability or organ dysfunction is recognized.
If intra-abdominal hypertension is present, abdominal opening can be a hemodynamically critical phase; anticipate deterioration and communicate promptly with the surgical team.

bullets: Correct fluid and electrolyte disturbances with individualized replacement. The obstruction review describes Ringer lactate as a commonly suitable fluid, while emphasizing that its volume guidance is rough and should be individualized.
Follow clinical response, including pulse, blood pressure, and urine output, while recognizing that intra-abdominal hypertension can make urine output unsatisfactory despite rehydration.
Tailor hemodynamic therapy to risk and response; colorectal evidence describes goal-directed approaches but does not establish a fixed fluid total for emergency obstruction.

bullets: For open colorectal surgery, thoracic epidural analgesia is an option, not a default for every urgent obstruction case; consider coagulation status and the patient's overall condition.
Use a multimodal, opioid-sparing approach when appropriate. The colorectal guideline supports implementing the pain plan before induction and describes scheduled acetaminophen and NSAIDs as options.
Choose NSAIDs cautiously in patients who are frail, dehydrated, or salt-depleted; the obstruction review flags potential harm in these groups.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Colectomy may be performed open or minimally invasively; use a minimally invasive approach when appropriate and expertise is available. Robotic surgery is feasible, but its advantages over standard laparoscopy are not fully established.

For laparoscopic or robotic cases, plan for pneumoperitoneum and positioning-related cardiorespiratory effects, including reduced compliance and increased airway pressures. Tailor ventilation and reassess after insufflation or position changes.

Prioritize hemodynamic stability and individualized fluid management: avoid both volume overload and undue restriction, and consider goal-directed therapy for high-risk patients or anticipated significant intravascular losses.

Build recovery around opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, PONV prevention, early oral intake and mobilization. If neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Colectomy encompasses colon resection by open or minimally invasive approaches; minimally invasive surgery is preferred when appropriate and expertise is available. Conversion to open surgery may occur.
Robotic surgery is feasible, but comparative benefit over standard laparoscopy remains uncertain; reported tradeoffs include longer operating times and higher cost.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiopulmonary disease, functional reserve, anemia, electrolyte or nutritional abnormalities, and the urgency of surgery. Emergency presentations may allow less time for optimization and require assessment for sepsis or hypovolemia.

For elective surgery, counsel patients before surgery about expected clinical milestones and discharge criteria. Consider multimodal prehabilitation for significant deconditioning or multiple comorbidities.

For elective colorectal resection, the 2023 ASCRS/SAGES guideline supports mechanical bowel preparation combined with oral antibiotics. This differs from the older review's position against routine mechanical preparation; follow applicable current institutional and surgical protocols.

bullets: For laparoscopic or robotic surgery, general anesthesia is described as standard to maintain ventilatory support; an endotracheal tube is preferred in the generic laparoscopic/robotic reference. These sources do not establish a colectomy-specific airway mandate.

After insufflation or position changes, reassess ventilation and airway pressures. The generic review describes increased airway pressures and possible endobronchial tube migration with insufflation or positional change.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pneumoperitoneum can produce hypercarbia, altered venous return and cardiac filling pressures, and reduced pulmonary compliance. Track the patient's response to insufflation rather than assuming uniform effects.
Trendelenburg may worsen respiratory mechanics and increase intraocular pressure; assess position-related effects and avoid unnecessary duration or degree of positioning.

Avoid intraoperative hypotension. The guideline notes association of MAP below 65 mm Hg, even briefly, with myocardial injury and acute kidney injury; this is a risk signal, not a universal individualized target.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: With sudden bradyarrhythmia at insufflation onset, recognize a possible vagal response; pneumoperitoneum-related hypercarbia can also contribute to tachyarrhythmias and acidosis. Escalate assessment of the patient and procedural conditions.

Unexpected hypoxemia, rising airway pressure, or asymmetric chest findings during laparoscopy warrant evaluation for tube displacement, obstruction, atelectasis, or capnothorax. The generic reference describes stopping insufflation as a possible response to capnothorax or severe hypercarbia, with escalation based on clinical severity.
Position-related facial, pharyngeal, or laryngopharyngeal edema and pressure or nerve injury are relevant concerns, particularly with steep Trendelenburg or prolonged robotic cases.

bullets: Individualize fluid administration to avoid both overload and hypovolemia. The guideline recommends balanced chloride-restricted crystalloids for maintenance and boluses, and does not recommend routine colloid boluses.

The generic laparoscopy reference notes that hemorrhage can occur with access-related solid-organ injury and may be less apparent with limited visualization; assess for bleeding when unexplained hemodynamic change occurs.

Thoracic epidural is an option for open surgery when a dedicated acute-pain team is available, but is not recommended routinely for laparoscopic surgery. Abdominal-wall blocks are among the opioid-sparing options described.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Excisional hemorrhoidectomy may be open (Milligan–Morgan) or closed (Ferguson); the choice and extent of excision are surgical decisions guided by symptoms and disease extent.

General, regional, or local anesthesia—with or without IV sedation—are described options. A systematic review favored local anesthesia with sedation for pain and urinary-retention outcomes versus spinal anesthesia, but patient-selection criteria are not established here.

Substantial postoperative pain is a central recovery concern; bleeding and urinary retention are recognized early complications. Avoid excessive excision, particularly with circumferential disease, because of anal stenosis risk.
Priorities after anesthesia include reassessing pain, voiding/retention risk, bleeding, and recovery from the anesthetic; use postanesthesia monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition.
