sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Excisional techniques include open Milligan–Morgan and closed Ferguson procedures. The closed technique reapproximates mucosa; the open wound is left open with hemostasis achieved using electrocautery.

Extent should follow symptoms and disease distribution; one or two excision areas may suffice. Avoid excessive removal, especially with circumferential disease, and preserve adequate mucosa and anoderm to reduce stenosis risk.

Operative priorities include identifying and protecting the internal sphincter, avoiding excessive tissue removal near the dentate line, and checking the suture line for hemostasis. These are surgical considerations, not anesthetic targets.

bullets: The anesthesiologist is responsible for determining medical status and developing the anesthesia-care plan. The supplied standards do not provide hemorrhoidectomy-specific selection criteria or a detailed preoperative assessment protocol.

Discuss anesthetic options in the context of the individual and procedure. The available review identifies general, spinal, caudal, nerve-block, local, and combined techniques, but does not define which patients should receive each.

bullets: Low anterior resection is a rectal resection; a minimally invasive approach is appropriate when expertise is available. The available evidence includes laparoscopic LAR studies but does not establish one approach for every patient.

bullets: Anastomotic leakage is a reported postoperative complication in elective laparoscopic colorectal surgery. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Orthognathic surgery repositions the maxilla, mandible, or both to correct dentofacial deformity and malocclusion. A bimaxillary procedure combines maxillary and mandibular osteotomies, with the repositioned bones fixed in place.

The nasal route is described to leave the face accessible for surgical alignment. Airway planning should account for potentially difficult laryngoscopy with retrognathia or limited mouth opening; the available review also cautions that nasal tubes can impede suctioning and ventilation during long procedures.

The dominant intraoperative concern is bleeding from a highly vascular operative region. Reviews describe controlled hypotension and hemostatic agents as strategies, but do not establish a universal target or regimen; fluid and blood management must be individualized.

Recovery priorities include airway observation, nausea and vomiting prevention—particularly when maxillomandibular fixation is present—and appropriate postanesthesia monitoring. If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative confirmation of recovery is recommended before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation repositions maxillary and/or mandibular bones to improve occlusion and facial harmony. Maxillary surgery commonly uses a Le Fort I osteotomy; mandibular advancement or setback addresses different jaw relationships.
Bimaxillary surgery involves maxillary and mandibular osteotomies performed independently or together; the bones are repositioned and fixed with titanium plates.

sources.label: Comprehensive anaesthesia management strategies for orthognathic surgical procedure

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess airway features relevant to laryngoscopy, particularly retrognathia, maxillary protrusion, and limited mouth opening. The review describes airway management as straightforward in most patients but recognizes these features as potential sources of difficulty.
Consider patient-specific PONV risk and the added concern of nausea or vomiting when MMF is used. The available sources do not establish a procedure-specific preoperative testing protocol.

The review identifies patient and setting factors relevant to DVT risk, including obesity, hormone therapy, and prolonged head-up positioning. It reports limited incidence data; individual assessment should not be replaced by a presumed universal risk level.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan access so the surgeon can view the face and align the jaws. The orthognathic review describes securing the nasotracheal tube to the forehead; it does not specify a universal table orientation or room layout.
Protect the eyes and pressure-prone areas during a prolonged operation. The review advises eye lubrication and covering, and protection of skin over bony prominences.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards. These include continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: A nasal tube is described as the approach for maxillofacial surgery when facial access is needed. Prepare the nasal cavity with a vasoconstrictor, as described in the review; the sources do not establish that one intubation technique is appropriate for every airway.

Videolaryngoscopy facilitates vocal-cord visualization. The review reports faster intubation with McGrath videolaryngoscopy than with Macintosh or GlideScope laryngoscopy in patients with an anticipated difficult airway, and increased success with videolaryngoscopy in patients with a simulated difficult airway.

Reconcile the need for facial access with the review’s warning that nasal-tube caliber, shape, and length can make suctioning and ventilation difficult during long procedures. The supplied evidence does not resolve that conflict into a single technique recommendation.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect bleeding to be a major concern because the maxillomandibular region is highly vascular and the operation involves bone and muscular dissection. The available abstract identifies blood loss and pain control as perioperative concerns.

If a throat pack is used, communicate its presence and confirm removal. The review describes reminder and checklist safeguards and recommends suctioning the oropharynx after removal to clear blood, clots, and debris.

Adequate analgesia is important to blood-pressure management. The review describes fentanyl and remifentanil for pain control and dexmedetomidine infusion as an added strategy to enhance analgesia and lower blood pressure; it does not provide a complete monitoring protocol.

sources.label: Comprehensive anaesthesia management strategies for orthognathic surgical procedure
Orthognathic Surgery: Anesthetic Considerations and Perioperative Management

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Bleeding and a deteriorating operative view are material concerns. The review describes hemostasis as improving the surgical field and potentially reducing operating time; it does not provide a case-specific blood-loss or transfusion threshold.
Protect against eye injury and pressure injury: the review identifies corneal injury from exposure or pressure and notes increased pressure-injury susceptibility with long procedures.
Nausea or vomiting in the presence of MMF raises aspiration risk. The available review abstract flags this hazard but does not provide a detailed rescue protocol.

sources.label: Comprehensive anaesthesia management strategies for orthognathic surgical procedure
Orthognathic Surgery: Anesthetic Considerations and Perioperative Management

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Controlled hypotension is described as a bleeding-reduction strategy, alongside hemostatic agents. The review describes reduction from baseline MAP but does not establish a universal target; decisions require patient-specific judgment.

The review cautions that positive fluid balance may contribute to complications and edema, while also reporting that fluid evidence is not necessarily specific to orthognathic surgery. It provides no general fluid regimen.

Tranexamic acid is discussed as a hemostatic agent, but the review reports no consensus on ideal timing or dose for orthognathic surgery. Do not treat cited study regimens or departmental practice as a universal recommendation.

sources.label: Comprehensive anaesthesia management strategies for orthognathic surgical procedure

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use a multimodal analgesia concept, including surgeon-administered local anesthetic infiltration and non-opioid options where appropriate. The review notes that opioids are rarely needed for postoperative pain in its described practice, not that they are never required.

Consider PONV prevention because orthognathic surgery may increase risk and nausea or vomiting is especially consequential with MMF. TIVA is reported to reduce PONV versus volatile anesthesia in a meta-analysis across different procedures.

The review describes ondansetron plus dexamethasone as a commonly used multimodal prophylaxis combination. It lists multiple alternatives, but this reference does not prescribe a drug combination or dosing regimen.

Nerve blocks are described in the newer abstract as beneficial for hemodynamic stability and reducing postoperative opioid need, but it does not provide comparative estimates or a specific block regimen.

Orthognathic Surgery: Anesthetic Considerations and Perioperative Management

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After throat-pack removal, suction the oropharynx to clear blood, clots, and debris. The orthognathic review also recommends positive pressure after extubation but does not give a full extubation-readiness protocol.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring rather than clinical assessment alone and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; the guideline specifies the adductor pollicis site.

Transfer to a PACU or equivalent recovery area, with ongoing observation and monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition. ASA standards require transport accompaniment and handoff to the receiving nurse.

bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is a review described by its authors as systematic. Its supplied account does not report included-study counts, search dates, or formal quality assessment; some recommendations reflect departmental practice or evidence from other procedures.

A newer review is available here only as an abstract, without study-level details, quantitative outcome estimates, or specific anesthetic protocols. It supports awareness of concerns, not a complete case-specific pathway.
Case-specific airway technique for a long bimaxillary operation and a detailed MMF-related emergency response are not resolved by the supplied sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adrenalectomy removes one or both adrenal glands; laparoscopic adrenalectomy is described as the standard approach for Conn’s and Cushing’s adrenal disease and for pheochromocytoma in current practice. Evidence here does not establish an adrenal-specific advantage for robotic assistance.

The anesthetic priorities vary with tumor function: pheochromocytoma carries marked hemodynamic risk around intubation, tumor dissection, and adrenal-vein ligation; Conn’s warrants attention to potassium and acid–base status; Cushing’s requires attention to airway, glucose, electrolytes, and glucocorticoid sufficiency.

Plan monitoring and resources for the actual endocrine phenotype and anticipated hemodynamic instability. Pheochromocytoma sources support invasive arterial pressure monitoring; do not treat an arterial line or other invasive access as universal for every adrenalectomy.

Recovery priorities include assessing for post-resection hypotension, monitoring glucose and electrolytes, and continuing indicated cortisol replacement. Routine extubation and disposition should reflect the patient’s perioperative course rather than a fixed pathway.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Adrenalectomy may be unilateral or bilateral and may be performed for catecholamine-, cortisol-, or aldosterone-secreting tumors, as well as adrenal carcinoma. The supplied evidence focuses mainly on functional tumors.

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is described as the gold standard for Conn’s and Cushing’s adrenal disease and as established standard care for pheochromocytoma. The pheochromocytoma review describes transabdominal and retroperitoneal minimally invasive approaches but does not establish a preferred access route.

sources.label: Anesthetic Considerations on Adrenal Gland Surgery
Management of Patients with Treatment of Pheochromocytoma: A Critical Appraisal

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish tumor function and review biochemical evaluation before planning anesthesia. Assess cardiovascular effects, blood pressure, volume status, electrolytes, glucose, and relevant end-organ disease according to phenotype.

For pheochromocytoma, preoperative adrenergic preparation is commonly recommended in cited guidelines, but the evidence does not establish a universally superior drug, target, or outcome benefit. Coordinate preparation with the endocrine, surgical, and anesthesia teams; avoid treating a particular blockade regimen as established by these reviews.

For Conn’s syndrome, identify and address hypokalemia and assess volume status; the review notes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis may prolong neuromuscular-blocker action. No potassium threshold for proceeding is established by the supplied evidence.

For Cushing’s syndrome, consider obesity, proximal weakness, difficult ventilation or intubation, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, skin fragility, and thromboembolic risk. Assess airway and respiratory risk and plan careful positioning and glycemic/electrolyte surveillance.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Anticipate pneumoperitoneum and position-dependent changes in venous return and respiratory mechanics. The available sources do not define a single adrenalectomy position; lateral decubitus is among positions used in laparoscopic and robotic surgery, with positioning determined by operative approach.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring, including ECG, oxygenation, ventilation/capnography, and regular blood-pressure assessment. Add invasive monitoring when indicated by the tumor phenotype and anticipated instability; pheochromocytoma reviews support arterial pressure monitoring.

For robotic cases, secure the patient and protect pressure points and the face; coordinate positioning and table movement before docking. These are general robotic precautions, not adrenal-specific requirements.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Management of Patients with Treatment of Pheochromocytoma: A Critical Appraisal
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For Cushing’s syndrome, plan general endotracheal anesthesia, with or without epidural. Central obesity and proximal muscle weakness can make mask ventilation and intubation difficult; assess and prepare accordingly.

For pheochromocytoma, use smooth induction and endotracheal intubation to limit sympathetic stimulation; intubation and tumor handling are critical periods for hypertensive episodes. The reviews do not establish a single precise anesthetic protocol.

Pneumoperitoneum can reduce compliance and functional residual capacity and increase shunt and dead space. Follow ventilation, oxygenation, airway pressures, and carbon dioxide; adjust ventilation to the observed physiologic response.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: In pheochromocytoma, closely anticipate hemodynamic responses at intubation, tumor dissection, and adrenal-vein ligation. Tumor handling may provoke hypertension or arrhythmia; communicate with the surgeon and respond to the observed event.

After tumor removal, falling catecholamine levels and pre-existing volume depletion or blockade may contribute to hypotension. Anticipate the transition and maintain communication during adrenal-vein ligation and resection.

For Conn’s syndrome, follow potassium and acid–base status and avoid hyperventilation that worsens respiratory alkalosis and hypokalemia. For Cushing’s syndrome, monitor glucose and electrolytes closely.

Pneumoperitoneum can raise systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure, impair venous return, and reduce renal perfusion and urine output. Interpret hemodynamics in light of insufflation and position rather than relying on a single volume surrogate.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize severe pressure changes or arrhythmias during pheochromocytoma manipulation and hypotension after resection as key hazards. Escalate promptly with the surgical team and manage according to the clinical event; these reviews do not provide a universal response algorithm.

Monitor for hypokalemia-related conduction or neuromuscular effects in Conn’s syndrome, and for glucocorticoid deficiency in patients undergoing adrenalectomy for Cushing’s disease or bilateral adrenalectomy.
During laparoscopy, consider positional or insufflation-related pulmonary and hemodynamic changes, endobronchial tube migration, and access-related hemorrhage or organ injury if deterioration occurs.

Anesthetic Considerations on Adrenal Gland Surgery
Cushing’s surgery: Role of the anesthesiologist
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Avoid assuming a fixed fluid volume or filling-pressure target. Assess perfusion in context: pheochromocytoma preparation may include correction of preoperative hypovolemia, while pneumoperitoneum and position can distort usual hemodynamic surrogates.
After pheochromocytoma tumor removal, anticipate severe hypotension; maintain adequate blood volume and reassess hemodynamics. The reviews do not establish a quantified fluid regimen.

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy sources do not establish procedure-specific blood-loss estimates or transfusion thresholds. Ensure resources are appropriate to the individual case and operative assessment rather than applying a universal crossmatch or transfusion rule.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use an individualized multimodal approach for laparoscopic port-site and visceral pain; general laparoscopic guidance describes acetaminophen, NSAIDs when appropriate, and port-site local anesthetic as options. The adrenal-specific reviews do not define a required regimen.
Consider postoperative nausea and vomiting prophylaxis based on patient and procedural risk; laparoscopy is identified as an independent PONV risk factor in the general review.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Extubation and destination should reflect airway, respiratory, hemodynamic, and metabolic status. Pheochromocytoma sources leave the extubation location to clinical judgment and do not establish fixed extubation criteria.

When neuromuscular blockade has been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; the recommendation applies to cases in which blockade is used.

In recovery, monitor blood pressure, glucose, and relevant electrolytes; continue cortisol replacement when indicated and assess for adrenal insufficiency, especially after bilateral adrenalectomy or adrenalectomy for Cushing’s syndrome.
Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, using monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The adrenal-specific sources are narrative reviews, not procedure-specific comparative trials or graded practice guidelines. Their recommendations should be interpreted within their stated scope and evidence limitations.

Pheochromocytoma preparation is an area of unresolved evidence: reviewed studies are heterogeneous, and no consensus blood-pressure target is reported. Avoid presenting a particular blocker, target, or regimen as universally established.
General laparoscopic/robotic and anesthesia-monitoring sources inform shared perioperative principles but do not resolve adrenal-specific positioning, access, fluid, or recovery protocols.
Case-specific targets for potassium correction, fluid administration, and transfusion are not established in the available sources.
The supplied sources do not compare robotic with conventional laparoscopic adrenalectomy or establish a robot-specific anesthetic protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Surgical resection is the definitive treatment. Minimally invasive adrenalectomy is standard for most adrenal pheochromocytomas; open surgery is more likely for large or invasive masses and many paragangliomas.
General anesthesia is required. The central anesthetic priority is limiting responses to stimulation and tumor handling while maintaining hemodynamic stability.

Expect potentially severe hypertension and arrhythmias during stimulation or tumor dissection, followed by hypotension after tumor devascularization and removal. Close communication across these transitions is important.
Plan monitored recovery with attention to blood pressure, glucose, and electrolytes. The need for ICU care depends on postoperative stability; sources differ on routine ICU disposition.

sources.label: Management of Patients with Treatment of Pheochromocytoma: A Critical Appraisal
Actualities in the anaesthetic management of pheochromocytoma/ paraganglioma

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Resection is the only curative treatment described. Minimally invasive adrenalectomy is established for most adrenal tumors; choice of transabdominal or retroperitoneal access depends on the case and surgical expertise.
Open surgery is more likely for large or invasive adrenal masses and most paragangliomas. Complex resections are best situated in experienced centers.
Bilateral cortical-sparing surgery may be considered in selected familial or bilateral disease to preserve adrenal tissue; this is a surgical planning issue, not a universal approach.

sources.label: Management of Patients with Treatment of Pheochromocytoma: A Critical Appraisal
Actualities in the anaesthetic management of pheochromocytoma/ paraganglioma
Pheochromocytoma resection: Current concepts in anesthetic management

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiovascular effects and end-organ status, including ECG, cardiac function, renal function, glucose, and electrolytes. Echocardiography is emphasized in the reviews because cardiomyopathy and diastolic dysfunction may alter perioperative risk.

Preoperative alpha blockade is guideline-supported practice in cited reviews, with beta blockade, when needed for tachyarrhythmia, only after adequate alpha blockade. However, evidence that preparation improves current postoperative outcomes or prevents intraoperative instability is contested; individualize preparation with the treating team.

Review drugs and conditions that may affect catecholamine release or metabolism. Chronic volume depletion, catecholamine-related hyperglycemia, tumor size, and catecholamine burden may affect planning; no universal pressure target is established across the sources.

sources.label: Actualities in the anaesthetic management of pheochromocytoma/ paraganglioma
Management of Patients with Treatment of Pheochromocytoma: A Critical Appraisal

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use continuous ECG and standard anesthetic monitoring, with an arterial line for real-time blood-pressure monitoring. Pheochromocytoma reviews recommend arterial placement before induction; another review describes differing clinician practice, so the timing should account for the patient and placement-related stress.

Central access is commonly used for vasoactive drugs and may assist fluid management, but the sources do not establish it as mandatory for every patient. Consider advanced cardiac-output monitoring or TEE selectively when myocardial dysfunction or instability makes it useful.
No specific patient position is established in the available procedure-specific sources; coordinate positioning with surgical access and patient factors.

Actualities in the anaesthetic management of pheochromocytoma/ paraganglioma
Implications and considerations during pheochromocytoma resection: A challenge to the anesthesiologist
Pheochromocytoma resection: Current concepts in anesthetic management

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is required. Ensure adequate analgesia when awake and sufficient anesthetic depth for intubation and other stimulating maneuvers; airway technique and a specific induction sequence are not established in the procedure-specific review.

Avoid or use caution with agents reported to increase catecholamine release or provoke histamine-related stimulation; the reviews identify ketamine, desflurane, and large morphine boluses among concerns. These are review-level cautions, not a substitute for individualized drug selection.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation; the adductor pollicis is the recommended monitoring site. These recommendations do not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Pheochromocytoma resection: Current concepts in anesthetic management

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Laryngoscopy, incision, pneumoperitoneum, and tumor manipulation can provoke catecholamine-mediated hypertension, bradycardia, tachyarrhythmias, or myocardial dysfunction. Maintain sufficient anesthetic depth and communicate anticipated stimulation with the surgeon.

Have short-acting vasodilator options available for significant hypertensive episodes and agents for rate control when indicated. Sources name nitroprusside, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, phentolamine, and beta blockers; they do not establish one universal regimen or threshold.

Adrenal-vein ligation and tumor removal mark a transition to hypotension risk from volume depletion, residual blockade, anesthetic vasodilation, and catecholamine withdrawal. Stop blood-pressure-lowering infusions promptly and coordinate the transition with the surgeon.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: During tumor handling, anticipate severe hypertension, bradycardia or tachyarrhythmias, and possible reduced cardiac output or ventricular dysfunction. Maintain close communication with the surgeon.

Post-resection hypotension may be profound or resistant to catecholamines. Assess for inadequate volume, bleeding, and persistent vasodilation; sources describe fluid resuscitation and direct-acting vasopressors, with vasopressin considered for refractory shock.
Monitor for postoperative hypertension, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte disturbance. After bilateral adrenalectomy, consider adrenal insufficiency and steroid replacement in a hypotensive patient.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Chronic intravascular-volume depletion is a recognized concern; preoperative salt and fluid intake and intraoperative volume replacement are described. Tailor administration to hemodynamics and cardiac function rather than applying a fixed total.

At adrenal-vein ligation or tumor removal, anticipate hypotension from contracted plasma volume, surgical bleeding, and anesthetic-induced vasodilation. Coordinate fluid resuscitation with the surgeon and promptly discontinue vasodilators; for persistent hypotension, TEE may assess ventricular filling.
The sources provide no procedure-specific blood-loss, transfusion, or universal fluid-volume protocol; prepare according to tumor and operative circumstances.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Analgesic requirements vary with the surgical approach and patient factors. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is associated with lower analgesic requirements than open surgery, but the review does not specify a postoperative analgesia regimen.

Choose analgesics with hemodynamic context in mind. Reviews caution that morphine-related histamine release may provoke catecholamine release; this is a reason for caution, not evidence for a single required alternative.

No case-specific PONV prevention regimen is established in the available sources. Avoid treating metoclopramide as a routine default in this setting because a review identifies it as a potential trigger.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Extubation at the end of an uncomplicated operation is common; persistent hemodynamic instability may require postoperative ventilation. Base extubation and destination on current stability and recovery.

Continue close monitoring of circulation, consciousness, oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, glucose, and electrolytes in PACU or an equivalent setting; higher-acuity care is appropriate when instability requires it.

PACU or equivalent care includes continued observation, appropriate monitoring, and transfer communication. Do not assume ICU admission is required for every stable patient: the procedure reviews differ on routine disposition.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The pheochromocytoma anesthesia sources are narrative reviews or current-opinion articles, not a standardized protocol. They describe limited randomized evidence and disagreement over some preparation and intraoperative management choices.

A systematic review reports inconsistent definitions of intraoperative instability and no consensus on preparation targets; its appraisal also questions whether pressure normalization improves postoperative outcomes. Recommendations therefore require clinical judgment rather than uncritical adoption of a single source.

Procedure-specific sources do not establish a standard position, airway protocol, bleeding plan, or postoperative analgesic regimen. Fixed drug doses, infusion rates, fluid totals, and universal ICU disposition are not established by this draft.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Bronchoscopy is the diagnostic and retrieval procedure. In adults who are stable, flexible bronchoscopy is commonly the initial approach; rigid bronchoscopy is favored when there is acute respiratory distress, a large or sharp or proximal object, difficult retrieval, or failure of flexible extraction.

The dominant immediate hazards are loss of airway patency and inadequate ventilation or oxygenation during retrieval. Plan airway-restoration and emergency surgical-airway contingencies with the bronchoscopist before beginning.

Anesthetic and ventilation approaches vary with patient status, object characteristics, and extraction route; the available adult sources do not establish spontaneous ventilation, paralysis, or a particular anesthetic drug regimen as universal.

After retrieval, confirm airway patency and inspect for additional objects, retained fragments, injury, stenosis, granulation, or bleeding. Use PACU monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition; the sources provide no foreign-body-specific emergence or recovery protocol.

Bronchoscopic management of airway foreign bodies in adults: a narrative educational review
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and management of airway foreign-body aspiration. In adults with stable status, flexible bronchoscopy is commonly the initial approach; rigid bronchoscopy remains an important alternative and backup.

Favor rigid bronchoscopy for acute respiratory distress or asphyxia, expected difficult flexible retrieval, failed flexible retrieval, or large, sharp, or proximal objects. Selection depends on clinical status, object features, location, and available expertise.
Plan the extraction route, retrieval tools, and contingency approach with the procedural team. Larger objects may require en-bloc removal with temporary loss of airway control.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach
Bronchoscopic management of airway foreign bodies in adults: a narrative educational review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess respiratory status and the degree of obstruction, and establish the suspected object's location, size, shape, and material. These factors inform procedure selection, extraction tools, and backup planning.

Symptoms and history may not reliably establish aspiration. When suspicion remains high despite negative CT, bronchoscopy may still be indicated; imaging and procedural planning should be interpreted in clinical context.
Agree in advance on how ventilation and airway patency will be maintained, who will restore airway control if a device must be removed, and what emergency surgical-airway option is available.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach
Bronchoscopic management of airway foreign bodies in adults: a narrative educational review

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate the bronchoscopist, assistants, nursing, and anesthesia teams; ensure the selected bronchoscopy and retrieval equipment and the agreed airway rescue resources are available. The sources do not establish a routine patient position for adult foreign-body extraction.

Apply monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA basic standards call for continuous assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; for general anesthesia, expired carbon dioxide is continually monitored unless the procedure or equipment invalidates it.

When general anesthesia is used, ASA standards also specify ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach
Bronchoscopic management of airway foreign bodies in adults: a narrative educational review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Possible adult approaches include conscious sedation with spontaneous ventilation, general anesthesia with a laryngeal mask airway, endotracheal intubation with positive-pressure ventilation, and rigid bronchoscopy with jet ventilation. Match the approach to patient needs and extraction requirements rather than treating one mode as universal.

Anticipate temporary loss of airway control during some large-object extractions. Positive-pressure or jet ventilation may need to be held during critical extraction phases, and either can occasionally move an object distally.

Maintain communication during extraction. An object lodged at the subglottis or retropharynx can produce complete obstruction; have a plan for direct-vision removal if it reaches the oropharynx and for emergency surgical airway management if it cannot be promptly extracted.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Prioritize maintaining airway patency, ventilation, and oxygenation through the extraction. For en-bloc removal or other phases requiring ventilation interruption, coordinate timing and airway restoration with the bronchoscopist.
Use continuous visualization and controlled object-specific maneuvers. Avoid pushing the object distally; keep it in view during withdrawal, especially through the glottis and retropharynx.
For sharp objects, retrieval technique should reduce airway contact and protect the vocal cords; rigid bronchoscopy can provide a protective barrel in selected cases.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach
Bronchoscopic management of airway foreign bodies in adults: a narrative educational review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Important hazards include airway obstruction or asphyxiation, object migration or loss, airway injury, bleeding, pneumothorax, and injury to vocal cords or oropharynx. A sudden failure to ventilate or oxygenate requires immediate team attention to airway patency and the planned rescue route.

If attempted withdrawal of a large object obstructs the trachea, the adult review describes advancing it into one mainstem bronchus to restore ventilation before further extraction attempts; this is a source-described contingency, not a routine maneuver.
After retrieval, reassess for retained fragments, stenosis, granulation, or bleeding. Follow-up imaging and/or bronchoscopy is recommended by the adult review to ensure resolution.

sources.label: Foreign body aspiration in adult airways: therapeutic approach

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The adult review reports bleeding in a minority of foreign-body extraction bronchoscopies and describes local endobronchial control options. Rigid bronchoscopy may assist with tamponade and large-bore suction in accessible large airways.

No procedure-specific fluid regimen, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold is established in the available adult sources; manage perfusion and any significant bleeding according to the individual clinical situation.

bullets: Awake flexible bronchoscopic tracheal intubation is an option when anticipated difficulty makes securing the airway before induction advantageous; it preserves spontaneous ventilation and airway tone while the airway is secured.
Prioritize adequate local airway anesthesia and multidisciplinary planning with a backup strategy tailored to the procedure and available resources.
Important hazards include obstruction or loss of airway control, hypoxemia, topicalization-related impairment of protective reflexes, and blood or secretions obscuring the bronchoscopic view.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Awake flexible bronchoscopic intubation is an airway-securing approach for selected anticipated difficult airways. The rationale is to avoid inducing anesthesia before tracheal access is established when loss of airway tone or spontaneous ventilation would be hazardous.

The usual bronchoscopic sequence is to topicalize the airway, advance the scope under vision into the trachea, railroad the tracheal tube, and confirm tracheal placement. The supplied sources do not establish one route or device as universal.
Awake supraglottic-airway-guided bronchoscopy is a distinct, case-series technique rather than a default substitute for conventional awake flexible bronchoscopic intubation.

Stridor, inability to lie flat, altered breathing position, or other signs of severe obstruction warrant particular caution. Scope contact or local anesthetic near the cords may precipitate total obstruction in severe obstruction, according to the ENT chapter.
Plan the airway approach with the relevant teams and identify a backup strategy based on procedural demands, pathology, patient status, and available resources.

bullets: Topical airway anesthesia is central to awake flexible intubation. Select topicalization methods according to route, anatomy, and the airway structures requiring coverage; the review cautions that one method may not provide adequate density in every patient.

A flexible scope can be advanced orally or nasally, with the tube railroaded over it under vision. For nasal passage, consider mucosal bleeding and visualization; for any route, avoid forcing tube passage when resistance is encountered.

Oxygenation should be maintained and ventilation assessed throughout the awake phase. The case-series oxygen insufflation practice is not a universal protocol; oxygen delivery and monitoring should suit the patient, equipment, and procedure.

If the view or tube passage is inadequate, pause and reassess oxygenation, airway patency, topicalization, route, and the agreed alternative plan. Do not treat repeated attempts as a substitute for changing strategy.

Recognize evolving obstruction or hypoxemia early and escalate to the pre-agreed oxygenation and airway rescue options, including emergency surgical access when indicated. The supplied sources do not support a single universal rescue algorithm.

Topicalization may blunt protective reflexes and create aspiration concern, particularly in patients already at risk. Evaluate this risk against the hazards of alternative airway strategies rather than treating topical anesthesia as categorically safe or contraindicated.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: FESS is an endoscopic operation used for chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, and other paranasal sinus disease. A clear operative view and avoidance of injury to adjacent orbital, vascular, and cerebrospinal-fluid structures are central concerns.
This is shared-airway surgery in a narrow field where bleeding can impair visualization. Bleeding and altered anatomy can also increase the risk of injury to nearby structures.

Propofol-based TIVA is supported by the review as a means of improving the operative field and reducing blood loss, but TIVA versus inhalational anesthesia should be selected for the individual case rather than treated as a universal rule.

Plan recovery around possible blood and secretions in the airway, aspiration risk, and postoperative nausea or vomiting. Nasal surgery sources describe awake extubation and end-of-procedure airway inspection and suction; the precise airway strategy remains case-dependent.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: FESS uses an endoscopic approach to treat chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, and other paranasal sinus pathology. The restricted operative field makes visualization and hemostasis important.

The surgical objective is to maintain visualization and minimize bleeding while avoiding injury to orbital, vascular, and cerebrospinal-fluid structures. Some procedures may extend toward the central skull base.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Mastoidectomy is generally performed under general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; the bed is typically turned 180 degrees after induction. The operation uses drilling to open mastoid air cells, with the aim of creating a “safe and dry ear.”

The surgical priority is safe dissection around the facial nerve and adjacent temporal-bone landmarks. Relevant complications include facial nerve injury, hearing loss, vertigo, CSF leak, and bleeding.

Discuss facial nerve monitoring with the surgeon before induction. Monitoring is often used, but is not described as mandatory; the source advises avoiding long-acting paralytic use when monitoring is planned.

Recovery priorities include assessing facial function and recognizing pain, vertigo, and associated nausea or vomiting. Use PACU monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition; the procedure source provides no specific emergence regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Mastoidectomy opens postauricular mastoid air cells by removing thin bony partitions. Indications in the source include acute or chronic mastoiditis and cholesteatoma; mastoidectomy may also provide an approach for other ear or skull-base procedures.

Canal-wall-up surgery preserves the posterior bony ear canal; canal-wall-down surgery removes it to create a common cavity. Approach selection depends on anatomy, disease extent, hearing or balance risk, and likely follow-up.

The described operating-room equipment includes an operating microscope, high-speed drill with cutting and diamond burrs, and otologic instruments. The source does not establish a single approach for all disease patterns.

During transport, the patient should be accompanied by an anesthesia team member, continually evaluated and treated, with support appropriate to the patient’s condition. Provide a verbal handoff and document arrival status.

PACU assessment should include oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; procedure-related observation should also consider facial weakness, vertigo, nausea or vomiting, and wound or dressing concerns.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Panfacial fracture repair commonly requires open reduction and internal fixation. The airway route and tube position should be planned with the surgeon around the operative field, injuries, and any planned maxillomandibular fixation (MMF); no single route fits every case.

The dominant perioperative hazards are a potentially difficult or contaminated airway, evolving edema, aspiration of blood or secretions, associated cervical-spine or head injury, and hemorrhage. Reassessment and a credible rescue-airway plan are central priorities.

Secure an airway strategy that preserves surgical access without sacrificing airway protection. Awake intubation, intubation after induction, alternative tube routes, and a surgical airway are options selected for the individual injury pattern and airway assessment—not automatic steps.

Base postoperative ventilation and extubation planning on perioperative status, associated injuries, surgery duration, airway and oral edema, and ability to maintain the airway. Confirm throat-pack removal; for postoperative MMF, keep wire cutters at bedside and train staff in their use.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation is fracture reduction and fixation; airway planning must accommodate the surgical approach and required access to the face, oral cavity, and dentition. Discuss the operative route, airway route, and whether postoperative MMF is intended with the surgeon before proceeding.

Possible airway routes include oral or nasal tracheal intubation, submental intubation, or tracheostomy; the choice depends on access needs, anatomy, contraindications, and whether postoperative ventilation or further procedures are anticipated. Submental intubation is described as an alternative when nasal intubation is contraindicated and a clear intraoral field is needed, but not for long-term ventilation.
Discuss the operative approach and anesthetic plan with the surgeon preoperatively, and select the tube route according to surgical requirements and the presence of nasal or skull-base fractures.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Complete trauma assessment and review associated injuries before selecting the anesthetic and airway approach. Specifically assess mouth opening, dentition and occlusion, neck movement and cervical-spine status, airway edema or distortion, nasal patency, and relevant imaging; reassess if the clinical picture changes.

Blood, debris, vomitus, secretions, restricted mouth opening, tissue injury, and edema can impair mask ventilation or laryngoscopy and increase aspiration risk. Swallowed blood may contribute to a full stomach; weigh any gastric evacuation approach against the patient’s condition and the risks of instrumentation or provoking vomiting.

Treat cervical-spine injury as unresolved until cleared and incorporate appropriate precautions during airway access. Review head injury and other associated trauma because they may affect airway decisions, postoperative ventilation, and destination after surgery.

Do not assume nasal intubation is appropriate merely because MMF is planned. Nasal or skull-base injury may change the route; the sources caution against blind nasal instrumentation when a sphenoid-sinus or cribriform-plate fracture is possible.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Before induction or airway instrumentation, agree on the primary airway approach, backup options, and who will perform a rescue surgical airway if required. Ensure difficult-airway and surgical-airway equipment is available; plan for suction and blood/debris contamination.

Choose the airway plan according to the injuries and airway status; discuss the surgical route, intubation route, and planned postoperative MMF with the surgical team. For postoperative MMF, keep wire cutters at the bedside and train staff in their use.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring and assess oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature throughout anesthesia. The supplied sources do not establish a case-specific position, vascular-access configuration, or indication for invasive monitoring; individualize these to injury severity and anticipated course.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose awake versus anesthetized intubation from the airway assessment, patient cooperation, injury pattern, and available expertise. Awake fibreoptic intubation is a described option, but blood, vomitus, and secretions can obscure the view and make fibreoptic techniques impractical; it is not a universal default.

When mouth opening is adequate and the airway is judged manageable, direct or video laryngoscopy with oral intubation is among the described approaches. RSI is not a universal prescription: aspiration concerns must be balanced against airway difficulty, the ability to ventilate, and the risk of losing spontaneous ventilation.

Select oral, nasal, or alternative tube routing to meet surgical access requirements while respecting nasal and skull-base injuries. If an intraoral field must be cleared and nasal intubation is unsuitable, submental intubation or a surgical airway may be considered in selected cases; submental routing is not suitable when prolonged postoperative ventilation is expected.

Maintain a rescue plan that accounts for obstruction, contamination, and failed intubation. Supraglottic devices can provide rescue oxygenation but do not protect reliably against aspiration and may be difficult to use when trauma leaves little intraoral space; establish a definitive airway when needed.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect a prolonged, shared-airway procedure in some cases; coordinate tube access and ventilation with surgical manipulation. The retrospective series reported a broad range of operative durations, which does not establish a fixed expected duration for an individual case.
Reassess the airway because tissue displacement, hematoma, or edema can cause delayed compromise. Significant hemorrhage is possible in midfacial fractures; have high-volume suction available.

Account for temperature and positioning-related protection during a long operation, but determine the actual positioning and monitoring additions from the planned repair and patient factors; the trauma series does not report a specific positioning or monitoring protocol.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Airway obstruction can arise from displaced fractures, tongue displacement, blood or debris, hematoma, edema, or laryngotracheal injury. Reassess rather than relying on an earlier airway examination; use suction and escalate airway support when patency or oxygenation is threatened.

For a contaminated airway, prepare high-volume suction and consider suction-assisted laryngoscopy techniques within local expertise. Blood or secretions can impair visualization with both direct and video techniques; instrumentation and removal of material should avoid worsening trauma or pushing debris deeper.
For patients with postoperative MMF, monitor for desaturation, significant dyspnea, or severe nausea/vomiting. Keep wire cutters or scissors at bedside and teach staff which wires to cut.

Confirm throat-pack removal and inspect/suction the airway before emergence. Retained packs and airway soiling are preventable hazards; a general ENT chapter describes fatal obstruction after failure to account for packs, supporting explicit team communication and confirmation.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Facial trauma surgery can involve significant bleeding. Review relevant investigations and ensure blood availability appropriate to the injury burden and anticipated operation; the sources do not support a universal crossmatch requirement, fluid total, or transfusion threshold.

Manage circulation and hemorrhage according to observed loss, physiology, associated injuries, and available clinical information. A single-center retrospective series reported blood loss and transfusion experience, but those observations are not targets or a reliable prediction for an individual operation.

bullets: Provide an individualized analgesia plan that accounts for the extent of fixation, associated injuries, airway status, and postoperative route of medication. The supplied trauma sources do not establish a specific analgesic regimen.
For patients with postoperative MMF, monitor for severe nausea/vomiting as part of postoperative airway observation. The sources provide no specific perioperative analgesic regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Base extubation versus continued ventilation on airway and oral edema, ability to maintain patency, associated injuries, operative course, and overall status. Patients with extensive edema or other reasons they cannot maintain the airway may require continued ventilation and a higher-acuity destination.

When extubation is selected, the trauma series describes waiting until the patient is fully awake, has intact airway reflexes, and can respond to commands. Consider anticipated edema and reintubation difficulty; the review discusses cuff-leak assessment when laryngeal edema is anticipated.

At the end of surgery, confirm throat-pack removal and inspect and suction the oro- and nasopharynx and tracheobronchial tree. For postoperative MMF, keep wire cutters at bedside and train staff in their use.

PACU or equivalent care should include reassessment and monitoring appropriate to condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Communicate the airway course, associated injuries, edema concerns, and MMF status to the receiving team.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Microlaryngoscopy for vocal-fold lesions is generally performed under general anesthesia; airway strategy must balance ventilation and oxygenation with an unobstructed surgical field.
The dominant hazards are obstruction or loss of ventilation, hypoxemia and hypercapnia—especially with tubeless or jet techniques—and airway fire when laser energy is used.
Plan jointly with the surgeon for airway access, ventilation method, rescue options and any laser-specific precautions; no single technique suits every lesion or patient.
Recovery deserves close attention to oxygenation, ventilation and airway patency: coughing, laryngospasm and desaturation are recognized concerns after laryngeal procedures.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Microlaryngoscopy uses specialized laryngoscopes and magnification to remove vocal-fold lesions; reported indications include nodules, polyps, cysts, granulomas and papillomas. Some phonosurgical procedures are performed awake, but microlaryngoscopy and lesion excision require general anesthesia.

The airway is shared. Select a secured-airway or tubeless approach according to lesion, airway anatomy, procedure demands, ventilation needs, laser use and team expertise; be prepared for the plan to change intraoperatively.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess symptoms and available endoscopic or imaging findings for lesion size, location, mobility and airway narrowing. Stridor, positional breathing difficulty, inability to lie flat or dysphagia may signal important obstruction; hoarseness alone is nonspecific.

Review prior laryngeal surgery and radiation, neck mobility, dentition and comorbidities that may complicate airway management. Radiation-related edema, fibrosis and reduced neck mobility can make airway management more difficult.

Agree with the surgeon on airway device, ventilation and rescue options before induction. Anticipated obstruction warrants appropriate difficult-airway equipment and a rigid bronchoscope available as a backup.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate microscope, suspension laryngoscope, airway equipment and laser precautions as applicable. The available sources do not establish a specific patient position for this procedure; agree on table orientation and access with the surgical team.

Apply applicable basic anesthetic monitoring: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; use quantitative oxygenation assessment and continual expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the procedure or equipment.

If an ETT or laryngeal mask is used, verify position clinically and with expired carbon dioxide; maintain continual quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis from placement until removal or transfer begins.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: A cuffed ETT secures the airway but can obstruct visualization. Use the smallest tube that supports ventilation; the source describes a 5.0- or 5.5-mm microlaryngeal tube as adequate in most cases, while recognizing increased resistance and the need to assess for leaks.

For laryngeal laser procedures, use a laser-resistant ETT compatible with the particular laser if an ETT is selected. Reduce inspired oxygen concentration to less than 30% and discontinue nitrous oxide; allow approximately 5 minutes for equilibration, depending on fresh-gas flow, circuit length, and initial oxygen concentration. Fill the ETT cuff with saline tinted with methylene blue to signal cuff rupture.

Tubeless options include spontaneous ventilation, intermittent apnea and jet ventilation. Jet ventilation can improve exposure but complicates CO₂ assessment and carries risks including hypercapnia and barotrauma; maintain a feasible oxygenation and reintubation plan.

TIVA with propofol and/or remifentanil is described as an option for an open airway; technique selection is individualized. Topical/local anesthetic may reduce airway reflexes, but the sources do not establish a mandatory drug or regimen.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain oxygenation and ventilation while preserving surgical exposure. Induction, positive-pressure ventilation or paralysis may precipitate dynamic obstruction in susceptible anatomy, so assess the airway and adapt the technique with the surgeon.

With jet ventilation, monitor oxygenation and ventilation using available measures, including chest excursion and CO₂ trends where interpretable; hypercapnia may be more likely with obesity or pre-existing obstructive lung disease.
When laser is used, coordinate laser activation with the anesthetic team and confirm fire-risk measures before activation; the source describes allowing time for FiO₂ equilibration after adjustment.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Potential complications include airway obstruction, laryngospasm, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, jet-related barotrauma and airway fire. Recognize deterioration promptly and escalate with the surgical team to restore oxygenation and airway control.

For a suspected laser airway fire, stop laser use and prioritize airway management and removal of burning material; the supplied sources do not provide a complete, validated fire-response protocol. Review the applicable institutional protocol with the team.

Jet ventilation complications include CO₂ retention, low oxygen saturation and barotrauma; pressure monitoring and experienced operation are emphasized, but the sources do not establish a universal jet setting or response algorithm.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Myringotomy opens the tympanic membrane to drain middle-ear fluid; a tympanostomy tube may then be inserted. Adults may tolerate the procedure under local anesthesia in a clinic, while general anesthesia is also used; the available sources do not establish one adult default.

Choose the anesthetic and setting according to the patient, indication, and procedural circumstances. The main anesthesia priority supported here is safe management of a shared, potentially reactive airway if general anesthesia is used; procedure-specific adult airway-risk estimates are not provided.

The procedure is brief and typically outpatient, but neither duration nor airway technique should be treated as a fixed adult standard. The supplied procedure sources give no adult anesthetic regimen or case-specific physiologic targets.

Recovery priorities are observation appropriate to the anesthetic and patient, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness. Grogginess and nausea may occur; the sources do not establish a procedure-specific emergence or PONV regimen.

bullets: The surgeon makes a small incision in the tympanic membrane, drains or suctions middle-ear fluid, and may place a tube through the incision to facilitate drainage and pressure equalization.

Adult indications described include chronic eustachian tube dysfunction with chronic effusion after medical management has not adequately improved symptoms and follow-up studies. Adult indications are less well-defined than pediatric indications in the source.
Adult procedures may be performed in a clinic under local anesthesia; general anesthesia is another described approach. The sources do not resolve which is preferable for a given adult or setting.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Neck dissection removes cervical lymph-node levels according to disease distribution; radical dissection also removes the sternocleidomastoid, internal jugular vein and accessory nerve, while modified and selective procedures preserve more structures.
Key intraoperative hazards include major-vessel bleeding, blood-pressure variation with carotid-bulb manipulation, chyle leak, pneumothorax and cranial-nerve injury.
Airway planning should account for obstruction, altered anatomy and prior treatment; significant concern may warrant a planned awake airway approach in coordination with the surgical team.

Recovery priorities are appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and attention to surgical complications including hematoma and chyle fistula; the supplied evidence does not establish a neck-dissection-specific extubation or postoperative airway protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Radical neck dissection removes levels I–V with the SCM, IJV and CN XI. Modified radical dissection removes levels I–V while preserving at least one of those structures; selective dissection removes selected nodal levels.

The cited review describes neck dissection as indicated for clinically positive nodal disease or advanced primary tumor stage in node-negative disease. It identifies unresectable disease, including skull-base or deep-neck-musculature invasion, as an absolute contraindication.
The operative field is the head and neck, shared with the anesthesia team; procedure extent and structures to be preserved or sacrificed should be established with the surgeon.

Review imaging and oncologic staging, and consider medical comorbidity and anticoagulation management. Carotid involvement can affect resectability; the source describes it as an absolute or relative contraindication depending on circumstances.

Prior radiotherapy or other treatment may contribute to distorted anatomy or contractures affecting airway access; the supplied sources do not quantify these risks or establish a specific preoperative pathway.

Maintain basic anesthetic monitoring, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; ECG is continuous and blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standards.

bullets: Carotid-bulb manipulation may cause significant blood-pressure variation; anticipate communication with the surgeon during this phase. The source supplies no target or treatment regimen.

bullets: Important operative hazards include injury to the IJV or carotid, chyle leak—particularly where the thoracic duct enters the left IJV—and pneumothorax during dissection near the lung apex.

Cranial-nerve injury is a recognized complication. In the retrospective cohort, 14 documented iatrogenic cranial-nerve injuries occurred among 925 cases; documentation-based ascertainment may have missed injuries.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Parotidectomy ranges from partial/superficial removal to total gland excision; approach depends on lesion extent and pathology. Facial nerve identification and preservation are central priorities, alongside oncologic safety when malignancy is present.

The main procedure-specific anesthetic challenge is preserving conditions for facial nerve assessment while maintaining a secure airway and coordinating with the surgeon. Facial nerve monitoring is used in many centers; the source advises avoiding muscle relaxants when nerve function is being monitored.
Examine and document baseline facial function. Anticipate potentially challenging intubation with deep-lobe or parapharyngeal-space tumors, or extensive lesions causing trismus.

The available procedure-specific source does not establish a drug regimen, fluid target, hemodynamic target, or extubation technique. Recovery should include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and a documented handoff, with immediate assessment of facial nerve function.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Operations include partial/superficial parotidectomy, total parotidectomy, and radical parotidectomy. The selected extent reflects lesion location, disease extent, and oncologic requirements; these approaches are not interchangeable.

Facial nerve identification and preservation are defining operative concerns. Radical parotidectomy may include nerve removal when preoperative paralysis or circumferential malignant involvement is present.
A suction drain and compressive dressing may be used; counsel patients about facial weakness, possible contour change, and the drain/dressing as part of the procedure-specific discussion.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Document facial function before surgery, ideally with photographs. Facial paralysis, trismus, formication, or numbness are concerning features in the assessment of a parotid mass.
Review imaging and disease extent for operative planning. Deep-lobe lesions may be subtle on examination; deep-lobe or extensive lesions can also make airway management more difficult.
Discuss facial nerve injury risk in context: the source describes greater risk with extensive malignant tumors and more facial weakness after total than superficial parotidectomy.
The supplied evidence does not describe pregnancy-specific parotidectomy anesthesia management; pregnancy-related decisions require applicable obstetric guidance and individualized assessment.

bullets: Position with the neck slightly extended and the head turned away from the operative side. The endotracheal tube is fixed contralaterally to leave access to the operative field.

Coordinate with the surgeon about the monitoring method and avoid muscle relaxants when monitoring requires observable facial nerve function. Direct observation remains relevant even when electronic monitoring is used.
Apply standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA basic standards require ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

bullets: General anesthesia with an endotracheal tube is described for parotidectomy. Assess airway anatomy and access in advance when a deep-lobe/parapharyngeal lesion or trismus is present.

bullets: Key surgical phases include flap elevation, gland mobilization, facial nerve localization and dissection, lesion/gland removal, hemostasis, drain placement, and closure. The supplied procedure source does not establish anesthetic physiologic targets for these phases.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting

Hematoma is an important postoperative complication; meticulous hemostasis is emphasized, and surgical reintervention may be required to control bleeding. New or expanding swelling merits urgent surgical assessment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Septoplasty and inferior turbinate reduction address structural nasal obstruction. Limited septoplasty may be performed in an office setting with topical and injected local anesthesia; more extensive or bony work may require an operating-room setting and general anesthesia.

This is shared-airway surgery. Blood and debris can contaminate the airway, and airway access may be constrained once surgery begins; agree on airway protection, surgical access, and a backup plan with the surgeon.

Prioritize oxygenation and ventilation monitoring, communication about local vasoconstrictor use, and protection from blood contamination. The supplied evidence does not establish a universal airway device or anesthetic technique for this operation.

Plan emergence around airway cleanliness and patency. Nasal surgery is commonly extubated awake in the cited airway review; postanesthesia recovery requires ongoing assessment appropriate to the patient's condition.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Septoplasty corrects septal deviation; inferior turbinate reduction may be performed alone or with other nasal procedures. bullets: Clarify obstruction symptoms, prior treatment and response, and whether findings suggest structural obstruction or an inflammatory cause. Consider whether turbinate enlargement is inflammatory and whether medical treatment has been tried. Significant systemic illness or cardiopulmonary disease may make an office procedure less suitable and require a more monitored setting.

bullets: For office-based procedures, the review describes a reclining chair, adequate working space and lighting, and emergency equipment, particularly when sedatives are used. These details apply to the office setting, not as a complete operating-room setup standard.

Follow basic anesthetic monitoring standards: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose airway management in collaboration with the surgeon, balancing access and airway security. The supplied review discusses tracheal tubes and flexible laryngeal mask airways for nasal/sinus surgery, but notes risks with either approach; it does not establish one device as best for every septoplasty or turbinate case.

A tracheal tube secures the lower airway, but its cuff does not guarantee freedom from contamination: blood may track past a throat pack along the tube. A correctly placed flexible LMA may protect the supraglottic and glottic airway, but malposition or dislodgement can cause obstruction or blood contamination.

Account for any throat pack explicitly and confirm its removal. Inspect and suction the oro- and nasopharynx before emergence; the airway review identifies retained packs and residual blood or clot as potentially serious hazards.

Anesthesia type should reflect patient status, procedural complexity, and team expertise. A single-center retrospective study included selected adult ASA I–II patients receiving deep sedation or general anesthesia; its design and exclusions do not establish either approach as routine for broader populations.

With substantial nasal/sinus bleeding, the airway review describes considering gastric evacuation before awakening to reduce retained blood and associated aspiration or emesis concerns. This is a review statement, not a universal instruction for every case.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Tonsillectomy is a shared-airway procedure. Tracheal tubes are commonly used in ENT surgery; an oral RAE tube is suited to pharyngeal surgery with a gag. Flexible LMA use for tonsillectomy is an experienced-team alternative, not a universal default.

The central intraoperative hazards are a shared and potentially obstructed airway, and contamination with blood or debris. Planning and communication should account for surgical access, airway protection, suction, and the possibility of difficult recovery after intra-oral surgery.

Recovery priorities include airway patency, oxygenation, ventilation, and vigilance for bleeding or respiratory events. Extubation approach should be chosen deliberately; the chapter describes awake extubation as usual and deep extubation as an option used by some anaesthetists.

For pain, the procedure-specific guideline supports paracetamol and NSAIDs as basic analgesia, a single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose, and opioids as postoperative rescue rather than routine first-line analgesia. It supplies no dosing instructions.

Described tonsil-removal approaches include cold dissection and electrocautery, as well as newer methods such as coblation and vessel-seal techniques. The review could not recommend a specific surgical technique to reduce pain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult epiglottitis can progress rapidly to life-threatening upper-airway obstruction. Airway intervention is not automatic for every adult, but when required it should be planned and performed by experienced clinicians with immediate surgical-airway capability.

For a threatened airway requiring intubation, the available review supports a monitored operating-room setting, an upright initial position, and preservation of spontaneous ventilation during airway management; no single anesthetic technique is established for every adult.

The dominant peri-procedural hazard is sudden worsening or total loss of airway patency, including with examination, induction, or positioning. Prioritize oxygenation and a prepared rescue pathway over nonessential diagnostic steps.

After airway security, plan monitored critical-care recovery. Extubation assessment in the available procedure-specific review includes a cuff-leak test and usually a second-look laryngoscopy; a fixed extubation timeline is not established.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: This is management of a potentially threatened airway from acute supraglottic infection, not a routine elective intubation. Assess whether intervention is needed; most adults in the cited chapter did not undergo airway intervention, but apparently stable patients may still deteriorate.

When securing the airway is indicated, the objective is controlled airway security with experienced anesthesia and otolaryngology support and a surgical-airway plan. The sources do not establish one universally preferred intubation technique for all adults.
An adult with severe airway distress may require an awake surgical airway rather than repeated or poorly supported intubation attempts; choice depends on presentation and local expertise.

sources.label: Epiglottitis, Acute Laryngitis, and Croup

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Keep a patient with suspected adult epiglottitis sitting; do not require supine positioning for assessment. Stridor, drooling, and tachypnea are associated with need for airway intervention, and stridor is a warning sign of upper-airway occlusion.

In respiratory distress, do not delay airway security for radiography or other diagnostic procedures. Contrast CT for suspected deep-neck infection or epiglottic abscess is considered only after the airway is secure.
An epiglottic abscess is a relevant adult severity modifier; assess for deep-neck extension when clinically appropriate, without allowing investigation to destabilize a threatened airway.

sources.label: Epiglottitis, Acute Laryngitis, and Croup
Acute epiglottitis: Trends, diagnosis and management

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For a planned intubation, use a monitored operating-room setting and verify immediate availability of a team capable of tracheotomy. The review does not support relying on an unprepared bedside or remote rescue arrangement.
Maintain the patient upright initially when tolerated; forced supine positioning can precipitate obstruction. Do not interpret this as a prohibition on repositioning after airway security.

Apply standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; verify tube or laryngeal-mask position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide.

sources.label: Acute epiglottitis: Trends, diagnosis and management
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Maintain spontaneous ventilation during airway management when feasible; the epiglottitis review advises avoiding muscle relaxants. This is a procedure-specific airway precaution, not a general prohibition on neuromuscular blockade in other settings.

The 2012 review describes fibreoptic nasal intubation or rigid bronchoscopy with a substantially reduced-diameter tube as preferred approaches. A later chapter also describes awake fibreoptic intubation in a cooperative patient and allows direct or video-assisted laryngoscopy; these sources do not resolve technique selection for every adult presentation.

Every intubation attempt requires immediate surgical-airway readiness. Swelling and secretions may impair visualization, and a failed attempt can precipitate acute obstruction; escalate rather than persist through repeated unsuccessful attempts.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Treat examination, induction, and changes in position as critical phases because each can worsen upper-airway obstruction. Maintain close observation of oxygenation and ventilation and be prepared to secure or rescue the airway.

Once an ETT or laryngeal mask is placed, ASA standards require continual end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis through extubation/removal or initiation of transfer, unless the nature of the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates it.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Tympanoplasty repairs a tympanic-membrane perforation, with or without ossicular reconstruction, to reduce reinfection and restore hearing. It is typically performed under general anesthesia; local anesthesia with conscious sedation has also been studied in selected adults.
Approach and graft choice depend on perforation and ear-canal anatomy and surgeon preference. Pre- and postoperative hearing assessment provides a comparison of outcome.

Key procedure-related risks include graft failure or recurrence, hearing loss, dizziness, and facial-nerve or chorda-tympani injury. The supplied evidence does not establish specific anesthetic targets or a tympanoplasty-specific airway technique.
