overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Percutaneous ASD closure is generally performed for suitable secundum defects using femoral venous access, fluoroscopy and echocardiographic guidance; TEE is usual, with ICE an alternative.

Anesthesia may be general anesthesia or sedation. ICE-guided procedures can permit moderate sedation; the supplied sources do not establish a routine airway technique or anesthetic drug regimen for ASD closure.

Priorities are confirming suitable anatomy and hemodynamic benefit, recognizing pulmonary vascular disease that may make closure unsafe, and maintaining imaging guidance to assess device position and surrounding structures.

After deployment, confirm device position by imaging and observe for complications such as arrhythmia, thromboembolism, or device embolization. Postprocedure antiplatelet practice varies; the source review describes therapy for at least six months but notes uncertainty.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: This reference addresses transcatheter ASD closure. Available devices are designed for secundum ASDs; primum, sinus venosus, and coronary sinus defects generally require surgical closure, with selected exceptions. Device suitability depends on anatomy and adequate supporting rims.

The described percutaneous route is usually femoral venous. Fluoroscopy and TEE guide the procedure; ICE is an alternative in larger patients. Imaging is used during and after deployment to evaluate position and effects on nearby structures.

bullets: Review imaging for defect size and location, septal rims, and associated anomalies. TTE is usually adequate initially in children with good windows; adults often require TEE, and 3D TEE, MRI, or CT may also be considered.

Assess pulmonary pressure, PVR, and shunt direction before deciding on closure. The review states closure should not be performed with PA systolic pressure or PVR above two-thirds systemic, or net right-to-left shunting. It describes possible consideration in selected patients with Qp:Qs ≥1.5 and lesser pulmonary vascular disease; this requires appropriate specialist assessment.

For PAH or left ventricular diastolic dysfunction, the review notes that test balloon occlusion or fenestrated closure may be considered. These are procedural-selection considerations, not a substitute for individualized cardiac assessment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) uses catheter-delivered lesions around the pulmonary veins, most commonly radiofrequency or cryoballoon; pulsed-field ablation is also described. Additional left-atrial lesion sets depend on the clinical substrate and operator plan.

General anesthesia is commonly selected for AF ablation to limit movement and support mapping, but sedation is also used. Match depth and airway approach to procedure, patient risks, and the need to preserve phrenic-nerve assessment during cryoablation.

Coordinate intraprocedural heparin and ACT monitoring with the electrophysiologist; maintain vigilance for transseptal or catheter-related perforation, tamponade, thromboembolism, air embolism, and vascular bleeding.

Prioritize prompt recognition of hemodynamic or neurologic change, access-site hemostasis, and a focused recovery assessment. Delayed fever, dysphagia, chest pain, or neurologic symptoms after ablation warrant urgent evaluation for esophageal injury or fistula.

sections.title: Procedure & approach

RF generally creates point-to-point lesions around each ostium; cryoballoon treatment freezes tissue after balloon positioning and vein occlusion are assessed. PFA is a nonthermal option, but the supplied evidence is early and does not establish it as the standard approach.

PVI alone is usually sufficient for paroxysmal AF; persistent AF may receive additional left-atrial substrate ablation. Confirm the planned lesion set and energy source with the procedural team rather than assuming posterior-wall isolation is routine.

Left-atrial access involves femoral venous catheter passage and transseptal puncture. TOE or ICE may guide access in selected cases; the cited review describes fluoroscopic guidance and imaging when septal crossing is difficult, not a single mandatory imaging method.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Typical CTI-dependent atrial flutter is treated with a right-atrial radiofrequency line between the tricuspid annulus and inferior vena cava; the procedural endpoint is complete bidirectional CTI block.

This is generally a shorter, right-sided EP procedure: transseptal puncture and TOE are usually unnecessary, and sedation or general anesthesia may be used according to patient and procedural factors.

Priorities are maintaining patient comfort and procedural conditions, monitoring circulation and rhythm, and remaining alert to vascular injury, perforation/tamponade, and conduction-system injury—particularly with septal lesion placement.

Recovery should include appropriate postanesthesia observation and attention to access-site bleeding and rhythm; uncomplicated AFL ablation may allow same-day discharge, but disposition remains case-specific.

bullets: For CTI-dependent flutter, the operator uses femoral venous access and creates a linear lesion from the ventricular side of the tricuspid annulus toward the inferior vena cava, interrupting the re-entrant circuit.

A complete bidirectional conduction block is the success endpoint; non-inducibility alone does not establish a complete line. The EP team may assess block by pacing in both directions and use more than one assessment method.

bullets: Use an EP laboratory equipped for catheter ablation and immediate cardiac resuscitation. The described resources include fluoroscopy, EP recording/stimulation equipment, an RF generator, defibrillator, temporary pacing, and resuscitation equipment.

Plan monitoring to match the anesthetic and patient risk. Basic standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes; during moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure or equipment invalidates it.
The flutter source does not specify patient positioning. Do not treat a particular position or additional invasive monitor as a procedure-wide requirement.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Typical CTI ablation may be performed with sedation or general anesthesia; choice depends on the patient, expected procedure, and local practice. The evidence does not support imposing intubation, paralysis, or general anesthesia on every case.

If moderate or deep sedation is used, maintain ongoing clinical assessment of ventilation and use expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless it is precluded or invalidated. Select airway support according to the actual anesthetic and clinical circumstances.
No CTI-specific airway device, sedative combination, or drug-dose regimen is established by the supplied flutter sources.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Coordinate with the EP operator during mapping, lesion delivery, and endpoint assessment. Procedural stimulation and mapping may influence the choice and depth of anesthesia; the EP source describes conscious sedation and general anesthesia as variable approaches.
The EP team should confirm complete CTI block, not simply termination of flutter. Anesthesia should remain coordinated with the operator while pacing and other endpoint assessments are performed.
Avoid assuming that more septal lesion placement is benign: the flutter source identifies increased risk of right coronary artery injury and AV-node damage at more septal sites.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Potential complications include access-site hemorrhage or vascular injury, cardiac perforation, tamponade, thromboembolism, and inadvertent complete heart block. The available incidence statements cover EP catheterization or RF ablation broadly and should not be presented as CTI-specific estimates.

A new hemodynamic concern or suspected effusion warrants prompt communication with the EP team and escalation using the laboratory's available echo, pericardiocentesis, and surgical support. This is a readiness priority, not a prescribed resuscitation algorithm.

After right atrial flutter ablation, check for re-induction with programmed stimulation and burst pacing and confirm complete block for linear lesions. Provide postoperative monitoring and early recognition of complications.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The EP laboratory should have fluids and infusion capability available, but the flutter source gives no administration regimen or target. Individualize fluid management to the patient and procedural course rather than applying a fixed volume.

Blood loss and transfusion are not characterized for this procedure in the flutter review. Assess bleeding and access-site concerns in context; the sources do not establish a routine transfusion preparation or threshold for uncomplicated CTI ablation.

Do not infer a universal anticoagulation regimen or ACT target for CTI ablation from left-sided-ablation guidance. Coordinate the case-specific plan with the EP team; the flutter review notes that anticoagulant therapy may need to be discontinued.

bullets: Use an individualized comfort and analgesia approach. The general EP review describes simple analgesics and local anesthetic infiltration at catheter puncture sites as postoperative options; it does not establish a CTI-specific regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For monitored anesthesia care, recovery is guided by the patient's respiratory, circulatory, and consciousness status. After general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this requirement applies when neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used.

Provide postanesthesia care with monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature; document recovery and hand over the procedural and anesthetic course.
Uncomplicated cases may be considered for same-day discharge when the responsible team judges recovery and procedural findings suitable; the source does not define CTI-specific discharge criteria.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Diagnostic cardiac catheterization is a fluoroscopy-guided, catheter-based procedure; the supplied sources support different details for general cath-lab procedures and for right-heart catheterization (RHC), so the intended study and anesthetic should be defined for the individual case.

For diagnostic RHC, local anesthesia is generally sufficient and sedation is rarely required; the supplied evidence does not establish this as the approach for every coronary angiography or left-heart catheterization.

Priorities include maintaining reliable hemodynamic assessment, avoiding unnecessary sedation-related changes, and accounting for contrast-associated renal risk when relevant. The evidence does not establish one fluid regimen or contrast-volume target for all patients.

Recovery should follow the patient's anesthetic and clinical condition. General postanesthesia standards support continued assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; the provided sources do not supply a diagnostic-cath-specific access-site or discharge protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Confirm with the proceduralist whether the study is coronary angiography, hemodynamic catheterization, or a combination, and what measurements or imaging are required. The supplied source details do not define a single diagnostic coronary-catheterization workflow.
For RHC, tailor measurements to a predefined diagnostic question; the review describes pressures, cardiac output, and mixed venous oxygen saturation as typical components of a complete study.
When interpreting RHC results, integrate the measurements with non-invasive data and the clinical question rather than relying on a single value or calculation.

bullets: Establish the indication and study requirements with the cardiology team, and assess comorbidities and the patient's current medical status as part of the anesthesia evaluation.

Review renal function when iodinated contrast is expected. The cath-lab review identifies impaired renal function as a concern and supports adequate hydration before and after contrast, without providing a universal regimen.
For diagnostic RHC, anticoagulation decisions for patients already taking anticoagulants should be individualized; the review notes that evidence for uninterrupted anticoagulation is limited.

bullets: The cath-lab environment may be remote from the main operating room and exposed to fluoroscopy. Confirm room familiarity, team communication, equipment availability, and a means to observe and communicate with the patient.

The procedure room may contain fluoroscopy, catheters, and dye-injection equipment. For RHC, the described measurement position is fully supine; record deviations because position can alter pressures and cardiac-output measurements.

When anesthesia or MAC is provided, apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards. These include continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.
Use radiation protection practices appropriate to the procedure and staff role; the cath-lab review describes distance, limiting exposure time, and shielding as core principles.

bullets: Do not assume general anesthesia or an advanced airway is required. The anesthesia technique depends on the procedure and patient; for diagnostic RHC, local anesthesia is generally sufficient and sedation is rarely needed.
If moderate or deep sedation is used, assess ventilation continuously, including expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

bullets: For RHC pressure acquisition, measure at end-expiration without breath-holding or Valsalva. With large respiratory swings, the review advises averaging across several respiratory cycles.
For RHC, maintain a consistent transducer reference and verify waveform quality; the review identifies leveling and damping errors as sources of measurement distortion.
For anesthetized patients, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature in accordance with basic monitoring standards.

bullets: Contrast-related adverse reactions and renal dysfunction are relevant hazards when contrast is used. The supplied cath-lab source describes contrast reactions and the possibility of worsened renal impairment, but does not provide a complete management algorithm.

During the initial phase of recovery, use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry and monitor according to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Elective external cardioversion is a brief, painful procedure using a synchronized shock to restore sinus rhythm; stable patients require deep sedation or anesthesia.

Synchronize every cardioversion shock to the ECG R wave. Priorities during sedation are continuous assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation, with ECG and appropriate ventilation monitoring.
Key immediate hazards include respiratory depression or apnea, hypotension, post-shock rhythm disturbance, and thromboembolism when anticoagulation is inadequate.
Recovery should include rhythm assessment, continued postanesthesia monitoring, and a clear anticoagulation plan; check pacemaker or ICD function when applicable.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: External electrical cardioversion delivers selected energy through chest electrodes or paddles. It is used principally to convert atrial fibrillation or flutter to sinus rhythm; other rhythm indications require appropriate clinical selection.
For cardioversion, confirm synchronized mode and R-wave sensing before shock delivery. Unsynchronized delivery during the vulnerable phase can induce ventricular fibrillation.
Elective cardioversion in a stable patient is painful and requires deep sedation or anesthesia; the evidence supplied does not establish one universal anesthetic or airway technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the indication, rhythm, clinical stability, AF duration, and anticoagulation status before proceeding. The supplied cardioversion review describes embolic risk when anticoagulation is insufficient; it does not provide a current society protocol for individual eligibility decisions.

Review reversible rhythm modifiers, including electrolyte imbalance and hypoxia, and consider thyroid disease as a recurrence modifier. The sources do not establish routine testing requirements for every patient.
Assess for digitalis toxicity: the cardioversion review identifies it as a contraindication because of resistant VF risk. This does not establish a routine digoxin-level testing protocol.
For a pacemaker or ICD, assess device function and leads before cardioversion and arrange post-shock function checks; device-specific precautions should be coordinated with the responsible team.

bullets: Use ECG, pulse oximetry, and non-invasive blood pressure monitoring. ASA basic standards require continuous ECG display during anesthesia and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes.
During moderate or deep sedation, monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment makes this invalid or impractical. Provide supplemental oxygen as clinically appropriate.

Have emergency airway and resuscitation equipment available. The supplied trial kept endotracheal-intubation equipment and cardiorespiratory drugs ready; it does not establish a required room layout or patient position.

bullets: Choose sedation depth and airway support according to the patient and clinical circumstances; the cardioversion review does not specify an airway technique. Do not treat a natural airway or intubation as a universal requirement.

Anticipate apnea or respiratory depression during sedation and be prepared to support ventilation. In one small elective trial, respiratory depression was more frequent in the propofol group; no patient required intubation, within that study population.

Maintain ongoing assessment of ventilation and oxygenation during recovery as well as during sedation; pulse oximetry is required during the initial phase of recovery under the cited postanesthesia standard.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The critical procedural safety step is confirming synchronization to the R wave before shock delivery; unsynchronized shock can coincide with the T wave and precipitate VF.

Observe closely for post-shock hemodynamic change. In the elective comparative trial, blood pressure fell after cardioversion in both anesthetic groups, with values approaching baseline during follow-up; the authors characterized the drops as clinically insignificant in that enrolled population.

If cardioversion fails or the post-shock rhythm is unstable, reassess the rhythm and escalate to the responsible cardiology and anesthesia teams. The supplied evidence does not establish a universal repeat-shock sequence.

bullets: Anesthetic management for an EP study should be matched to the study’s purpose and the importance of preserving arrhythmia inducibility; the supplied sources do not define a single technique for standalone diagnostic studies.

When induction or mapping is critical, avoid unnecessarily deepening anesthesia: some focal atrial and ventricular ectopic rhythms may be suppressed, although effects vary by arrhythmia and anesthetic.
Prioritize continuous ECG and appropriate anesthetic monitoring, with capacity to respond to induced tachyarrhythmia, hemodynamic deterioration, airway compromise, and catheter-related complications.
Recovery planning should reflect the actual anesthetic and clinical course; no EP-study-specific emergence or disposition protocol is established by the supplied sources.

bullets: ICD implantation may use local anesthesia with sedation or general anesthesia; the choice depends on the patient, indication, cardiac function, procedural complexity, and whether device testing is planned.

bullets: ILR placement is generally an outpatient procedure performed by an electrophysiologist using local anesthesia; conscious sedation is possible but usually unnecessary.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Transvenous lead extraction is usually a percutaneous, stepwise procedure: manual traction is attempted first, with locking devices and extraction sheaths used when fibrosis or adhesions prevent removal.
Infection is the most frequent indication. Lead burden, dwell time, device type, and pacing dependency inform procedural and anesthetic planning.

The dominant acute hazards are major-vein or cardiac injury, haemorrhage, and tamponade. Recognize instability promptly, release lead traction, assess for bleeding, and escalate urgently to the planned surgical rescue pathway.

Recovery depends on procedural stability: uncomplicated patients may be awakened and sent to the ward after PACU care; complications may require high-dependency or ICU care. Post-extraction imaging and infection management remain important.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Extraction is generally performed percutaneously through the implant site. The sequence may progress from manual traction to a locking device and then to powered or non-powered sheaths when adhesions prevent lead release; tool choice depends on the lead–tissue interface, fibrosis, lead characteristics, dwell time, and operator experience.

Infection is the leading indication in the cited registry; other indications include lead malfunction or recall, venous access problems, severe tricuspid regurgitation, chronic pain, and access needed for MRI or radiotherapy.

Extraction strategy should account for the number, type, location, and dwell time of leads, as well as pacing dependency. Clinical success may allow a small residual fragment; it is not identical to complete removal of every lead component.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the indication, cardiac history, functional status, device type and programming, lead number and dwell time, and pacing dependency. Longer dwell time and lead characteristics help predict fibrosis, adhesion, and calcification.

Echocardiography can assess ventricular function, lead course, vegetations, shunts, and tricuspid regurgitation. The cited review recommends a full blood count, coagulation testing, and cross-match; interpret these measures in the context of the patient and local pathway.

Assess infection status and whether temporary pacing or reimplantation planning is needed. For pacemaker-dependent patients, establish a case-specific pacing plan before extraction; do not assume extraction can proceed without pacing support.

Risk rises with older leads and can also be affected by lead configuration and patient factors. The review reports higher major-complication risk in its highest EROS category; scores inform risk discussion, not a guarantee of an individual outcome.

bullets: Use a setting and team that can support rapid rescue. A hybrid operating theatre is described as ideal; pre-procedure discussion should include surgical response, possible cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) strategy and availability, blood availability, and whether an SVC occlusion balloon may be needed.

Position supine and drape to preserve access to the implant vein, femoral vessels, and sternotomy site. The multidisciplinary team includes cardiac surgery and perfusion support appropriate to the anticipated risk.

The review describes intra-arterial, central venous, and femoral venous access, with a larger femoral venous sheath advised because of intrathoracic central-vein haemorrhage risk. Select access and monitoring to the case; these details do not establish that every patient needs every line or sheath.
General anaesthesia is common in the cited review; high-risk cases should have TOE monitoring. The evidence does not support treating TOE or an arterial line as mandatory for every risk category.

bullets: A tracheal tube under general anaesthesia is common, particularly when procedural complexity or patient risk warrants it. The cited review also permits sedation for low-risk cases, provided rapid initiation of general anaesthesia and intubation is available if complications develop.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: TOE is most useful for identifying the cause of haemodynamic instability and guiding assessment. Lead traction can distort right-heart anatomy or the tricuspid valve; release of traction usually resolves lead-tension-related inversion.

If instability persists after traction is released, promptly assess for pericardial or pleural fluid and new or worsened tricuspid regurgitation. The likely compartment depends on the injured structure and whether the SVC injury is intra- or extra-pericardial.
After extraction, assess for valve injury, residual fragments, and pericardial or pleural fluid. TOE may need repositioning or withdrawal during fluoroscopy to avoid obscuring the area of interest.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: SVC injury is a particularly serious hazard and may present with sudden severe hypotension, haemothorax, tamponade, or both. Prioritize recognition and immediate escalation to the pre-agreed surgical rescue pathway; an occlusion balloon may provide temporary stability but must not delay surgery.

Pericardial bleeding can cause rapid collapse; thoracic bleeding may deteriorate more gradually but can also cause collapse. Uncontrolled haemorrhage requires urgent surgical management, with delay in chest opening potentially fatal.

Other reported complications include cardiac avulsion, vascular laceration, pericardial effusion, haemothorax, thromboembolism, air embolism, valve injury, and retained or migrated lead fragments. Confirm the post-extraction structural and imaging assessment before routine disposition.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TEER is usually performed in a catheterization lab or hybrid operating room through femoral venous access and transseptal passage, with clip placement guided by fluoroscopy and continuous TEE. General anesthesia with tracheal intubation is typical to facilitate TEE.

Priorities are to maintain cardiac output, avoid hypotension and bradycardia, and avoid reflex fluid loading that may worsen MR. Keep ventilation stable during device positioning and leaflet grasping.

Key hazards include tamponade after transseptal puncture, bleeding, embolic events, TEE-related injury, clip malposition, and iatrogenic mitral stenosis. New hemodynamic instability warrants urgent assessment for pericardial tamponade.

Most patients can be awakened at procedure end and recover in PACU; routine ICU admission is no longer usual. Intermediate-care or coronary-care units are suitable for most. Perform transthoracic echocardiography within 24 h to confirm success and assess residual MR, new mitral stenosis, and any unclosed septal defect’s flow volume and direction.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TEER places one or more clips across the free edges of the mitral leaflets to reduce regurgitation. The typical route is femoral venous access, transseptal puncture, delivery into the left atrium, and leaflet grasping under TEE and fluoroscopy.

TEE is central to procedural guidance: it supports transseptal access, clip alignment and grasping, and assessment of residual MR and new mitral stenosis. Two- and three-dimensional imaging are described as important for positioning.

The procedural endpoint balances reduction of MR against the risk of creating mitral stenosis. Clip number and placement are anatomy- and result-dependent; the available review does not establish a universal clip count for an individual case.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review MR mechanism and severity, ventricular function, mitral anatomy and access suitability with the structural heart team. The review identifies favorable anatomy and high surgical risk as relevant to selection; eligibility is a team decision rather than an anesthesia-only determination.

For secondary MR, confirm optimization of heart-failure therapy and management of concomitant coronary disease; the review describes repair when symptoms persist and MR remains severe. Assess LV function because correction of MR can increase LV afterload, particularly with impaired systolic function.

Reconcile antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and heart-failure medications with the procedural team. The supplied review describes differing medication approaches; it does not support applying one stop or restart schedule to every patient.

Consider frailty, renal function, pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid regurgitation, rhythm, and baseline hemodynamics in planning. The review notes that pulmonary hypertension and tricuspid regurgitation are common, but does not support routine preprocedural intervention on those findings to improve TEER outcome.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use a catheterization lab or hybrid operating room equipped for fluoroscopy and TEE. The patient is typically supine with arms by the sides; secure monitoring and vascular lines because equipment, drapes, and personnel may restrict access.

TEE is continuous procedural imaging. An arterial catheter is appropriate for continuous blood-pressure monitoring and ACT sampling. Central venous access and urinary catheterization are not routine in the cited review; select additional access for patient-specific need.

External defibrillator pads are advised in the review because intracardiac wires and catheters can provoke malignant arrhythmias. Ensure the team has access to pericardiocentesis capability; the procedure-specific review recommends a complete TEE examination for tamponade before completion.

bullets: General anesthesia with tracheal intubation is typical because sustained TEE access is required. Non-intubated approaches are reported but are described as not routine; they should not be treated as an equivalent default.
General anesthesia with an endotracheal tube is recommended because TEE is important for device placement.

Maintain stable ventilation and avoid ventilatory changes during critical delivery-system and clip-deployment phases. Low tidal volumes are described as reducing cardiac movement and facilitating grasping; use the procedural team’s timing cues rather than assuming routine apnea.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Preserve cardiac output while avoiding conditions that worsen MR. The review cautions against bradycardia and notes that hypotension, hypovolemia, hypertension, and hypervolemia can change the apparent MR assessment; coordinate hemodynamic conditions with the proceduralist.

Avoid reflexive fluid loading for hypotension: volume loading may exacerbate MR. The review describes selected use of diuretics or inotropes in some patients to reduce filling pressures or support ventricular function, while explicitly noting that effects on procedural success are insufficiently studied.

Anticoagulation is coordinated with the interventional team, with ACT measurement available. The cited review reports an institutional ACT target, not a universal anesthesia target; do not generalize a numeric target across cases or institutions.

During transseptal puncture, delivery-system advancement, leaflet grasping, and clip assessment, maintain close communication among anesthesia, interventional cardiology, and imaging. The review describes direct left-atrial pressure trends as an adjunct to TEE when assessing dynamic MR changes.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Delayed pericardial tamponade is a feared complication; urgent transthoracic echocardiography is mandatory with postprocedural hemodynamic instability.

Clip malposition may require repositioning, removal, or an additional clip; additional leaflet capture must be balanced against iatrogenic mitral stenosis. TEE is used to assess leaflet insertion, residual MR, and new stenosis.

Other important hazards include TEE-related esophageal or gastric injury, access-site or retroperitoneal bleeding, embolic complications, and septal shunting. New neurologic dysfunction or organ malperfusion should prompt consideration of embolization; unexplained hypotension or anemia warrants assessment for occult bleeding.

bullets: There is no source-supported fixed crystalloid volume for TEER. Individualize fluid to hemodynamics and ventricular function; account for procedural flushing fluid, which may be substantial, and avoid unnecessary loading that could worsen MR or cause pulmonary edema.

Assess bleeding risk and access sites, including the possibility of occult retroperitoneal bleeding. Have a response pathway for significant hemorrhage and hemodynamic deterioration; the sources do not establish a universal blood-product preparation or transfusion threshold.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: High-risk PCI is catheter-based coronary revascularization; when mechanical circulatory support (MCS) is planned, the support strategy and anesthetic technique are individualized. PCI commonly uses mild sedation, while general anesthesia or deeper sedation may be selected for patient or procedural needs.

The dominant physiologic concern is hemodynamic deterioration in patients selected for support because of severe coronary disease, impaired LV function, heart failure, or anticipated technically challenging PCI. VA-ECMO provides support but can increase LV afterload.

Key procedural hazards include coronary thrombosis or perforation, tamponade, and complications of large-bore vascular access such as bleeding and limb ischemia. Contrast exposure is relevant to renal risk, particularly with impaired renal function.

Recovery location and airway disposition depend on postprocedure stability and ongoing support. ICU care was used for some registry patients, but the available sources do not establish a universal ICU, extubation, or MCS-weaning protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Permanent pacemaker implantation uses fluoroscopic venous access to create a subcutaneous pocket and position pacing leads. Local anesthesia is commonly used; the available evidence does not establish one sedation or airway technique for every implant.

Anesthetic planning should account for cardiac function, anticipated procedure complexity, airway and respiratory risks, and the need to maintain comfort while limiting avoidable hemodynamic disturbance. More involved CRT procedures may warrant a different anesthetic approach than an uncomplicated implant.

Important hazards include device-pocket hematoma and uncommon but potentially serious cardiac perforation or tamponade. Anticoagulation decisions should be coordinated with the procedural team; evidence in device surgery does not support routine heparin bridging for patients on warfarin.

Recovery requires appropriate postanesthesia observation and assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. The supplied evidence does not establish pacemaker-specific imaging, interrogation, or activity instructions.

Device selection may depend on ventricular function and anticipated pacing burden. The review discusses physiologic or conduction-system pacing in patients with LV dysfunction when a significant proportion of ventricular pacing is expected; it is not an implant-specific selection protocol.

Anticoagulation management is a procedural-team decision. In the cited device-surgery trial, continued warfarin was associated with fewer clinically significant pocket hematomas than heparin bridging; evidence did not show continued DOAC therapy to be superior to interruption.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: SVT ablation is a catheter-based electrophysiology procedure; radiofrequency ablation is described in the supplied SVT evidence. The sources address SVT generally and do not establish separate anesthesia protocols for AVNRT versus AVRT.

Sedation depth is a procedural trade-off: comfort and analgesia must be balanced against the possibility that deeper anesthesia may reduce inducibility. The EP team and anesthesia clinician should align the approach with the planned mapping and ablation phases.

Priorities during the procedure include maintaining appropriate monitoring and promptly recognizing hemodynamic change, conduction disturbance or heart block, vascular-access injury, and cardiac perforation/tamponade.

After anesthesia, recovery should include appropriate observation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness, with rhythm and procedural concerns handed over to the receiving team. Uncomplicated SVT ablation may allow same-day discharge, but disposition is case-specific.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TAVR replaces a stenotic aortic valve by catheter; transfemoral access is the most common approach, with alternative access selected when vascular anatomy is unsuitable.
Anesthetic approach is individualized: GA remains common, while MAC is used in selected uncomplicated transfemoral cases; immediate conversion capability is important when MAC is chosen.
Priorities include preserving perfusion during severe AS, anticipating transient instability with rapid pacing, and having a coordinated response to coronary, vascular, and conduction complications.

Recovery requires monitored assessment for hemodynamic change, neurologic events, access complications, and new conduction abnormalities; pacing needs and disposition depend on the patient and course.

bullets: TAVR is a transcatheter treatment for severe aortic stenosis. The common retrograde transfemoral route may be unsuitable with severe peripheral vascular disease, tortuosity, or aortic disease; alternative routes include subclavian/axillary, transaortic, transapical, transcaval, and transcarotid access.

Deployment behavior is valve-specific: balloon-expandable Sapien deployment uses rapid ventricular pacing; the self-expanding CoreValve/Evolut-R can be released gradually and recaptured or repositioned.
Imaging supports guidance and post-deployment evaluation. Assess valve seating, gradients, and transvalvular or paravalvular leak using the modalities selected by the procedural team.

bullets: Persistent or sudden hemodynamic change should prompt urgent communication and assessment for vascular injury, bleeding, coronary occlusion, tamponade, annular rupture, or valve malposition; advanced support may be needed.

Conduction injury, including AV block, may require immediate or postoperative pacing. Risk is higher with baseline conduction abnormalities and is reported more commonly with CoreValve than Sapien in the reviewed literature.

Valve migration, paravalvular leak, or coronary obstruction require procedural-team assessment and may need additional intervention. The available sources do not establish a single anesthetic response for these events.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TEE-guided cardioversion uses transesophageal imaging before nonemergent direct-current cardioversion (DCCV) to assess for intracardiac thrombus, including left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus. For AF lasting longer than 48 hours, the cited review describes oral anticoagulation for at least three weeks before and four weeks after electrical cardioversion, or TOE to exclude LAA thrombus if the patient is not anticoagulated.

The anesthetic priority is to provide adequate conditions for probe insertion and examination while maintaining ventilation and oxygenation; sedation depth for TEE and the shock should be tailored to the patient and procedure. Sources describe both carefully monitored moderate sedation for TEE and deep sedation or general anesthesia for cardioversion.

Important immediate hazards include apnea or airway obstruction, aspiration, and TEE-related pharyngeal or esophageal injury. Cardioversion also warrants readiness for hypotension or bradycardia and possible post-shock pacing.

After anesthesia, recovery priorities include monitoring oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness; confirm the post-cardioversion rhythm and provide an appropriate monitored recovery destination. The available sources do not establish a TEE-specific oral-intake or gag-reflex timetable.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: VT catheter ablation uses electroanatomic mapping and endocardial ablation; epicardial access may be needed when the substrate is not reachable endocardially. Mapping strategy depends in part on whether VT is inducible and hemodynamically tolerated.

VT ablation is usually performed under general anesthesia (GA) or monitored anesthesia care (MAC), depending on the patient and operator. GA is preferred for prolonged, complex procedures in patients with unstable rhythms or poor cardiopulmonary reserve; anesthetic choice can affect VT induction, electro-anatomic map quality, and catheter stability.

The dominant immediate hazard is hemodynamic compromise during sustained or induced VT; tamponade, vascular injury, and bleeding are additional procedural concerns. Anticipate the need for prompt recognition and escalation of support.

Recovery location and monitoring should reflect respiratory and hemodynamic status and support requirements. The available evidence does not establish routine ICU admission, extubation criteria, or a single post-procedure pathway for every VT ablation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Ablation may target scar-related reentry or a focal source. Endocardial and, when indicated, epicardial approaches are used; non-ischemic scar may extend into mid-myocardial or epicardial tissue and may require strategies beyond endocardial ablation.

When VT is inducible and tolerated, activation and entrainment mapping may be performed during VT. For unstable or difficult-to-induce VT, substrate mapping can identify targets without relying on repeated VT induction.
Epicardial access is a selected approach, not an assumed component of every case. Planning may use CT to assess a needle trajectory; epicardial access carries risk of injury to adjacent structures.

bullets: Review the cardiomyopathy and available cardiac imaging to understand scar distribution, ventricular function, and procedural risk. The review describes contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI as a key tool for scar characterization and planning.

Assess the likelihood that VT induction or sustained VT will be poorly tolerated. MCS may be considered for selected high-risk patients, using individualized assessment rather than a fixed ejection-fraction threshold.
Coordinate the anesthetic and electrophysiology plans before the procedure, including the anticipated mapping strategy and response to hemodynamic compromise.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Percutaneous LAA occlusion is performed through transseptal catheter access, with TEE or ICE and fluoroscopy guiding assessment, sizing, deployment, and confirmation of device position and seal.

Anesthetic technique varies: conventional procedures commonly use general anesthesia and tracheal intubation, while SGA or selected conscious-sedation approaches are described. TEE access and patient-specific airway and aspiration considerations matter when selecting a technique.

Use TEE to assess device position and pericardial effusion, and ensure trained staff are prepared to manage potential cardiac tamponade. Maintain close hemodynamic monitoring during device release to reduce the risk of device displacement.

Recovery priorities are assessment for effusion and device position, hemodynamic and access-site observation, and an explicit postimplant antithrombotic plan. Same-day discharge is reported in a small feasibility series, not established as a universal pathway.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For a superficial cutaneous abscess in an immunocompetent patient without complicating risks, incision and drainage under local anesthetic is generally sufficient; the procedure is the accepted treatment.

Anorectal abscesses require prompt drainage. Small superficial cases may be managed in a clinic or emergency department with local infiltration; deep, extensive, or higher-risk cases warrant management under anesthesia.
Procedural pain is a major practical concern. In anorectal disease, assess for systemic sepsis and comorbidity; patient comfort during drainage helps permit thorough examination of the cavity.
Recovery priorities include reassessing the wound, providing wound-care instructions and adequate analgesia, and applying postanesthesia monitoring standards when anesthesia care has been provided.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For superficial cutaneous abscesses, drainage is the central treatment; local anesthetic is generally sufficient only for the population specified in the review: immunocompetent patients without confounding risks.

For anorectal abscesses, select the setting and anesthetic support according to depth, extent, sepsis severity, and patient risk. The anorectal review advises an examination under anesthesia before drainage when feasible; it does not establish a universal anesthetic technique.

For anorectal drainage, the approach is anatomy-specific. The source describes lateral decubitus or knee-elbow positioning for outpatient perianal or ischiorectal drainage, and lithotomy, Lloyd-Davies, or prone jackknife for larger/deeper cases or EUA.

The anorectal review advises adequate drainage while avoiding sphincter injury and generally avoiding probing the cavity to identify a fistula tract; inflammation can create false tracts and probing can risk sphincter injury.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For anorectal disease, assess sepsis severity and perform a disease-specific history and examination, including perineal and digital rectal examination. Relevant history includes sphincter function, prior anorectal procedures, blood-thinner use, and personal or family history of inflammatory bowel disease.

The anorectal source recommends laboratory assessment including CBC, creatinine, inflammatory markers, blood glucose, and HbA1c. Diabetes and other immunocompromised states are identified as risk modifiers; this is not an anesthesia-specific testing protocol.
Consider occult, recurrent, or complex disease and Crohn disease where clinically relevant; the source recommends selective imaging rather than routine imaging for all patients.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The sources do not define a procedure-specific room configuration. Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic actually provided; the ASA standard applies to general, regional, and monitored anesthesia care.

During anesthesia, qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present, and oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature must be continually evaluated. Blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the stated standard.
For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The available abscess sources do not specify an airway device or a comparative anesthetic technique. Airway management should therefore not be inferred from the procedure name alone; technique selection remains dependent on the individual case and the intended level of anesthesia.

If general anesthesia is used, assess ventilation continually; when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, with quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis through transfer preparation as specified by the standard.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Plan for substantial procedural pain, particularly during cavity exploration and disruption of loculations. Local anesthetic can be less effective within the acidic abscess environment; the review describes perimeter infiltration as an advocated approach, not a proven universal regimen.

For anorectal drainage, the source describes saline irrigation and hemostasis by direct pressure, cautery, or lignocaine with adrenaline. These are reported procedural options, not an anesthesia-specific protocol.

Routine packing is not recommended by the anorectal source unless needed for hemostasis; it reports increased pain and no benefit in healing or fistula formation. The older superficial cutaneous review notes that evidence for packing is lacking, so do not treat its case-specific packing choice as a standard.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anorectal abscess may be associated with sepsis, perineal cellulitis, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, or Fournier gangrene. The source supports prompt recognition and severity-based timing, but does not provide an anesthesia resuscitation algorithm.

Postoperative anorectal complications include hemorrhage, urinary retention, surgical-site infection, sphincter-related incontinence, pudendal nerve injury, and anal stricture. Escalation and management details are not specified in the supplied source.

Fistula assessment requires caution: the source notes that probing amid inflammation and induration can create false tracts and risk sphincter injury; primary fistulotomy is described as controversial and dependent on anatomy and expertise.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The anorectal source describes local hemostatic measures but provides no fluid regimen, blood-loss thresholds, transfusion guidance, or intraoperative physiologic targets. No universal fluid or blood-management prescription can be derived from these sources.

sources.label: Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthesia is important to procedural comfort, but the evidence review found no randomized trials then evaluating optimal pain control for superficial cutaneous abscess I&D. Its cited local-anesthetic approaches are based on textbooks or expert opinion, not comparative proof.

After anorectal drainage, provide adequate analgesia and wound-care instructions; the source does not specify an analgesic drug or regimen. PONV prevention or treatment is not addressed in the abscess-specific sources.

sources.label: Evidence-based approach to abscess management
Anorectal Abscess — StatPearls [Internet], NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The abscess sources do not establish emergence timing or a recovery-room protocol. After anesthesia care, use an appropriate postanesthesia-care area, transport monitoring/support appropriate to condition, and continual recovery evaluation.

During the initial phase of recovery from anesthesia, the ASA standard requires a quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry. Continue observation appropriate to the patient’s condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.
For anorectal wound care, the source advises absorbent dressings, hygiene, sitz baths, adequate analgesia, and follow-up until healing; it notes healing may take up to eight weeks.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The superficial cutaneous abscess article is an older evidence-based narrative review focused mainly on immunocompetent patients without confounding risks. It is not an anesthesia reference and reports no anesthesia-specific assessment or airway protocol.

The anorectal source is an educational review, not an anesthesia guideline; it supplies procedural and disease-management details but does not specify anesthetic regimens, monitoring standards, or emergence guidance. Its anorectal recommendations should not be generalized to all soft-tissue sites.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia-care sources provide general standards, not abscess-specific anesthetic choices. The supplied ERAS material concerns major gastrointestinal surgery and does not provide procedure-specific recommendations relevant to abscess I&D.
Comparative anesthetic technique, drug choice, airway strategy for complex cases, and PONV management are not established by the supplied abscess-specific evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Appendectomy may be performed laparoscopically or open. General anesthesia is commonly used for laparoscopy to support ventilation during CO₂ insufflation; neuraxial techniques have been reported in selected patients, but the available studies do not establish them as routine alternatives.

For laparoscopy, insufflation and positioning can alter pulmonary mechanics, CO₂ clearance, venous return, and hemodynamics. Priorities are appropriate ventilation and monitoring, attention to positioning, and prompt recognition of deterioration.

An endotracheal tube is preferred for laparoscopic surgery in the supplied educational review; insufflation and position changes can affect tube position, cuff pressure, and ventilation. Airway choice and ventilation should reflect the procedure and patient rather than a universal rule.

Recovery priorities include multimodal pain control, PONV prevention, appropriate PACU observation, and confirmation of adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: This reference covers adult appendectomy performed laparoscopically or open. The supplied material supports general anesthesia as a usual approach for laparoscopy; open appendectomy is also described under general or spinal anesthesia in a small cohort. These sources do not establish a preferred anesthetic for every patient or operative approach.

Neuraxial anesthesia has been studied or reported for appendectomy, but the laparoscopic randomized study was small and largely involved healthy patients. Its findings should not be generalized to complicated disease or higher-risk patients as proof of equivalent routine care.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the patient’s medical status and develop an anesthesia plan in context of the intended operation and the patient’s condition. The available sources do not provide an appendectomy-specific preoperative assessment protocol or a universal risk-stratification scheme.

Complicated appendicitis, obesity, and coexisting disease warrant particular attention when considering whether evidence from selected neuraxial studies applies. The laparoscopic study excluded patients with ASA status III or higher and had few perforated cases; it does not supply a validated aspiration-risk or urgency algorithm.
The cited laparoscopic appendectomy trial excluded pregnant patients; the supplied sources do not provide pregnancy-specific appendectomy anesthetic recommendations.

sources.label: Basic Standards for Preanesthesia Care
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic appendectomy, anticipate CO₂ insufflation. Positioning is not universal: the cited trial used Trendelenburg with a 15° turn, while other laparoscopic procedures may use different positions; insufflation and positioning can have hemodynamic and pulmonary effects.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring, including ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. For general anesthesia, the ASA standards specify continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart rate determination at least every five minutes, and continual ventilation evaluation.
Consider additional hemodynamic monitoring according to patient status and anticipated needs; the laparoscopic review gives examples but does not make invasive monitoring routine for appendectomy.

sources.label: Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The laparoscopic review describes general anesthesia as standard for ventilatory support and favors an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway. This supports a common approach, not a rule that every appendectomy or every patient requires intubation.

During insufflation or position changes, reassess ventilation and airway-device position as clinically indicated; the review describes possible endobronchial migration, increased cuff pressure, and atelectasis. Maintain expired CO₂ monitoring during general anesthesia unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.

The review describes lung-protective ventilation and adjustment of minute ventilation for CO₂ absorption, but specific settings should be individualized to respiratory mechanics and clinical context rather than treated as appendectomy-specific targets.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can increase systemic vascular resistance and cardiac filling pressures while IVC compression can reduce preload and venous return. Peritoneal stretch may provoke vagal bradyarrhythmias; hypercarbia may contribute to tachyarrhythmias and acidosis-related cardiovascular effects.

CO₂ absorption and cephalad diaphragmatic displacement can impair pulmonary compliance and promote ventilation/perfusion mismatch. Follow ventilation and oxygenation throughout insufflation and position changes, and communicate with the surgical team if physiology deteriorates.

The supplied material does not establish appendectomy-specific intraoperative targets or a universal insufflation-pressure strategy. Individualize management to physiology and coordinate changes in insufflation or positioning with the procedural team.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Potential laparoscopic hazards include vagal events at insufflation, impaired respiratory mechanics, airway-device changes, and access-related solid-organ injury or hemorrhage. Recognize evolving instability and coordinate prompt evaluation with the surgical team; the supplied review does not provide an appendectomy-specific rescue algorithm.

Subcutaneous emphysema or capnothorax may present with crepitus, rising airway pressures, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia. The review describes stopping insufflation as often followed by resolution in some cases and notes that significant cases may require further intervention; escalation depends on the clinical situation.

The case fields identify conversion to open surgery as a concern, but the supplied appendectomy study does not establish its frequency: all operations in that small study were completed laparoscopically. Be prepared to adapt the anesthetic to changes in operative approach without assuming conversion will occur.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Spinal/epidural block as an alternative to general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy: a prospective randomized clinical study

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, while warning that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg. Do not infer a fixed fluid volume for appendectomy from the supplied material.

Access-related hemorrhage is a recognized laparoscopic hazard, and limited visualization may make injury less apparent. Assess perfusion and suspected blood loss in context; the sources provide no appendectomy-specific transfusion threshold or hemorrhage protocol.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Laparoscopic pain may include somatic port-site pain and visceral pain from peritoneal stretch or tissue manipulation. The educational review describes multimodal nonopioid analgesia and port-site local anesthetic as options; tailor technique to the patient and operation.

PONV prevention is a relevant recovery priority in laparoscopy. The supplied material supports prophylactic antiemetic use but does not establish a single drug combination or regimen for all patients.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring when available and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; the cited ASA guideline overview recommends a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9. This does not apply to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide PACU or equivalent care after anesthesia, with continued assessment appropriate to the patient’s condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Handoff and documentation are part of the postanesthesia standards.

Monitor for pain, PONV, and residual neuromuscular weakness as applicable. The appendectomy sources report postoperative outcomes, but do not provide a universal discharge threshold or a procedure-specific PACU protocol.

sources.label: New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific laparoscopic anesthesia source is a small randomized study comparing general with combined spinal/epidural anesthesia in selected adults; its authors caution about limited perforated cases, obesity, complicated appendicitis, and generalizability. It is not a practice guideline.

The open-appendectomy comparison is a small, single-center, nonrandomized cohort restricted to adults with ASA I or II status and immediate recovery outcomes. Its observed comparisons do not establish a universal anesthetic choice.

The laparoscopic and robotic surgery review supplies general physiologic and perioperative context rather than appendectomy-specific recommendations; ASA standards support basic monitoring and postanesthesia care, while the neuromuscular-blockade source applies only when such drugs are used.

Appendicitis-specific decisions for perforation or sepsis, including aspiration-risk assessment, antimicrobial selection, and coordinated perioperative management, are not resolved by the supplied sources.

Comparing the Quality of Patient Recovery After Open Appendectomy Under General Versus Spinal Anesthesia: Prospective Cohort Study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The cited review addresses colorectal surgery and covers open and laparoscopic approaches, including laparoscopic-assisted surgery and possible conversion to open surgery. The supplied procedure-specific evidence is colorectal-focused; its applicability to small-bowel resection is not established.

Priorities include maintaining perfusion and oxygenation, individualized fluid and electrolyte management, and normothermia. Avoid assuming one fluid volume or a single anesthetic technique for all cases.

Obstruction, perforation, malnutrition, anemia, electrolyte disturbance, and comorbidity can materially alter perioperative risk. Routine mechanical bowel preparation is generally discouraged, with a reported rectal-resection/diverting-stoma exception.

Recovery priorities include opioid-sparing analgesia where appropriate, early feeding and mobilization within the care pathway, and surveillance for ileus, infection, respiratory complications, and anastomotic problems.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The available procedure-specific review addresses colorectal operations for malignant, inflammatory, ischemic, diverticular, traumatic, and obstructive conditions. It includes open and laparoscopic approaches; laparoscopy may require conversion to open surgery.

Stoma planning is relevant when a diverting or permanent stoma is anticipated; the review supports preoperative enterostomal education and site marking. The need for anastomosis, diversion, or other operative details is not established by these anesthesia sources.

Do not assume routine mechanical bowel preparation. The colorectal review discourages routine preparation; the rectal/pelvic review describes a qualified exception for rectal resection with diverting stoma, reflecting a procedure-specific unresolved issue.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess and address anemia, electrolyte imbalance, nutritional deficiency—particularly hypoalbuminemia—and weight loss when clinical urgency allows. Poor nutritional status is associated with increased postoperative complications.

For urgent obstruction or perforation, assess physiological deterioration and consider sepsis and hypovolemia; the review identifies history, examination, monitored parameters, blood gas analysis, and serum electrolytes as inputs to severity assessment.

Identify and optimize relevant comorbidities, including cardiac and respiratory disease; the colorectal review notes these are common. Elective fitness assessment may include functional reserve evaluation, but no single risk score or test is a universal requirement in the supplied sources.

For elective rectal/pelvic surgery, clear fluids are permitted up to 2 hours and solid food up to 6 hours before induction. A clear fluid containing complex carbohydrates 2 hours before anesthesia is recommended unless aspiration risk is increased, such as with bowel obstruction.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG is displayed during anesthesia, and blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every five minutes.

Position carefully and maintain positioning during laparoscopic surgery. The review notes reported brachial plexus injury and lower-limb compartment syndrome after laparoscopic large-bowel surgery; this supports attention to positioning, not a particular position or positioning device.

Maintain temperature monitoring and active thermoregulation as appropriate; normothermia is described as standard care in colon surgery. The sources do not establish a case-specific room configuration, vascular-access plan, or routine arterial-line indication.
Avoid routine nasogastric tube placement in colorectal surgery according to both perioperative reviews; this is not a prohibition when a clinical indication exists.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The supplied colorectal review does not specify an airway device or airway-management technique, and the rectal/pelvic review likewise gives no airway device or technique. Therefore, these sources do not establish routine intubation, rapid-sequence induction, or a ventilation regimen for every resection.

If general anesthesia is provided, follow applicable monitoring standards, including continual ventilation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. The source provides monitoring standards, not a bowel-resection ventilation prescription.

Aspiration risk is specifically raised for bowel obstruction in the rectal/pelvic review, but the supplied evidence does not define an induction method or thresholds for selecting one. Individual airway planning remains necessary.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The review's central anesthetic priorities are to minimize stress responses, maintain systemic and colonic blood flow and oxygenation, manage fluids and electrolytes carefully, provide multimodal analgesia, and limit postoperative gut dysfunction.

Hemodynamic optimization and goal-directed management are discussed as approaches associated with fewer gastrointestinal complications; the review describes a range of possible endpoints rather than a single target.

Prevent hypothermia with active thermoregulation in open and laparoscopic surgery. The review associates hypothermia with an exaggerated stress response and immune suppression; the rectal/pelvic review also links it with wound infection, cardiac ischemia, and bleeding.
No specific anesthetic agent is recommended by the colorectal review. Comparative findings are mixed and do not establish a preferred volatile or intravenous technique for routine practice.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant postoperative concerns include ileus and impaired bowel function, infectious complications, and anastomotic leakage. These are risks to recognize and assess in context; the supplied reviews do not provide a case-specific diagnostic or treatment algorithm.

Opioids can inhibit bowel motility and contribute to nausea, vomiting, and constipation, potentially delaying bowel recovery and oral intake. Consider opioid-sparing strategies within the patient's surgical and analgesic context.
For laparoscopic cases, maintain positioning and remain alert to positioning-related injury; the cited reports establish a hazard, not its incidence or a specific prevention protocol.

In PACU or an equivalent recovery location, continually evaluate the patient, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Escalation should follow the patient's findings and local clinical pathways; no bowel-specific emergency algorithm is supplied.

sources.label: Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize perioperative fluid therapy to maintenance needs, losses, and pathophysiological changes of major bowel surgery. The colorectal review explicitly gives no fixed fluid formula.

Optimize fluid balance and avoid fluid excess; the rectal/pelvic review describes targeting cardiac output and allowing vasopressors for arterial hypotension. This does not establish a universal fluid total or perfusion target.

The colorectal review describes restrictive postoperative fluid therapy as beneficial and cautions against excess fluid used solely to correct vasodilator-related hypotension. Interpret this alongside the need to maintain perfusion and individualize therapy.

Bowel surgery can involve fluid deficit in urgent presentations and changes in colonic blood flow related to volume status, hemorrhage, and sepsis. The sources provide no transfusion threshold, blood-loss estimate, or universal blood-preparation protocol.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For open colorectal surgery, thoracic epidural analgesia is recommended in the review and is associated with better gastrointestinal recovery. Its suitability depends on the patient, operation, and overall analgesic plan.

For laparoscopic surgery, evidence is insufficient to identify one preferred postoperative analgesic method. Epidural, systemic or intrathecal techniques, wound approaches, and TAP block are described, but the source reports limited or conflicting evidence for some comparisons.

Acetaminophen/paracetamol and NSAIDs are described as components of multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. The colorectal review notes concern about increased anastomotic-leak risk with COX-2 inhibitors; it does not justify treating all NSAIDs as interchangeable or universally appropriate.

Assess PONV risk and use prophylaxis according to risk. The rectal/pelvic review recommends prophylactic antiemetic treatment for patients with two or more identified risk factors; this is a review recommendation, not a universal regimen.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The colorectal review does not establish a specific extubation protocol. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site.

Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location, with appropriate monitoring and continuing evaluation. A qualified anesthesia-care-team member accompanies transport and gives a verbal handoff on arrival.

Recovery care should include attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Early oral feeding and mobilization are elements of enhanced recovery described in the rectal/pelvic review. Their application should follow the operative and patient-specific plan; the source does not define a universal pathway for all small- and large-bowel resections.

sources.label: Anesthesia and perioperative management of colorectal surgical patients – A clinical review (Part 1)
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The main procedure-specific source is a clinical review of colorectal surgery, published in 2012; it is not a dedicated small-bowel resection guideline. The rectal/pelvic ERAS review addresses elective rectal/pelvic surgery, not every bowel-resection population.

For laparoscopic colorectal surgery, the review reports insufficient evidence to recommend a specific postoperative analgesic method. It also states that there is no evidence to recommend specific anesthetic or analgesic agents for colorectal surgery.

The bowel-preparation sources do not fully agree: routine preparation is discouraged generally, while the rectal/pelvic review describes a possible exception for rectal resection with diverting stoma and notes the need for further study.

Case-specific airway, ventilation, drug-selection, and extubation protocols are not established by the procedure-specific sources. The available ASA materials provide general monitoring, postanesthesia-care, and neuromuscular-blockade guidance rather than bowel-resection-specific anesthetic recipes.
Workflow limitation: case-specific targets and protocols are not established in the available sources.

Best practice in major elective rectal/pelvic surgery: enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)
