overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The evidence covers image-guided needle sampling and localization as well as surgical excisional biopsy; it does not establish one anesthetic technique for the full range of breast operations. Excisional biopsy may be performed under local or general anesthesia.

Percutaneous biopsy is generally performed with local anesthesia. Bleeding, bruising, pain, infection, and vasovagal reactions are the relevant procedure-specific concerns described in the sources; these findings should not be assumed to quantify risk in larger operations.

For image-guided biopsy, positioning and access depend on the imaging modality and lesion. Do not infer routine operating-room positioning or airway management for lumpectomy or mastectomy from these percutaneous-procedure sources.

When anesthesia is given, apply general anesthesia monitoring and recovery standards as appropriate. The available sources do not establish a breast-surgery-specific fluid, analgesia, PONV, or recovery regimen.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Distinguish percutaneous sampling from surgical excision: image-guided FNS, CNB, and VAB sample tissue; excisional biopsy removes the lesion. Do not treat their anesthetic requirements as interchangeable.

Preoperative localization is used for nonpalpable lesions requiring surgery. The source describes wire localization, carbon marking, radiotracer injection, and radioactive or magnetic seeds; localization method and coordination are procedure-specific.

Percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy is performed supine or in a decubitus/lateral position; MRI-guided VAB is performed prone. These are image-guided procedure positions, not evidence for the position used in an operating-room breast operation.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Breast Biopsy Procedure Toolkit: Ultrasound, 2D Stereotactic, 3D Tomosynthesis, and MRI-Guided Procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For percutaneous breast biopsy, explain the reason for the procedure, devices used, and possible adverse events, side effects, and complications; verify allergies to local anesthetic drugs. Local anesthesia is administered for CNB and VAB; it is optional for FNS.

Review bleeding history and antiplatelet or anticoagulant use for biopsy; decisions about interruption should be made with the prescribing physician and local guidance. The supplied sources do not establish a medication plan for breast surgery.

For MRI-guided biopsy, screen for MRI contraindications, relevant implants, prior contrast reactions, and renal impairment. This is specific to the MRI procedure and does not substitute for a broader anesthetic assessment.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Breast Biopsy Procedure Toolkit: Ultrasound, 2D Stereotactic, 3D Tomosynthesis, and MRI-Guided Procedures

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For image-guided procedures, positioning and equipment depend on modality: mammography/tomosynthesis may use prone or upright systems, while MRI biopsy uses a dedicated breast coil and prone positioning. These descriptions do not establish operating-room setup for excision.

For any anesthetic, use appropriate monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ASA standards also require ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

When general anesthesia is delivered with an anesthesia machine, the cited ASA standard specifies oxygen analysis with a low-oxygen alarm and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not establish an airway device, general-anesthetic technique, or ventilation strategy for lumpectomy or mastectomy. Select technique for the actual procedure and patient; do not infer an LMA-versus-ETT rule from the supplied evidence.

If an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is used, ASA standards require verification of placement clinically and by identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas, with continual quantitative end-tidal carbon dioxide analysis through removal or transfer.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging
Breast Biopsy Procedure Toolkit: Ultrasound, 2D Stereotactic, 3D Tomosynthesis, and MRI-Guided Procedures
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For percutaneous core biopsy, tell the patient about the firing noise to reduce the chance of movement. The source describes sequential sampling for CNB and vacuum-assisted sampling without removing the needle for VAB.

Vasovagal reactions are a procedure-specific concern, reported more often with upright biopsy systems than dedicated prone tables. This evidence concerns biopsy positioning, not an anesthetic event rate for breast surgery.
The supplied sources do not describe physiologic targets or phase-specific anesthetic management for lumpectomy or mastectomy.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For percutaneous biopsy, common reported effects include minor pain and bruising; larger hematoma or infection is uncommon in the cited review. Do not transfer these rates to excisional surgery.

Bleeding after biopsy is usually self-limited or managed with manual compression; severe bleeding requiring surgery is described as very rare. The source does not provide a surgical-mastectomy bleeding protocol.

A very rare chest-wall injury, including pneumothorax, is described with free-hand or ultrasound-guided biopsy; the source notes risk is practically null with mammography- or MRI-guided biopsy. This is a modality-specific hazard, not a general operative risk estimate.

sources.label: Image-guided breast biopsy and localisation: recommendations for information to women and referring physicians by the European Society of Breast Imaging

bullets: The image-guided biopsy sources provide no IV-fluid regimen or intraoperative fluid-management guidance. They do not establish fluid volumes, blood-loss expectations, or transfusion criteria for lumpectomy or mastectomy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Laparoscopic diagnostic procedures and adhesiolysis use abdominal insufflation; general anesthesia is the usual approach in the general laparoscopic-surgery reference, with an endotracheal tube preferred when higher ventilatory pressures or PEEP may be needed.

Prioritize ventilation and hemodynamic assessment as pneumoperitoneum and positioning can impair respiratory mechanics, alter venous return and filling pressures, and provoke hypercarbia-related effects.

Remain alert to access-related injury or hemorrhage, vagal bradyarrhythmia at insufflation, and respiratory or hemodynamic changes suggesting gas-related complications; escalate promptly when deterioration occurs.
Plan recovery around oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; address PONV and pain, and assess residual neuromuscular blockade before extubation if a blocker was used.

bullets: This reference concerns abdominal laparoscopy, including diagnostic procedures and possible adhesiolysis. The available general anesthesia source addresses laparoscopic and robotic surgery broadly, not this operation’s specific operative steps or adhesiolysis technique.

bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the patient and technique. For anesthesia, ECG display is continuous and blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standards.

bullets: The broad laparoscopic-surgery reference describes general anesthesia as standard and prefers an ETT when higher pressures or PEEP may be required. This is not evidence that every short diagnostic procedure has an identical airway requirement.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: At insufflation, anticipate changes in venous return, intrathoracic pressure, and cardiac filling pressures. Peritoneal stretch may trigger vagal bradyarrhythmia; monitor closely during initiation and respond to clinically significant instability.
CO₂ absorption can produce hypercarbia and acidosis, with cardiovascular effects; monitor ventilation and end-tidal CO₂ and reassess when the clinical trajectory is unexpected.

Pneumoperitoneum, lung compression, and Trendelenburg can worsen atelectasis and airway pressures. Interpret pressures in context of chest-wall and lung mechanics rather than treating a single pressure value as a universal target.

bullets: Consider access-related organ injury or hemorrhage when instability or unexpected findings arise; limited visualization can obscure injury. The sources do not give an adhesiolysis-specific injury or conversion protocol.

The review lists findings and describes management ranging from observation to decompression or surgery depending on the case; it does not provide a universal response algorithm.
Recognize insufflation-associated vagal bradyarrhythmia and hypercarbia-related cardiovascular effects; promptly assess the patient and coordinate with the surgical team when instability develops.

bullets: Percutaneous feeding access may be placed into the stomach by PEG or an interventional-radiology approach, or into the jejunum; surgical jejunostomy has open, laparoscopic, and other approaches. Enteral access is considered when oral intake is inadequate or unsuitable. Relevant concerns include aspiration risk, anatomy that may make access difficult, coagulopathy, ascites, and prior gastric or abdominal surgery.

Important procedural hazards include bleeding, infection, and injury to adjacent organs; aspiration and tube-related complications also matter. Avoid assuming that transillumination, a particular airway technique, or general anesthesia applies to every approach.

bullets: Laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair generally combines reduction/mobilization, hiatal closure and fundoplication. A 360° Nissen is common, but motility findings can inform selection of a partial wrap.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can increase SVR and filling pressures, reduce venous return through IVC compression, and produce hypercarbia-related cardiovascular effects. The net response varies with position, volume status and patient factors.

Peritoneal stretch may cause a vagal response and bradyarrhythmia; hypercarbia can produce tachyarrhythmia and acidosis-related effects. Recognize a temporal relationship to insufflation or traction and communicate promptly with the surgeon.

Dissection around the hiatus and mediastinum places the pleura, esophagus, stomach, spleen and vagus nerve at risk. Surgical sources emphasize careful mobilization and protection of the vagus and spleen.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Capnothorax is a recognized laparoscopic antireflux complication. Consider it with rising airway pressure, hypoxemia or hypercapnia, unequal chest expansion or related signs; the general review describes a range of responses from observation to decompression or surgery according to severity.

Pleural rupture is described as common in the procedure-specific technical account, which says thoracic drainage is usually unnecessary and mentions positive-pressure lung recruitment at the end of surgery. This does not establish a universal response; assess the clinical effect and coordinate with the surgeon.

Bleeding or visceral injury may occur during access, reduction or fundus mobilization. Limited laparoscopic visualization can obscure access injury; surgical guidance emphasizes gentle dissection and prompt conversion for uncontrolled bleeding.

sources.label: Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No hiatal-repair-specific fluid regimen, hemodynamic target or transfusion threshold is provided. The general laparoscopic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed administration, while cautioning that conventional measures such as urine output can be poor volume surrogates during pneumoperitoneum.

Expect generally limited blood loss but remain alert to splenic, hepatic or access-related injury; the procedure-specific source notes that uncontrolled bleeding may require conversion. There is no source-supported routine crossmatch or blood-loss estimate.

sources.label: Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Pain may arise from port sites and visceral manipulation. The general laparoscopic review describes multimodal analgesia, including acetaminophen, NSAIDs and port-site local anesthetic, as opioid-sparing options; the procedure-specific source reports pain is often mild but provides no regimen.

Laparoscopy increases PONV risk, so provide risk-informed prophylaxis and treatment. The available evidence does not support a mandatory number or specific combination of antiemetics for every patient.

Assess postoperative swallowing and bloating. Dysphagia is often transient; Nissen is associated with gas bloat and impaired ability to belch or vomit, which may affect counseling and symptom interpretation.

Laparoscopic hernioplasty of hiatal hernia - PMC - NIH
Hiatal Hernia – StatPearls

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied procedure-specific sources do not define an emergence or extubation technique. Avoid presenting deep extubation, a particular drug, or a specific cough-suppression method as established case-specific practice.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, ASA guideline recommendations summarized by APSF support quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide monitored postanesthesia care with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature; assess for PONV, dysphagia, gas bloat and respiratory complications. Diet advancement is surgical-protocol dependent.

bullets: The procedure-specific 2016 article is a technical letter, not an anesthesia reference or comparative study; its brief anesthesia description cannot establish an anesthetic regimen or outcome.

StatPearls is an educational clinical review, not an anesthesia source. Its operative and postoperative discussion informs procedure context, but it explicitly lacks airway, anesthetic, fluid and emergence guidance.
The laparoscopic/robotic review provides general physiologic and anesthetic context, not hiatal-repair-specific targets. Its recommendations should not be mistaken for a procedure-specific protocol.

The provided sources do not resolve case-specific aspiration/RSI decisions, optimal positioning despite conflicting descriptions, or an emergence strategy. These remain individualized decisions rather than universal requirements.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open anterior repair may be performed under local, regional, or general anesthesia; local anesthesia is a supported option for open repair. Minimally invasive repair is generally performed under general anesthesia.
Approach selection depends on patient factors and surgical expertise. Laparoscopic approaches can assess and repair bilateral hernias and may be useful after a prior open repair.

For minimally invasive surgery, prioritize the physiologic effects of CO₂ insufflation and positioning: changes in ventilation and airway pressures, hemodynamics, and risks related to patient position.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, pain control, ambulation, and assessment for urinary retention; if neuromuscular blockade is used, confirm adequate recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open anterior repair is an option for local anesthesia; the review specifically encourages local anesthesia for open anterior repairs. General or regional anesthesia are also described options, without a complete protocol for any technique.

Laparoscopic TAPP and TEP are the described minimally invasive approaches; robotic-assisted repair follows similar principles and commonly uses a robotic TAPP approach. The supplied sources describe general anesthesia for minimally invasive repair.

Approach is a surgical-anesthetic decision informed by comorbidities, BMI, recurrence, bilaterality, and surgeon proficiency. Laparoscopy can access both sides and may use a different tissue plane after a prior open repair.

sources.label: Current options in inguinal hernia repair in adult patients
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess whether the patient can undergo general anesthesia and tolerate insufflation if minimally invasive repair is planned. Adhesions, prior radiation, ascites, large inguinoscrotal hernia, and incarcerated or strangulated hernia may increase difficulty or risk.

Clarify prior repair and planned approach. Recurrence after prior minimally invasive repair generally favors open repair in the cited review; approach remains dependent on surgical expertise and circumstances.

Incarceration or strangulation warrants heightened procedural planning: the review identifies these as factors that can complicate minimally invasive repair and lead to conversion. The supplied sources do not establish a universal aspiration or rapid-sequence induction protocol for this situation.

sources.label: Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For minimally invasive repair, prepare for laparoscopic or robotic equipment and coordinate positioning with the surgeon. The patient is described as supine; robotic-assisted repair uses Trendelenburg before docking.
Protect pressure points and the face, secure the patient against sliding, and account for restricted access after robotic docking. The table must not move while the robot is docked.

Use standard anesthesia monitoring. ASA standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

sources.label: Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is the described usual approach for minimally invasive repair. For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, an endotracheal tube is preferred over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; the hernia review itself does not specify an airway device.
Insufflation and position changes can alter respiratory mechanics and tube position. Reassess ventilation and airway pressures when these conditions change.

Ventilation may require adjustment for CO₂ absorption and reduced compliance during pneumoperitoneum. The general laparoscopic review describes a lung-protective approach and an end-tidal CO₂ goal, but these are not hernia-specific prescriptions and require clinical individualization.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pneumoperitoneum can increase systemic vascular resistance and filling pressures while inferior vena cava compression may reduce venous return. Interpret hemodynamic changes in the context of insufflation and position.

CO₂ absorption and diaphragmatic displacement reduce pulmonary compliance and functional residual capacity; atelectasis and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may follow. Trendelenburg can worsen these effects.

Be alert to bradyarrhythmia at insufflation onset from vagal response and tachyarrhythmia with hypercarbia. Recognize a significant change and escalate with the surgical team; the available sources do not establish a case-specific treatment algorithm.

Surgical hazards include injury to vessels, nerves, bladder, or bowel during access, dissection, or reduction. The minimally invasive review emphasizes careful dissection and avoidance of nerve- and vessel-containing regions.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider airway or pulmonary complications when airway pressures rise, oxygenation worsens, or ventilation changes after insufflation or repositioning; the laparoscopic review describes endobronchial migration, tube obstruction, and atelectasis.

Subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax are recognized insufflation-related hazards. The source describes crepitus and respiratory or hemodynamic changes as warning features; significant cases require close monitoring and escalation.

Vascular or visceral injury may be difficult to identify because access and limited visualization can obscure bleeding. Conversion to open surgery may be required for injury or difficult dissection, including incarceration or strangulation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Minimally Invasive Inguinal Hernia Repair

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic review supports balanced crystalloid and goal-directed administration, while cautioning that excess fluid may contribute to facial, pharyngeal, or laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg.

Potential hemorrhage includes injury during needle or port access; assess perfusion in context because common bedside measures may be unreliable during pneumoperitoneum. The supplied sources do not establish a hernia-specific fluid total or transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For open repair, local anesthesia is described as suitable. Local and regional anesthesia are described as providing preemptive analgesia and a more comfortable postoperative period; patients receiving either are reported to require fewer postoperative analgesics than those receiving general anesthesia. The review provides no complete anesthetic protocol.

For laparoscopic approaches, pain may arise from port sites and visceral tissue manipulation. A multimodal strategy and port-site local anesthetic are described options; the supplied review gives no specific drug doses.
Laparoscopy is an independent PONV risk factor; prophylactic antiemetic administration is recommended in the general laparoscopic review.

sources.label: Current options in inguinal hernia repair in adult patients
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

After anesthesia, provide postanesthesia care with monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Assess pain, ambulation, and urinary retention during recovery; urinary retention is specifically associated with spinal anesthesia in the hernia review. No case-specific discharge criteria are provided.

title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)
aliases: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lower-extremity amputation may be performed under general or regional anesthesia; the choice is individualized. Regional techniques include neuraxial anesthesia and peripheral nerve blocks, but the available sources do not establish a single preferred technique for every patient or amputation level.

The dominant risk context is substantial comorbidity—particularly peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, cardiac disease, renal impairment, and infection. Assess physiologic reserve and the urgency of source control when selecting an anesthetic approach.

Regional anesthesia can support analgesia and may reduce some perioperative morbidity, but comparative findings are mixed and do not establish a mortality benefit. Consider block coverage, tourniquet use, contraindications, and the risk of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity.

Recovery priorities include adequate acute stump pain control, surveillance for hemodynamic and wound complications, and attention to phantom limb pain. Use postanesthesia monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Amputation level and staging depend on tissue viability, infection, and whether adequate bone coverage can be obtained. A staged open amputation may be used for source control in septic shock; a single-stage operation may be suitable when the patient and soft tissues permit.

The reviewed regional approaches are level- and coverage-dependent. For BKA, adductor-canal saphenous and popliteal sciatic blocks are described; the review cautions that tourniquet ischemic pain and discomfort limit their use as the sole anesthetic.

For AKA, comprehensive peripheral block coverage may involve femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, sciatic, and obturator nerves. The review notes added time, local-anesthetic exposure, and toxicity risk with multiple blocks; these descriptions are not a universal technique recommendation.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, and functional reserve, and account for diabetes and preoperative infection as relevant comorbidities and risk factors in major lower-extremity amputation.

For diabetes and suspected infection, consider glycemic optimization and early antibiotic treatment as part of preoperative care. In PVD, the indication and level relate to nonhealing tissue when blood-flow restoration is not an option; assess healing potential and tissue condition rather than relying on one measure alone.

Review anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy and evaluate for coagulopathy or systemic infection before considering neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques. The review describes circumstances in urgent cases where neuraxial anesthesia may be avoided; it does not provide medication interruption intervals.

For traumatic injury, evaluate for concomitant life-threatening injuries, bleeding, and resuscitation needs. Discuss likely functional outcome and the risks of major amputation with the patient or designated advocates when circumstances allow.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The chapter describes supine positioning and use of an appropriately sized tourniquet when appropriate. Some patients have no vascular inflow, in which case a tourniquet is not necessary; protect the skin before application.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; temperature monitoring is required when clinically significant change is intended, anticipated, or suspected.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General or regional anesthesia are described options. The available procedure-specific sources do not establish an airway device, ventilation strategy, or universal sedation approach; select these according to the planned anesthetic and patient condition.

For general anesthesia, ASA monitoring standards require ongoing ventilation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by patient, procedure, or equipment. Verify endotracheal-tube or laryngeal-mask position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide when used.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect a high-risk cardiovascular population. One observational study summarized in the review found less intraoperative hypotension and vasopressor administration with regional anesthesia than with alternative modalities, but the regional group combined spinal anesthesia and peripheral blocks; this does not establish a technique-specific effect.

Consider tourniquet-related discomfort and ischemic pain when selecting regional coverage. The evidence describes stable hemodynamics in a small high-risk BKA study without a tourniquet, but does not establish that result for other patients or tourniquet conditions.
The surgical approach may be staged in unstable or septic patients to obtain source control; coordinate timing and anesthetic decisions with the surgical team as clinical status evolves.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Major concerns include cardiopulmonary complications, wound infection, prolonged ICU care, and revision. Risk context includes cardiac disease, renal impairment, infection, and proximal amputation; reported mortality varies by population and should not be treated as an individual prediction.

If stump pain persists, consider non-anesthetic causes as well as inadequate analgesia, including infection, wound dehiscence, reduced blood flow, osteomyelitis, hematoma, or inadequate tissue coverage.

Peripheral blocks require attention to coverage and local-anesthetic toxicity risk, especially when multiple nerves or substantial volumes are involved. The review’s case reports do not establish routine management for patients with sepsis, thrombocytopenia, or respiratory infection.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The sources do not establish a procedure-specific fluid regimen, transfusion threshold, or blood-ordering rule. Assess bleeding and resuscitation needs in the clinical context; the chapter specifically identifies hemostasis and adequate resuscitation for traumatic injuries.

The review summarizes studies associating regional anesthesia with reduced blood loss or transfusion in some settings, but the comparative evidence is mixed and does not provide a patient-specific estimate or mandate an anesthetic technique.
Perfusion and tissue viability inform level selection and healing potential; TcPO₂ may contribute to assessment but does not capture the whole patient or limb condition.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan acute stump analgesia before the anesthetic or block regresses. The review favors regional anesthesia for acute stump pain and describes multimodal planning, while noting that opioids alone may be insufficient; the sources do not establish one universal drug regimen.

For BKA, combined saphenous/adductor-canal and sciatic coverage is described for perioperative pain; continuous catheters may extend analgesia. Evidence for long-term prevention of phantom limb pain remains limited.

Discuss phantom limb pain and residual limb pain as distinct but potentially overlapping recovery problems. Early acute-pain-service involvement and a preemptive approach are emphasized in the review; no intervention is guaranteed to prevent chronic pain.

A retrospective BKA comparison reported lower pain scores, opioid use, and postoperative nausea and vomiting with combined femoral and sciatic blocks than with general anesthesia; this observational finding does not establish a universal technique choice.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not specify emergence or extubation criteria. For general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, apply quantitative recovery guidance; do not impose that requirement on cases without blockade.

After anesthesia, use PACU or equivalent care, including ICU when appropriate. Continue condition-appropriate monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; evaluate pain and the operative wound.

Provide a structured handoff covering the preoperative condition, surgical and anesthetic course, adverse events, blood loss and resuscitative measures, and the planned destination. A receiving clinician should accept responsibility before anesthesia-team departure.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia review is a narrative review focused on major lower-extremity amputation and regional anesthesia, especially peripheral nerve blocks; it is not a guideline or meta-analysis. Its summarized studies vary in design and population.

Comparative outcome evidence is unresolved: studies report possible morbidity advantages with regional techniques, while mortality findings are controversial. Many studies combine neuraxial and peripheral techniques, limiting technique-specific conclusions.

The StatPearls chapter is an educational surgical review rather than an anesthesia reference. ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards provide general requirements, not amputation-specific anesthetic plans.

The available sources do not resolve individualized airway/ventilation planning, anesthetic technique selection for a particular patient, or perioperative anticoagulant management for regional procedures.
The procedure-specific chapter does not specify vascular-access strategy or monitoring standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: This is emergency abdominal surgery for a potentially life-threatening intra-abdominal condition such as perforation. The operative approach is pathology- and patient-dependent; consider laparoscopy when appropriate rather than assuming an open operation.

Priorities are to recognize physiologic instability and sepsis, assess electrolyte and acid–base derangements, and anticipate regurgitation and aspiration risk associated with emergency abdominal disease.

When general anesthesia is required, manage the airway with the elevated aspiration risk in mind and select induction drugs to maintain hemodynamic stability. The sources do not establish a single mandatory induction drug or a universal RSI rule for every patient.

Recovery planning starts intraoperatively: maintain normothermia, reassess extubation suitability with the multidisciplinary team, and select postoperative care according to instability and ongoing support needs; ICU care is likely appropriate for many emergency-laparotomy patients.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The emergency-laparotomy guidance covers non-elective, potentially life-threatening intra-abdominal conditions, including perforation. It does not prescribe a single operation or surgical approach.

Approach selection is individualized to patient factors, pathology, imaging, and surgical expertise. Laparoscopy may be considered when appropriate; evidence associating it with better outcomes is largely observational and susceptible to confounding.

For critically ill patients unlikely to tolerate prolonged definitive surgery, damage-control strategies may control sepsis or hemorrhage and defer definitive management. Decisions are individualized; the guideline notes limited evidence and potential burdens of multiple operations and prolonged ICU care.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess for electrolyte and acid–base disturbances: the perforation-peritonitis source describes hypokalemia with chloride loss, hyperkalemia in hypotensive metabolic acidosis or renal insufficiency, and metabolic acidosis related to shock or reduced renal function. It identifies blood-gas and electrolyte assessment with correction as important.

Treat suspected or established sepsis and physiologic instability as major anesthetic risk modifiers. Emergency abdominal patients also have elevated aspiration risk associated with obstruction or distension, sepsis, opioids, and emergency surgery.
Consider intra-abdominal fungal infection in the clinical assessment; the perforation-peritonitis letter describes poor prognosis and advises early recognition, while noting nonspecific presentation.

The available sources do not provide a complete perforation-specific preoperative assessment or resuscitation protocol. Use clinical assessment and applicable local pathways rather than inferring required tests or a fixed optimization interval from this reference.

sources.label: Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis
Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Consider early arterial and/or central venous pressure catheters for physiologic assessment and titration or delivery of fluids and vasopressors; the guideline does not make either line universal.

Follow basic anesthetic monitoring standards: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and assess blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.
Measure core temperature and use active warming and warmed IV fluids to maintain normothermia. Record fluid balance during and after surgery.
The supplied sources do not specify a patient position or procedure-specific room arrangement; select these with the surgical team and the planned approach.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Emergency-laparotomy patients are at increased risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Where rapid-sequence induction/intubation is chosen, the consensus guideline supports a fast-acting neuromuscular blocker; it does not establish that RSI is mandatory for every individual or specify one induction agent.
If using controlled ventilation, the guideline recommends tidal volume based on predicted body weight and initial PEEP, with subsequent titration to flow-volume loops and clinical evaluation.

For general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas; continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to postoperative care.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Induction and ongoing anesthesia require attention to hemodynamic stability in patients with sepsis or other physiologic derangement. The sources advise selecting induction drugs to maintain stability but do not establish ketamine or another agent as universally preferred.

In sepsis present or suspected during emergency laparotomy, the guideline describes norepinephrine as the first-choice vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; epinephrine or vasopressin 0.03 U/min may be added to norepinephrine. Apply this guidance in context rather than as an automatic drug sequence.

Correct electrolyte disturbances throughout the perioperative period. The perforation-peritonitis letter links metabolic and electrolyte disturbances to arrhythmia, hemodynamic disturbance, and delayed recovery.

Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the guideline's pre-incision interval unless appropriate therapy is already underway; select and continue therapy according to local or national guidance, pathology, and operative contamination.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Maintain vigilance for aspiration and hemodynamic instability; if instability occurs, assess the patient's physiology and escalate support according to local emergency practice. The sources do not provide a perforation-specific collapse-resuscitation algorithm.
Consider acid–base and electrolyte derangements when evaluating arrhythmia or hemodynamic disturbance; shock and reduced renal function are described contributors to metabolic acidosis.

Prevent and detect hypothermia with temperature monitoring and active warming. At the end of surgery, evaluate extubation suitability in light of blood loss, ventilatory needs, acid–base status, temperature, and ongoing support requirements.
Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring when a neuromuscular blocker is used, and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: For emergency laparotomy, prefer balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline for resuscitation and intravascular volume maintenance; the guideline grades this as a weak recommendation based on low evidence and notes that evidence is inferred from other populations.

Individualize fluid boluses using objective measures of hypovolemia and avoid both volume overload and inadequate perfusion. The available guidance does not establish a fixed fluid volume for perforation cases.

Use a restrictive red-cell transfusion approach as the guideline recommends, with exceptions based on individual clinical status and comorbidities. Do not treat an unsupported fixed hemoglobin target as routine.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use an individualized multimodal analgesic plan, including acetaminophen and NSAIDs when not contraindicated; consider wound catheters or abdominal-wall blocks to reduce opioid demand.

Assess sepsis and coagulation abnormalities before considering thoracic epidural or spinal techniques. The emergency-laparotomy guideline advises individualized assessment rather than routine neuraxial placement.
Treat emergency-laparotomy patients as high risk for PONV and use multimodal prevention while minimizing triggers and opioid exposure.

To reduce ileus burden, consider opioid-sparing analgesia as part of a broader recovery strategy. The perforation-peritonitis letter also discusses epidural analgesia, but does not establish an emergent epidural as appropriate for every patient.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Make extubation a multidisciplinary end-of-surgery decision. Consider respiratory status, blood loss, temperature, acid–base condition, and ongoing fluid or hemodynamic support rather than relying on a single criterion.

Choose postoperative destination using preoperative risk, procedure impact, instability, and ongoing therapeutic or supportive needs. ICU care may be appropriate for many patients, but is not a universal disposition.

For postanesthesia transfer, provide appropriate monitoring and support, communicate the anesthetic and surgical course, and continue observation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature in the receiving area.
Consider nasogastric tubes individually, reassess their need daily, and remove as early as possible; routine postoperative use is not supported by the perforation-peritonitis letter.

sources.label: Consensus Guidelines for Perioperative Care for Emergency Laparotomy Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS®) Society Recommendations Part 2—Emergency Laparotomy: Intra- and Postoperative Care
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Anesthetic management for patients with perforation peritonitis

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most case-relevant source is an international emergency-laparotomy ERAS consensus guideline covering intra- and postoperative care; it includes perforation among indications but notes that much evidence is extrapolated and some emergency-laparotomy evidence is limited.

The perforation-peritonitis-specific source is a short letter to the editor, not a full protocol or primary clinical study. Use its metabolic, fungal-infection, transfusion, and postoperative-care discussion within those limits.

The supplied ERAS gastrointestinal reviews provide abstract-level or limited content rather than detailed case-specific recommendations. ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general standards, not perforation-specific treatment protocols.

Case-specific induction-agent preference, a universal RSI requirement, a fixed fluid prescription, and routine postoperative intubation are not established by the supplied evidence. Specific antimicrobial selection and a complete preoperative optimization pathway are also not provided here.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pilonidal surgery ranges from drainage of an acute abscess to definitive treatment of chronic disease. The operative approach matters: these sources describe local anesthesia for selected drainage and pit-picking procedures, and general anesthesia for the reviewed modified cleft-lift technique.
For definitive excision and closure, the review supports off-midline techniques over midline closure; it reports no evidence that one off-midline method is superior to the others.

Prone positioning is reported for the reviewed cleft-lift operation, but the surgical reviews provide no anesthesia-specific airway technique, physiologic targets, or complication-management protocol. Do not infer a routine airway or anesthetic recipe from them.

Recovery priorities in the available evidence are surgical wound healing and follow-up: open wounds can require prolonged healing and frequent dressing changes, while dehiscence and recurrence are reported after closure procedures.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Acute abscess management is distinct from definitive treatment of chronic sinus disease. The surgical review favors simple incision and drainage for an acute abscess; complete excision during acute swelling may create a very large wound defect.

Definitive options include excision with healing by secondary intention or closure. Midline primary suture is not recommended in the reviewed guidelines; off-midline closure options include Karydakis, cleft lift, and Limberg flap.

For the authors’ modified Bascom cleft lift, the described workflow uses general anesthesia and prone positioning with moderate waist flexion. This is a description of that technique, not a universal anesthetic requirement for pilonidal procedures.

bullets: Clarify whether the planned procedure is acute abscess drainage, a minimally invasive intervention, or definitive excision and closure; these are distinct approaches, and the sources do not provide one anesthesia plan applicable to all of them.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Port placement is typically performed through venous access using a Seldinger technique, with the catheter connected to a subcutaneous pocket; removal is mentioned in the evidence, but its technique is not described.

Anesthesia varies: local anesthesia or superficial cervical plexus block with intravenous sedoanalgesia has been studied, while another cohort reports general anesthesia. These sources do not establish one preferred technique.
Key procedural hazards include arterial puncture, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, and catheter malposition; guidewire and catheter position need attention during placement.
Recovery priorities include monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic, assessment for access-related complications, and confirmation of recovery status before discharge from postanesthesia care.

Rare serious access complications in the audit included pericardial or pleural placement with haemothorax and guidewire migration; these qualify possible hazards but do not establish routine treatment.
If a complication is suspected, maintain appropriate monitoring and escalate for procedural and medical assessment. The available sources do not provide a unified port-specific rescue algorithm.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robotic cholecystectomy is a minimally invasive upper-abdominal operation. General anesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is commonly described; robotic docking makes access and patient movement more constrained.

Key physiologic concerns are CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, impaired respiratory mechanics and hypercarbia, and reduced venous return in reverse Trendelenburg. Coordinate positioning, ventilation, and insufflation with the surgeon.

Plan access and escalation before docking, including a team-practiced robotic-cart removal drill. If neuromuscular blockade is used, coordinate its maintenance and reversal with the surgical team and assess recovery quantitatively before extubation.
Prioritize multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention, then monitor recovery for oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, nausea, and shoulder or port-site pain.

bullets: This is robotic-assisted laparoscopic gallbladder surgery; the supplied sources discuss laparoscopic cholecystectomy and robotic surgery broadly, not a dedicated robotic-cholecystectomy anesthetic protocol.
Robotic instrumentation and docking constrain movement and access; establish the surgical and anesthesia team’s communication and emergency cart-removal plan before the case.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess history, examination, functional status, and relevant cardiopulmonary and metabolic disease; optimize conditions where possible and plan airway and access before draping or docking restricts them.

Significant cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease warrants careful assessment and team judgment. The review identifies increased intracranial pressure as a reason to avoid laparoscopic surgery; these are general review statements, not a robotic-cholecystectomy selection rule.
Pregnancy requires individualized maternal and surgical assessment; the supplied review discusses laparoscopic cholecystectomy in pregnancy but does not establish a trimester-based rule.

sources.label: Do Small Incisions Need Only Minimal Anesthesia?—Anesthetic Management in Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Reverse Trendelenburg is commonly used for cholecystectomy. Anticipate reduced venous return and hypotension, particularly if intravascular volume is low; agree positioning and access arrangements with the surgeon before docking.
Pad pressure points and protect the face; robot arms and a docked system can restrict access, and the table should not be moved while docked.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring, including ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation, and capnography; monitor neuromuscular blockade when used. Consider advanced hemodynamic monitoring according to patient risk and procedure needs, not routinely.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is the approach described for laparoscopic surgery; an endotracheal tube is preferred in the educational reference to permit higher ventilation pressures and PEEP.

Pneumoperitoneum and positioning can impair compliance and increase ventilation requirements. Track ventilation and end-tidal CO₂; consider arterial CO₂ assessment when clinical circumstances make end-tidal values unreliable.
Recheck tube position when positioning or insufflation changes; cephalad movement of the diaphragm and carina can produce endobronchial migration.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation can cause vagal bradycardia from peritoneal stretch; hypercarbia and acidosis may contribute to tachyarrhythmia or impaired cardiac function. Communicate abrupt changes promptly with the surgeon and reassess insufflation and patient physiology.

Pneumoperitoneum and reverse Trendelenburg can reduce venous return while raising airway pressures and impairing respiratory mechanics. Follow gas exchange and hemodynamics through insufflation, position changes, and desufflation.

For robotic cases, immobility and timing of reversal require coordination with the surgeon. The sources differ on routine depth/continuation of blockade; use clinical judgment and quantitative monitoring if blockade is administered.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider tube migration, atelectasis, or impaired compliance with rising airway pressures or hypoxemia. Reassess airway position, ventilation, and surgical position with the team.

Gas-related complications include subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax. Recognize signs such as crepitus, increased airway pressure, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia; alert the surgeon and assess for airway or hemodynamic compromise.

Vascular injury, gas embolism, or sudden cardiovascular collapse require immediate team escalation and surgical coordination. A docked robot can impede access; follow the locally rehearsed undocking response rather than assuming access is immediate.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The educational reference describes balanced crystalloid with goal-directed administration and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, or laryngeal edema. Individualize administration to the patient and operative course.

Bleeding may follow port or needle access injury and can be difficult to recognize when visualization is limited. Heart rate, blood pressure, CVP, and urine output are imperfect volume surrogates during pneumoperitoneum; interpret them in context.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal basic analgesia appropriate to the patient; the review cites paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, with opioids reserved for rescue when needed.

Port-site local anesthetic infiltration is supported in the cited procedure-specific recommendations. Shoulder-tip pain may reflect diaphragmatic irritation and residual gas; thorough gas evacuation is described as a preventive measure.
Laparoscopy is a PONV risk factor; provide prophylaxis based on the patient’s risk and local practice. The available sources do not establish a mandatory drug combination for robotic cholecystectomy.

bullets: Detach robotic arms before reversal of neuromuscular blockade. When a blocker has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited guideline summary.

Consider delayed extubation or further airway assessment if facial or laryngeal edema is suspected, particularly after prolonged or extreme positioning; the review describes assessment and observation as relevant in that setting.

Provide postanesthesia care with evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; pulse oximetry is required during the initial phase of recovery under the cited standard.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robotic ventral or incisional hernia repair is generally performed under general anesthesia with CO₂ pneumoperitoneum; mesh is placed in a preperitoneal or retromuscular plane, with the approach determined by defect and tissue characteristics.

Key physiologic stresses include raised intra-abdominal pressure and CO₂ absorption, with potential cardiovascular effects, reduced pulmonary compliance, hypercarbia, and position-related edema or pressure injury. Assess the patient and operative conditions rather than assuming one uniform response.

Before docking, establish safe patient access and protect the face, ventilation tubing, and pressure points. Maintain complete neuromuscular blockade while the robotic platform is docked. Do not move the operating-room table while docked.

Recovery priorities include assessing ventilation and oxygenation, residual neuromuscular block when applicable, pain, PONV, and position-related facial or airway edema. Use an appropriate postanesthesia care setting and ongoing assessment.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Robotic ventral/incisional repairs use a minimally invasive sublay approach. Described options include preperitoneal repair (r-TAPP), retromuscular approaches (including r-TARM and r-E-TEP), and robotic transversus abdominis release (RoboTAR). These are surgical options, not interchangeable anesthesia protocols.

Approach depends on hernia location, size, prior operations, tissue planes, and the need for component separation. The technique review describes TAPP as dependent on a robust preperitoneal layer and RoboTAR for selected medium- or large-sized incisional hernias requiring component separation.

For expected intestinal adhesions, the technique review advises considering direct-vision transabdominal adhesiolysis before E-TEP to reduce bowel-injury risk during sac or posterior-element dissection.
The supplied hernia-specific sources address ventral and incisional repairs; they do not establish an anesthesia approach specific to robotic inguinal hernia repair.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the defect and prior abdominal operations with the surgical team; prior operations and anticipated adhesions may affect access and the operative dissection plan.

Consider obesity and cardiopulmonary stress in planning. The hernia cohort discusses obesity, intra-abdominal pressure, and cardiopulmonary stress; the technique review notes that a bulging abdomen or obesity can make caudal access technically difficult.

Review positioning tolerance and pressure-injury risks where flexion or Trendelenburg is planned. Available sources describe these positions but do not establish a universal position or duration for all robotic hernia repairs.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The described ventral/incisional procedures use supine positioning. Table flexion, or legs-down positioning with slight Trendelenburg if hip flexion is unavailable, may be used to improve working geometry; choose positioning with attention to patient comfort and operative access.

Plan arm positioning and protect the face, airway tubing, and pressure points before docking. Robot arms can create pressure or accidental-extubation hazards, and access to the patient is constrained while docked.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

Keep the operating table stationary while the robot is docked. Make an access and communication plan for any urgent need to reach the patient; the provided sources do not supply a procedure-specific undocking algorithm.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is reported for the described robotic hernia procedures. A general laparoscopic/robotic anesthesia review favors an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; airway choice remains dependent on the procedure and patient.

Pneumoperitoneum and position can reduce pulmonary compliance and promote atelectasis; CO₂ absorption can increase carbon dioxide. Reassess ventilation after insufflation and position changes rather than assuming unchanged mechanics.

For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, a commonly used lung-protective strategy is 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight with PEEP 5–10 cm H₂O, titrated according to driving pressure and respiratory compliance; these are not hernia-specific targets.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify correct positioning by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation or removal, or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, continually analyze end-tidal CO₂ using a quantitative method.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation may increase systemic vascular resistance and filling pressures, while inferior vena cava compression can reduce venous return. Peritoneal stretch may cause vagal bradyarrhythmia; hypercarbia may contribute to tachyarrhythmia or acidosis.

Reduced compliance, atelectasis, increased airway pressures, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may accompany insufflation and Trendelenburg. Interpret airway pressures in context and reassess after operative or position changes.
Surgical descriptions use CO₂ pneumoperitoneum and report reducing pressure during selected closure steps. Those operative technique details do not define a universal anesthetic pressure target.
Maintain adequate neuromuscular relaxation through docking when blockade is used, and coordinate the end of blockade with undocking and the operative phase.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: At insufflation onset, a pronounced vagal response can produce bradyarrhythmia and, rarely, cardiac arrest. Recognize the temporal association and promptly coordinate assessment with the surgical team; the supplied review does not provide a case-specific rescue algorithm.

Position or insufflation can be associated with endobronchial intubation, tube obstruction, or atelectasis. Reassess airway position and ventilation when airway pressures, oxygenation, or ventilation change.

Consider subcutaneous emphysema or capnothorax when crepitus, rising airway pressure, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or asymmetric chest movement occurs. The review notes that these may resolve after insufflation is stopped, but significant cases require close monitoring and assessment for airway or hemodynamic compromise.

Bowel injury during adhesiolysis and trocar or access-related bleeding are surgical hazards. Limited visualization can obscure access injury; coordinate prompt evaluation with the surgeon when suspected.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The general laparoscopic/robotic review describes balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration. It cautions that heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are poor surrogates for intravascular volume during pneumoperitoneum.
Avoid assuming that minimally invasive access eliminates hemorrhage risk. Solid-organ injury during Veress needle or port access is described, and limited visualization may delay recognition.

Excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, particularly with Trendelenburg. Individualize fluid administration to clinical circumstances; the hernia-specific cohort provides no fluid or blood-loss regimen.

bullets: Pain may be somatic at port sites and visceral from peritoneal stretch or abdominal tissue manipulation. A multimodal approach including acetaminophen and NSAIDs is described in the general review to limit opioid use; selection should reflect patient and procedure factors.
TAP blocks are described as an option for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches, not as a required component of every robotic repair. The hernia cohort does not specify an analgesic regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred to clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Assess for facial, pharyngeal, or laryngopharyngeal edema after substantial Trendelenburg exposure, especially alongside fluid-related edema risk. The supplied hernia sources do not establish a routine delayed-extubation protocol.

After anesthesia, use a PACU or equivalent care area, with continuing assessment appropriate to the patient's condition and attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Evaluate pain, PONV, and bowel transit in recovery; the hernia cohort reported unscheduled presentations for pain and delayed intestinal transit, but these observations do not define a routine treatment protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Soft-tissue mass excision ranges from a localized excision under local anesthesia to larger or complex procedures; the available procedure study reports local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia, but does not establish which patients need which technique.

Priorities supported by the procedure sources are careful dissection near neurovascular structures, hemostasis, and limiting traction or thermal injury; reported complications include seroma, hematoma, and nerve injury.

Do not assume general anesthesia, an advanced airway, or neuromuscular blockade for a small superficial mass; the supplied sources do not define case-specific selection criteria or an anesthesia regimen.
Recovery should include assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and patient condition; the procedure literature does not define a specific emergence, analgesic, or PACU protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative approach depends on lesion site and extent. Excision may be diagnostic as well as therapeutic when complete tissue architecture is needed; the supplied sources do not specify a single approach for all soft-tissue masses.

For lipomas, one described limited-incision method uses circumferential dissection, full mobilization before delivery, meticulous hemostasis, irrigation, and layered closure. This is a reported technique, not a universal standard.

For a rapidly growing presumed lipoma, the source describes radiologic evaluation to help distinguish it from malignant neoplasms. The available material does not establish a sarcoma staging, margin, or frozen-section protocol.

bullets: Clarify lesion location, depth, size, vascularity, and proximity to neurovascular structures with the surgical team; these factors affect planning, but the sources provide no universal anesthesia-selection rule.

Consider whether complete excision is appropriate or whether a diagnostic alternative is needed for a large or complex lesion near vital structures. This is a source-described concern, not a fixed contraindication to excision.
Assess patient-specific medical status and develop the anesthesia plan; the provided standards identify this responsibility but do not supply a procedure-specific assessment protocol.

bullets: Positioning and room setup are site-dependent. A cutaneous excision reference calls for comfortable positioning, appropriate surgical lighting, and a setup at the surgeon’s appropriate height; it does not establish positioning for every deep mass.
For MAC or general anesthesia, apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.
The supplied sources do not support routine invasive monitoring or a particular vascular-access plan for this procedure.

Avoid unnecessary traction and thermal injury during limited-incision dissection; the source describes careful mobilization and preference for scissors or forceps over electrocautery for dissection.

Maintain attention to bleeding and potential hematoma. The excisional-biopsy reference identifies bleeding as the most common intraoperative concern and notes that persistent bleeding may require further local control.

For expanding, tense postoperative hematoma, the reference describes prompt evacuation and wound-bed re-exploration to reduce risk of tissue ischemia, infection, and edge necrosis; this is procedural guidance, not an anesthetic algorithm.

bullets: Postanesthesia care applies after general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care. During transport, the patient should be evaluated and treated with monitoring and support appropriate to condition; on PACU arrival, reassessment and handoff are required.
During the initial recovery phase, the postanesthesia standard requires a quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry; ongoing observation should reflect the patient’s condition.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended and recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Splenectomy may be open, laparoscopic, or robotic; minimally invasive approaches are favored for scheduled procedures, particularly for hematologic conditions. The approach and position are surgical decisions, with open surgery described supine.
Prioritize anticipation and recognition of hemorrhage, especially with splenomegaly or portal hypertension, and protect the pancreas and other adjacent structures during dissection.
For laparoscopic surgery, insufflation and position can impair respiratory mechanics and alter venous return and hemodynamics; monitor and respond to the individual patient's physiology.
Recovery priorities include surveillance for bleeding, pancreatic complications, thromboembolism, and infection; vaccination and ongoing infection-prevention measures matter after splenectomy.

sources.label: Splenectomy
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Splenectomy removes the spleen and can be open, laparoscopic, or robotic-assisted. The review describes minimally invasive approaches as favored over open surgery, especially for scheduled hematologic procedures; this does not establish that a particular approach suits every patient.

For laparoscopic cases, positioning is not settled: right lateral decubitus can facilitate posterior and hilar dissection, while other positions offer different operative access. Selection depends on surgeon preference and the likelihood of conversion.
Open surgery is described supine. Laparoscopic access and dissection vary; the review describes open cutdown as preferred when splenomegaly makes access more hazardous.

sources.label: Splenectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess spleen size and relevant comorbidity. For elective laparoscopic splenectomy, the review calls for preoperative abdominal ultrasonography; it notes CT assessment for accessory spleens in patients with ITP or malignancy.

Splenomegaly can restrict operative space and complicate dissection or extraction; it is associated with more blood loss and conversion. Portal hypertension also increases bleeding and conversion concerns.

Review vaccination status and optimize relevant anemia, nutritional deficiencies, comorbidities, and clotting or bleeding abnormalities. Elective vaccination against encapsulated organisms is recommended approximately two weeks before surgery in the cited review.

sources.label: Splenectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning for laparoscopic splenectomy is technique-dependent; right lateral decubitus is one described option, not a universal requirement. Open surgery is described supine.

The procedure review lists arterial line, Foley catheter, gastric tube, and sequential compression devices for open and laparoscopic procedures. It gives no individualized criteria or monitoring targets; select invasive monitoring according to the case and patient.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

sources.label: Splenectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is described for laparoscopic and robotic procedures; endotracheal intubation is specified for open surgery in the procedure review and was used in the reported laparoscopic series. The laparoscopic-surgery reference describes an endotracheal tube as preferred to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP.

With pneumoperitoneum, reduced lung compliance and functional residual capacity, atelectasis, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may complicate ventilation. The general laparoscopy reference describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption; no splenectomy-specific ventilatory target is established here.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For laparoscopy, insufflation and positioning can affect preload, venous return, airway pressures, and gas exchange. Monitor for clinically important changes during insufflation and position changes rather than assuming a uniform response.

Dissection and mobilization are bleeding-risk phases; the review identifies splenic capsule or short-gastric-vessel injury as common sources of intraoperative bleeding. Adequate hemostasis and readiness to change approach are central priorities.

Hilar dissection requires attention to the pancreatic tail and neighboring organs. The procedure review describes laparoscopic hilar division with a vascular-load stapler, with clips or hemostatic agents for staple-line bleeding; it does not establish an anesthetic-specific intervention.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Hemorrhage may follow mobilization or splenomegaly and portal hypertension. If bleeding is not controlled promptly, the procedure review supports considering conversion; it supplies no anesthesia-specific hemorrhage algorithm.

Pancreatic injury can lead to pancreatitis, fluid collection, or pancreatic fistula; stomach and colon are also among commonly injured structures. Suspected pancreatic injury warrants surgical assessment; the review describes drain placement when injury is suspected.

Laparoscopic access and insufflation can cause solid-organ injury or hemorrhage that is obscured by limited visualization; gas-related thoracic complications are also described in the general laparoscopy reference. Recognize unexpected hemodynamic or respiratory deterioration and escalate evaluation with the surgical team.

Postoperative concerns include venous thromboembolism, infection including overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, and intra-abdominal abscess. The review describes lifelong preventive measures and monitoring after splenectomy.
