sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The procedure-specific review provides no fluid, blood-product, or hemodynamic management protocol. Anticipate blood loss in higher-risk anatomy and tailor access and product availability to the clinical context rather than applying a fixed volume or transfusion rule.

For laparoscopic procedures, the general reference supports balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, especially with Trendelenburg.
The cited retrospective laparoscopic series reports a local intraoperative blood-salvage protocol, but it does not establish a general transfusion strategy or threshold for splenectomy.

bullets: The splenectomy review provides no specific analgesia regimen. The general laparoscopy reference describes multimodal analgesia, including acetaminophen and NSAIDs, with local anesthetic at port sites as options to reduce opioid use; select according to patient and procedure factors.
A transversus abdominis plane block may be offered for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches; the general laparoscopy reference does not make neuraxial anesthesia routine.
Laparoscopy is an independent PONV risk factor; the general reference recommends prophylactic antiemetic administration, without specifying a splenectomy-specific regimen.

bullets: The splenectomy review gives no specific emergence, extubation, or recovery-room protocol. Recovery planning should reflect the operative course and patient status; the source does not establish routine ICU disposition for all cases.

After anesthesia, patients should receive postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location, with ongoing assessment appropriate to their condition and particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Provide ongoing surveillance for bleeding, pancreatic complications, infection, and thrombosis. The splenectomy review describes vaccination and often antibiotic prophylaxis as longer-term prevention measures, not substitutes for immediate postoperative assessment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Most thyroidectomies use general endotracheal anesthesia; selected patients may have surgery with superficial cervical blocks and mild or no sedation.
Priorities are thyroid-function optimization and anticipating airway difficulty from large, substernal, deviated, or compressed tracheas.
Key intraoperative hazards include thyroid storm in inadequately controlled hyperthyroidism, bleeding, and airway compromise associated with goiter or surgical complications.
Recovery priorities are smooth emergence and prompt recognition of neck hematoma, vocal-cord dysfunction, tracheomalacia, and symptomatic hypocalcemia.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Thyroidectomy removes all or part of the gland. Indications include hyperthyroidism, thyroid cancer, and a benign large goiter with potential tracheal compression; operative complexity ranges from nodule excision to sternotomy for a large retrosternal goiter.

General endotracheal anesthesia is usual. The source also describes selected, motivated patients undergoing surgery with bilateral superficial cervical blocks and mild or no sedation; this is not a basis for imposing general anesthesia on every case.
The sources do not establish a single anesthetic technique for every patient; choice depends on the operation and airway, thyroid, and patient factors.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: For elective thyroid surgery, assess thyroid function and clinical signs of imbalance, aiming for euthyroidism. Hyperthyroidism carries risks of tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and thyroid storm during gland dissection; preoperative optimization may use antithyroid medications and beta blockers.

Ask about dyspnea, orthopnea, dysphagia, stridor, and positional symptoms. Identify goiter size and substernal extension; review imaging or laryngoscopy when available and coordinate airway planning with the surgeon.

Review voice symptoms and relevant prior neck treatment or surgery as part of the clinical airway and laryngeal assessment. Large, long-standing compressive goiters raise concern for tracheomalacia after resection.

Consider associated endocrine disease in thyroid cancer, including MEN type 2 and possible pheochromocytoma or hyperparathyroidism; the source describes screening for relevant clinical and biochemical clues.

sources.label: Anesthesia and thyroid surgery: The never ending challenges
Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning commonly uses a padded head support and shoulder roll for neck extension. Reassess airway-device position after neck hyperextension for surgical exposure.

Have difficult-airway equipment available. When recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring is requested, a NIM endotracheal tube may be used; optimize electrode contact with the vocal cords and verify position.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards require continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.
Protect the eyes, particularly with Graves’ exophthalmos. The available sources do not establish a thyroidectomy-specific need for invasive monitoring or a fixed room configuration.

sources.label: Anesthesia and thyroid surgery: The never ending challenges
Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan airway management around goiter size, substernal extension, tracheal deviation or compression, and positional symptoms. For severe compression, the source discusses intubation with spontaneous ventilation; this is a selective strategy, not a universal approach.

A NIM tube requires accurate electrode alignment. Use only enough neuromuscular blockade to facilitate intubation as appropriate, allow recovery before nerve monitoring, and avoid further paralytic agents while monitoring is underway.

If a large-goiter airway deteriorates after intubation, use the preidentified position that reduces obstruction and escalate airway support. An endotracheal tube proximal to an obstruction may not fully secure the airway.
Long-standing compression can leave a vulnerable trachea after extubation. Consider tracheomalacia in immediate respiratory distress or expiratory stridor and be prepared to re-establish the airway.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: In patients with suspected hyperthyroidism, watch for abrupt hypertension, tachycardia or arrhythmia, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, and hyperthermia during gland manipulation. These findings warrant prompt escalation for possible thyroid storm and supportive management.
Avoid contributing adrenergic stressors where feasible in a patient at risk of storm; the source specifically identifies ketamine, ephedrine, atropine, and hypercapnia as potential triggers.
PONV prevention matters because retching can increase venous pressure and postoperative bleeding risk. TIVA is identified as an option with antiemetic properties, rather than a required technique.
For nerve monitoring, maintain conditions that permit reliable vocal-cord EMG assessment; anesthetic depth and neuromuscular-block recovery need consideration.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Expanding postoperative neck hematoma is a life-threatening airway emergency. Recognize acute respiratory distress or compression and escalate immediately for wound decompression, airway management, and surgical hemostasis.
Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction commonly alters voice; bilateral vocal-cord paralysis can cause stridor and respiratory distress requiring emergent airway intervention.

After total thyroidectomy, parathyroid injury can cause symptomatic hypocalcemia. Monitor for paresthesia, spasms, tetany, altered mental status, seizures, laryngospasm, or QT prolongation; the source notes PACU PTH testing and early calcium/vitamin D supplementation for patients at risk.

Pneumothorax is rare but is a consideration with retrosternal-goiter dissection; unexplained hypoxemia, hypotension, increased airway pressure, difficult ventilation, or absent breath sounds should prompt urgent assessment and escalation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy
Anesthesia and thyroid surgery: The never ending challenges

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Major hemorrhage is uncommon but becomes more plausible with large retrosternal goiter dissection or adjacent-vessel injury. Maintain vigilance for bleeding and airway consequences rather than assuming low blood loss makes postoperative surveillance unnecessary.
The supplied thyroidectomy sources specify no routine fluid regimen, fluid volume, or transfusion threshold. Individualize fluid and blood management to the clinical and operative context.

If thyroid storm is suspected, the source includes hydration among supportive measures, alongside cooling, beta blockade, and steroids; this reference does not prescribe a fixed fluid amount or stand-alone algorithm.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Thyroidectomy
Anesthesia and thyroid surgery: The never ending challenges

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Superficial cervical plexus block and wound infiltration are described options for postoperative analgesia; the source reports opioid-sparing benefits for superficial blocks. Deep cervical blocks are discouraged in the cited review because of potential complications and lack of added analgesic benefit over superficial blocks.
Multimodal analgesia and opioid-sparing approaches are relevant because this population has substantial PONV concern; select techniques in light of bleeding risk and patient-specific considerations.

Use antiemetic prophylaxis as clinically appropriate. Retching can increase venous pressure and risk of postoperative bleeding; the source lists TIVA as one possible approach with antiemetic properties.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Aim for smooth emergence because coughing and bucking increase venous pressure and may contribute to wound bleeding. Assess airway patency and respiratory status closely after extubation, particularly when there was tracheal compression or long-standing goiter.
When feasible, assess vocal-cord function after surgery; some surgeons request laryngoscopy to assess bilateral movement. New stridor or respiratory distress requires immediate airway evaluation.
Continue focused observation for hematoma and airway compromise in recovery. Most hematomas occur early, but the source reports that some present within the first postoperative day.

For any neuromuscular blocker used, quantitative monitoring guidance recommends confirming train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.
PACU care should include ongoing assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

bullets: The principal procedure-specific sources are educational clinical summaries/reviews, not identified as formal guidelines or trials; they do not grade evidence or provide systematic-review methods.

The sources differ in emphasis: one describes selected regional-block cases, while the older review presents general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation as the safest contemporary approach. Neither supports treating one technique as mandatory for every patient.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia-care sources provide general standards, not thyroidectomy-specific complication-management or recovery protocols. The neuromuscular-blockade guideline applies when blockade is used, not to every anesthetic.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Tracheostomy establishes an airway through the anterior tracheal wall by an open surgical or percutaneous approach. Open procedures are usually performed in an operating room; percutaneous placement is commonly performed at the bedside in an ICU.

The key anesthetic priorities are coordinated airway transition, reliable confirmation of tracheostomy-tube position, and avoidance of loss of ventilation or airway access. End-tidal carbon dioxide and, for percutaneous placement, bronchoscopic visualization support confirmation.

Important hazards include operative bleeding, false passage or airway loss during tube exchange, posterior-wall injury, and rare airway fire when electrocautery is used in an oxygen-enriched environment.

Recovery planning centers on a secured, patent tracheostomy airway, surveillance for bleeding, obstruction or displacement, and appropriate postanesthesia or ICU care. The source does not establish a specific anesthetic emergence or analgesia regimen.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Tracheostomy creates an opening in the anterior tracheal wall, usually between the second and third rings. The approaches described are open surgery and percutaneous placement using a modified Seldinger technique.

Open tracheostomy is traditionally performed in the operating room; selected cases may be performed under local anesthesia. Percutaneous placement is usually performed at the ICU bedside, though it may also be done in the operating room.

The choice of approach depends on the clinical situation, anatomy, procedural expertise and setting. In the COVID-era review, evidence did not establish superiority of open over percutaneous technique; that review’s infection-control context should not be treated as a general approach mandate.
Initial placement generally uses a cuffed, nonfenestrated tracheostomy tube. The operative technique and airway plan should be coordinated between the proceduralist and airway operator.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the indication and whether the patient is already intubated; assess current airway access, neck anatomy, prior surgery or radiation, and coagulation status. These factors can affect approach and procedural difficulty.

For a planned case, review whether the patient can tolerate the brief ventilation interruption that may be needed during tracheal entry or dilation. The available sources do not establish a universal threshold for tolerance.

In life-threatening airway emergencies, the source states that no condition is an absolute contraindication to tracheostomy; management remains dependent on the emergency and available airway options.

The COVID-era review recommends multidisciplinary discussion for its population and describes infectious-risk planning. Those recommendations are specific to COVID-19-era practice and do not establish routine timing or testing requirements for other patients.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For neck access, supine positioning with neck extension is described; a shoulder roll or chest bump can improve anterior tracheal access. Individualize positioning when neck mobility or anatomy limits extension.

Have tracheostomy equipment and appropriate tube options available. For percutaneous placement, the described technique uses flexible bronchoscopy to visualize needle and guidewire placement and confirm tube position.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; for general anesthesia, expired carbon dioxide monitoring is continued unless invalidated by the patient, procedure or equipment.

For a transmissible respiratory pathogen or other aerosol-risk context, use infection precautions and room controls appropriate to the circumstance and local policy; the COVID-era review describes negative-pressure rooms when available.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open procedures are usually performed under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, but selected upper-airway-compromise cases may be managed awake under local anesthesia with spontaneous breathing. Percutaneous procedures are typically performed in intubated, sedated patients, with or without neuromuscular blockade.

For percutaneous placement, the described conventional technique withdraws the ETT under bronchoscopic guidance before needle entry; coordinate ETT movement and tracheal access with the proceduralist. The precise airway sequence may vary by approach.

Ventilation may be interrupted briefly during tracheal entry or percutaneous dilation if clinically feasible. Once the tracheostomy tube is inserted, confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reconfirm ventilation.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation is conditional on blockade use; it does not impose paralysis for every tracheostomy.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The airway transition is a critical phase: coordinate ETT withdrawal, tracheal entry, tracheostomy-tube insertion and connection to the breathing circuit. Confirm tube position and ventilation after the transition.

Bleeding can obscure the operative field or impede bronchoscopy. The source emphasizes correction of coagulopathy when possible and meticulous hemostasis; it does not supply a universal fluid or transfusion regimen for this reference.

When electrocautery is used, coordinate with the surgical team to reduce airway-fire risk from oxygen and ignition sources. The supplied sources do not establish a universal inspired-oxygen threshold for all tracheostomies.
Tracheostomy may reduce airway resistance and facilitate ventilator weaning, but the source does not provide case-specific physiologic targets or a ventilation prescription.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anticipate bleeding, false passage, tube obstruction, displacement and loss of airway access. Tube displacement into soft tissue or a false passage may require airway re-establishment; the source identifies flexible-laryngoscopic guidance as preferable for reintubation when required.
Posterior-wall disruption, false passage or apical injury can lead to pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Bronchoscopy can help prevent posterior-wall injury during percutaneous placement.

If airway fire occurs, the source describes immediate circuit removal, mask ventilation and airway inspection for thermal injury. This is a source-reported response, not a substitute for local emergency protocols.

Early tube changes are discouraged unless necessary because the immature tract increases the risk of false passage and airway compromise. The source describes the initial tube change as typically occurring on postoperative days 5 to 7; this is not a universal timing instruction for an individual patient.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Bleeding is identified as the most common intraoperative complication. Assess and manage hemostasis in the context of the patient’s coagulation status and procedural findings.

The tracheostomy overview provides no fluid regimen or specific fluid-management guidance. Fluid administration and perfusion goals therefore remain patient- and context-dependent rather than fixed by these sources.

The COVID-era review likewise does not specify fluid-management regimens, blood-product thresholds or transfusion practice; its discussion of anticoagulation is specific to COVID-associated illness and does not define a general perioperative anticoagulation protocol.

bullets: The tracheostomy source provides no analgesic regimen or specific postoperative pain-management recommendation. It therefore does not support a standard drug or dose for this procedure.

The supplied sources do not provide a procedure-specific PONV assessment or prophylaxis regimen; manage these issues according to the patient and applicable practice guidance rather than infer a tracheostomy-specific protocol.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure establishes a tracheostomy airway, which is connected to the ventilator as appropriate. Confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reassess ventilation; the source does not specify when or how anesthesia should be discontinued or the ETT removed.

Plan recovery in a PACU or equivalent area such as an ICU, with transport monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition. The ASA postanesthesia standards call for attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature.

Postprocedure surveillance includes tube patency and position, bleeding, and subcutaneous air. Humidified gas, suctioning and routine stoma or cannula care are described as measures to reduce obstruction risk.

bullets: The principal procedure source is a clinical overview, not an anesthesia-specific guideline or formal systematic review. It describes approaches, airway considerations and complications but does not provide detailed anesthetic emergence, analgesia or fluid protocols.

The second procedure source concerns COVID-19-associated respiratory failure and is a narrative review combining prior outbreak literature with institutional experience. Its timing and infection-control discussion should not be generalized as routine practice outside its scope.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adult primary umbilical hernia repair, open surgery may be performed with local anesthesia plus monitored anesthesia care (LA + MAC); laparoscopic and robotic approaches are also described. The anesthetic approach depends on the patient, operation, resources, and preference.

For laparoscopic or robotic abdominal surgery, general anesthesia is described as standard; an endotracheal tube is preferred over a supraglottic airway to support ventilation when insufflation raises ventilatory demands.

With abdominal insufflation, prioritize assessment of ventilation and hemodynamics: CO₂ absorption, altered respiratory mechanics, pressure effects, and positioning can all affect physiology. Adapt support to the operation and observed response.

Plan recovery around pain and PONV, and assess for residual neuromuscular blockade if a blocker was used. Quantitative confirmation of recovery applies to NMB cases, not to every local or neuraxial technique.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The hernia-specific source addresses elective repair of primary adult umbilical hernias and distinguishes these from incisional umbilical hernias. It describes open repair, laparoscopic repair, and several robotic approaches; it does not establish one approach as universally preferred.

For open primary umbilical repair, LA + MAC is a described option, particularly for older patients with substantial comorbidity. Regional anesthesia is also discussed as an approach in settings where resources or general anesthesia are limited. Neither is established here as a universal regimen.

The general laparoscopic/robotic review supplies relevant anesthesia considerations but is not a hernia-specific protocol. Do not infer a required anesthetic technique for every repair from approach alone.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the patient’s comorbidities and preferences alongside the planned approach and local expertise/resources. The source describes LA + MAC as an option, not a default; in the authors’ practice, patient preference was the stated contraindication to offering it for most open repairs.

For hernia decision-making, the source discusses obesity, smoking, hernia size, and infection risk. It recommends counseling about smoking and weight loss but says repair should not be denied solely because a patient cannot or adamantly refuses to make those changes.

Acute incarceration with strangulation may require urgent or emergent treatment; bowel-containing hernias warrant more cautious management than those incarcerated with fat. The source does not provide an anesthesia-specific induction protocol for these circumstances.
The supplied hernia source concerns primary umbilical hernia, so its selection and risk discussion does not resolve assessment for ventral or prior-incisional repairs.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic or robotic surgery, the general review recommends standard ASA monitors. Consider additional hemodynamic monitoring only when patient or procedural circumstances warrant it; the source does not prescribe routine arterial access.

Potential laparoscopic/robotic positions include Trendelenburg, reverse Trendelenburg, lateral decubitus, lithotomy, and flexed position. Position-related venous return changes and pressure injury are relevant; protect pressure points and coordinate table movement when a robot is docked.

Basic monitoring standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes. These standards apply across anesthetic techniques, including MAC.
The supplied sources do not establish hernia-specific room equipment, warming, urinary-catheter use, or access requirements.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open repair may be performed under LA + MAC in selected patients; this evidence does not justify imposing intubation or neuromuscular blockade on local-anesthetic cases. During moderate or deep sedation, ventilation assessment includes clinical observation and expired CO₂ monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

For laparoscopic/robotic surgery, general anesthesia is described as standard; the review prefers an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP. This is approach-specific guidance, not a mandate for open minimal-anesthetic repair.

Insufflation and position changes can alter airway pressures and tube position; the review notes possible endobronchial migration and increased cuff pressure. Reassess ventilation and airway status as the operation and position evolve.

sources.label: Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: At insufflation, pneumoperitoneum can increase intrathoracic pressure and cardiac filling pressures; inferior vena cava compression may reduce preload and venous return. Interpret hemodynamic changes in the context of insufflation, position, and the patient’s response.

CO₂ absorption and altered respiratory mechanics can increase CO₂ and airway pressures, while reduced compliance, atelectasis, and ventilation/perfusion mismatch may develop. The review describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption; exact ventilator settings must reflect the individual case.

Insufflation onset can produce a pronounced vagal response and bradyarrhythmias; hypercarbia can contribute to tachyarrhythmias. Recognize abrupt changes and coordinate promptly with the surgical team regarding the operative stimulus and insufflation.
The supplied sources do not characterize abdominal-wall closure physiology or closure-related ventilation changes specifically for hernia repair.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For laparoscopic access, solid-organ injury and hemorrhage may be obscured by limited visualization. Keep access-related injury in the differential when physiology changes unexpectedly and communicate concerns with the surgeon.

CO₂-related complications described include subcutaneous emphysema and capnothorax. Findings may include crepitus, increased airway pressure, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or unequal chest expansion; monitor for airway compromise and significant hemodynamic change and escalate for assessment.

Residual neuromuscular blockade is associated with upper-airway obstruction, reintubation, atelectasis, pneumonia, and prolonged PACU stay. If NMB is used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; the guideline favors adductor pollicis monitoring and confirmation of recovery before extubation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The laparoscopic/robotic review favors balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, worsened by Trendelenburg. This is general MIS guidance, not a hernia-specific fluid prescription.

During pneumoperitoneum, heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are described as poor surrogate predictors of intravascular volume. Interpret these measures alongside the operative and physiologic context rather than as isolated volume indicators.

MIS is associated with less bleeding and reduced transfusion need, but access-related hemorrhage remains possible. The supplied evidence gives no hernia-specific blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or fluid total.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For laparoscopic procedures, the review describes multimodal analgesia including acetaminophen and NSAIDs to limit opioid use, with local anesthetic at port sites as an option. It does not establish a hernia-specific drug regimen.
TAP blocks are described as an option for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches. The source does not establish a TAP block as mandatory or as a universal technique for open hernia repair.

Laparoscopy is identified as an independent PONV risk factor, and the review recommends prophylactic antiemetic administration. The supplied evidence does not specify an individualized prophylaxis regimen.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: If neuromuscular blockers were administered, use quantitative monitoring to confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited guideline recommends TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 and the adductor pollicis monitoring site; these recommendations do not apply to cases without NMB.

After anesthesia, patients should receive postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent unless specifically ordered otherwise by the responsible anesthesiologist. Continue appropriate observation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

During transport to the PACU, a knowledgeable Anesthesia Care Team member must accompany the patient and provide monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition. Re-evaluate the patient on arrival and provide a verbal report to the responsible nurse. The hernia-specific article does not provide detailed emergence or postoperative-care instructions.

Elective Umbilical Hernia Repair in Adults in the 21st Century

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The hernia-specific article is a perspective/review, not an anesthesia guideline or randomized anesthesia trial. It reports no randomized trials comparing LA + MAC with general or regional anesthesia for umbilical hernia repair; its institutional feasibility cohort included 53 veteran patients, limiting generalizability.

The hernia-specific source addresses primary umbilical hernias exclusively; the general MIS review supports contextual laparoscopic/robotic considerations but does not establish hernia-specific management. Evidence for ventral and incisional hernia anesthesia is therefore not resolved by these sources.
The ERAS sources concern major abdominal or gastrointestinal surgery and provide broad principles or consensus context in the supplied material, not detailed hernia-specific recommendations.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Debridement ranges from bedside sharp removal to surgical excision in the operating room. Surgical debridement removes nonviable tissue down to intact structures; the extent and method depend on the wound and patient.

For surgical cases, plan adequate anesthesia and account for pain and bleeding. Tissue and vessel injury with bleeding are common during surgical debridement; wound-care sources do not establish an anesthetic technique for a particular patient or wound.

Choose the anesthetic and monitoring to fit the planned procedure and patient; available sources do not establish a default airway, ventilation strategy, invasive monitoring plan, or fluid regimen for debridement.

After anesthesia, use an appropriate postanesthesia-care setting and monitor recovery according to the patient's condition. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited guideline supports quantitative confirmation of recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Debridement removes adherent dead tissue, scabs, or foreign bodies; the selected method should reflect the wound and patient rather than assume one technique is suitable for all cases. Debridement supports wound assessment and healing, but repeated, unselected surgical removal may impair healing.

Sharp debridement may be performed on an outpatient basis and can leave nonviable tissue behind. Surgical debridement is more extensive and, in the cited wound primer, is performed in the operating room; pronounced findings warrant adequate anesthesia in an operating room in the position paper.

The wound primer notes that surgical debridement often requires general anesthesia or local infiltrate. The position paper advises discussing general anesthesia as an option; neither source establishes a universal anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify wound extent, the proposed method and setting, patient comorbidities, pain, and the patient's overall condition. The cited position paper also identifies available resources and clinician competencies as factors in method selection.

Assess bleeding risk before surgical debridement, including coagulation disorders and anticoagulant treatment, and incorporate findings into procedural planning. The source identifies significant bleeding as a particular complication but gives no thresholds or medication-interruption schedule.

Assess pain and consider individualized, adequate analgesia. Pyoderma gangrenosum during its inflammatory phase is identified as a condition in which debridement may worsen disease through pathergy; the source says medically controlled inflammation changes that consideration.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For pronounced findings requiring surgical debridement, the wound-care position paper recommends an operating-room setting with adequate anesthesia. It does not provide positioning, access, warming, or room-equipment specifications.

Apply the relevant basic anesthesia monitoring standards for the anesthetic delivered: oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature are continually evaluated, with blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes.

Do not infer that an arterial line is routinely required for this procedure. The monitoring standard describes intra-arterial pressure as one possible means of continually evaluating circulation during general anesthesia, not a debridement-specific indication.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The provided wound-debridement sources do not specify airway choice, induction, ventilation, or criteria for general versus local anesthesia beyond noting that surgical debridement may require general anesthesia or local infiltrate. Select technique for the individual procedure and patient; no routine intubation or paralysis is established here.

For general anesthesia, follow the basic ventilation-monitoring standard, including continual evaluation of ventilation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the standard's stated exceptions apply.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to local-anesthetic or other cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Surgical debridement may involve removal down to intact tissue, with tissue and vessel injury and bleeding commonly occurring. The supplied wound sources do not define physiologic targets or procedure-specific critical phases.
After surgical debridement, the position paper describes hemostasis by manual compression or hemostatic wound dressings and recommends a short-term clinical check that bleeding is controlled.

The primer notes that sharp or surgical debridement often causes bleeding; it provides no bleeding rate or quantified complication risk. Avoid extrapolating this observation to an expected blood loss for an individual case.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Bleeding is a recognized complication of surgical debridement. Reassess hemostasis clinically after the procedure; the wound position paper does not supply a blood-loss threshold or a transfusion algorithm.
Consider pathergy in susceptible wounds, particularly pyoderma gangrenosum during active inflammation. The source advises that debridement can be performed when inflammation is medically controlled.
Worsening wound findings may include increased exudate, pain, odor, bleeding, and tissue friability.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize fluid and blood-product planning to the patient, wound, and observed losses. The supplied sources do not establish a fluid volume, transfusion threshold, or blood-product preparation rule for debridement.

Account for bleeding risk before the procedure and assess hemostasis after surgical debridement. The wound paper describes clinical bleeding control rather than a quantitative perfusion or blood-loss endpoint.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Assess pain regularly with an appropriate instrument and plan analgesia individually. The position paper gives visual analog and numeric rating scales as examples.
For minor procedures, topical lidocaine–prilocaine cream may be sufficient; the position paper specifies an adequate application time of not less than 30–60 minutes.
Discuss general anesthesia as an option for surgical debridement when appropriate. No PONV prevention or treatment regimen is supplied for this procedure.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied debridement sources do not provide emergence criteria or procedure-specific postoperative anesthesia care. Use the appropriate postanesthesia-care setting unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise.

During recovery, evaluate the patient continually with monitoring appropriate to medical condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A quantitative oxygenation method such as pulse oximetry is required in the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation as described in the cited guideline overview. The source does not establish a debridement-specific discharge or extubation protocol.

bullets: The most procedure-relevant source is an ICW professional-society position paper on chronic-wound debridement nomenclature and wound-care practice, not an anesthesia reference. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Diagnostic EGD is usually performed with conscious sedation; deeper sedation may be used when clinically selected. The endoscope creates a shared airway and can partially obstruct it.

Prioritize airway access, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring, and readiness to rescue deeper-than-intended sedation. Positioning and oxygen-delivery choices must account for limited airway access.
Assess aspiration and cardiopulmonary risk before the procedure; consider a protected airway when aspiration risk is especially high or the procedure is prolonged or technically challenging.
Recovery priorities are ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and consciousness, with monitoring for sedation or instrumentation complications and use of discharge criteria.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: EGD (also termed OGD in the sources) provides direct visualization and mucosal sampling for diagnosis, therapy and surveillance of upper-GI symptoms. The procedure and intended sedation level should be agreed with the patient as part of consent.

Most diagnostic examinations use conscious sedation; unsedated examination with topical pharyngeal anesthetic is also described. Sedation practice varies, and the sources do not establish one regimen as the routine choice for every adult EGD.

This is a shared-airway procedure with reduced airway access. The scope is a foreign body in the aerodigestive tract and may cause partial obstruction; stimulation and required sedation depth can change during the examination.

sources.label: Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management
Guidelines for sedation and anesthesia in GI endoscopy
Hypoxia During Upper GI Endoscopy: There is Still Room for Improvement

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review prior adverse reactions to sedation, medications and interactions, cardiopulmonary disease, sleep apnea, neuromuscular or swallowing impairment, obesity, airway features, baseline consciousness and recent oral intake. Consider ASA class as one risk modifier; ASA III or above is associated with increased adverse-event risk in GI endoscopy.

Review the last oral intake and assess for impaired gastric emptying or esophageal motility disorders. A review describes minimum fasting periods of 2 hours for clear liquids and 6 hours for food, extended to at least 12 hours for known or suspected delayed gastric emptying or motility disorders and 48 hours in achalasia. The ASGE guideline reports no direct evidence linking fasting duration to pulmonary-aspiration risk and no universally accepted practice standard; it cites ASA guidance of at least 2 hours after clear liquids and 6 hours after light meals.

Reflux, dysphagia, food impaction, GI bleeding and anemia are identified as airway-related risk modifiers; obesity, pulmonary disease, reduced cardiac output and fever may increase vulnerability to rapid desaturation during apnea. Pregnancy testing is recommended in the appropriate clinical setting for women of childbearing age; the sources do not make pregnancy a universal contraindication.

sources.label: Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Expect lateral, semi-prone or prone positioning and plan for restricted access to the airway. Position is not standardized in the supplied sources; select it with the endoscopist while preserving feasible airway access.

Have appropriate airway and resuscitation equipment immediately available, and ensure the team can communicate and respond despite endoscopist access needs. Bite blocks can dislodge teeth; assess dentition and use appropriate protection.

For moderate or deep sedation, monitor oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, pulse, blood pressure and responsiveness. ASA standards call for at least every-five-minute blood pressure and heart-rate assessment during anesthesia; consider capnography particularly for deep sedation, without treating its benefit in moderate sedation as established.

Supplemental oxygen is required by the ASGE guideline when deep sedation is targeted and should be administered if hypoxemia is anticipated or develops. The sources do not establish one optimal oxygen-delivery device for EGD.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan for partial obstruction from the endoscope and sedation-related loss of upper-airway tone, compounded by limited access in common positions. The airway plan should be chosen for the patient and intended sedation depth rather than assumed to be a natural airway in every case.

Maintain the ability to rescue deeper-than-intended sedation. The ASGE guideline identifies chin lift, jaw thrust and oral or nasal airway insertion as potential rescue interventions; it does not establish one maneuver as universally most effective for EGD.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation continuously by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure or equipment precludes or invalidates it. Pulse oximetry alone does not substitute for ventilation assessment.

Consider general anesthesia, with or without endotracheal intubation, when aspiration risk is especially high or the examination is likely to be prolonged or technically challenging. This is a consideration, not a universal EGD airway technique.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The initial insertion can provoke gagging, coughing or laryngospasm, while required sedation depth can change as stimulation changes. Titrate sedation cautiously to the lowest effective dose, particularly in elderly or comorbid patients.

Apnea or hypoventilation can lead to rapid desaturation, especially in patients with limited oxygen-loading capacity or increased oxygen demand. Vigilance and timely recognition are priorities; the supplied sources do not prescribe a procedure-specific intervention algorithm.

Cardiopulmonary events include hypoxia, hypotension, vasovagal episodes and dysrhythmias. A vagal response is possible during instrumentation, but the sources do not establish a specific EGD treatment regimen.

sources.label: Hypoxia During Upper GI Endoscopy: There is Still Room for Improvement
Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: The principal sedation-related hazards are oversedation with respiratory depression or hypoxia, airway compromise, laryngospasm, aspiration and hemodynamic events. Maintain readiness to recognize deterioration and escalate airway or resuscitation support.

Dental trauma can occur, particularly with poor dentition or loose teeth. Temporomandibular-joint dislocation is rare; new jaw pain or inability to close the mouth after the procedure warrants assessment.

Perforation is uncommon but potentially serious. Disproportionate or persistent chest or abdominal pain, distension, dysphagia, shortness of breath, voice change or systemic deterioration after EGD should prompt urgent evaluation and appropriate multidisciplinary escalation.

sources.label: Complications of diagnostic upper Gastrointestinal endoscopy: common and rare – recognition, assessment and management
Guidelines for sedation and anesthesia in GI endoscopy

bullets: The available sources do not provide a routine EGD fluid regimen or case-specific fluid targets. Manage fluids and perfusion according to the patient’s clinical state and the actual procedure rather than importing an unsupported fixed volume.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ERCP combines upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and x-rays to diagnose and treat disease involving the bile ducts, pancreatic ducts, ampulla, and related structures. The anesthetic approach ranges from monitored sedation with spontaneous breathing to general anesthesia with an airway device; no single approach is established as superior.

Priorities are maintaining immobility and adequate oxygenation and ventilation while accommodating procedural complexity and position. ERCP may be performed prone or semi-prone, which can limit airway access and affect cardiopulmonary physiology.

Respiratory depression, airway obstruction, hypoxemia, and aspiration are important sedation-related hazards. Select airway support and monitoring according to patient risk, anticipated procedure, and position rather than treating intubation as mandatory for every ERCP.

Recovery requires observation for sedation- and instrumentation-related adverse effects, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness. The supplied sources do not establish an ERCP-specific postoperative monitoring protocol or discharge criteria.

For general anesthesia, apply basic anesthetic monitoring: continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every five minutes. For a secured airway, monitor exhaled carbon dioxide continually.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation continuously by clinical observation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment makes it invalid or impractical. sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose among spontaneous ventilation, a supraglottic airway, and tracheal intubation using patient-specific aspiration and respiratory risks, procedural complexity, position, and access. Available evidence does not establish one approach as universally superior.

Consider a secured airway for high aspiration or major bleeding risk, concurrent gastric outlet obstruction, transluminal access or drainage, and prolonged or highly complex procedures. A cuffed endotracheal tube provides stable ventilation access and protection from aspirated gastric contents or blood.

A supraglottic airway may facilitate ventilation without tracheal intubation, but seal, displacement, and aspiration remain considerations. In prone positioning, LMA manipulation requires care and it does not protect against aspiration of gastric fluid.

For spontaneously breathing patients, supplemental oxygen and respiratory support should be matched to risk. High-flow nasal oxygen can reduce hypoxia in some studies, but effectiveness in obese and other high-risk patients and effects on hypercarbia remain uncertain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Transvaginal cerclage is the usual approach. When appropriate, regional anesthesia is commonly favored over general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; either technique may be used when carefully selected.

Priorities include confirming the indication and excluding labor, ruptured membranes, and infection; pregnancy-related aspiration risk and aortocaval compression should inform anesthetic and positioning decisions.

Lithotomy, with Trendelenburg when needed to reduce bulging membranes, is described for transvaginal placement. Fetal heart rate is assessed before and after; continuous intraoperative fetal monitoring is generally not performed.

Recovery priorities are obstetric reassessment and observation for contractions, bleeding, membrane rupture, infection, and neuraxial-block resolution; pain is often limited and acetaminophen is commonly used.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Endometrial ablation destroys functional endometrium to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding. Second-generation devices use different energy sources and generally do not require hysteroscopic surgical skills; the approach depends on the device and uterine cavity.

Many second-generation procedures are performed as outpatient procedures under local anesthesia, sometimes with minimal conscious sedation. General anesthesia is an alternative setting, not an approach established as necessary for every ablation.
Priorities include confirming suitability, reviewing uterine anatomy and endometrial assessment, and counseling about alternatives, outcomes, contraception, and the intended anesthetic setting.

Recognize pain, vasovagal symptoms during cervical instrumentation, uterine perforation, and hemorrhage as relevant concerns. Recovery planning should account for pain, nausea/vomiting, and the patient's readiness for discharge.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hysteroscopy directly visualizes the uterine cavity for diagnosis and, in selected cases, treatment. Office diagnostic hysteroscopy commonly uses vaginoscopy, without a speculum or tenaculum; sedation is not routine.

The principal physiologic hazard is absorption of distension fluid, which can cause fluid overload and electrolyte or plasma disturbances, including hyponatremia with hypotonic solutions. Monitor fluid status and communicate concerns with the procedural team.

Procedure-related priorities include minimizing pain and excessive distension, recognizing vasovagal events, and identifying possible uterine perforation or gas embolism. The anesthetic approach depends on whether the procedure is diagnostic or operative and its setting.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Hysteroscopy provides direct visualization of the vagina, cervix, and uterine cavity. Office procedures are used mainly for abnormal uterine bleeding and may also diagnose or treat selected intrauterine lesions.

Office procedures may include sampling, adhesiolysis, and removal of polyps, small leiomyomas, retained products, or intrauterine devices. The planned intervention affects procedural extent; sources do not define a universal anesthetic technique for each.

Vaginoscopy is the recommended standard outpatient diagnostic technique: the scope passes through the vagina and cervix without a speculum or tenaculum. It may reduce procedural pain with similar efficacy to conventional hysteroscopy.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify diagnostic versus operative intent, anticipated procedural extent, expected discomfort, and patient preferences. Counsel on goals and anticipated discomfort; the office guideline recommends verbal reassurance during the procedure.

Relevant history includes medical conditions, chronic pain, prior cervical procedures, and sexual-abuse history. Consider pain tolerance and cervical stenosis when assessing whether an office procedure under local anesthesia is appropriate.

The office guideline advises ruling out pregnancy or timing the procedure immediately after menstruation, and postponing hysteroscopy during active pelvic or genital infection until treatment. These are procedure-selection considerations, not an anesthesia regimen.

For patients with cardiac or pulmonary comorbidities that compromise hemodynamic stability, the office guideline advises considering earlier termination at specified fluid deficits; these are qualified recommendations, not universal thresholds.

bullets: Office setup should provide space for equipment and staff, patient changing space, a restroom, a comfortable recovery area, and emergency equipment. The article does not specify a universal operating-room layout.

bullets: Use the minimum distension pressure needed for adequate visualization; excessive distension may cause pain. Smaller-diameter scopes generally cause less discomfort and require less cervical dilation.

bullets: Fluid absorption can cause overload, hyponatremia, and cerebral edema; possible manifestations include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, shortness of breath, or headache. Hypotonic electrolyte-free solutions are particularly associated with hyponatremia and cerebral edema.

Uterine perforation is a recognized diagnostic and operative complication, with greater risk when resection extends into the myometrium. The supplied sources do not establish a universal anesthesia response pathway.

Gas embolism is chiefly associated with surgical hysteroscopy. If suspected, the source advises stopping the procedure, removing the causative gas or solvent to reduce cavity expansion, and notifying the anesthesia team immediately.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy or adnexal surgery is performed through abdominal ports with CO₂ insufflation. General anesthesia with endotracheal intubation is usual for laparoscopy; the approach and extent of ovarian surgery depend on the operative indication.

The main anesthetic challenges are the combined effects of pneumoperitoneum and pelvic positioning on respiratory mechanics and circulation, including reduced compliance, increased airway pressures, and CO₂-related changes. Reassess ventilation and tube position as conditions change.

Anticipate access-related hemorrhage and insufflation or positioning complications; prioritize recognition of deteriorating ventilation, oxygenation, or hemodynamics and escalation with the surgical team.

Plan recovery around multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia where appropriate, PONV risk mitigation, and postanesthesia monitoring. Confirm adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when neuromuscular blockers have been used.

bullets: General anesthesia with endotracheal intubation is usual for laparoscopy. The general reference prefers an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; technique should reflect the patient and operation.

Insufflation and cephalad diaphragmatic displacement can reduce functional residual capacity and compliance, increase airway pressures, and worsen atelectasis, particularly with Trendelenburg. sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Insufflation changes cardiopulmonary loading: intrathoracic pressure and cardiac filling pressures rise, while IVC compression may reduce preload and venous return. Hemodynamic responses can vary with insufflation and patient position.

CO₂ absorption can cause hypercarbia and acidosis. The general reference describes effects including altered vascular tone, contractility, and arrhythmia susceptibility; interpret changes alongside ventilation, insufflation, and hemodynamic context.

At insufflation onset, peritoneal stretch may provoke a vagal response and bradyarrhythmia; hypercarbia can be associated with tachyarrhythmia. Recognize abrupt changes and coordinate promptly with the surgeon regarding insufflation and operative conditions.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: A rising airway pressure, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia can accompany impaired respiratory mechanics, tube migration, obstruction, or gas-related thoracic complications. Assess the airway and ventilation and escalate with the surgical team when the change is unexplained or significant.

Access-related solid-organ injury and hemorrhage may be difficult to see in the laparoscopic field. Maintain awareness of the possibility when hemodynamics change or bleeding is suspected; the supplied reference does not provide a procedure-specific hemorrhage algorithm.

Trendelenburg-related concerns described in the general reference include facial, laryngopharyngeal, and conjunctival edema, visual injury, nerve injury, and compartment syndrome. The supplied evidence does not establish incidence or a cystectomy-specific prevention protocol.

bullets: The general laparoscopy reference describes balanced crystalloid with goal-directed administration and cautions that excessive fluid can contribute to facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema, worsened by Trendelenburg. It does not establish a fixed volume for ovarian surgery.

Heart rate, blood pressure, central venous pressure, and urine output are described as poor stand-alone surrogates for intravascular volume during pneumoperitoneum. Interpret them in the full clinical context.

Laparoscopy is associated with less bleeding and reduced transfusion need overall, but access injury can cause hemorrhage and limited visualization may obscure it. The available evidence gives no cystectomy-specific blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or blood-preparation rule.

bullets: Laparoscopic pain may be somatic from port sites and visceral from peritoneal stretch and tissue manipulation. Laparoscopy is an independent PONV risk factor, and the general reference recommends prophylactic antiemetic administration. The supplied sources do not establish one mandatory drug combination or regimen for every patient.

bullets: When neuromuscular blockers are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery to TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis should be confirmed before extubation. This applies to cases using neuromuscular blockade, not to local or neuraxial techniques without it.

After anesthesia, patients should receive postanesthesia care with monitoring appropriate to condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. The ASA standard requires quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase.

In an ovarian-cystectomy randomized trial, nausea/vomiting and the QoR-15 pain domain were reported as recovery outcomes, with QoR-15 assessed at 24 hours. The abstract does not describe an emergence protocol, PACU management, discharge criteria, or postoperative-care protocols.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Postpartum tubal ligation is commonly performed through an infraumbilical mini-laparotomy; the enlarged postpartum uterus can bring the tubes within reach of the incision.

When feasible, consider neuraxial anesthesia, including a functional labor epidural; individualize technique and timing to the patient’s condition and preferences. The evidence does not establish a universally superior technique.

Key perioperative concerns include aspiration risk, postpartum hemodynamic status and blood loss, and the possibility that labor epidural anesthesia may be inadequate or fail as time from delivery increases.

After anesthesia, admit the patient to the PACU or an equivalent area unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Re-evaluate the patient on arrival and continually in recovery; monitor according to the patient’s medical condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature. Use a quantitative method of assessing oxygenation, such as pulse oximetry, during the initial phase of recovery.

Recovery priorities include respiratory and hemodynamic reassessment, adequate analgesia and PONV control, and monitoring for urinary, bowel, bleeding, and positioning-related problems.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation supports the vaginal vault by securing mesh to the vagina and the anterior longitudinal ligament at the sacral promontory. Open abdominal repair is described through a Pfannenstiel or low midline incision; laparoscopic repair uses a minimally invasive abdominal approach.

Robotic assistance is described as an option for intracorporeal suturing. The available robotic series report variable operative times and complications; they do not establish a preferred approach or a routine anesthesia protocol.

Surgical exposure may involve dissection of the promontory and adjacent vaginal spaces. The source describes identifying the ureter and major vessels before promontory dissection and avoiding excessive lateral or leftward dissection.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess comorbidities and the planned approach, including ability to tolerate general anesthesia, pneumoperitoneum, and the required position. The procedure cohort reports approach selection influenced by BMI and comorbidities, but does not define a general selection rule.

Clarify the surgeon’s bowel-preparation plan rather than assuming a universal policy: one procedural review says adequate preparation may aid promontory exposure, while ERAS review material lists avoidance of bowel preparation.

Review anticoagulation and VTE risk in the context of the patient and local pathway. A cohort reports low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis for at-risk patients, but supplies no regimen or timing for an individual patient.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, the procedural source describes general anesthesia in modified lithotomy, with vaginal and rectal access. Pelvic MIS may use Trendelenburg; the precise position and degree should follow the operative approach and patient tolerance.

Plan padding and securement before docking; protect the face from robot arms and avoid moving the table while the robot is docked. Position-related nerve injury, pressure injury, and edema are described concerns.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. The ASA standard calls for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.
A urinary catheter is part of the described laparoscopic setup; the source notes that it can also permit bladder filling to help identify bladder margins or lesions.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy procedural review specifies general anesthesia but does not state an airway device or ventilation plan. A general laparoscopic/robotic reference prefers an endotracheal tube to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; apply this as approach-level context, not a sacrocolpopexy-specific protocol.

Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg can reduce pulmonary compliance and functional residual capacity, increase airway pressures, and promote atelectasis. The generic MIS source describes lung-protective ventilation as commonly used, with settings titrated to mechanics rather than a case-specific target.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not imply paralysis is required for every approach.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During insufflation, anticipate changes in preload, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac filling pressures, and rhythm; Trendelenburg can further alter venous return and filling pressures. Reassess when position or insufflation changes.

CO₂ absorption and restricted respiratory mechanics may produce hypercarbia and increased airway pressures. The general MIS reference describes increasing minute ventilation to compensate for CO₂ absorption and notes permissive hypercapnia may be acceptable to avoid barotrauma; no sacrocolpopexy-specific targets are established.

Promontory dissection is a critical phase for presacral or median sacral vessel bleeding and potential injury to nearby major vessels or ureter. Maintain communication with the surgeon if bleeding or unexpected anatomy compromises exposure.

Position and insufflation can also affect renal perfusion and urine output; the generic MIS review describes reduced renal perfusion with parenchymal compression. Interpret urine output in the operative context rather than as a stand-alone measure of intravascular volume.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Presacral hemorrhage is a high-consequence hazard. A retrospective cohort reports two presacral-vein hemorrhages, controlled surgically with a Z-suture and warm-sponge pressure; this describes study events, not a universal response protocol.

Potential operative injuries include bowel or rectum, bladder, ureter, and vessels. If injury or major bleeding is suspected, coordinate promptly with the surgeon and support assessment and management according to the evolving clinical situation; the supplied procedure sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue algorithm.

During robotic surgery, limited access after docking makes advance communication about undocking and access to the patient important. The generic robotic reference identifies accidental extubation and face pressure injury from robot arms as hazards.

After steep Trendelenburg, assess for airway or facial edema, visual symptoms, and position-related nerve injury. The source describes these as potential complications, not as an indication for a particular routine extubation test.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The general MIS reference describes balanced crystalloid and goal-directed fluid administration, cautioning that excess fluid may worsen facial, pharyngeal, and laryngeal edema in Trendelenburg. It provides no procedure-specific volume or transfusion protocol.

In a prospective series of 132 laparoscopic sacrocolpopexies beyond the learning curve, reported blood loss was 185 mL (SD 124). A separate cohort estimated blood loss from the difference between pre- and postoperative hemoglobin and did not report a separate measured quantity. These observational series results are not an individualized blood-loss prediction.

bullets: A multimodal, opioid-sparing approach is consistent with the generic MIS reference, which describes acetaminophen and NSAIDs, with local anesthetic at port sites. The supplied sacrocolpopexy procedural source does not establish a procedure-specific regimen.
The generic review says a TAP block can be offered for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches; this is not evidence for a mandatory block or for a specific open-surgery technique.

Laparoscopy is identified as an independent PONV risk factor in the general MIS reference, which supports considering prophylaxis while individualizing the plan. No sacrocolpopexy-specific antiemetic regimen is provided.

bullets: No sacrocolpopexy-specific emergence or extubation criteria are reported. Reassess ventilation, oxygenation, circulation, consciousness, temperature, and position-related concerns before disposition.
When neuromuscular blockers have been used, confirm quantitative TOF recovery to at least 0.9 before extubation; this guidance applies to NMB use, not to cases performed without it.
Transfer to PACU or equivalent care with appropriate monitoring and support, a knowledgeable anesthesia team member accompanying the patient, and communication of the operative and anesthetic course.

Postoperative observation should include pain, nausea, urinary function, bowel recovery, and VTE prevention in context. The cohort reports catheter removal on postoperative day one, but catheter timing is not established as a universal anesthesia instruction.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For ruptured ectopic pregnancy, the available procedure-specific source describes urgent definitive surgery, principally laparotomy; laparoscopy may be attempted, with conversion possible if bleeding obscures the view.
The dominant immediate hazard is hemorrhagic shock. Control of bleeding is definitive; resuscitation supports the patient while surgery is expedited.
Anticipate concealed blood loss and deterioration, including around induction; tailor anesthetic technique to stability, aspiration risk, available expertise, and the urgency of source control.

Recovery priorities are reassessment of hemodynamics and ongoing bleeding, adequate analgesia, and appropriate postanesthesia monitoring; critical illness or major hemorrhage may require higher-acuity care.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Salpingectomy removes the affected fallopian tube. The strongest procedure-specific evidence here concerns urgent surgery for acute ruptured ectopic pregnancy, principally laparotomy; it does not establish a routine approach for other salpingectomy indications.

Laparoscopy is described in a single ruptured-pregnancy report, with conversion to laparotomy when bleeding impaired visualization. This illustrates a possible need for conversion, not a standard approach or conversion threshold.

For a stable patient with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, one practical review describes spinal anesthesia as acceptable. It does not support extrapolating that option to instability or significant bleeding.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Rapidly establish clinical stability and whether rupture or ongoing hemorrhage is suspected; an initially reassuring appearance may not exclude substantial blood loss. Do not let further optimization displace necessary definitive surgery.

Assess airway and aspiration risk, hemodynamic status, hemoglobin, and available blood products; obtain large-bore IV access. The source gives practical access advice, but the necessary resources depend on presentation and setting.

Treat the patient as potentially having a full stomach when aspiration risk is present. Pregnancy, pain, or vomiting may inform assessment, but the supplied evidence does not establish a universal airway technique for every salpingectomy.
Coordinate with the surgical team and assemble senior assistance when instability or hemorrhage is possible; use local emergency and blood-management pathways.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Have functioning anesthesia equipment and suction immediately available; prepare for urgent escalation if hemorrhage or airway difficulty develops. The practical review also emphasizes checklist use and essential equipment readiness.

Use routine anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique and patient. ASA basic standards require continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment are specified.

Consider invasive blood-pressure monitoring when active bleeding or instability makes beat-to-beat assessment useful; a case report describes this use, not a routine requirement. The supplied ectopic-pregnancy review gives no positioning recommendation.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Select general, regional, or other airway/anesthetic management in context of rupture, hemodynamic stability, aspiration risk, surgical approach, and available expertise. The procedure-specific review suggests general anesthesia according to stability; this is not a universal mandate for every salpingectomy.

When general anesthesia is selected and aspiration risk is significant, the source advises full-stomach precautions and rapid-sequence induction. It emphasizes preoxygenation and permits mask ventilation while awaiting paralysis using low airway pressures.

If tracheal intubation fails, the review describes attempting mask ventilation and, if possible, a supraglottic airway; laparotomy with an SGA is described as acceptable after failed intubation. This is contingency guidance, not a preferred routine airway.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect hemodynamic deterioration during induction or loss of compensatory sympathetic tone, even when pre-induction observations appear stable. Communicate changes promptly and prioritize timely surgical control of bleeding.
Titrate anesthetic depth to the evolving circulation. The review cautions that unstable patients may require less anesthetic and that requirements can rise as resuscitation restores stability.

An intentionally light anesthetic may increase awareness risk; once stability permits, deepen anesthesia and address analgesia. If awareness is suspected or reported, the review supports postoperative counseling.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Hemorrhagic shock is the principal time-critical threat. Recognize poor response to initial resuscitation or worsening instability and escalate urgently with the surgical team rather than relying on anesthetic support alone.
Significant blood loss may lead to coagulopathy and progression to complex shock. Reassess the clinical course and laboratory results as available, and involve local hemorrhage resources when needed.

Aspiration risk and failed intubation require preparation for oxygenation and ventilation alternatives. The source prioritizes adequate ventilation and oxygenation rather than intubation at all costs.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for ruptured ectopic pregnancy at district level

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Begin resuscitation while proceeding to definitive hemostasis; resuscitation is supportive and does not replace source control. Use locally available blood-management procedures and reassess response.

The practical review describes crystalloid and blood-component resuscitation, with emergency blood available; it does not justify a universal fluid total or fixed component strategy across patients and settings.

Consider antifibrinolytic therapy and blood-conservation options within the applicable local protocol and clinical context. The source discusses TXA during massive hemorrhage and low-technology autotransfusion where appropriate; these are not universal instructions.

Vasopressor support may be needed alongside fluid and blood resuscitation. The practical review discusses escalation for persistent hypotension; the supplied sources do not establish a single agent or universal target for this operation.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Provide adequate postoperative analgesia, individualized to hemodynamic status, surgical approach, and contraindications. The procedure-specific review recommends multimodal analgesia once the patient is stable but supplies no regimen.
Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia is an ERAS component in gynecologic surgery, but the review does not establish a salpingectomy-specific drug combination or dose.

The available evidence does not define ectopic-pregnancy-specific PONV prevention or treatment. Individualize management rather than importing findings from heterogeneous gynecologic ERAS studies as a procedure-specific protocol.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Base extubation and destination on recovery of ventilation, oxygenation, consciousness, and hemodynamic stability. The ectopic-pregnancy review does not supply a detailed extubation protocol.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and confirm adequate recovery before extubation when neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used; this guidance does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia care in PACU or an equivalent setting, with monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition; consider higher-acuity disposition when major hemorrhage or coagulopathy requires it.
