overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) is an open abdominal operation. General anesthesia is represented in procedure-specific evidence, while neuraxial and regional techniques are options rather than universal requirements.
Priorities include preoperative anemia and VTE risk assessment, maintaining euvolemia and normothermia, and limiting opioid-related effects through multimodal care.
Recovery planning should address pain and PONV, early mobilization, urinary-catheter removal when appropriate, and thromboprophylaxis tailored to the patient and operation.
Procedure-specific evidence does not establish a universal airway, monitoring beyond basic standards, fluid volume, transfusion approach, or anesthetic regimen; these require individual assessment.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TAH is an open approach to hysterectomy. The supplied guidance discusses abdominal hysterectomy alongside vaginal and minimally invasive procedures; approach selection is not prescribed for an individual patient.

The stated indications in the case record are not independently substantiated by these sources. The ACOG document covers hysterectomy in benign and gynecologic oncology care but does not provide a TAH indication algorithm.
Favor a minimally invasive approach when feasible according to the ACOG pathway, while recognizing that this is a surgical approach consideration, not an anesthesia mandate.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess and address anemia, obesity, tobacco and alcohol use, and sleep apnea; provide patient education and coordinate pain and recovery expectations with the surgical and anesthesia teams.

Assess VTE risk; prophylaxis should be individualized. The ACOG pathway names risk assessment models and recommends mechanical measures and early ambulation postoperatively, with pharmacologic prophylaxis also an option.

Avoid treating bowel preparation as routine anesthesia preparation: evidence of benefit is limited and the source describes individualized decision-making. Follow the applicable institutional fasting pathway.
Review hormonal contraception and other VTE modifiers without routine discontinuation of hormone therapy; balance risks and use prophylaxis decisions appropriate to the patient's risk and procedure.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The supplied procedure-specific sources do not establish a room layout, patient position, access plan, or routine invasive-monitoring threshold for TAH.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and assess blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.

For general anesthesia, use pulse oximetry and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring as specified by the basic standards; additional monitoring should follow patient condition and clinical judgment, not a BMI cutoff inferred from this evidence.

bullets: The sources do not specify an airway technique for TAH or establish that every patient requires tracheal intubation. A small TAH trial used general anesthesia and tracheal intubation, which describes that study rather than a universal requirement.

If an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is used, verify placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, and maintain quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis through the specified perioperative interval.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain euvolemia and normothermia in coordination with the surgical team. Both fluid overload and hypovolemia have potential physiologic consequences in the ACOG guidance.
Use active measures to avoid hypothermia; even mild temperature reduction is associated in the guidance with increased wound infection, arrhythmia, and blood-loss incidence.

The available material does not define TAH-specific hemodynamic targets, phases of vessel ligation, or management of uterine vasopressin or oxytocin effects; anticipate and manage changes in the context of the actual surgical events.

bullets: The supplied sources do not report TAH-specific rates or management protocols for hemorrhage, ureteral injury, or bladder injury.
Plan for PONV and opioid-related adverse effects through multimodal, opioid-sparing care and antiemetics; the sources do not establish one mandatory regimen.

Postoperative urinary retention and urinary tract infection are reported in gynecologic fast-track surgery literature. Monitor clinically and respond to the patient's course; these findings do not establish TAH-specific incidence.

Recognize residual neuromuscular blockade as a potential cause of upper-airway obstruction, reintubation, atelectasis, and pneumonia when blocking drugs are used; escalate evaluation and support according to the patient's condition.

bullets: Use a goal-directed clinical assessment to maintain euvolemia rather than a fixed crystalloid volume. The ACOG pathway identifies risks at both ends of the volume balance.
When IV fluids are needed, balanced crystalloids such as Ringer’s lactate are preferred over large volumes of 0.9% saline. Stop IV fluids within 24 hours when oral intake is adequate.

No supplied source establishes a routine crossmatch, expected blood loss, transfusion threshold, or TAH-specific antifibrinolytic strategy. Determine blood-product preparation from patient, procedure, and local policy.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use judicious opioids when appropriate and emphasize stepwise, multimodal, nonopioid strategies. For women undergoing TAH, preemptive acetaminophen, gabapentin, NSAIDs, and COX-2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce total narcotic requirements and improve pain and satisfaction.

For open gynecologic surgery, postoperative spinal or thoracic epidural analgesia may be considered. Neuraxial techniques are not feasible or appropriate for every procedure and can limit mobilization.

TAP blocks are an option, but findings are mixed. A small randomized TAH trial found lower 24-hour morphine use in its TAP group than in its epidural and parenteral groups; its protocol and population do not establish a universal preferred technique.
Include PONV prophylaxis appropriate to patient risk and local practice. The supplied ACOG pathway supports antiemetics but does not prescribe a universal drug combination.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation. This guidance addresses neuromuscular blockade generally, not TAH specifically.

Provide appropriate postanesthesia evaluation and monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; transfer with monitoring and support appropriate to the patient's condition.

Prioritize pain control, early ambulation, oral intake as tolerated, and timely removal of urinary catheters when used. For laparotomy for abdominal or pelvic malignancy, the ACOG guidance specifies extended VTE prophylaxis.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The ACOG source is ERAS guidance for gynecologic surgery, not a procedure-specific anesthesia manual; it explicitly does not define airway, positioning, access, or monitoring protocols.

The TAH randomized trial is narrow evidence: 60 selected patients, with exclusions including BMI of 30 or greater, and study-specific analgesia regimens. Its comparative results should not be converted into routine doses or a universal technique.

The gynecologic ERAS systematic review reported moderate overall quality and insufficient data for meta-analysis; results span different procedures and approaches and are not a TAH-specific anesthesia guideline.

The AHRQ anesthesiology evidence-review material supplied here is only an abstract and does not state specific recommendations or regimens. Adult-focused applicability is not consistently defined across sources; the TAH trial includes adults aged 18–60, while the broader guidance does not explicitly define an adult-only population.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Vaginal hysterectomy removes the uterus through the vaginal canal without abdominal incisions; it is often preferred for benign disease when feasible, especially uterine prolapse and favorable pelvic anatomy.

Do not assume a single anesthetic technique: general anesthesia is common for hysterectomy, while spinal or epidural anesthesia may be appropriate for selected vaginal procedures; the available sources give no selection criteria or regimen.

Prioritize hemodynamic and blood-loss surveillance, and maintain awareness of bladder and ureter injury risk. The supplied sources do not establish vaginal-hysterectomy-specific anesthetic targets or a standard intraoperative fluid or transfusion protocol.

Plan recovery around multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia, early oral intake and mobilization when appropriate, and timely urinary-catheter removal; monitor for pain, urinary dysfunction, bleeding, and other complications.

Guidelines for postoperative care in gynecologic/oncology surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The vaginal route provides access through the vaginal canal and avoids abdominal incisions. For benign conditions, it is often preferred when anatomy and other factors make it feasible, particularly with uterine prolapse.

Route selection is individualized. Consider the indication, uterine size and mobility, pelvic anatomy, prior surgery, comorbidities, surgeon expertise, available resources, and patient preference; a large uterus or adhesions may affect feasibility or prompt consideration of another approach.

Vaginal access does not generally require abdominal laparoscopic or robotic equipment unless a combined procedure is planned. The sources do not provide a procedure-specific operative sequence for anesthesia planning.

sources.label: Surgical Approaches to Hysterectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the indication, uterine size and mobility, pelvic anatomy, prior pelvic or abdominal surgery, comorbidities, and patient preferences as they bear on route and anesthetic planning.

Evaluate medical fitness and optimize relevant conditions. Significant cardiopulmonary disease warrants particular consideration; obesity, prior surgery and adhesions, and large uterine size are relative considerations, not automatic exclusions.

Review relevant imaging and pathology, assess cardiopulmonary status when indicated, and coordinate anticoagulant management with the appropriate specialists. The supplied sources do not provide a vaginal-hysterectomy-specific risk score or anticoagulant interruption schedule.

sources.label: Surgical Approaches to Hysterectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For any anesthetic, qualified anesthesia personnel should remain present and continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Apply monitoring appropriate to the selected technique and patient.

ASA basic standards include continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes during anesthesia. For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is common across hysterectomy procedures, but spinal or epidural anesthesia may be appropriate for specific vaginal procedures. The sources do not establish a preferred technique for vaginal hysterectomy or provide selection criteria.

Choose airway management and ventilation according to the anesthetic technique and individual clinical circumstances. The supplied procedure-specific review does not give an airway protocol for vaginal hysterectomy.

If general anesthesia is used, continually evaluate ventilation; ASA standards call for expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. Confirm airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted.

sources.label: Surgical Approaches to Hysterectomy — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain awareness of blood loss and hemodynamic status during dissection and control of uterine and other pelvic vessels. The source identifies potential bleeding sites but does not supply a vaginal-hysterectomy-specific sequence or blood-loss target.

Bladder and ureter injury are relevant surgical hazards. The source highlights the ureter’s proximity to uterine arteries and cardinal ligaments; it does not specify an anesthetic intervention to prevent injury.

The supplied references do not establish vaginal-hysterectomy-specific ventilation, hemodynamic, temperature, or anesthetic-depth targets. Use the applicable general monitoring standards and clinical judgment rather than inferring targets from another surgical approach.

sources.label: Surgical Approaches to Hysterectomy — StatPearls

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For a felon with abscess, tension, or fluctuance, the source-supported procedure is incision and drainage; cellulitis without abscess is managed differently.
A digital block before I&D is the only anesthetic technique specifically described for felon drainage; a finger tourniquet may aid visualization.
Prioritize complete drainage while protecting digital neurovascular structures, flexor tendon sheath, and nail matrix; edema and pus can compromise perfusion.
Aftercare described for felon includes wound packing and splinting, followed by reassessment; the available procedure source does not establish an airway or general-anesthetic plan.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For felon with abscess formation, tension, or fluctuance, drain the infected material. Cellulitis without abscess is not described as an I&D indication in this source.

The described approach targets maximal volar swelling and tenderness. Deep felon drainage uses a lateral incision with specified separation from the DIP joint and nail plate; superficial felon may use a volar longitudinal incision.

Bluntly separate fingertip septae as needed for complete drainage, irrigate, and pack and splint the wound. The source discourages fish-mouth, hockey-stick, and transverse palmar incisions because of reported injury and scarring.
This approach is supported for felon only; it should not be treated as a procedure description for flexor tendon sheath infection or palmar-space abscess.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care, ASA postanesthesia standards call for appropriate recovery-area care, handoff, and continuing assessment; the specific destination and discharge decision depend on the applicable care arrangements.

Flexor-tendon postoperative care described in the review emphasizes splint protection and staged, therapist-supervised movement. The reported protocol is not established as a universal adult rehabilitation schedule.
The supplied sources do not establish a tendon-repair-specific emergence or PACU checklist; evaluate recovery and discharge according to the anesthetic delivered and applicable standards.

The anesthesia-preference evidence is a survey of surgeons’ reported practice, with a directly acknowledged conflict between its Results section and table; it cannot resolve comparative effectiveness or individual selection.

The general hand-anesthesia review covers bedside procedures and blocks but does not prescribe a particular anesthetic technique for each operation. Case-specific adult anesthesia selection and regimen therefore remain unresolved by these sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hepatic resection removes part of the liver for benign or malignant lesions; it may be performed open or by a minimally invasive approach.
General anaesthesia with tracheal intubation and controlled ventilation is usual. Tailor invasive access and monitoring to patient risk, resection extent, approach, and duration.

The major intraoperative hazards are sudden, substantial bleeding—particularly hepatic-vein backflow during transection—and hemodynamic instability during vascular occlusion or release. Balance venous-pressure reduction against perfusion and air-embolism risk.
After resection, watch for bleeding, bile leak, metabolic disturbance, and post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF); extent of resection and clinical condition guide the level of postoperative care.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Resection is used for benign lesions and primary or secondary malignancy; colorectal liver metastases are identified as the main indication in the review.

Laparoscopic and robotic approaches share the indications of open surgery. Approach selection should account for the possibility of conversion and the need for prompt vascular control if bleeding occurs.
The review reports less blood loss, pain, wound infection, and length of stay with minimally invasive resection than open surgery, while noting that complication types and incidence are similar.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess underlying liver disease, functional reserve, comorbidities, frailty, anaemia, and nutrition. Cirrhosis and chemotherapy-associated liver injury increase PHLF risk; no single test reliably predicts postoperative liver dysfunction.

CT or MRI can estimate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; interpret it alongside liver function and post-hepatectomy liver failure risk. The review cites minimum FLR volumes of 20% with normal liver function, 30–40% with severe steatohepatitis or prior hepatotoxic chemotherapy, and at least 50% with cirrhosis.

CTP class, MELD, and ICG retention may inform multidisciplinary selection, but none should be treated as a stand-alone clearance rule. PVE and other augmentation strategies may be considered when FLR is inadequate.
Optimize relevant comorbidities and consider chemotherapy-related hepatic and cardiac effects; the review states surgery should be delayed until 4–6 weeks after neoadjuvant treatment.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Ensure large-bore IV access and ready access to blood products because hemorrhage may be sudden and catastrophic. Decide on arterial and central access according to patient, procedure, and monitoring needs rather than treating either line as universal.

Use standard anaesthetic monitoring and add invasive haemodynamic monitoring when justified. Avoid hypothermia; temperature and coagulation effects matter in a procedure with substantial bleeding potential.
Trendelenburg is one reported means of lowering CVP, not a mandatory position. During minimally invasive surgery, pneumoperitoneum can make CVP readings unreliable.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube and controlled ventilation is the usual technique described for hepatic resection.

For laparoscopic or robotic cases, assess tolerance of prolonged CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, particularly with cardiac or respiratory dysfunction. Standard laparoscopy sources describe altered respiratory mechanics and increased ventilatory requirements during insufflation.
Use appropriate capnography and verify tracheal-tube position. The supplied sources do not establish a liver-resection-specific ventilator prescription.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During parenchymal transection, hepatic-vein backflow is a major bleeding source. Venous-pressure reduction is used to limit bleeding, but must be balanced against systemic perfusion and organ blood flow.

Pringle manoeuvre interrupts hepatic arterial and portal inflow and can alter venous return and systemic vascular resistance. Communicate with the surgeon at clamp and release, anticipating hemodynamic change.

Occlusion strategy and duration depend on liver condition and surgical circumstances. The review describes intermittent clamping with reperfusion intervals; prolonged continuous inflow interruption risks ischaemia–reperfusion injury.
Total vascular exclusion can produce profound volume shifts and is reserved in the review for selected situations, including persistent major hepatic-vein bleeding or required IVC resection.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Be prepared for abrupt major haemorrhage, including from hepatic-vein injury. In minimally invasive surgery, rapid vascular control may be difficult; escalate promptly with the surgical team when bleeding is suspected.

Consider venous air embolism when sudden haemodynamic or end-tidal CO₂ changes occur, particularly during low-CVP transection or reperfusion. Source-described signs include a fall in end-tidal CO₂, oxygenation changes, and arrhythmias; use local emergency escalation and surgical coordination.
Monitor for PHLF, bile leak, postoperative haemorrhage, renal dysfunction, and metabolic disturbance. The review describes PHLF by rising INR and bilirubin on or after postoperative day 5.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: ERAS guidance summarized in the review recommends balanced crystalloids, low CVP during resection, and euvolaemia after resection. Avoid carrying restrictive intraoperative fluid practice into recovery once hemostasis is achieved.

Low-CVP practice is debated: evidence summarized in the source suggests reduced blood loss and transfusion but not improved clinical outcomes, and another analysis found CVP monitoring did not affect blood loss. Individualize the strategy and preserve end-organ perfusion.
Do not treat CVP as a stand-alone volume measure during pneumoperitoneum. After transection, assess and restore circulating volume according to bleeding, hemodynamics, and perfusion needs.
Use blood-conservation and transfusion decisions in the context of actual blood loss, physiology, and coagulation assessment; the supplied sources do not establish a universal transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery
Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia tailored to open versus minimally invasive surgery. The ERAS review does not recommend routine thoracic epidural analgesia for open liver resection; it identifies intrathecal opioids and peri-incisional catheters as alternatives.
Paracetamol and NSAIDs may be components when appropriate to liver function, renal function, and other contraindications; the source urges caution with extensive resection and liver disease.
Use multimodal PONV prevention; the ERAS guidance summarized recommends two antiemetics.

sources.label: Perioperative management for hepatic resection surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Postoperative destination should reflect resection extent, approach, and patient condition. More extensive or open resections generally need closer monitoring than smaller minimally invasive resections.

Do not apply a fixed extubation rule based only on resection category: the source material provides no standardized liver-resection emergence or extubation criteria. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative TOF recovery before extubation.

Recovery care should include surveillance for bleeding, bile leak, glucose disturbance, and evolving PHLF; early oral intake and mobilization are included in the ERAS recommendations summarized by the review.
Postanaesthesia monitoring must address oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with an appropriate PACU or equivalent care location.

Anesthetic Considerations in Hepatectomies under Hepatic Vascular Control

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is an educational perioperative review, not a trial. Its summary of ERAS recommendations and low-CVP evidence should be interpreted with the stated debate and limits on demonstrated clinical outcomes.
The vascular-control source is an older narrative review and does not establish an optimal anaesthetic technique; some reported evidence comes from small studies or nonclinical populations.

Case-specific targets and standardized rescue or extubation protocols are not established across the supplied evidence; decisions remain individualized to procedure, patient physiology, and local practice.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Liver transplantation is a major operation conducted under general anesthesia. The anesthetic course is organized around dissection, anhepatic, and graft-reperfusion phases, each with changing hemodynamic and coagulation demands.

Priorities include anticipating dissection-related bleeding, managing preload changes during caval clamping when used, and preparing for abrupt cardiovascular instability at reperfusion, including arrhythmia and right-heart stress.

An arterial line and central access are usual components of monitoring and access; additional cardiac monitoring and bypass resources depend on the patient's physiology, operative approach, and local practice.

Most recipients proceed to ICU care for ongoing hemodynamic and hematologic monitoring. Extubation is individualized; when neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative recovery should be confirmed before extubation.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Liver transplantation is a treatment for end-stage liver disease and also addresses selected cases of acute liver failure and hepatic malignancy. Selection and allocation depend on clinical criteria; the supplied review describes MELD-based allocation and Milan criteria for primary liver tumours.

The operative phases are hepatectomy (dissection), anhepatic, and reperfusion (neohepatic). In classic transplantation, caval clamping affects preload and venovenous bypass may be used; the piggyback approach may have less hemodynamic fluctuation.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess disease severity and allocation context, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, encephalopathy, ascites, and the patient's coagulation profile. MELD incorporates creatinine, bilirubin, INR, and sodium; acute liver failure prioritization is described separately from MELD.

Cirrhosis may produce low SVR with compensatory high cardiac output, while pulmonary hypertension, cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and hepatorenal syndrome can materially alter anesthetic risk and monitoring needs.

Coagulation abnormalities may include hypocoagulability, hypercoagulability, or DIC; do not infer bleeding risk from a single conventional test in isolation. Review notes that severe anemia is also usual in the described cirrhotic population.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan reliable large-bore access, central access, rapid fluid-delivery capability, warming equipment, infusion pumps, and immediate defibrillation capability according to anticipated needs. The supplied review identifies an arterial line and central line for every recipient.

Choose cardiac monitoring with the patient's risks and local expertise in mind. One source describes TEE as standard of care, while another says it is not routine; PA catheter monitoring is specifically indicated in the supplied material for portopulmonary hypertension.

Use frequent blood sampling and point-of-care testing for acid-base status, electrolytes, hemoglobin, and coagulation, including viscoelastic testing where available. Positioning details are not provided in the transplant sources.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is the described technique. RSI is usually preferred in the review because delayed gastric emptying and related aspiration risks are common considerations; selection and conduct should account for hemodynamics and the individual presentation rather than presume a universal indication.

Titrate induction agents carefully to avoid further reduction in SVR. The review identifies intravenous propofol and etomidate as preferred short-acting induction agents and notes agent-specific hemodynamic and pharmacokinetic considerations.

Maintain standard anesthetic monitoring, including continual ventilation assessment and quantitative expired CO₂ monitoring for general anesthesia, subject to the stated standard's exceptions. The transplant sources do not establish a case-specific ventilation prescription.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During dissection, hemorrhage and instability can follow manipulation of the diseased liver, caval compression, or vascular torque. Optimize circulating volume and support perfusion while preparing for the hemodynamic changes of the next phase.

During the anhepatic phase, caval clamping in classic transplantation can reduce preload and cardiac output; acidosis and coagulopathy may worsen. Follow potassium and ionized calcium and coordinate phase-specific volume and hemodynamic management with the surgical team.

Reperfusion may abruptly reduce SVR and contractility while increasing pulmonary pressures; returning cold, acidotic, hyperkalemic blood and preservation-solution contents can precipitate dysrhythmia or right-heart dysfunction. Confirm readiness and communicate closely with the surgical team before graft flow is restored.

sources.label: Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations
Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: In liver transplantation, post-reperfusion syndrome is defined as a 30% decrease in MAP for at least one minute within the first five minutes after graft reperfusion; it can cause severe arrhythmias or asystole.

Consider pulmonary hypertension and right-heart dysfunction when instability occurs around reperfusion: severely cold or acidotic reperfused blood, or excess volume returning to the right heart, can raise pulmonary pressures and cause right-heart dysfunction. TEE may help evaluate cardiovascular collapse, including pulmonary hypertension, hypovolemia, myocardial depression, clot, or air embolism.

Persistent bleeding may reflect surgical sources, coagulopathy, or hyperfibrinolysis; distinguish these before targeted correction. Graft dysfunction and ongoing hemorrhage require close postoperative surveillance and may prompt further intervention.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use repeated volume and perfusion assessment; avoid assuming either liberal or restrictive fluid therapy is universally appropriate. The review reports risks from excessive fluid, including pulmonary or graft edema, and renal-failure risk with restrictive therapy; it states that no ideal fluid prescription or monitoring system is established.

Manage bleeding and coagulation with clinical assessment and viscoelastic testing where available. Sources conflict on some transfusion strategies: one describes avoiding plasma and lowering CVP in the pre-anhepatic phase, while another describes PRBC and FFP replacement; these do not support a universal ratio or empiric transfusion rule.

Anticipate citrate-associated hypocalcemia during blood-product administration and changing potassium and acid-base status across phases; monitor and respond to measured values and clinical context. Avoid excess transfusion because congestion may impair graft function.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for Liver Transplantation: An Update
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use a multimodal analgesic approach appropriate to graft function, renal status, bleeding risk, and recovery goals. The supplied ERAS review recommends multimodal analgesia for transplantation but does not provide a transplant-specific drug regimen.

Neuraxial epidural analgesia is not recommended in the supplied transplant ERAS table because of bleeding risk. If systemic analgesia is used, account for renal and hepatic dysfunction; the sources do not establish a universal postoperative opioid or NSAID plan.
The ERAS review recommends dual antiemetic therapy, with an additional agent if required; individual contraindications and the patient's risk profile still apply.

sources.label: A review of the current ERAS guidelines for liver resection, liver transplantation and pancreatoduodenectomy
Adult Liver Transplantation: Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Plan postoperative ICU care for ongoing hemodynamic and hematologic monitoring. Extubation at the conclusion of surgery may be considered in selected patients, but the sources do not establish universal criteria or a fixed timing protocol.

When a neuromuscular blocking drug has been used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Transfer and recovery should include appropriate monitoring, handoff, and reassessment in the receiving ICU or equivalent care area; recovery standards require continued attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The transplant-specific sources are an educational clinical summary and a narrative review, not formal procedure-specific anesthesia guidelines; neither provides evidence grading or a systematic review method.

Monitoring and fluid practices are not fully settled in the supplied evidence. TEE use and some fluid/transfusion approaches differ between sources; clinical claims above retain this uncertainty rather than presenting one approach as universal.

The sources do not specify positioning, a universal setup configuration, case-specific fluid targets, or a detailed extubation protocol. These details require local expertise and individual clinical judgment; their absence does not establish that a fixed target should exist.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open cholecystectomy may be planned or converted from a laparoscopic operation; the described approaches are a right subcostal (Kocher) or upper midline incision. General anesthesia is the usual technique described for the operation.

The dominant procedural hazards are uncertain or variable biliary anatomy, bile duct injury, bleeding, and liver injury during exposure. Careful identification of anatomy and inspection of the gallbladder bed are central surgical priorities.

In critically ill patients, an open approach may avoid the cardiovascular and ventilatory effects of pneumoperitoneum; the supplied sources do not establish a procedure-specific anesthetic response or target.

The larger incision is usually more painful than laparoscopic surgery and is associated with more wound complications. Recovery requires postanesthesia assessment and monitoring appropriate to the patient's condition.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open surgery may be selected in advance or used after conversion from laparoscopy. Reasons for conversion include unclear anatomy, extensive inflammation or adhesions, anatomical variation, bile duct injury, retained duct stones, uncontrolled bleeding, or need for duct exploration.

Planned open surgery is described for cirrhosis, gallbladder cancer, extensive upper abdominal adhesions, selected comorbidities, and critically ill patients. These are source-described selection contexts, not a complete set of indications or contraindications.
Exposure is through a right subcostal (Kocher) or upper midline incision, using packs and retractors. The source emphasizes avoiding liver injury from retraction.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the indication, prior upper abdominal operations and adhesions, comorbidities, and whether the planned approach is open or may convert. The surgical workup described includes ultrasound, with CT, HIDA scanning, blood work, and history and examination as appropriate.

Assess and optimize hemodynamic status before surgery; the source specifies stabilization and resuscitation when needed. It also describes possible antibiotics and thrombosis prophylaxis as elements of standard surgical preparation, without giving an individualized anesthetic protocol.
Planned open surgery may be used for patients with cirrhosis; the source does not specify how cirrhosis-related conditions should alter anesthetic management.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use an operating room equipped for open abdominal surgery. The surgical source describes packs and retractors and recommends that cholangiography equipment be available when intraoperative cholangiography is needed.

The supplied open-cholecystectomy source does not specify patient positioning, vascular access, or a procedure-specific monitoring package. Select access and monitoring according to the patient's condition and anticipated operative course rather than assuming routine arterial or central venous lines.

For anesthesia, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ASA basic standards include ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure source describes general anesthesia but does not establish an airway device, induction method, or ventilation targets for open cholecystectomy. Airway and ventilation planning therefore require individual clinical judgment; no universal rapid-sequence technique is supported by these sources.

When general anesthesia is used, assess ventilation continually; verify endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, and continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide monitoring through the specified intraoperative period.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Critical surgical steps include exposure and identification of the gallbladder, Calot triangle, and bile ducts, followed by cystic duct and artery division and separation of the gallbladder from the liver bed. The source stresses obtaining a critical view before division.

Anatomical variation is a material surgical hazard: the source reports altered biliary anatomy and describes potential common bile duct misidentification and right hepatic artery injury. This supports careful communication around difficult anatomy, not an anesthesia-specific intervention.

An open approach may avoid pneumoperitoneum-related decreases in cardiac return and increases in ventilation pressures in critically ill patients. The source does not provide ventilation or hemodynamic targets for this operation.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant operative complications include bleeding, liver injury, bile leak, bile duct injury, and retained duct stones. The surgeon inspects the liver bed for bleeding and bile leakage; anesthesia should maintain communication with the surgical team if these concerns arise.

The source reports more wound infection, hematoma, and hernia with open than routine laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and a higher overall complication rate in a cited study. These observations identify recovery concerns but are not individualized risk estimates.

During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, bile duct injury or uncontrolled bleeding may prompt conversion to open surgery; the source does not provide an anesthesia-specific complication-management protocol.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Patients should be hemodynamically stabilized and resuscitated if needed before surgery. The source does not specify an intraoperative fluid-management regimen.

Uncontrolled bleeding is a stated reason to convert to open surgery, and the liver bed is inspected for bleeding and bile leaks. The source does not specify an anesthesia-specific blood-product or blood-loss strategy.

sources.label: Open Cholecystectomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Open cholecystectomy is usually more painful than laparoscopic surgery. The supplied procedure source does not specify an analgesic regimen, and the available evidence does not establish thoracic epidural analgesia as a universal standard for this operation.

A two-patient report describes thoracic paravertebral block in selected high-risk adults, but its authors identify the small case number as a limitation. It cannot establish routine analgesic or anesthetic practice. The supplied procedure source gives no PONV regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The open-cholecystectomy source does not specify an emergence or extubation approach. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

After anesthesia, admission to a PACU or equivalent is expected except by specific anesthesiologist order. During initial recovery, use quantitative oxygenation assessment and monitor according to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

The open operation's larger incision makes wound infection and hematoma relevant postoperative concerns; assess the surgical wound and clinical status during recovery. No procedure-specific PACU schedule or discharge criteria are supplied.

bullets: The principal procedure source is an educational narrative review of open cholecystectomy, not an anesthesia protocol. It explicitly leaves airway, positioning, monitoring, anesthetic drugs, ventilation, fluid management, and emergence unspecified.

The paravertebral-block source is a two-patient case report in selected adults; it cannot define routine technique. Liver and pancreatic ERAS or anesthesia sources address different operations and are not used here to prescribe open-cholecystectomy management.

General ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade sources support applicable monitoring and recovery principles; they do not supply a procedure-specific anesthetic plan. Case-specific targets and choices remain dependent on clinical assessment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes the pancreatic head and adjacent structures, followed by pancreatic, biliary, and gastrointestinal reconstruction; it may be performed open, laparoscopically, or robotically.

General anesthesia is described for the operation. Priorities include appropriate monitoring, maintaining temperature, and avoiding both excessive and inadequate fluid administration; the available evidence does not establish one universal anesthetic recipe.
Major operative hazards include vascular injury and bleeding during dissection, while pancreatic fistula and delayed gastric emptying are important postoperative complications.

Recovery priorities include glycemic management, early feeding as tolerated, and surveillance for anastomotic complications. Analgesia should be individualized: the sources differ on thoracic epidural use in pancreaticoduodenectomy.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation combines resection with reconstruction: pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy are described in the technical illustration. The precise extent of resection varies with disease and anatomy.
Open, laparoscopic, and robotic approaches are used. The illustrated sequence is one institution’s standard open technique, not a universal operative sequence.

Vascular resection and reconstruction may be undertaken in selected cases with venous involvement; the cited robotic article describes selected institutional practice, not a general approach for all such patients.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess nutritional status; the ERAS review recommends nutritional assessment and several weeks of preoperative support for nutritional deficiency in pancreaticoduodenectomy patients. The form and duration of support depend on clinical circumstances.

Review jaundice, biliary obstruction, and any prior biliary intervention. The ERAS review does not recommend routine preoperative biliary drainage; it lists specific indications, including cholangitis, required neoadjuvant therapy, or higher bilirubin.

The anesthesia assessment should establish medical status and an anesthesia-care plan. Procedure-specific sources also describe assessing tumor extent and vascular anatomy, but do not supply a complete anesthesia risk-stratification protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The technical description uses supine positioning with the right arm tucked. Positioning must be adapted to the chosen approach and operative requirements; the robotic vascular-resection source describes a different position after laparoscopic preparation.

A procedure-specific description supports arterial pressure monitoring, with or without a central venous catheter, and Foley catheter use. It does not establish that central access is mandatory for every case.
Basic anesthetic monitoring standards require ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The technical review describes induction of general anesthesia but gives no airway device or airway strategy. Select airway management according to the patient, aspiration risk, and operative circumstances rather than treating an RSI or specific tube as universal.

With general anesthesia, confirm airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide. Continual end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis is required from placement of an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask through extubation or transfer preparation.
The procedure-specific sources do not establish a preferred ventilation strategy or targets for pancreaticoduodenectomy; these should not be inferred from the operative technique descriptions.

sources.label: Whipple pancreatoduodenectomy: A technical illustration

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Dissection around the mesenteric and portal vessels is a critical phase: vascular injury can cause bleeding, and vascular anatomy may differ from preoperative imaging. Maintain communication about anticipated vascular involvement and changes in the operative plan.

The technical review emphasizes checking hepatic arterial flow before gastroduodenal artery ligation when celiac or superior mesenteric artery stenosis may alter flow. This is an operative consideration, not an anesthesia-specific monitoring target.
ERAS guidance supports goal-directed fluid therapy and maintaining normothermia. The sources do not define a single hemodynamic target or a fixed temperature-management recipe for every patient.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Pancreatic fistula and delayed gastric emptying are prominent postoperative concerns. The available material supports monitoring and clinical evaluation, but does not establish an anesthetic maneuver that prevents either complication.

After portal or superior mesenteric venous reconstruction, the cited institutional article identifies mesenteric venous hypertension and venous thrombosis as concerns. Its surveillance and treatment descriptions are local practice and should not be generalized as a universal protocol.

For suspected major vascular injury, recognize the potential for rapid blood loss, communicate immediately with the surgical team, and escalate to available institutional hemorrhage support. The sources provide no universal transfusion threshold or rescue algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use an individualized, goal-directed approach. The ERAS review warns that excessive fluid may contribute to edema, pulmonary complications, anastomotic complications, and bleeding; it also notes renal-failure risk with restrictive therapy in its broader surgical discussion.

Anticipate bleeding during mesenteric dissection and possible portal or superior mesenteric venous work. Neither the operative technical review nor the vascular-resection article provides a general transfusion threshold or universal blood-product plan.

The available sources do not establish a fixed fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, or hemodynamic target for this operation; these are case- and context-dependent rather than universal reference values.

bullets: Multimodal analgesia and limiting intravenous opioids are described within an ERAS pathway. The sources do not establish one regional technique as appropriate for every patient or approach.

Thoracic epidural use is unresolved in the supplied procedure-specific guidance: one editorial describes combined general and epidural anesthesia in the authors’ practice, while the ERAS review’s pancreaticoduodenectomy table includes both support for and a statement against thoracic epidural anesthesia. Do not characterize it as an undisputed gold standard.

bullets: The procedural review does not specify emergence or extubation criteria. For patients who receive neuromuscular blocking drugs, confirm a TOF ratio of ≥0.9 before extubation.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, ASA guideline recommendations summarized in the supplied source support quantitative monitoring and confirming a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

After anesthesia, admit patients to a PACU or equivalent care area unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Continually evaluate and monitor the patient using methods appropriate to their condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature.
Postoperative priorities include glycemic control and early oral feeding when appropriate; evaluate delayed gastric emptying and nutritional needs if oral feeding is not tolerated.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The supplied adult ACDF evidence describes elective procedures under general anesthesia. Cervical plexus block is discussed as an adjunct; sole-block approaches are described as uncommon and not established as routine.

Treat anesthesia duration as a risk-assessment consideration, not a modifiable target or proof of causation: longer duration was associated with higher adjusted odds of selected adverse outcomes in an observational cohort.
Cervical plexus block may improve analgesia and reduce opioid requirements when used with general anesthesia, but the review does not establish a preferred universal technique or regimen.

Recovery priorities supported by general standards are ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature; when neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ACDF is the anterior cervical discectomy and fusion procedure represented in the supplied elective adult cohort. The available cohort evidence concerns general anesthesia; it does not define surgical indications, levels, approach details or a preferred anesthetic technique.

Cervical plexus block has been described as an adjunct to general anesthesia for cervical spine surgery. The regional-anesthesia review favors superficial or intermediate approaches and cautions that deep cervical block can have serious complications; this does not establish a routine ACDF block protocol.

bullets: Apply the adult scope of the available ACDF cohort and perform individualized preanesthetic assessment. The general ASA preanesthesia standard assigns the anesthesiologist responsibility for determining medical status and developing the anesthesia-care plan; it does not supply ACDF-specific selection criteria.

Consider duration in overall risk assessment, especially alongside patient and procedural factors. The reported association is observational and should not be interpreted as a reason to avoid a lengthy procedure or as evidence that a particular anesthetic change prevents complications.

bullets: Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring and maintain qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout anesthesia. The supplied ACDF study and regional review do not provide a procedure-specific positioning, access or enhanced-monitoring protocol.

During anesthesia, continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature, with ECG displayed and blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes under the basic monitoring standard.

bullets: The adult observational cohort found higher adjusted odds of any complication and return to the operating room in its longest anesthesia-time group versus its shortest. bullets: In the cohort, the longest anesthesia-time group had higher observed rates of pulmonary complications, transfusion, sepsis, wound complications, prolonged stay and return to the operating room than the shortest group. The study did not test a management strategy for preventing these events.

If a cervical plexus block is chosen, recognize the block-specific hazards reported in the review, including systemic local-anesthetic toxicity and possible nerve damage after intraneural injection. The source does not provide an ACDF-specific rescue algorithm.

bullets: A cervical plexus block may be considered as an adjunct for analgesia and opioid sparing, with technique and suitability discussed in context. The review reports benefit but does not establish optimal dosing or a universal block regimen.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Endovascular AVM embolization selectively delivers liquid embolic material through feeding arteries to obliterate or reduce the nidus; it may be staged or precede resection.
Immobility and stable physiology are priorities. General anesthesia is commonly used for INR procedures; no anesthetic mode is established as superior.
Key hazards are hemorrhage from embolic passage into draining veins, stroke or injury to normal-brain supply, and rupture during flow changes.

After embolization, close neurologic observation and procedure-specific blood-pressure management are important; the available review describes slightly low postoperative pressure without a numeric target.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Selective catheterization of AVM feeding arteries permits controlled injection of radiopaque liquid embolic material; the intended result is nidus obliteration or reduction.
Embolization may be performed with diagnostic angiography or in a later session. Staging is used in some approaches to limit risks from rapid flow alteration; treatment is individualized.
The source describing combined embolization and resection is a procedural protocol, not comparative evidence establishing a universal embolization strategy or extent.

bullets: Review lesion evaluation and treatment plan with the neurointerventional team; the procedural source describes selection using grading scales and multidisciplinary assessment.
Assess baseline neurologic status, airway and cardiopulmonary reserve, blood pressure, coagulation, and prior contrast or medication reactions as part of INR preparation.
Determine whether treatment is staged and whether resection is planned; embolization can carry risks from altered flow, venous outflow obstruction, and compromise of normal-brain arterial supply.

bullets: Use the neurointerventional angiography environment with fluoroscopic imaging; the procedural protocol places patients supine for diagnostic angiography and embolization.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is common for INR and can provide immobility and controlled ventilation, but the review does not establish it as superior to other anesthetic modes.

When using general anesthesia, controlled ventilation may support normocapnia or mild hypocapnia. Avoid treating hyperventilation as a universal requirement; its use is described as a possible flow-redistribution maneuver.

Select anesthetic technique according to procedural complexity, duration, immobilization needs, patient status, and interventionist preference; be prepared for airway or hemodynamic complications in the remote suite.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Injection and changing flow are critical phases. The interventionist is directed to avoid reflux into non-AVM arteries and distal embolization into draining veins.
Liquid embolic passage into a drainage vein is identified as a serious hemorrhage mechanism. Mild intraoperative hypotension may be helpful according to the review, but it supplies no target.
Onyx is described as less influenced by blood pressure than glue; this material-specific statement does not establish a general blood-pressure strategy for all embolic agents.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Maintain readiness to recognize and escalate suspected hemorrhage, arterial occlusion, or neurologic change; the procedural risks include rupture, stroke, venous outflow obstruction, and injury to normal-brain supply.
Contrast reaction and contrast-associated kidney injury are relevant peri-procedural concerns; assess prior reactions and attend to hydration and renal risk in context.
For a new postoperative neurologic deficit, repeat neurologic assessment and obtain imaging as clinically indicated; the review specifically notes CT or other imaging when a deficit is detected.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain appropriate hydration in view of contrast exposure and individual renal and cardiovascular risk; the available review provides no universal fluid volume or regimen.

Manage blood pressure in coordination with the interventionist. The AVM review describes slightly low postoperative pressure, but gives no numeric target; avoid importing targets from other neurovascular procedures.
The available procedural protocol advises having blood consent and products available for resection, but does not specify transfusion thresholds or an embolization-specific blood-loss plan.

bullets: The supplied sources do not establish an AVM embolization-specific postoperative analgesic or PONV regimen. Individualize symptom management and avoid delaying neurologic assessment.

bullets: Plan emergence to permit prompt neurologic assessment when appropriate, while avoiding abrupt hemodynamic stress; the review identifies smooth recovery for immediate examination as a general INR consideration.

Continue procedure-appropriate blood-pressure and neurologic monitoring after anesthesia; postanesthesia standards require continual evaluation using methods appropriate to the patient's condition.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Awake craniotomy permits cortical or subcortical mapping during resection near eloquent function. Common approaches are asleep–awake–asleep (AAA) and monitored anesthesia care (MAC); technique depends on patient, procedure, and team.

The central anesthetic priorities are reliable cooperation and mapping, effective scalp and incision analgesia, and preservation of spontaneous ventilation and a rapidly accessible airway during the awake phase.

Important intraoperative hazards include stimulation-associated seizure, airway obstruction or hypoventilation, pain, anxiety, and nausea or vomiting. Preserve access to the patient and be prepared to pause mapping and escalate support.

After surgery, promptly assess neurologic function and provide monitored postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient. Do not assume ICU admission is routine; disposition depends on clinical status and local care arrangements.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Awake craniotomy is used principally for tumor resection near eloquent cortex and for selected epilepsy surgery, enabling functional mapping while the patient performs tasks such as naming, reading, or moving a limb.

AAA uses general anesthesia or deep sedation for the initial stage, an awake mapping stage, then anesthesia or MAC for closure. MAC keeps the patient spontaneously breathing with sedation adjusted around mapping; neither approach is established as universally preferable.
The surgical and anesthesia teams should coordinate the transition into mapping and restoration of consciousness, including the planned tasks and signals that mapping can proceed.

Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess willingness, ability to cooperate, psychological readiness, tolerance of prolonged positioning, pain concerns, and airway risks. Explain the stages, expected sensations, scalp block, and functional tasks; preparation is part of the anesthetic strategy.
Evaluate airway difficulty and obstructive sleep apnea, as airway access may be restricted by head fixation and position. Discuss an emergency airway plan before the patient is positioned.

Review seizure history and planned electrocorticography with the team. Evidence for routine antiepileptic prophylaxis in awake craniotomy is limited; medication decisions should not be inferred from this reference.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan positioning with the surgeon and ensure the face remains visible. Supine, half-sitting, or lateral positions are described; head fixation and position can complicate airway access.

Keep airway equipment immediately available and arrange the room so the anesthesiologist can communicate with and observe the awake patient. Protect pressure points and maintain comfort during prolonged positioning.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment. Arterial access and EEG-derived depth monitoring may be considered according to the procedure and patient; sources do not establish either as mandatory in every case.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: In AAA, an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway may be used during the asleep phase and removed for awake mapping, with airway support re-established for closure if needed. MAC is an alternative; choose the approach with airway access and transition risks in view.

During mapping, target a responsive patient with adequate spontaneous ventilation. Sedation that is too deep risks respiratory depression and hypercapnia; excessive lightness may permit anxiety or movement.

Continually assess ventilation and expired carbon dioxide during moderate or deep sedation unless precluded by the clinical circumstances. Airway obstruction may require simple airway maneuvers or escalation; access can be difficult once the head is fixed.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Scalp incision through dural opening and the transition to mapping require adequate analgesia and a smooth emergence. Restore the patient to an appropriate level of consciousness before functional testing.
Coordinate cortical stimulation and task performance with the surgeon and, where involved, speech or neurophysiology specialists. Sedative choices can affect testing or electrocorticographic signals.

A stimulation-associated seizure can interrupt mapping and threaten patient safety. Alert the surgical team; the review describes cortical irrigation with cold saline and, if needed, IV propofol as measures used in this setting.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For airway obstruction or hypoventilation, assess ventilation and oxygenation, reduce contributing sedation where appropriate, and escalate airway support if needed. Hypercarbia and obstruction can worsen brain swelling.

Pain, panic, nausea, or vomiting can impair cooperation and mapping. Reassess the block and surgical stimulus, communicate with the patient and team, and be prepared to pause or alter the anesthetic approach.

If cooperation cannot be maintained or an emergency compromises the airway, mapping may not be possible and conversion to general anesthesia may be required. The fixed head may make airway intervention challenging.

sources.label: Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The available awake-craniotomy sources do not establish a procedure-specific fluid, blood-loss, or transfusion regimen. Manage these according to the patient, operative course, and applicable local practice rather than adopting a fixed volume.
Consider arterial pressure monitoring according to patient and procedural needs; the sources do not support making an arterial line universal for awake craniotomy.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Scalp nerve block and/or incision-line infiltration are core analgesic components. Confirm coverage for the planned incision and pin sites; sedation alone does not substitute for adequate local analgesia.

Pain may persist despite a block, particularly with dural manipulation, traction, temporalis dissection, or a prolonged procedure. Additional analgesia should be balanced against its potential to impair cooperation.
Antiemetic prevention or treatment may be considered, especially when opioids are used. Nausea and vomiting can also be associated with anxiety and surgical stimulation.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Anaesthesiologist’s Approach to Awake Craniotomy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For mapping, emergence should be smooth enough for reliable neurologic testing; restore consciousness to the preoperative state. After resection, sedation may be continued until surgery is complete when clinically appropriate.

Assess speech and motor function after surgery and monitor for seizure, pain, nausea, and respiratory problems. Level of care should reflect the patient’s condition and complications rather than an assumed routine ICU destination.
Provide postanesthesia observation with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; document recovery and hand off the anesthetic and surgical course.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For chronic subdural hematoma, burr-hole craniostomy evacuates the collection by opening the dura and using suction and irrigation; general anesthesia is common, with local anesthesia a feasible alternative.
Choose the anesthetic approach in light of neurologic status and patient factors; the available evidence does not establish a selection algorithm for local versus general anesthesia.

When general anesthesia is used, preserve oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation, and attend to potential raised intracranial pressure; the sources do not establish burr-hole-specific physiologic targets.
Plan recovery around reassessment of consciousness and the patient’s clinical condition. Anesthesia standards allow an ICU or equivalent area to provide postanesthesia care when appropriate.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For chronic subdural hematoma, burr-hole craniostomy is described as the most common evacuation technique. The review describes one or two openings on the cerebral convexity, followed by dural incision and evacuation with suction and irrigation.

General anesthesia is common, while local anesthesia is a feasible alternative. The choice should not be treated as a fixed rule: the anesthesia review identifies no validated criteria for selecting one approach.
The supplied procedure reviews concern chronic subdural hematoma. They do not establish a single approach for exploratory burr holes, acute hematoma decompression, or other indications.

bullets: Establish the neurologic condition and review available imaging as part of the preanesthetic assessment. In head trauma, the neuroanesthesia manual specifically calls for assessment of associated injuries and review of CT/MRI in its intracranial aneurysm preparation discussion; it does not provide a burr-hole-specific assessment protocol.

Chronic subdural hematoma populations may be older and medically complex. Reported antiplatelet or anticoagulant use varied across studies, and the review found no reported information on whether or how these agents were reversed.

Assess airway and trauma-related concerns when relevant. The manual describes full-stomach precautions and possible cervical-spine injury in severe head trauma; those observations do not establish a universal airway technique for burr-hole surgery.

bullets: Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical circumstances. ASA basic standards require continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

The cSDH anesthesia review does not specify patient positioning, vascular access, or a procedure-specific monitoring regimen. An arterial line or other additional monitoring should therefore not be represented as routine on the basis of these sources.

bullets: The review describes general anesthesia for burr-hole evacuation as involving pharmacologic agents and endotracheal intubation. It does not establish an induction sequence or a universal airway plan.

Local anesthesia, sometimes accompanied by sedation, is represented in the cSDH literature. The review does not supply a monitoring protocol for local anesthesia or criteria for conversion; do not assume every case requires intubation or general anesthesia.

bullets: Reported postoperative complications in the anesthesia comparison literature varied and included cardiopulmonary events, infection, and pneumocephalus. Event definitions and reporting were not uniform, so these data do not define a case-specific complication-management protocol.

Delayed awakening, confusion, and postoperative delirium are discussed as potential concerns in older patients receiving general anesthesia; delirium was not consistently assessed with standardized tools.
If neuromuscular blockers are used, residual blockade is a recognized source of airway and respiratory complications; use quantitative assessment rather than relying on clinical signs alone.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Posterior cervical laminectomy and laminoplasty decompress multilevel cervical myelopathy; laminoplasty is generally considered when decompression is needed without fusion and alignment is suitable.

Prone positioning and cervical manipulation make neutral-to-slight flexion, protection from pressure injury, and avoidance of hypotension important; the available source does not establish a universal blood-pressure target.
Cervical pathology may limit neck movement and increase intubation difficulty. Avoid excessive extension; video laryngoscopy or fiberoptic-assisted intubation can help maintain neutral positioning.
SSEP/MEP monitoring may support detection of cord compromise; recovery priorities include a prompt neurological assessment and attention to new root-level weakness, particularly C5 palsy.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Posterior cervical laminectomy, laminectomy with fusion, and laminoplasty are approaches to cervical myelopathy. Posterior decompression is indirect: adequate cord drift away from anterior compression depends on sagittal alignment.

The review describes posterior approaches as most advantageous for multilevel myelopathy involving three or more motion segments. Significant kyphosis may limit cord drift; approach selection remains a surgical decision based on anatomy and imaging.

Laminoplasty preserves posterior elements while expanding the canal and is described for patients who do not require fusion. Laminectomy with fusion may be considered where significant neck pain or risk of progressive kyphosis informs the surgical plan.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the neurological baseline and review the degree of myelopathy, prior cervical surgery, and cervical stability. These findings affect positioning and airway planning.

Review sagittal alignment and symptoms with the surgical team: posterior decompression may be less suitable when kyphosis prevents adequate cord drift. The cited review describes laminoplasty particularly for lordotic alignment and little spondylotic neck pain.

Assess neck range of motion, airway difficulty, and neurological symptoms with extension. For severe myelopathy or poor tolerance of extension, the review advises considering awake fiberoptic intubation; it does not make this mandatory for all patients.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For the posterior approach, plan prone positioning with the neck neutral to slightly flexed and immobilized as appropriate. Keep pressure off the eyes and face, use lateral chest and abdominal bolsters to avoid abdominal compression, and consider reverse Trendelenburg while watching for hypotension.
Avoid exceeding the patient’s tolerated preoperative extension. Shoulder taping can create longitudinal tension; monitoring may help identify positioning-related brachial plexus compromise.

SSEP or MEP monitoring is recommended by the review for patients with myelopathy. In severe disease, consider a post-intubation, pre-positioning baseline; arterial pressure monitoring may be appropriate, particularly with cardiovascular lability.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Secure the airway supine before turning prone. Avoid excessive cervical extension; video laryngoscopy or fiberoptic-assisted intubation may help maintain neutral positioning when cervical pathology limits movement.

After prone positioning, reassess airway security and access to the patient. The cervical-surgery summary identifies prone positioning and the possibility of significant blood loss with multiple instrumented levels; it does not provide a procedure-specific ventilation regimen.

For cord monitoring, the cervical-surgery anesthesia summary favors TIVA and advises limiting volatile anesthetic if used; it also advises avoiding nitrous oxide. Select the technique with the monitoring team and clinical context in mind.
