sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid hypotension and maintain adequate spinal-cord perfusion throughout the case, including before incision when prone positioning or reverse Trendelenburg may provoke hypotension. The source does not establish a universal blood-pressure target.

For patients with myelopathy, SSEP or MEP spinal cord monitoring is recommended; the review notes controversy about MEP use but says available data indicate MEPs may add useful information to SSEPs when available.

Positioning, decompression, and surgical manipulation all warrant attention to neurological monitoring and hemodynamics. The available sources support avoiding hypotension but do not provide a case-specific anesthetic depth, neuromuscular-blockade, or cord-perfusion target.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Positioning-related cord compromise and brachial plexopathy are relevant hazards. Avoid excessive neck extension and shoulder traction; use the planned monitoring and communicate concerning signal changes promptly with the surgical and monitoring teams.

Segmental root palsy, most often involving C5, is reported after laminoplasty. New postoperative weakness or sensory symptoms warrant prompt neurological assessment and communication with the surgical team.

Postoperative axial neck pain is a recognized concern, and laminoplasty is not designed to treat painful spondylosis. Counsel and plan recovery in the context of preoperative symptoms and the surgical approach.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain adequate blood pressure for spinal-cord perfusion; avoid hypotensive anesthesia. Individualize hemodynamic support to the patient and operative context rather than applying a fixed target from this evidence.

Reverse Trendelenburg may lower cervical venous pressure but can be accompanied by hypotension. Maintain vigilance before surgical stimulation, when the review says hypotension is commonly encountered.
Avoid abdominal compression and use positioning that limits venous congestion. The sources do not provide a case-specific fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan postoperative analgesia that supports comfort and neurological assessment. A review describes cervical plexus block as an adjunct to general anesthesia for cervical surgery, but does not establish it as a routine requirement for posterior decompression.

Discuss any regional analgesic technique with the surgeon when rapid postoperative neurological examination is important. The review notes that motor block from epidural local anesthetic may impede assessment.
The procedure-specific review does not provide a complete postoperative analgesia regimen or PONV protocol; select these according to patient and institutional context.

Posterior Surgery for Cervical Myelopathy: Laminectomy ...

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Return the patient to a position suitable for airway management before extubation. Aim for a smooth emergence that permits neurological assessment, while individualizing extubation to airway, respiratory, and neurological status.
Assess neurological status early in recovery and communicate new deficits promptly. Continue observation for root-level palsy and other approach-related concerns.

Use postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient’s condition, with evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; transfer and handoff should communicate the perioperative course.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The procedure-specific source is a 2008 narrative review, not an anesthesia guideline, and does not provide a systematic-review method. Its recommendations and numerical outcomes draw on cited studies and author experience.
The cervical-surgery anesthesia material is an educational summary of several procedures; it supports general airway and anesthetic considerations but is not specific to laminoplasty alone.

The regional-anesthesia article is a review, and it notes that regional anesthesia for spinal surgery has not been extensively evaluated. It does not establish a single best analgesic technique for this operation.
Available sources do not establish a laminoplasty-specific extubation protocol, fluid regimen, analgesic regimen, or neuromonitoring alarm threshold.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Craniotomy may be performed under general anesthesia; awake approaches are used when cortical or subcortical mapping is needed, particularly for tumors near eloquent function.

The anesthetic priorities are to preserve cerebral perfusion, avoid preventable increases in intracranial pressure, and accommodate the surgeon’s need for brain relaxation and timely neurological assessment.

Important hazards include stimulation-related hemodynamic changes, brain swelling or hemorrhage, seizures, and venous air embolism in susceptible operative settings; sudden deterioration requires prompt communication and escalation.
Recovery should permit prompt neurological assessment when appropriate, while avoiding coughing or straining and providing observation suited to the patient’s condition.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Craniotomy for tumor resection or tissue diagnosis may be undertaken with general anesthesia, sedation with local anesthesia, or local anesthesia alone. The appropriate approach depends on the surgical and mapping requirements.

For tumors near eloquent cortex, awake craniotomy permits functional mapping during resection. Described approaches include asleep–awake–asleep and monitored anesthetic care; awake techniques require patient cooperation and an experienced team.

Coordinate the anesthetic plan with the surgeon, including whether mapping, neuromonitoring, or a rapid postoperative examination is required. Available sources do not establish one anesthetic technique as appropriate for all tumor resections.

sources.label: Local anesthetics for brain tumor resection: current perspectives

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review imaging and discuss tumor size, location, and vascularity with the surgeon; these features affect the operative approach and anticipated bleeding or air-embolism risk.

Assess baseline neurological status and symptoms that may be consistent with raised intracranial pressure. For an awake approach, evaluate airway and ability to cooperate; difficult airway or obstructive sleep apnea makes candidacy less favorable.

Review steroid use and relevant metabolic or hematologic concerns. The source manual specifically notes glucose monitoring in patients receiving steroids or with diabetes, and laboratory assessment as indicated; it does not supply a comprehensive contemporary preoperative testing protocol.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Confirm the operative position and head-frame plan in advance. Position is surgeon- and tumor-dependent; the manual describes prone positioning for many posterior fossa procedures and emphasizes padding and careful airway security when the head is remote.
Pin placement is a highly stimulating phase. Plan analgesia/anesthetic depth with the team before clamp application; local infiltration is one described adjunct.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and case. The manual recommends invasive arterial pressure monitoring for full craniotomy; this is a source-specific educational recommendation, not a universal line-placement rule. Basic standards require continuous ECG display and regular blood pressure and heart-rate assessment.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For general anesthesia, secure the endotracheal tube and tape the eyes carefully because the head will be away from the anesthesiologist. Verify tube placement clinically and by identifying carbon dioxide in expired gas, and continually monitor end-tidal CO₂ until extubation or transfer.

During awake craniotomy, airway access can be difficult with the head turned and secured. Keep an airway rescue plan and equipment immediately available; do not assume that an airway intervention will be straightforward in the operative position.

Avoid unintended hypercapnia, which can worsen brain swelling, while coordinating ventilation goals with the surgeon. The supplied manual describes hypocapnia, whereas the case material proposes normocapnia; the available sources do not resolve a universal target.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Anticipate hemodynamic responses to pin fixation, incision, and closure. Scalp block or infiltration can reduce nociceptive and autonomic responses, but the optimal technique is not established by comparative evidence.

Maintain cerebral perfusion and avoid avoidable hypotension or hypertension, with goals agreed with the surgical team and individualized to the patient and operative phase. The supplied material does not validate a single blood-pressure target for all tumor craniotomies.

Brain swelling, hemorrhage, and seizures may arise during resection. Maintain communication with the surgeon and neuromonitoring team so changes in anesthetic or neuromuscular blockade do not compromise mapping.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: A sudden end-tidal carbon-dioxide decrease, particularly with cardiovascular change, can signal venous air embolism in a susceptible operative setting. Recognize the change promptly and alert the surgical team; the supplied sources do not establish a complete response algorithm.

New swelling, bleeding, seizure activity, or unexplained hemodynamic change warrants immediate communication and reassessment of the operative and anesthetic situation. Awake-craniotomy complications include respiratory depression and airway obstruction, with urgent intervention emphasized for airway compromise.

During awake mapping, seizures are a recognized complication, particularly with cortical stimulation. The review describes cold-saline irrigation and low-dose propofol as reported interventions; these are source-described options, not a universal protocol.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The educational manual describes glucose-free isotonic crystalloid and minimizing crystalloid to limit brain edema. This is not a comparative, procedure-specific fluid guideline; choose fluid and volume to the clinical context rather than applying a fixed regimen.

Anticipated blood loss depends on tumor and approach; the manual contrasts substantial bleeding with vascular meningiomas against lower bleeding risk in typical glioma debulking. Ensure blood availability is proportionate to the operation and team assessment, not a universal crossmatch rule.

The sources do not establish a transfusion threshold or a universal perfusion target for tumor craniotomy. The manual advises monitoring blood loss and hematocrit and transfusing if needed; decisions remain dependent on the patient and operative course.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Scalp block or incision-line infiltration can provide analgesia and blunt responses to painful phases. A complete scalp block involves six sensory nerves, but no evidence supplied establishes one block technique as superior.

Use multimodal postoperative analgesia while preserving wakefulness and ventilation needed for neurological assessment. Opioids may impair cooperation during mapping and can contribute to sedation or hypercapnia.

Nausea and vomiting are reported complications and may interfere with recovery; anticipate symptom management as part of postoperative care. The sources do not provide a craniotomy-specific antiemetic regimen.

sources.label: Anesthetic considerations for awake craniotomy
Local anesthetics for brain tumor resection: current perspectives

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When early awakening is appropriate, aim for a smooth emergence and avoid coughing, straining, and ventilator fighting. The manual advises delayed emergence when preoperative consciousness, brain swelling, operative extent, or other clinical conditions make early extubation unsuitable.

Plan recovery location and observation according to neurological status and overall condition. Postanesthesia standards require continual evaluation with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

If a neuromuscular blocking drug was used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The case-specific evidence consists largely of narrative reviews and an educational neuroanesthesia manual, rather than a single contemporary guideline for adult tumor craniotomy. The manual provides no publication date, references, or evidence grading.

Awake-craniotomy reviews address selected patients and do not establish the routine anesthetic for all tumor resections. The local-anesthetic review also notes a lack of comparative evidence establishing superiority of scalp block over field infiltration.

Available sources conflict on ventilation emphasis: the manual describes mild-to-moderate hypocapnia as usual, while awake-craniotomy material cautions that respiratory depression and hypercapnia can contribute to brain edema. A universal case-specific carbon-dioxide target is not established.
Sources do not provide a validated universal blood-pressure target, transfusion threshold, or postoperative neurological-check interval for adult tumor craniotomy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Surgical clipping uses a craniotomy to place a clip across the aneurysm neck. It is selected according to aneurysm anatomy and patient factors, often when endovascular treatment is unsuitable.
The central anesthetic balance is limiting aneurysm transmural pressure and re-rupture risk while preserving cerebral perfusion and obtaining adequate brain relaxation.

Avoid abrupt arterial-pressure changes, particularly hypertensive responses before the aneurysm is secured; avoid hypotension that may compromise cerebral perfusion. Individualize targets to ICP, neurologic grade, and the operative phase.
After clipping, prioritize prompt neurologic assessment and monitored neurocritical care, with attention to hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, delayed cerebral ischemia, and seizures.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Aneurysm clipping is performed through a craniotomy; the clip excludes the aneurysm neck from circulation. Choice of clipping versus endovascular treatment depends on aneurysm size, location, morphology, perforator relationships, calcification or thrombosis, and overall patient risk.

Approach and position are anatomy-dependent. Pterional approaches are commonly used for anterior-circulation aneurysms; posterior-circulation approaches may use a retrosigmoid route and park-bench positioning. Confirm the planned approach and position with the surgical team.
Clipping is often considered for complex or wide-necked aneurysms and selected middle cerebral artery aneurysms; the choice remains multidisciplinary rather than determined by a single feature.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess neurologic grade and review CT and angiography for hemorrhage burden, mass effect, hydrocephalus, aneurysm anatomy, and collateral circulation. Higher-grade SAH may involve raised ICP, brain swelling, impaired autoregulation, and increased ischemia risk.

Consider SAH-associated cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmia, pulmonary complications, and fluid, electrolyte, or glucose derangements. Correct relevant abnormalities without delaying urgent definitive treatment.
Coordinate arterial-pressure goals and rupture-response roles with the surgeon. A preoperative rupture simulation is suggested as preparation; it does not replace individualized planning.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan positioning around aneurysm location and surgical exposure, with attention to venous drainage and avoiding excessive neck flexion or rotation. For anterior approaches, the source describes supine positioning with the head turned away; posterior approaches commonly use park-bench positioning.

Use continuous arterial-pressure monitoring for clipping; establish it before induction when indicated by the clinical and procedural risk. Sources differ on whether pre-induction placement is needed for every patient.

Ensure reliable venous access, ECG, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring, temperature monitoring, and access to processed EEG where used. Neurophysiologic monitoring may include SSEPs and MEPs; consider anesthetic effects and communicate changes promptly.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For clipping under general anesthesia, plan tracheal intubation and a controlled, smooth induction. Use adequate anesthetic depth and analgesia to blunt laryngoscopy and pin-placement responses while avoiding hypotension, especially with myocardial dysfunction.

Avoid inadvertent hypo- or hypercarbia. Hypercarbia may increase ICP; aggressive hypocarbia may raise aneurysm transmural pressure and impair perfusion. Controlled, modest hyperventilation may be used for brain relaxation when appropriate, not as an automatic pre-dural-opening maneuver.

TIVA is commonly favored when evoked-potential monitoring is used, but it is not established as universally superior. Volatile agents can affect evoked potentials in a dose-dependent manner; neuromuscular blockers disrupt MEP monitoring.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Before aneurysm security, avoid rapid pressure increases and avoid relative hypotension that could threaten cerebral perfusion. The appropriate pressure range depends on ICP, neurologic grade, baseline physiology, and surgical phase; communicate targets with the surgeon.

Brain relaxation may involve head elevation, careful fluid management, controlled ventilation, osmotherapy, and CSF drainage when appropriate. Avoid excessive volatile-agent concentrations and excessive or rapid CSF drainage; choose measures in context of perfusion and rupture risk.

Temporary clipping risks focal ischemia. Coordinate clip duration and reperfusion strategy with the surgeon, use evoked-potential or EEG information when available, and respond to changes with reassessment of clip/retractor position and perfusion. A single universally safe occlusion duration is not established.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For suspected intraoperative rupture, alert the surgeon, maintain coordinated communication, and support rapid surgical control while managing pressure and perfusion deliberately. The reviewed source describes brief pressure reduction as one possible aid to visualization, not a universal response.

If evoked potentials change during clipping, promptly communicate with the surgeon and assess for clip-related ischemia or retractor effects; blood-pressure augmentation, clip adjustment, or retractor adjustment may be considered according to the situation.

Postoperative neurologic decline warrants urgent evaluation for hydrocephalus, edema, delayed cerebral ischemia, or seizure. Neurocritical care surveillance is important; DCI may occur with or without angiographic vasospasm.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain euvolemia and avoid hypovolemia; use isotonic fluid choices appropriate to the clinical context. The available reviews do not establish a routine fluid volume, transfusion threshold, or blood-product regimen for clipping.

Have blood availability appropriate to the anticipated operation and patient. Complex aneurysm trapping or reconstruction can involve prolonged occlusion and major blood loss, but this should not be generalized to every clipping procedure.

Osmotherapy may be used for raised ICP or brain relaxation, with mannitol and hypertonic saline both discussed in the sources. Select and monitor therapy in context; no universal agent or dose is established here.

sources.label: Perioperative Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Narrative Review
Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use analgesia judiciously to blunt responses to laryngoscopy and cranial-pin placement while preserving hemodynamic stability and the ability to assess neurologic function. Local anesthetic pin-site infiltration or scalp block may be useful adjuncts.

Scalp block is described as reducing pain stimuli and anesthetic/opioid requirements and supporting postoperative analgesia. Technique and local-anesthetic selection should follow applicable institutional practice and patient-specific assessment.
The supplied clipping sources do not specify a postoperative analgesia regimen or a PONV prevention strategy; do not infer one from these materials.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Aim for smooth, timely emergence that permits neurologic assessment while avoiding coughing, straining, or marked hypertension. The supplied clipping reviews do not establish a specific emergence drug regimen or extubation rule.

Plan postoperative care in a neurointensive-care or equivalent high-dependency setting with close neurologic observation. Ongoing aSAH care and surveillance should be coordinated with the neurocritical-care team.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative recovery before extubation, using adductor-pollicis monitoring. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to every anesthetic technique.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific source is an educational review of clipping anesthesia, not a formal guideline or trial. It does not describe systematic-review methods or formal evidence grading.

A second source is a narrative review that explicitly reflects clinical interpretation and experience. Its recommendations are useful context, not a substitute for current institutional or specialty guidance.

Sources differ on whether an arterial line must precede induction in every patient and on temporary-clipping pressure and duration strategies. Individualize these decisions; a universally safe clipping duration or single pressure target is not established by the supplied evidence.

The sources do not provide a validated case-specific emergence/extubation protocol or a postoperative analgesia and PONV regimen. These are substantive limits of this draft; no absent universal fluid total or fixed drug regimen is implied.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adults with acute TBI may require general anesthesia for emergent craniotomy or decompressive craniectomy; the available review does not define procedure-selection criteria.
Priorities are preventing secondary brain injury: avoid and promptly correct hypotension and hypoxia, maintain controlled ventilation, and recognize and treat raised ICP.
Secure the airway when severe TBI is a concern; RSI and video laryngoscopy are options, not a universal mandatory recipe. Avoid both unwanted hyperventilation and hypercapnia.
Moderate–severe TBI patients commonly remain sedated and intubated after surgery for airway protection, ventilation, and safe transfer to neurocritical care.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The adult TBI operative pathway may include emergent craniotomy or decompressive craniectomy. The supplied review describes these procedures but does not establish indications or selection criteria for one approach over another.

Coordinate timing and positioning with the surgical team in light of the injury pattern and associated trauma; the review identifies assessment of positioning needs but gives no default position for this operation.

Plan for possible hemodynamic change at decompression. The review describes hypotension and asystole as potential events around decompression and discusses anticipatory fluid or blood administration; this is not a fixed-volume instruction.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Use trauma assessment to identify airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, hypothermia, and associated injuries. Hemorrhagic shock or cardiovascular compromise may threaten cerebral perfusion and complicate anesthesia.
Document neurologic status and its trajectory, including GCS, pupils, motor and sensory function, and lateralizing findings; mild or moderate injury does not exclude subsequent deterioration.
Review imaging, laboratory results, coagulopathy risks, and associated injuries; establish access to blood products. Correcting extracranial hemorrhagic shock remains an important competing priority.

Consider cervical-spine injury in trauma assessment and airway planning. The educational manual advises treating severe-trauma/head-injury patients as having an unstable cervical spine until radiologically excluded.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare for urgent surgery with reliable IV access and immediately available blood products. Central access may be useful, but its placement should not delay decompression.

Monitor ECG, oxygenation, expired CO₂, blood pressure—preferably invasively—and core temperature; monitor neuromuscular blockade when used. Additional cerebral oxygenation monitors are not described as standard.
Position according to the operative approach while protecting alignment and pressure areas; the sources do not establish a single required position for traumatic craniotomy.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For concern about severe TBI, the review supports definitive tracheal intubation. RSI may reduce aspiration risk; modified RSI with low-volume/low-pressure breaths may be considered when ICP is high. These statements do not make RSI compulsory in every patient.

Video laryngoscopy may facilitate intubation; have difficult-airway equipment available and maintain cervical stabilization when indicated. Avoid nasotracheal intubation when skull-fracture status is unknown or fracture is suspected.

Do not use 30–35 mmHg as a routine PaCO₂ target for every TBI patient. ACS 2024 guidance gives an initial PaCO₂ target of 35–45 mmHg when intracranial hypertension is absent; raised ICP, severe metabolic acidosis and significant pulmonary disease require an individualized strategy. Therapeutic hyperventilation belongs in an ICP-directed rescue or tiered pathway, not a universal ventilation recipe.
Use arterial blood gas assessment when CO₂ abnormality is suspected or the end-tidal value may be unreliable, particularly during hypotension.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts
ACS Best Practices Guidelines: The Management of Traumatic Brain Injury (2024)

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid and promptly correct systemic and cerebral hypotension. The review discusses different severe-TBI pressure thresholds and recent support for a higher systolic target or MAP-based alternative; interpret targets in the clinical context rather than treating one value as universal.

Maintain controlled ventilation: unwanted hyperventilation may cause cerebral ischemia, while hypercapnia may increase cerebral blood flow, ICP, and edema. Use temporary hypocapnia only as a bridge for high ICP.

Recognize and treat an ICP crisis promptly, whether or not an ICP monitor is present. The review defines high ICP and describes hyperosmolar therapy as an option, with serial sodium monitoring and attention to therapy-related complications.
Maintenance practice is not settled by comparative trials. The review describes low-dose volatile anesthesia as typical and notes that TIVA may be used in refractory ICP; avoid nitrous oxide.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Treat hypotension as a threat to cerebral perfusion. If hypotension remains unexplained after considering hemorrhage, the review suggests point-of-care ultrasound to assess systolic dysfunction.

Be alert to hemorrhage and coagulopathy, including substantial scalp or intracranial blood loss. The available review supports laboratory assessment and blood-product availability but does not specify a single transfusion trigger.
A sudden respiratory or pupillary change, hypertension, bradycardia, or arrhythmia may signal an ICP crisis; escalate recognition and treatment promptly because herniation and death are risks.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use isotonic fluids and blood products as clinically indicated to support perfusion and replace losses. Avoid hypotonic fluids; the review advises against albumin in this setting.

Hyperosmolar therapy can reduce ICP but has trade-offs: mannitol may cause hypovolemia and hyponatremia and is contraindicated in renal failure; monitor sodium with either mannitol or hypertonic saline.

Anemia is associated with worse outcomes, but the review states there is no standard transfusion threshold. Base blood replacement on the full clinical and bleeding context rather than a fixed case-specific target from this source.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Avoid long-acting opioids when an early postoperative neurologic examination is needed. A scalp block may be used as an adjunct to reduce painful stimulation, anesthetic and opioid requirements, and hemodynamic variability.
The supplied sources do not establish a TBI-specific PONV regimen or a complete postoperative analgesic protocol; individualize these while preserving neurologic assessment.

sources.label: An Overview of Adult Acute Traumatic Neurologic Injury for the Anesthesiologist: What is Known, What is New, and Emerging Concepts
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Moderate–severe TBI patients often remain sedated and intubated because brain injury evolves and airway protection or ventilation may still be needed. Extubation is therefore selective, not the default endpoint.

Account for residual neuromuscular blockade when interpreting the neurologic examination; reversal is individualized. If neuromuscular blockers were used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative confirmation of recovery before extubation.

Arrange transfer to ICU or equivalent postanesthesia care with condition-appropriate monitoring, support, and handoff. The receiving team should receive the preoperative condition and surgical/anesthetic course.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal TBI source is an adult acute neurotrauma review, not a formal anesthesia guideline or trial. It reports that OR-specific evidence is sparse and recommendations are often extrapolated; interpret its practice descriptions accordingly.

The neuroanesthesia manual is an educational source without a stated date, references, or evidence grading; its older detailed recipes should not override the more recent review or applicable standards.
The monitoring and postanesthesia sources establish general standards, not TBI-specific treatment protocols; the neuromuscular-blockade source applies only when such drugs are used.
The available sources do not define criteria for selecting craniotomy versus decompressive craniectomy or a complete TBI-specific PONV and analgesia pathway.

The Brain Trauma Foundation Level II B recommendation advises against prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 25 mmHg or less. Its older statements on temporary hyperventilation and brain-oxygen monitoring are restated with an explicit warning that they do not meet current evidence standards. Do not present all these statements as equally graded recommendations.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: DBS lead placement is commonly performed with the patient awake for microelectrode recording and stimulation testing; sedation may be used during parts of the procedure, but the anesthetic must permit meaningful neurologic assessment.

Priorities are a cooperative patient, reliable airway access despite the fixed head frame, and stable hemodynamics. Intracranial hemorrhage is a major concern; sedation-related respiratory compromise and seizure are also relevant hazards.

Use local anesthesia for pin sites and scalp/incision discomfort, with anesthetic drugs selected and timed in coordination with the surgical and neurophysiology teams because agents can alter recordings and testing.

Recovery priorities include reassessment for new neurologic change and appropriate postoperative imaging to check lead position and exclude hemorrhage or pneumocephalus; routine recovery monitoring should follow applicable anesthesia standards.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Stereotactic leads are advanced along a planned trajectory to a selected target. Microelectrode recordings help identify target activity; stimulation testing assesses symptom response and adverse effects. Common movement-disorder targets include the STN, GPi, and ventralis intermedius nucleus.

Awake implantation with monitored anesthesia care is a common approach. General anesthesia is used in selected circumstances, but can prevent clinical stimulation testing; whether mapping is feasible under anesthesia depends on the technique and local team practice.

Lead placement and pulse-generator implantation may be staged. Available reviews describe variation in staging and timing; do not assume that generator implantation is a universal same-day or general-anesthetic phase.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm the indication, planned target, intended mapping/testing approach, ability to cooperate, and multidisciplinary plan. Explain the awake phases and assess anxiety and cognitive or psychiatric factors that could affect cooperation.

Review airway history, obstructive sleep apnea, respiratory function, autonomic symptoms, and comorbidities. Frame placement and positioning may make later airway intervention difficult; plan access before the frame is fixed.

Coordinate disease-specific medication withholding with the neurosurgical team. Some patients need an “off-medication” state for mapping, but symptoms may worsen; the available sources do not establish a single hold interval or a universal postoperative restart instruction.

Review MRI compatibility and relevant implanted metal or devices before imaging. Anxiety, distress, and poorly controlled blood pressure may increase hemorrhage risk; individualize assessment and management.

sources.label: Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare for stereotactic frame or neuronavigation, imaging, and microelectrode-recording equipment, with neurophysiology participation. Maintain communication and access for neurologic testing during awake portions.
Position supine or semi-sitting with the frame secured to the operating table, as appropriate to the case. Pad and support the patient; positioning should preserve comfort and airway patency.

Use standard anesthesia monitoring appropriate to the technique and patient. For moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment makes this invalid or impractical.

Control blood pressure around electrode insertion and mapping in coordination with the team. The review describes possible targets but states that optimal pressure is not well defined; use patient- and case-specific judgment rather than treating a review value as universal.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For awake mapping, MAC commonly avoids airway manipulation, with oxygen delivered by nasal cannula or facemask. This approach requires continued observation and a plan for rescue because access becomes restricted by the frame.

Agree on an airway rescue strategy before frame placement when intervention may be required. The reviews describe nasal oxygen, facemask, LMA, and fiberoptic intubation as options in context; choice depends on the patient, frame, aspiration risk, and urgency.

If sedation is moderate or deep, monitor ventilation with clinical observation and expired CO₂ when feasible; sedation-related respiratory compromise can become difficult to manage with the head fixed in a frame.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Use local anesthetic at frame pins and scalp/incision sites to support awake tolerance and reduce reliance on systemic sedatives and opioids. Re-infiltration may be considered for discomfort during a prolonged case.

Sedation is commonly concentrated during opening and closing, with the patient awake for recording and stimulation. Many teams stop short-acting infusions before mapping when feasible, but reported practice varies; coordinate drug timing with neurophysiology and the surgeon.

Anesthetic effects on neuronal recordings are agent-, dose-, target-, and depth-dependent. Avoid assuming any sedative is entirely neutral: reports on dexmedetomidine differ, and propofol and benzodiazepines can depress or alter MER.
Keep the patient awake and cooperative during macrostimulation to assess clinical benefit and adverse effects, including paresthesia or abnormal motor activity.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Intracranial hemorrhage is a major procedural hazard. Watch for new neurologic change or sudden reduced consciousness, communicate promptly with the surgical team, and escalate evaluation; available sources describe postoperative imaging but do not provide a complete hemorrhage-response algorithm.

Seizure may occur, including during stimulation testing. Recognize the event, alert the procedural team, and prioritize patient safety and urgent clinical assessment; the sources do not establish a single management regimen.

Respiratory compromise is important because frame-limited airway access, sedation, neck position, seizure, or declining consciousness can impair ventilation. Reassess airway patency and oxygenation promptly and call for help early if deterioration occurs.

Venous air embolism and pneumocephalus are reported hazards. Unexplained hypoxia, tachycardia, coughing, chest symptoms, or hemodynamic change warrant immediate team assessment; the supplied sources do not support a procedure-specific response algorithm.

sources.label: Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No DBS-specific fluid regimen, expected blood loss, or transfusion protocol is established in the supplied reviews. Avoid inferring a fixed fluid total or blood-product plan; individualize to clinical status and operative events.

Avoid unnecessary fluid loading, particularly when positioning and procedure duration make comfort or bladder distension concerns relevant. This is not a prescribed restriction or a quantitative fluid target.

Maintain hemodynamic stability and address hypertension or distress before and during lead insertion. The review identifies blood-pressure control as important but says an optimal target is not defined; choose targets for the individual patient and procedural context.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Pin-site infiltration and scalp block are the principal described local analgesic measures. Sedation can supplement local anesthesia during incision and burr-hole work; systemic analgesia should be coordinated with mapping needs.

Choose antiemetics with attention to movement-disorder symptoms. The anesthesia review identifies dopamine-antagonist antiemetics as a concern and discusses non-dopamine-antagonist options; selection remains patient- and institution-specific.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal postoperative opioid regimen. Use analgesia compatible with neurologic assessment and the patient’s respiratory status.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for deep brain stimulation: a review
Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For awake implantation, preserve the ability to participate in testing through the mapping phase. Sedation may be resumed after electrodes are secured and testing is complete, according to the procedural plan.

Reassess neurologic status and investigate unexpected deficits or altered consciousness with the surgical team. Postoperative CT or MRI is commonly obtained to assess lead position and exclude hemorrhage or pneumocephalus.

Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Disposition and monitoring intensity should reflect patient condition and procedural events.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, apply quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases conducted without neuromuscular blockade.

Anesthetic Challenges for Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Approach

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The DBS-specific anesthetic evidence provided consists mainly of reviews rather than procedure-specific society standards. The 2015 source is a narrative review; the 2014 source is a systematic literature review, but it reports institutional variation and unresolved anesthetic effects on MER.

The reviews differ on how much sedation can be continued during recording and on dexmedetomidine’s effects. The draft therefore avoids a blanket “no sedatives” rule or any claim that a particular drug guarantees preserved mapping.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general anesthesia standards, not DBS-specific management guidance. The neuromuscular-blockade guidance applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
The supplied sources do not provide obstetric-specific DBS evidence. This draft is an adult-focused reference and does not establish pregnancy-specific management.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Epilepsy surgery may resect a seizure focus by craniotomy, either awake or under general anesthesia; electrocorticography (ECoG) and stimulation testing may be used to guide localization and resection.

Coordinate the anesthetic with the surgical and neurology teams: anesthetics can depress ECoG, while anesthetic choice and timing may need to change between mapping and the remainder of the operation.
Plan around seizure risk and antiepileptic drug interactions; continue prescribed anticonvulsants on the morning of surgery as directed, and avoid abrupt interruption.
Recovery priorities are an early, interpretable neurological assessment, prompt resumption of anticonvulsants, and recognition and evaluation of postoperative seizure activity.

sources.label: Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery
Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative aim is to remove a localized seizure focus. The reviewed approaches include cortical-electrode procedures for mapping or activation and resection by craniotomy.
Resection may be performed awake or under general anesthesia, with or without ECoG and stimulation testing. Awake craniotomy is considered when the focus is close to eloquent areas.
The available sources do not establish a single operative or anesthetic technique for all epilepsy resections; the approach depends on localization and the planned mapping.

sources.label: Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Document seizure history and control, baseline neurological status, comorbidities, and current neurologic medications. Review relevant prior records and imaging with the surgical team.

Continue anticonvulsants on the morning of surgery as scheduled and coordinate administration with the neurologist and surgeon. Do not infer that a particular drug level must be measured from these sources.

Antiepileptic therapy can affect sedation, cognition, hepatic drug metabolism, and neuromuscular-blocker duration; assess the medication history and potential interactions rather than assuming uniform effects.

Review imaging and the planned localization strategy. The sources describe diagnostic workups that may include MRI, PET, stereotactic electrodes, or other localization procedures, but do not set a universal workup for resection.

sources.label: Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Confirm whether ECoG and stimulation testing are planned and coordinate the anesthetic phase with the team performing them. The sources do not specify a required ECoG equipment layout or personnel configuration.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the selected technique. ASA standards require continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG is displayed and blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes.

sources.label: Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia and awake approaches are both described. The supplied evidence does not support a universal airway device or a requirement for intubation in every approach.
For an awake approach, assess cooperation, airway difficulty, and obstruction risks; emergency airway access may be challenging during awake craniotomy.

For general anesthesia, maintain standard ventilation monitoring and verify airway-device position using clinical assessment and expired carbon dioxide when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is used.

sources.label: Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery
Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Anesthetic drugs alter ECoG; agree with the surgical team on the mapping phase and how anesthetic technique will be managed around it. The sources do not establish a specific ECoG-compatible drug regimen.

A review describes propofol or thiopentone for induction and maintenance with nitrous oxide, opioid, and sub-MAC isoflurane or sevoflurane for epilepsy surgery. These are review-described options, not a case-specific protocol.

Avoid treating any one anesthetic as universally suitable or unsuitable based on these broad reviews. For example, the source's ketamine caution is discussed in its drug-specific and nonepilepsy-surgery material, not established as a procedure-specific epilepsy-resection rule.

sources.label: Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: A perioperative seizure is a key hazard. Priorities described in the review are airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, IV access, and close cardiorespiratory monitoring; escalate promptly if seizure activity persists or compromises ventilation or circulation.

Postoperative movements may have causes other than epileptic seizure, including shivering or pseudo-epileptic events. Assess the clinical context and do not equate movement alone with electrographic seizure.
Document baseline neurological status, cognition, communication and language, motor/sensory deficits, cranial nerve function, and pupil size.

sources.label: Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The epilepsy-specific material does not establish a fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold. Match fluid and blood preparation to the individual operation and clinical assessment.

For intracranial surgery generally, a preoperative review advises maintaining intravascular volume and avoiding hypotonic or glucose-containing fluids where reduced plasma osmolality could worsen cerebral edema; this is general intracranial guidance, not epilepsy-specific fluid evidence.
Use of mannitol and invasive hemodynamic monitoring should be driven by the operative and patient-specific circumstances; the supplied sources do not define an epilepsy-resection target.

sources.label: Epilepsy and nonepilepsy surgery: Recent advancements in anesthesia management
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: A scalp block may be used as an adjunct to general anesthesia or during awake craniotomy. The review describes reduced pain stimuli and hemodynamic variability, lower anesthetic and opioid requirements, and postoperative analgesia as its aims.

The regional-anesthesia review describes local anesthetic scalp block as an adjunct, not a complete postoperative pain or antiemetic plan; adapt analgesia to the operation and the need for neurological assessment.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Preoperative Assessment of Adult Patients for Intracranial Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Plan for timely awakening when appropriate so that neurological function can be assessed; avoid presenting rapid emergence as suitable regardless of intraoperative or preoperative status.
Restart anticonvulsants as early as possible after surgery and coordinate any interruption or replacement with the treating team.

Provide postanesthesia care with continuing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative train-of-four recovery to at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The epilepsy-specific anesthesia source is a review covering multiple epilepsy and nonepilepsy procedures, with no reported systematic search, evidence grading, or quantified comparative outcomes. Treat its recommendations as broad review-level guidance.

Other supporting sources are general intracranial-surgery reviews, a neuroanesthesia orientation manual, a regional-anesthesia review, and ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards. They inform general care but do not resolve several epilepsy-resection specifics.

The available sources do not specify an epilepsy-resection positioning protocol, airway-device requirement, detailed ECoG anesthetic protocol, or procedure-specific fluid and blood-management regimen.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a complete or approved clinical protocol.
The supplied sources do not specify positioning or invasive-monitoring choices specifically for epilepsy resection.
The supplied evidence does not establish a procedure-specific PONV regimen for epilepsy resection.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: EVD placement is an urgent means of diverting CSF and monitoring ICP in acute hydrocephalus or raised ICP, including cases associated with intracranial hemorrhage, SAH, or traumatic brain injury.

Placement is commonly performed urgently at the bedside or in the operating theatre. The catheter is introduced into a lateral ventricle and connected to an external drainage system; local anesthetic is described, but an anesthetic technique is not prescribed.
Key procedural hazards include hemorrhage, inaccurate or suboptimal catheter placement, and infection. For an unsecured aneurysmal SAH, excessive or rapid drainage is a specific concern.

After placement, priorities include correct drain leveling, interpretation of ICP and drainage, and surveillance for leakage, obstruction, and infection. Recovery location and monitoring should reflect the patient’s neurologic condition; ICU care is commonly relevant.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Perioperative management of hydrocephalus
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: EVDs may be used for acute hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and selected neurologic intensive-care conditions. Reported indications include hemorrhage with intraventricular extension, SAH, traumatic brain injury, and bacterial meningitis; the underlying pathology and ventricular anatomy affect the clinical context.

The catheter is placed in a frontal horn of a lateral ventricle, tunnelled beneath the scalp, and connected to an external drainage and collection system. A freehand surface-landmark approach is commonly described; imaging and navigation techniques are also reported.

The prescribed drainage height and strategy are pathology- and pressure-dependent. For unsecured aneurysmal SAH, the review specifically cautions against rapid CSF drainage because of potential effects on aneurysm transmural pressure and rebleeding risk.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Perioperative management of hydrocephalus

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish the neurologic baseline and assess for raised-ICP features, including change in consciousness or seizure activity. In urgent cases, the neurologic indication and urgency of CSF diversion are central context for anesthetic planning.

The available EVD review does not provide formal selection criteria, contraindications, or a preoperative risk-assessment protocol. It therefore does not establish an EVD-specific anticoagulation-reversal approach or anesthetic plan.

sources.label: Perioperative management of hydrocephalus
External ventricular drains: Management and complications

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Insertion may take place in the operating theatre or, when urgent, in a critical-care environment. The placement review describes supine positioning with the head of bed elevated; this is a reported technique, not a universal anesthetic positioning requirement.

For drain management, the external auditory meatus approximates the foramen of Monro when supine. Relevel the system after position changes; inaccurate leveling can distort ICP readings and cause under- or over-drainage.

When anesthesia is provided, apply basic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic technique and patient. ASA standards call for ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

sources.label: Perioperative management of hydrocephalus
External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The EVD-specific sources do not establish an airway plan, sedation depth, or choice between local anesthesia, monitored anesthesia care, and general anesthesia. These sources cannot support routine intubation or a universal sedation technique for placement.

If moderate or deep sedation is used, ASA basic monitoring standards call for continual observation of clinical signs and monitoring for expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Perioperative management of hydrocephalus
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Local anesthetic is described before the scalp incision, but the EVD literature supplied does not specify anesthetic drugs, doses, or a complete intraoperative anesthetic technique.

Opening pressure and the patient’s underlying pathology inform the drainage strategy. With continuous drainage, a transducer-based ICP waveform can be assessed; the review describes a pulsatile waveform after stabilization as the expected signal.

For unsecured aneurysmal SAH, drainage height requires particular attention: the cited review links overly rapid CSF drainage to altered transmural pressure and possible rebleeding. Do not treat EVD drainage as inherently pressure-regulated in a way that eliminates this hazard.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Placement complications include hemorrhage and inadvertent placement into brain tissue; other reported problems include suboptimal placement, displacement, and seizures. The review’s placement-complication estimate is not an individualized patient prediction.
Infection is a major EVD complication. The supplied reviews report different incidence ranges, so these figures should not be treated as a single pooled estimate or as a patient-specific risk.

Obstruction may present with reduced or absent CSF flow and a dampened ICP waveform. The review identifies clot or tissue debris, kinking, migration, and system failure among possible causes; clinical troubleshooting and any system manipulation require appropriate expertise and sterile technique.

Transport-clamping recommendations conflict between the supplied reviews. Follow the applicable institutional neurosurgical protocol and clarify the responsible team’s plan rather than applying a universal rule.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Perioperative management of hydrocephalus

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The EVD placement review does not describe systemic fluid management, blood-product use, or a bleeding-resuscitation regimen. No procedure-specific fluid total, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion target is established by the supplied evidence.

Hemorrhage is a recognized placement complication. The supplied sources do not provide an EVD-specific intraoperative response algorithm; recognize deterioration and escalate promptly to the neurosurgical and anesthesia teams.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthetic at the scalp incision is described. No EVD-specific systemic analgesic regimen or postoperative pain strategy is provided in the placement review.
The supplied EVD sources do not specify PONV prevention or treatment. Individualize any plan to the anesthetic and patient context rather than inferring an EVD-specific regimen.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The EVD-specific sources do not prescribe an emergence or extubation protocol. Recovery and airway disposition should be determined in the context of neurologic status and the anesthetic actually used.

The EVD review emphasizes ongoing drain monitoring, accurate leveling, system integrity, sterility, ICP waveform assessment, and surveillance of CSF drainage. ICU or equivalent postanesthesia care should be arranged as appropriate to the patient’s condition.

sources.label: External ventricular drains: Management and complications
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The EVD anesthesia evidence is limited: the placement-and-management review is not an anesthesia reference and supplies no airway, sedation, anesthetic regimen, or anesthesia-specific perioperative recommendations. These omissions remain unresolved in this draft.

The hydrocephalus source is an educational review that discusses adults and children but does not provide an anesthetic technique for drain insertion. It cannot establish a specific adult EVD anesthetic plan.
ASA basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general anesthesia-care principles, not EVD-specific anesthetic choices, drain management, or procedural targets.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Endovascular coil embolization treats intracranial aneurysms as an alternative to clipping. General anesthesia is common and supports immobility and image quality, but coiling may also be performed under local or general anesthesia; the sources do not establish one anesthetic mode as superior.

The main physiologic priorities are avoiding abrupt blood-pressure elevations that could contribute to rupture or re-bleeding, while preserving cerebral perfusion and adapting management to rupture status, ICP, and vasospasm.

Intraprocedural aneurysm rupture and thromboembolism are major hazards. Rapid recognition, coordination with the neurointerventionist, and prioritization of hemorrhage control or perfusion are central; reversal and blood-pressure decisions must reflect the procedural situation.

Recovery should enable prompt neurologic reassessment when feasible, with close observation for neurologic change, re-bleeding, vasospasm, and access-related complications. SAH-related disposition and blood-pressure management require a case-specific plan.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Coiling is an endovascular treatment in which detachable coils are delivered into the aneurysm. Stent-assisted and balloon-assisted coiling are also addressed in the complication literature; the supplied sources do not define selection criteria for an individual patient.
The procedure uses arterial catheter access, fluoroscopy, and digital subtraction angiography. Head movement can degrade image quality, making procedural immobility important.

General anesthesia is frequently used for immobility and image quality, but it is not established as obligatory for every coiling procedure. Anesthetic selection should reflect patient status, procedural needs, and the interventionist’s requirements.

sources.label: Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish whether the aneurysm is ruptured, the neurologic baseline and level of consciousness, and whether ICP is elevated. For SAH, the clinical condition and evolving complications affect procedural and anesthetic priorities.

Review coagulation and antithrombotic exposure because anticoagulation is commonly used during INR procedures. Clarify the planned antithrombotic strategy with the intervention team, particularly when stent-assisted treatment is contemplated.

Assess prior contrast or medication reactions and renal risk. Adequate hydration is identified as a preventive measure for contrast-associated kidney injury, but the sources do not prescribe a universal fluid regimen.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan for an interventional neuroradiology suite with specialized angiography equipment and potentially unfamiliar access and traffic flow. Ensure the airway and IV equipment remain accessible around the imaging setup.

A radial arterial line is commonly preferred for continuous pressure monitoring and blood sampling, but the source describes coordination with the interventionist when a femoral sheath may provide arterial access. An arterial line is not established here as mandatory for every case.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the selected technique; when general anesthesia is used, maintain continuous assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Positioning is not specified in the procedure-specific sources.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: When general anesthesia is selected, airway management and neuromuscular relaxation can support immobility and image quality. Coiling may also be performed under local anesthesia; the evidence does not support imposing intubation or paralysis on every patient.

Controlled ventilation under general anesthesia can support normocapnia or mild hypocapnia and help manage ICP. Avoid excessive hyperventilation because marked carbon-dioxide reduction can compromise cerebral oxygen availability and may cause iatrogenic ischemia.

Limit stimulation-related surges during airway instrumentation and emergence. The review identifies short-acting opioids or a short-acting beta-blocker as options to help control responses, without establishing a single regimen.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For an unruptured aneurysm, avoid acute blood-pressure elevation that could precipitate rupture; the source recommends careful, possibly invasive, pressure monitoring. It does not establish a universal target applicable across patients and procedures.

With ruptured aneurysm and SAH, re-bleeding and vasospasm are competing hazards. Interpret pressure goals in light of current neurologic status, ICP, and evidence of vasospasm, coordinating with the neurointerventionist and treating team.

A rise in blood pressure or pulse may accompany intraprocedural rupture but is not diagnostic by itself. Device stimulation or diminished anesthesia can also raise pressure; correlate with angiography and procedural findings.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Intraprocedural aneurysm rupture ranges from limited contrast leakage to severe hemorrhage and intracranial hypertension. When suspected, promptly communicate with the neurointerventionist and confirm the event using procedural imaging and clinical context.

For confirmed rupture, the review describes anticoagulant reversal as an initial measure, but cautions that protamine can cause adverse reactions and should not delay mechanical hemostasis. Reversal and hemorrhage-control decisions require immediate coordination with the procedural team.

Thromboembolism may present during or after coiling; angiographic flow defects and distal emboli are described, with electrophysiologic monitoring as an adjunct under general anesthesia. Escalate suspected ischemia promptly with the intervention team; the review discusses several rescue approaches but does not establish a universal algorithm.

sources.label: Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain hydration while considering cardiac status, renal risk, and the contrast burden. The available review supports adequate hydration to reduce contrast-associated nephropathy but gives no case-specific volume or fluid prescription.

Treat cerebral perfusion as dependent on both MAP and ICP; neurologic disease can impair autoregulation, so pressure changes may have variable effects. Avoid applying a single pressure target across ruptured, unruptured, and vasospasm states.
The review describes hypervolemia and hemodilution among possible thromboembolism treatments; these are not established as routine fluid strategies for all coiling procedures.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The supplied sources do not establish a coiling-specific postoperative analgesia or PONV regimen. Select care according to the patient's condition and the anesthetic used; do not infer that pain is invariably minimal from the endovascular approach.
For general anesthesia, short-acting opioids are described as one option to attenuate airway-stimulation responses; drug selection should also account for the goal of timely neurologic assessment.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Complications of endovascular treatment for intracranial aneurysms: Management and prevention

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Aim for a smooth recovery that permits neurologic assessment when clinically appropriate. Avoid coughing or straining that could cause hemodynamic stress; balance prompt examination against the patient's neurologic and respiratory status.

Perform repeated neurologic examinations after the procedure and obtain imaging if a deficit is detected. Monitor for vasospasm and manage post-coiling pressure according to rupture status and the treating team's plan.

Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent area, such as an ICU, and monitor the patient by methods appropriate to their medical condition; ICU disposition is not required for every coiling case.

sources.label: Anesthetic Consideration for Neurointerventional Procedures
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia source is a review of interventional neuroradiology practice, not a procedure-specific guideline; it reports no clear superior anesthetic mode and describes institutional practice. Its recommendations should not be treated as a universal regimen.

The aneurysm-complication review is not an anesthesia reference and does not provide a comprehensive anesthetic plan. Some management claims derive from cited retrospective studies, and it reports no systematic-review methodology or evidence grading.

The supplied procedure reviews do not specify an age range, so they do not establish adult-only evidence. The adult clinical framing here does not resolve the need for individualized, contemporary procedural decisions.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lumbar decompression is performed for symptomatic stenosis; laminectomy may be considered after conservative treatment fails. General anesthesia is common, with spinal anesthesia an alternative for selected elective cases.
Prone positioning is usual. Maintain an unobstructed abdomen and avoid pressure on the eyes; prone positioning can impair venous return and increase epidural venous pressure and bleeding risk.

For lumbar surgery under spinal anesthesia, coordinate with the surgical team about prone positioning and airway contingencies. When SSEP monitoring is used in decompressive surgery, account for its effects on anesthetic technique.

Plan recovery to permit assessment of neurologic status, while providing appropriate postanesthesia observation and monitoring. If neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.
