REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Lumbar spinal stenosis can cause lower-extremity and buttock pain, sometimes with low-back pain. Laminectomy is one surgical option after conservative treatment fails.

General anesthesia and neuraxial anesthesia are both described for lumbar laminectomy. The choice depends on the patient, procedure, and airway or other clinical considerations; the sources do not establish one universally preferred approach.

Spinal anesthesia is discussed as an option for selected elective lumbar cases; suitability depends on procedural extent and patient factors, and requires planning for airway rescue in the prone position.

sources.label: Neurosurgical Anesthesia: Optimizing Outcomes with Agent Selection
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: When spinal anesthesia is being considered, assess suitability during the initial surgical consultation and consider comorbidities and planned surgical extent. The cited eligibility algorithm identifies scoliosis, anxiety, high BMI, OSA, three or more fusion levels, and four or more decompression levels as characteristics that may preclude spinal anesthesia.

For possible spinal anesthesia, discuss expectations and risks with the patient and assess factors that may complicate its feasibility, including scoliosis, anxiety, high BMI, OSA, and extensive planned decompression.

The spinal-anesthesia review describes anticipated operative time and number of levels as selection considerations, but these are not universal exclusion rules. General anesthesia may be selected when airway management is expected to be challenging.

sources.label: Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Neurosurgical Anesthesia: Optimizing Outcomes with Agent Selection

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prone is the usual position. Coordinate positioning and contingency planning with the surgical team, especially if the chosen anesthetic limits immediate airway access.

Use appropriate padding and positioning supports; keep the abdomen free of compression, preserve head venous return, and avoid pressure on the eyes. These measures address prone-position effects described in the review, not a substitute for repeated clinical assessment.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique. ASA standards require continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; monitor temperature when significant change is anticipated, intended, or suspected.

sources.label: Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: With general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. After ETT or LMA placement, verify position clinically and by identifying carbon dioxide in expired gas, and use quantitative end-tidal CO₂ monitoring through extubation or initiation of transfer.

For spinal anesthesia with sedation, assess airway-obstruction risk and plan rescue access before prone positioning. The review describes an LMA as a rescue option and recommends that a fiberoptic bronchoscope be available when needed for a high-risk airway.

Do not impose general anesthesia, intubation, or neuromuscular blockade on a regional technique. If moderate or deep sedation is used, ASA standards call for observation of clinical signs and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless precluded or invalidated.

sources.label: Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid abdominal compression in the prone position: the review links it to reduced venous return and increased pressure in the epidural venous plexus, with increased bleeding risk.

Select maintenance technique in light of monitoring needs. Volatile agents can depress evoked potentials; the cited review favors TIVA, alone or balanced with low-dose volatile anesthetic, when SSEP monitoring is used.

If spinal anesthesia is chosen, confirm adequate block with the surgical team before sedation and incision, and allow time for the block to take effect. These are recommendations from a narrative review and should be applied with clinical judgment.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Neurosurgical Anesthesia: Optimizing Outcomes with Agent Selection
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Prone positioning can produce relative hypovolemia, hypotension, reduced cardiac index, and venous stasis. Reassess the patient and positioning if hemodynamic instability or unexpectedly increased bleeding occurs.

Under spinal anesthesia, airway obstruction or acute airway loss is a recognized concern in the prone position. Use the pre-agreed rescue plan and obtain prompt assistance; the source emphasizes contingency planning rather than providing a universal rescue algorithm.

Durotomy is discussed in the spinal-anesthesia review; cited comparisons did not find a significant difference in risk between spinal and general endotracheal anesthesia. This does not establish a procedure-specific response protocol.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Positioning that leaves the abdomen uncompressed is a supported measure to reduce venous engorgement and bleeding risk. No case-specific fluid regimen, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion protocol is established in the available lumbar-surgery sources.

Attend to hypotension risk in the prone position, particularly with regional anesthesia or relevant comorbidity. Individualize hemodynamic management; the sources do not establish a universal MAP target for elective lumbar decompression.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan postoperative analgesia while preserving the ability to assess neurologic status. Intrathecal opioid is described as an option; discuss its use with the surgeon and account for the need for appropriate postoperative observation.
Epidural local anesthetic may produce motor block and complicate postoperative neurologic assessment; discuss the technique with the surgeon and consider the need for timely examination.

The review of elective lumbar anesthesia reports potential short-term advantages of spinal anesthesia, including less PONV in some comparisons, but this does not establish a uniform patient-level benefit or an analgesic regimen.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Neurosurgical Anesthesia: Optimizing Outcomes with Agent Selection
Spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar spinal surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Coordinate emergence to support prompt postoperative neurologic assessment when clinically appropriate. Transfer the patient to a PACU or equivalent area with monitoring and handoff appropriate to condition.

Postanesthesia care standards call for continual assessment, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; use pulse oximetry during the initial recovery phase.

When neuromuscular blockade has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are supported by the ASA guideline overview. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthetic-selection source is a narrative review with heterogeneous findings; it explicitly reports no consensus or official guidance for an optimal anesthetic choice. Its findings should not be treated as a universal lumbar-laminectomy regimen.

The spinal-anesthesia source is a narrative review combined with institutional experience, not a guideline; it notes unresolved selection and dosing questions. The regional-anesthesia review also states that spinal-surgery regional techniques have not been extensively evaluated.

The provided evidence does not establish whether cauda equina features require a particular anesthetic pathway or give a detailed procedure-specific neurologic surveillance protocol. These questions need case-specific clinical judgment and evidence beyond this source set.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Mechanical thrombectomy is an emergency endovascular procedure to remove an occluding clot and restore cerebral blood flow. Anesthesia may be general anesthesia or conscious sedation; selection is individualized rather than a universal preference.

The dominant physiologic priority is preserving cerebral perfusion while avoiding blood-pressure extremes; permissive hypertension may be used before recanalization. The available sources do not establish a universal numerical target.

Sedation can preserve ongoing neurologic assessment but requires readiness to manage airway compromise or conversion to general anesthesia. General anesthesia can provide immobility and controlled ventilation, with possible induction-related delay and hemodynamic fluctuation.

After the procedure, prioritize frequent neurologic assessment and monitoring of blood pressure and vital signs in an ICU or specialized stroke unit; avoid oversedation that could obscure examination.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview
Common Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Thrombectomy treats selected acute ischemic strokes due to large-vessel occlusion, with the aim of reperfusing threatened brain tissue. The neurointerventionalist advances a catheter through the femoral artery under fluoroscopic guidance; clot removal may use a stent retriever or aspiration catheter, with angiography used to assess restored flow.

The anesthetic approach may be general anesthesia or conscious sedation. Choose according to the patient’s ability to tolerate the procedure, airway and aspiration risks, neurologic status, procedural complexity, local protocol, and team experience; the sources do not support a universal technique preference.

sources.label: Common Neurointerventional Procedures
Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Obtain a rapid neurologic baseline, including NIHSS where available, and review brain imaging for infarct location and size and to exclude hemorrhage. Coordinate assessment with ongoing procedural preparation; the review emphasizes avoiding unnecessary delay.

Review cardiovascular stability, comorbidities, anticoagulant and antiplatelet medications, and available blood glucose and coagulation results. The sources identify these as relevant assessment factors but do not provide a thrombectomy-specific medication interruption or correction protocol.

Individualize the choice of general anesthesia (GA) versus conscious sedation (CS) according to patient characteristics, local protocols, and clinician experience. GA may be useful with agitation, a predicted difficult airway, poor baseline oxygen saturation, dysphagia, or inability to follow commands. CS avoids intubation and mechanical ventilation risks.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use a neurointerventional environment with fluoroscopic imaging and access to appropriate anesthesia equipment, medications, and airway support. Coordinate readiness among anesthesia, neurology, and radiology teams.

The procedural arterial access described is femoral. Standard anesthetic monitoring includes ECG, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, temperature, and expired carbon dioxide as applicable to the anesthetic. An arterial catheter is preferred by the review, but the procedure should not be delayed solely for placement unless specifically indicated.
Positioning instructions specific to thrombectomy are not established in the supplied sources; use the procedural and imaging requirements without inferring a fixed position.

sources.label: Common Neurointerventional Procedures
Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: With conscious sedation, maintain an approach that permits neurologic assessment while watching for airway obstruction, respiratory depression, aspiration, and the need for urgent conversion. Conversion can create treatment delay and may require securing the airway in a suboptimal situation.

Use general anesthesia when patient or procedural factors make sedation unsuitable, including inability to protect the airway or significant aspiration risk. Endotracheal intubation provides a secure airway and controlled ventilation, but airway-device choice remains case-specific.

Avoid hypoxia and manage ventilation with attention to carbon dioxide: hypercapnia increases cerebral blood flow through vasodilation, whereas hypocapnia decreases it through vasoconstriction. The review gives no consensus ventilator settings; individualize ventilation to the patient and circumstances.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain cerebral perfusion by avoiding blood-pressure extremes, particularly hypotension before recanalization when collateral flow supports threatened tissue. The review gives a preoperative pressure range, while another source describes permissive hypertension; neither establishes a universal target applicable to every patient or phase.

Reassess blood pressure and neurologic status in the context of procedural progress and reperfusion. Avoid assuming a fixed post-recanalization systolic target from these sources; monitor and coordinate individualized postoperative pressure management.

Control glucose and temperature and maintain appropriate oxygenation. Hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, and hyperthermia can worsen secondary brain injury; the review emphasizes glucose control and normothermia. Routine supplemental oxygen is not supported for non-hypoxic patients in this review.
Use titrated, short-acting anesthetic agents when feasible to support prompt neurologic reassessment; avoid oversedation and communicate changes in patient status or procedural course across teams.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview
Common Neurointerventional Procedures

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Sudden neurologic or hemodynamic deterioration requires urgent assessment for hemorrhagic versus occlusive complications and escalation with the neurointerventional team. The supplied manual describes these as general interventional-neuroradiology catastrophes, not a thrombectomy-specific treatment algorithm.

During sedation, be prepared for aspiration or airway compromise and conversion to general anesthesia. Agitation, prolonged procedures, comorbidities, tandem occlusion, and multiple pharmacologic agents are reported as possible conversion predictors.

sources.label: Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use intravenous fluids as clinically needed to support blood pressure and cerebral perfusion; avoid hypotension and consider the patient's cardiovascular status. The review does not specify a fluid regimen or blood-loss protocol.

Anticoagulant and antiplatelet treatment involves balancing thromboembolic and bleeding risks; review medications and coagulation information with the procedural team. The sources do not establish a universal peri-procedural anticoagulation or reversal regimen for thrombectomy.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Analgesic and sedative choices should be titrated to procedural needs and neurologic assessability. The review describes opioid options and their potential respiratory or hemodynamic effects but does not establish a single regimen for thrombectomy.

After the procedure, treat pain while avoiding sedation that obscures the neurologic examination or delays recovery. The available procedure-specific review does not supply a PONV prevention protocol.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general anesthesia, favor timely recovery of consciousness for neurologic assessment when clinically appropriate; the source does not provide specific extubation criteria. After sedation, reassess neurologic status promptly.
Monitor patients in an intensive care unit or specialized stroke unit, with frequent neurological assessments and ongoing blood-pressure and other vital-sign monitoring.

For postanesthesia transfer, continue monitoring and support appropriate to the patient's condition, communicate the anesthetic and procedural course to the receiving team, and document status on arrival.

sources.label: Anesthetic Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke Undergoing Mechanical Thrombectomy: An Overview
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal thrombectomy anesthesia source is a narrative review, not a guideline or trial. It reports that there is no clear consensus on general anesthesia versus conscious sedation and that guidelines do not provide specific recommendations; anesthetic choice should therefore remain individualized.

An educational neurointerventional summary supports both sedation and general anesthesia for thrombectomy but provides limited case-specific anesthetic detail. Its general statement that general anesthesia and invasive arterial monitoring are common for intracranial procedures should not be read as a thrombectomy-specific mandate.

The anesthesia review's cited trial summaries do not establish that MAC is uniformly superior to general anesthesia: it reports similar functional outcomes in several comparisons and higher successful reperfusion with general anesthesia without corresponding functional-outcome improvement.

A specific post-recanalization blood-pressure target and thrombectomy-specific fluid, drug, anticoagulation, and extubation protocols are not established by the supplied evidence. Individualize these decisions with the stroke and neurointerventional teams.

Common Neurointerventional Procedures

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: MEPs are used during operations that place motor pathways at risk: transcranial electrical stimulation (TES) elicits responses recorded from peripheral muscles. The anesthetic and surgical teams should coordinate monitoring and interpret signals in that context.

A propofol–opioid TIVA approach is commonly used for IOM. Volatile anesthetics can suppress or abolish MEPs; avoid abrupt anesthetic changes and interpret signals with the anesthetic technique in mind.

Neuromuscular blockade can decrease or abolish muscle MEPs. Generally minimize or avoid it during recording, in coordination with the neurophysiologist; a weak or unavailable baseline is more likely with pre-existing motor weakness.

Treat an important signal change as a prompt for joint assessment, not an automatic diagnosis of injury: check technical, anesthetic, and physiologic causes, correlate with the surgical event, and promptly notify the surgeon when signals are lost or meaningfully altered.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: MEP monitoring is an intraoperative method for assessing motor-pathway function when the operation puts those pathways at risk. TES is commonly used; responses are recorded from selected peripheral muscles.

Recording sites and monitoring protocol depend on the operation and the neural structures at risk. The cited review describes multi-muscle recording; it does not establish one universal muscle set or protocol for all procedures.
MEP monitoring is not indicated for every operation. Select monitoring through discussion among the surgeon, monitoring personnel or neurophysiologist, and anesthesiologist.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Document relevant baseline motor function and discuss whether reliable responses are likely. Significant preoperative motor weakness can make MEP acquisition difficult or prevent a useful baseline.

Review seizure history, intracranial lesions or devices, and implanted cardiac devices with the monitoring team. The older review lists several of these as contraindications to TES; the available sources do not resolve device-specific eligibility or compatibility.

Agree before induction on the monitoring plan, intended anesthetic approach, and how the team will communicate signal changes. These sources do not provide a universal preoperative selection protocol for all MEP-monitored operations.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: TES uses scalp stimulation electrodes and muscle responses are recorded from peripheral electrode sites. The monitoring team should specify electrode locations and acquisition protocol for the case.
Obtain a post-positioning baseline when feasible, since positioning can alter signals; reassess signals after repositioning if a change occurs.
Consider technical artifacts as well as physiologic changes. Electrocautery, stimulation, cable contact, and equipment or electrode problems can affect recordings.

sources.label: Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Choose airway management for the procedure and patient; the available MEP sources do not establish that an endotracheal tube is required for every MEP-monitored case.

If a neuromuscular blocker is used to facilitate airway management, account for its effect on muscle MEPs and coordinate recording with the monitoring team. Avoid assuming elapsed time alone establishes recovery from blockade.

Maintain ventilation and oxygenation while avoiding abrupt changes that could confound signals. Very low PaCO₂ has been associated with cortical evoked-potential changes in the cited review; it advises obtaining baseline recordings before hyperventilation.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Propofol-based TIVA with an opioid is a commonly used approach. Propofol can itself suppress MEP generation at higher doses, so signal quality must be interpreted alongside anesthetic depth and changes in administration.

Volatile anesthetics suppress evoked responses. One review describes concentrations below 0.5 MAC as generally compatible with acceptable MEPs, while another warns that halogenated agents may abolish MEPs even at low doses. Prefer a stable technique and do not treat 0.5 MAC as a guaranteed safe threshold.

Avoid abrupt anesthetic boluses or concentration shifts when possible. Blood pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, hematocrit, and positioning may also affect recordings; maintain physiologic stability appropriate to the patient and operation.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: A sustained, reproducible signal change across recordings is more persuasive than an isolated fluctuation. MEP amplitude has high intertrial variability, and the optimal alarm criteria remain debated.

For a meaningful change, assess technical factors and electrodes, anesthetic changes, blood pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, and other relevant physiology; if no such cause is apparent, treat a surgical cause as possible and escalate promptly to the surgeon.

MEP alarm criteria vary by procedure and practice: one review reports absence of mMEP as an alarm sign for spinal surgery and a greater-than-50% amplitude decrement as a potential alarm sign for brain surgery in the authors’ laboratory. A spine review states that there is no clear consensus on meaningful change and describes a 50% increase in stimulus intensity needed to elicit tceMEPs as significant.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Avoid hypotension that could reduce neural perfusion or suppress evoked signals; respond to a signal change by evaluating blood pressure in the clinical context.
No MEP-specific universal MAP target, fluid regimen, transfusion threshold, or blood-loss protocol is established by the supplied MEP sources. Individualize these to the operation and patient.

sources.label: Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Opioids are commonly paired with propofol in TIVA approaches for IOM. Select analgesia for the procedure and patient while avoiding abrupt anesthetic changes that confound monitoring.

The general IOM review does not provide procedure-specific analgesia or detailed postoperative care. A spine-monitoring review describes a balanced TIVA approach including an opioid such as sufentanil and says the infusion is usually stopped 30–60 minutes before the end of surgery to provide analgesia at emergence.

sources.label: Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring: Basic Principles and Recent Update
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: When neuromuscular blockers have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone, with TOF ratio at least 0.9 confirmed at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to every MEP case.
Recovery location and monitoring should reflect the patient's condition and anesthetic course; reassess and communicate intraoperative signal findings to the receiving team.

sources.label: New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal sources are narrative reviews: one surveys IOM across procedures, and the other presents a practical approach to complex spine monitoring. They do not provide a single procedure-specific anesthetic guideline.

Signal criteria and anesthetic effects should be interpreted cautiously: the first review says optimal MEP alarm criteria remain debated, and the second describes authors' practice and recommendations rather than universal standards.

No supplied source establishes a universal airway plan, MAP goal, bite-block requirement, or procedure-independent drug regimen for MEP monitoring. Adult applicability is not specifically established for every source; apply only relevant general anesthesia standards and case-specific expertise.

Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Diagnostic neuroangiography uses catheter-based contrast imaging under fluoroscopy, most commonly through common femoral access; other arterial access may be selected when anatomy or access suitability requires it.
The central anesthetic priorities are patient immobility, preservation of an interpretable neurologic examination, and prompt recognition of neurologic or vascular change.

Conscious sedation with fentanyl and midazolam is described for most diagnostic procedures; general anesthesia may be needed when cooperation or procedural complexity makes sedation unsuitable. The sources do not establish a specific anesthetic regimen or airway technique.

Important hazards include stroke, catheter-related dissection or vasospasm, access-site bleeding, contrast-associated renal injury, and contrast reaction. Recovery should include neurologic and access-site assessment.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Diagnostic neuroangiography obtains fluoroscopic contrast images of intracranial and extracranial vessels and may inform subsequent endovascular treatment. It is generally reserved for selected diagnostic questions rather than routine use where noninvasive imaging is sufficient.

Common femoral access is typical in the cited institutional practices; transradial or transbrachial access may be used in selected circumstances. Access choice is procedural and anatomy dependent, not a fixed anesthetic requirement.

Catheter manipulation, contrast injection, and digital subtraction angiography require limiting motion; the team may need to coordinate patient instructions and sedation with imaging and neurologic assessment.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the diagnostic question with the referring and interventional teams. Document a focused neurologic baseline before sedation or anesthesia so pre-existing deficits can be distinguished from procedural change.

Review renal function, blood count, and coagulation testing when indicated by the clinical situation. Renal insufficiency, coagulopathy, and contrast allergy are described as relative contraindications; anticoagulants should be held when possible in coordination with the procedural team.

For contrast allergy, the reviews describe preprocedure prophylaxis but do not establish a universal regimen here. With renal insufficiency, they describe saline hydration and judicious use of iodinated contrast; neither a hydration volume nor an individualized renal-risk protocol is specified.

sources.label: Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The patient is positioned supine with a headrest. Instructions to remain still and, when appropriate, hold the breath can reduce motion artifact; a head strap is described for some uncooperative patients.

Fluoroscopy and DSA expose staff to radiation. The neuroanesthesia manual advises lead aprons and thyroid shields; arrange protection and a means of monitoring the patient if radiation exposure requires intermittent remote observation.

Apply applicable basic anesthesia monitoring. ASA standards require continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment; during moderate or deep sedation, expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring is required unless precluded or invalidated.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For cooperative patients, the neuroangiography reviews describe conscious sedation and analgesia using fentanyl and midazolam, with presedation assessment that includes airway evaluation. They do not supply a dose protocol.

General anesthesia may be required for complex neurointerventions or when cooperation is inadequate. The cited neuroangiography reviews do not specify an airway device, conversion plan, or general-anesthetic drug regimen; choose these based on the patient and procedure rather than treating them as routine.

Sedation can limit serial neurologic examination, while airway obstruction or patient motion can compromise the procedure. Match sedation depth to cooperation, airway assessment, and the need for neurologic reassessment.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual (page title: Orientation Manual; document title shown as Neuroanesthesia Orientation Manual.doc)

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Preserve the ability to detect neurologic change. The review recommends documenting assessment after automated pump injections, recognizing that sedation or anesthesia may reduce the reliability of the examination.

Vertebral artery catheterization is a particular procedural hazard because of dissection and vasospasm risk. Delayed contrast washout may indicate vasospasm, dissection, obturation, or thromboembolism; promptly communicate the finding to the interventionalist for assessment and management.

Meticulous inspection and flushing of catheter systems with heparinized saline is described to reduce air or thrombotic emboli. The sources do not establish a universal systemic heparin or activated-clotting-time target for diagnostic cases.

sources.label: Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Neurologic complications include transient or permanent deficits and stroke; risk is reported as higher with factors such as older age, severe atherosclerosis, symptomatic cerebrovascular disease, and acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. New neurologic change warrants prompt assessment with the procedural team.

Access and catheter complications include groin hematoma, arterial occlusion, dissection, and vasospasm. After the procedure, examine the access site and assess for neurologic change; escalate suspected vascular injury or deficit to the interventional team.

Contrast allergy and renal injury are recognized risks. The supplied sources identify risk reduction measures but do not provide a procedure-specific emergency treatment algorithm for a severe contrast reaction.

sources.label: Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: For renal insufficiency, the reviews describe prehydration with normal saline and minimizing iodinated contrast. They do not specify a routine volume or rate; individualize fluid administration to the patient’s clinical condition.

After diagnostic cerebral arteriography, achieve common femoral artery hemostasis with manual compression or a percutaneous closure device. At the authors’ institution, pressure is typically held for approximately 20 minutes with a 5-Fr system.
Hematoma can be clinically consequential, but the reviews provide no blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, or resuscitation protocol specific to diagnostic neuroangiography.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Fentanyl is included with midazolam in the described conscious-sedation approach. The sources do not provide a separate postoperative analgesic regimen; expected discomfort and analgesic needs should be assessed clinically.
A procedure-specific postoperative nausea and vomiting prevention strategy is not described in the available evidence.

sources.label: Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips
Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After angiography, perform and document a neurologic examination and check the access site. Significant neurologic change may require further imaging and coordinated evaluation.

Patients receiving anesthesia should recover in a PACU or equivalent area unless specifically ordered otherwise; transport, handoff, and monitoring should follow applicable postanesthesia standards, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

The neuroangiography sources do not specify an anesthetic emergence, reversal, extubation, or discharge protocol. Recovery and disposition should reflect the anesthetic, neurologic findings, and procedural course.

sources.label: Basic Neuroangiography: Review of Technique and Perioperative Patient Care
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Neuroangiography: Review of Anatomy, Periprocedural Management, Technique, and Tips

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The two procedure-specific sources are narrative reviews of neuroangiography technique and perioperative care, not anesthesia protocols. Their sedation and access descriptions include institutional preferences; neither provides comparative anesthesia evidence.

The neuroanesthesia manual gives broader interventional neuroradiology guidance but is an educational manual without stated publication date or evidence grading. Use it as contextual support, not as a substitute for current local procedural protocols.

The supplied sources do not establish an adult diagnostic-angiography-specific emergency protocol for severe contrast reaction, a universal anticoagulation/ACT strategy, or a standardized anesthetic technique. These remain matters for current specialty guidance and the procedural team.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: SCS implantation places epidural leads to deliver stimulation for refractory pain; permanent implantation generally follows a successful trial. Percutaneous leads are introduced through an epidural needle, while paddle leads require a different, generally surgical approach.

For paresthesia-mapped lead placement, patient feedback is an important positioning aid; use the least sedation that supports comfort and safety while preserving useful feedback when feasible. Paresthesia-free systems do not require this mapping, and selected cases may favor deeper anesthesia.

Lead placement is typically prone and fluoroscopy-guided. Prone sedation poses airway-access challenges; avoid assuming that an unprotected airway under deep sedation is appropriate. Plan anesthesia depth and airway contingencies for the patient, procedure, and ability to provide feedback.

Priorities include preventing neural injury, infection, and lead displacement, and recognizing possible epidural hematoma. Recovery should include appropriate postanesthesia observation, device/programming follow-up, and movement restrictions intended to reduce lead migration.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: SCS is used for selected patients with chronic refractory pain after conservative treatment and for certain ischemic conditions. Implantation is a two-step process: a trial followed, when successful, by permanent implantation; the techniques differ. A successful percutaneous trial requires a second procedure for permanent implantation.

Percutaneous cylindrical leads are advanced through an epidural needle under fluoroscopy. Paddle electrodes may require a surgical approach, including laminotomy; do not assume the percutaneous lead workflow or anesthesia considerations apply identically to paddle placement.

After lead positioning, permanent implantation may involve anchoring, tunneling to a subcutaneous pulse-generator pocket, connection, and wound closure. Pocket location is selected for patient comfort and access; the specific approach depends on the implant and surgical plan.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review pain distribution, prior spinal operations and hardware, and available imaging for anatomy at the intended access and lead levels. Spinal anatomy that prevents safe epidural access is a contraindication; imaging is used to map the epidural space and correlate anatomy with symptoms.
Confirm psychological evaluation and readiness to participate in follow-up, wound care, and device management. A trial is used to assess benefit and coverage before permanent implantation.

Assess infection and bleeding risks, including therapeutic anticoagulation. The review says anticoagulation typically requires interruption according to ASRA guidance and placement is contraindicated if it cannot be interrupted in specified high-risk circumstances; determine management using applicable current guidance and the patient's indication rather than a fixed interval.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare for prone lead placement with fluoroscopic visualization and a team able to maintain the sterile field while imaging is obtained. Positioning should permit the planned lead trajectory and safe access to the patient.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and patient. ASA basic standards require continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes are specified.

During moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation continuously by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it. Monitoring standards do not specify SCS-specific physiologic targets.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For traditional paresthesia mapping, plan sedation so the patient can respond and provide meaningful feedback when required. The consensus recommendation described in the review is an awake, conversant patient for percutaneous lead placement, while acknowledging selected exceptions.

An awake-feedback approach is not universal: paresthesia-free anatomical placement does not require mapping, and deep sedation or general anesthesia may be considered in selected circumstances. These choices trade patient comfort and immobility against loss of patient warning feedback.

Prone MAC can make airway access difficult, and deep sedation may leave the airway unprotected. Evaluate airway and respiratory risk, sedation feasibility, and the consequences of movement before choosing the technique; the sources do not prescribe a universal airway device or ventilation strategy.

sources.label: Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia
Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Lead advancement and localization are critical phases. Patient feedback may alert the clinician to needle or lead advancement toward neural structures or compression; careful epidural localization and appropriate fluoroscopic visualization are described as safeguards.

Balance immobility with feedback needs. Movement, poor needle control, and ineffective fluoroscopy are discussed as possible contributors to injury; use imaging views appropriate to the trajectory and level.

Once leads are positioned, tunneling and pulse-generator pocket work follow. The review describes that sedation may be deepened after lead implantation; the required depth and timing are case- and technique-dependent.

sources.label: Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Important complications include epidural hematoma, infection, lead migration or breakage, inadequate coverage, nerve injury, and paralysis. The source describes the most devastating complications as exceedingly rare, but does not establish a reliable incidence for this individual patient.

Maintain sterile technique and use the prescribed perioperative infection-prevention measures. Infection may require explantation of the system unless contamination is confined to superficial tissues.

New neurologic symptoms or concerning back pain after implantation require urgent clinical assessment for a potentially serious neuraxial complication. Available sources identify epidural hematoma and direct neural injury but do not provide a complete diagnostic or treatment algorithm.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The available SCS sources do not provide a fluid regimen, expected blood loss, or transfusion guidance. Manage these according to the patient's condition and operative circumstances rather than inferring a routine SCS prescription.

Bleeding risk is particularly consequential in the epidural space. Review antithrombotic therapy and coordinate interruption or continuation with the relevant current guidance and the prescribing team; the source does not support fixed stop or restart intervals here.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthetic may be used at the incision, and patient discomfort despite adequate local anesthesia can make light sedation impractical. No SCS-specific anesthetic drug regimen or postoperative analgesic protocol is established in the sources.
PONV prevention and treatment are not addressed in the SCS-specific material; select measures based on individual risk and local practice rather than assuming a procedure-specific regimen.

sources.label: Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Lead Placement Under Deep Sedation and General Anesthesia

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After anesthesia, recovery monitoring should address oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase. Transfer and handoff should be appropriate to the patient's condition.

For a percutaneous trial, programming is finalized in recovery before discharge. Permanent implantation requires device follow-up and wound management; movement restrictions intended to reduce lead migration are described, but patient-specific instructions should follow the implanting team's guidance.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are recommended; this does not imply that neuromuscular blockade is required for SCS.

Spinal Cord Stimulation — StatPearls
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia-specific source is a descriptive survey of practice patterns and reported complications, not a guideline or trial. Its authors lacked total case numbers and complication details, so it cannot establish overall risk or a preferred anesthetic technique.

The broader SCS review supports procedural and selection context but is not anesthesia-specific and notes limited formal evidence-based contraindication guidance. The monitoring and postanesthesia sources provide general standards, not SCS-specific anesthetic or discharge protocols.

The supplied sources do not define a single anesthetic technique for all SCS procedures, nor do they resolve patient-specific antithrombotic management, drug selection, fluid needs, or device-specific MRI compatibility. These require the applicable specialty guidance, device information, and individualized clinical planning.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TLIF/PLIF are posterior lumbar fusion approaches; the operation may include decompression, interbody work, and posterior instrumentation. The available sources describe a range of lumbar fusion complexity rather than one uniform technique.

For cases using spinal-cord or nerve-root monitoring, the anesthetic must support interpretable signals and timely postoperative neurologic assessment; TIVA is often selected, though a carefully balanced technique may also be suitable.
The major physiologic concerns are prone-position effects, blood loss, and maintaining end-organ perfusion; risk varies with patient comorbidity, operative extent, and duration.
Plan recovery for an early neurologic examination while also assessing oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, temperature, pain, and any new deficit.

sources.label: Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning
Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Lumbar fusion may be performed for degenerative disease and other spinal pathology. TLIF and PLIF are posterior approaches; minimally invasive and open operations differ in exposure and operative demands.

The surgical plan may include decompression, disc-space preparation, interbody placement, and instrumentation. Prior decompression at the same level can leave scar and adhesions that complicate exposure.
Extent, number of levels, approach, and pathology affect expected blood loss and operative burden; the sources do not establish a single anesthetic pathway for all TLIF/PLIF cases.

sources.label: Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning
Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess functional and cardiopulmonary reserve in relation to prone positioning, anticipated blood loss, anemia, and prolonged surgery. Use comorbidity and functional findings to guide further evaluation.

Review prior lumbar operations, pathology, planned levels, baseline neurologic findings, and the surgeon’s monitoring plan. Surgical complexity and prior same-level decompression can affect technical difficulty and recovery.

Consider anemia, nutrition, frailty, smoking and substance use, obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease as potential risk modifiers. The cited review supports assessment and optimization, not a universal exclusion rule.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For prone surgery, use a positioning system that permits abdominal excursion and avoids pressure on the eyes and other vulnerable structures. Prone positioning can alter venous return and cardiac loading.
For most multilevel fusions, the review recommends continuous arterial pressure monitoring and frequent blood-gas assessment; choose access and monitoring in light of case extent and comorbidity.

Use appropriate basic anesthetic monitoring, including continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Confirm an airway device with clinical assessment and exhaled carbon dioxide.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The supplied TLIF/PLIF and complex-fusion sources do not specify an airway device, intubation technique, or ventilation target. Select airway management according to the individual and planned positioning rather than treating a particular technique as universal.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify correct positioning by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to postoperative care, perform continual end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis using a quantitative method such as capnography, capnometry, or mass spectroscopy.

The sources do not establish a TLIF/PLIF-specific ventilation strategy or a routine neuromuscular-blockade policy. If blockade is used, quantitative recovery assessment before extubation is supported by general ASA guideline reporting.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Choose an anesthetic compatible with planned SSEP, MEP, or EMG monitoring. TIVA is often selected; a balanced technique with low volatile exposure can preserve monitoring in many cases.

Coordinate anesthetic changes and signal interpretation with the monitoring team. Boluses of opioids, sedatives, hypnotics, ketamine, or dexmedetomidine can transiently alter evoked-potential signals.

Treat a significant monitoring change as an urgent team communication and surgical reassessment issue; reversing a maneuver or changing correction may prevent neurologic injury. Avoid hypotension during prolonged prone anesthesia.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Prone positioning and lengthy surgery are associated with pressure injury and visual-loss concerns. Risk modifiers described include obesity, Wilson-frame positioning, higher blood loss, longer surgery, and crystalloid-only fluid management.

Potential surgical complications include dural tear, nerve-root injury, and misplaced screws. Adequate visualization and minimizing nerve-root or thecal retraction are emphasized in the MIS TLIF review.

Unexpected bleeding, hemodynamic deterioration, or monitoring changes warrant prompt communication and reassessment of surgical and anesthetic contributors. The available sources do not provide a single troubleshooting algorithm for these events.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Anticipate substantial variation in blood loss by procedure extent. Consider active warming, cell salvage, and proactive assessment of hemoglobin and coagulopathy during significant bleeding.

Balanced crystalloids are preferred to normal saline in the complex-fusion review because they are less likely to cause hyperchloremic acidosis and postoperative kidney injury. Individualize fluid composition and volume to the patient and operative course.
Avoid deliberate hypotension as a routine blood-loss strategy; the review links it with cardiac and neurologic complications. Individualize pressure goals to end-organ perfusion and comorbid risk.

Tranexamic acid is reported to reduce blood loss and transfusion in spine surgery, but the review states that an optimal dose is not established; any use and regimen require individualized clinical judgment.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use a multimodal analgesic plan tailored to opioid exposure, comorbidity, and surgical complexity. Scheduled acetaminophen and selected non-opioid agents are discussed; NSAID use requires consideration of bleeding and bone-healing concerns.

Gabapentinoids may reduce opioid requirements in some studies, but reported pain outcomes are equivocal and sedation or respiratory-depression concerns exist, especially with opioids; routine use is not well-supported.

Assess PONV risk and use an individualized prevention and rescue approach. The outpatient-fusion review discusses opioid limitation, non-opioid analgesia, hydration, and antiemetics as measures supporting early discharge.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Favor an emergence that permits timely motor and sensory assessment, while accounting for anesthetic effects, residual blockade if used, and the patient’s respiratory and hemodynamic status.

Recovery care should include continual assessment appropriate to the patient, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Provide an appropriate handoff and document the recovery course.

Document and assess the postoperative neurologic examination alongside pain, bleeding, and respiratory status. The supplied sources do not establish a TLIF/PLIF-specific imaging pathway for a new deficit.

sources.label: Perioperative Management for Complex Spine Fusion Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia source is a focused review of complex spine fusion that synthesizes varied evidence and expert opinion; recommendations and certainty are not uniform, and it is broader than TLIF/PLIF alone.

The lumbar-fusion review is not anesthesia-specific and describes outpatient evidence as scarce and largely retrospective, with selection bias. Its outpatient findings should not be treated as universal eligibility or anesthetic standards.
The neuroanesthesia manual is an educational source without stated date, references, or evidence grading; its spinal reconstruction discussion is not a contemporary TLIF/PLIF-specific guideline.

Lumbar spinal fusion in the outpatient setting: an update on management, surgical approaches and planning
