overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: SSEP monitoring uses peripheral nerve stimulation to assess sensory pathways from the periphery through the spinal cord and brainstem to the cortex. It does not by itself monitor motor pathways.

The main anesthetic priority is a stable, interpretable signal: avoid abrupt anesthetic changes, account for dose-dependent volatile suppression, and interpret recordings against anesthetic and physiologic changes.

An SSEP amplitude decrease of 50% or greater and/or latency increase of 10% or greater is commonly considered significant when not attributable to anesthetic or temperature changes. Criteria are empirical; changes should be sustained and reproducible, and a physiologically meaningful change should appear in more than one recording and preferably more than one modality.

Priorities when signals change are to promptly alert the surgical team, assess technical and anesthetic contributors, and review perfusion and temperature; recovery care should include focused neurologic reassessment.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: SSEPs are elicited by electrical stimulation of a peripheral nerve, commonly median or posterior tibial, with responses recorded along the pathway and at cortical sites. Monitoring is used when surgery places sensory pathways at risk.

SSEP findings are not a complete assessment of spinal cord function: an anterior pathway injury may occur while dorsal-column SSEP pathways remain intact. Interpret monitoring alongside the operation, examination when available, and other modalities selected by the clinical team.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review whether usable baseline signals are likely and identify pre-existing neurologic deficits or pathology that may limit amplitude or increase variability. The review notes this limitation in patients with neurologic deficits and several spinal disorders.
Agree the anesthetic approach and signal-change communication plan with the surgeon and monitoring team. Pre-existing neurologic impairment may also increase anesthetic effects on signals.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate stimulation and recording sites with the procedure level. Peripheral recordings can help distinguish technical or peripheral-conduction problems from a spinal-level change.

Obtain recordings after induction once the anesthetic state is steady and repeat a baseline after positioning. Position-related signal changes can occur; check electrode integrity and positioning if recordings deteriorate.
SSEP averaging takes time, so allow for acquisition when planning critical surgical steps and signal reassessment.

sources.label: Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The supplied SSEP sources do not establish a procedure-independent airway technique or a requirement for tracheal intubation. Select airway and ventilation management for the operation, positioning, patient, and anesthetic plan; maintain standard anesthetic monitoring.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, distinguish their effects on modalities: they do not directly alter SSEPs, but they can compromise MEP monitoring. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and confirmation of recovery before extubation apply when blockade is used.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Volatile anesthetics suppress cortical SSEP amplitude and increase latency in a dose-dependent manner. The review describes cortical monitoring as compatible with concentrations up to 0.5 MAC with nitrous oxide or up to 1.0 MAC without it; these are context-specific compatibility statements, not universal anesthetic targets.

Nitrous oxide can substantially reduce cortical amplitude and potentiate depression from volatile and many intravenous agents. Do not assume it is a signal-neutral adjunct; account for its contribution when interpreting a change.

Propofol–opioid infusion without nitrous oxide is described as an appealing approach because of its SSEP effects and emergence characteristics. Propofol and other intravenous agents can still alter recordings; use a steady regimen rather than treating any technique as signal-proof.

Temperature and perfusion affect signals. Hypothermia delays peripheral and central conduction, while amplitude responses are variable; hypotension below autoregulatory limits can reduce amplitude. Interpret changes against measured physiology rather than assuming a single universal MAP or temperature target.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Use a sustained, reproducible SSEP amplitude decrease of 50% or greater and/or latency increase of 10% or greater as a commonly used warning criterion when not attributable to anesthetic or temperature changes. Criteria are empirical; latency changes of 7–10% and amplitude reductions of 45–50% have also occurred without postoperative neurologic change.

For a concerning change, notify the surgeon and assess signal quality, electrodes, anesthetic concentration or recent boluses, blood pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, hematocrit, and temperature. If no technical or anesthetic cause is apparent, treat a surgical cause as a serious possibility.

Interpret signal loss with the operative event and other recordings; changes that are sustained, reproducible, and present across recordings or modalities carry greater concern than an isolated, transient fluctuation.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No SSEP-specific fluid, blood-loss, or transfusion protocol is established in the supplied sources. Avoid preventable hypotension and interpret signal changes alongside perfusion and hematocrit; the review does not define a universal pressure or hematocrit threshold.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Intravenous anesthetic regimens generally perturb SSEPs less than inhaled anesthetics, although propofol–sufentanil may substantially reduce amplitude. Remifentanil is described as producing less cortical amplitude depression and variability than fentanyl–nitrous oxide; continuous opioid infusion is favored to avoid marked concentration differences.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Where clinically feasible, facilitate timely postoperative neurologic assessment. The review describes propofol–opioid infusion as having favorable emergence characteristics, but the operation and patient condition determine extubation and recovery disposition.

Reassess new postoperative neurologic findings carefully in the context of the anesthetic course and surgical risk. During postanesthesia care, evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation does not impose blockade or reversal on cases where neuromuscular blockers were not used.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal pharmacologic and physiologic source is a narrative review, not a guideline. It notes small studies, limited evidence in neurologically impaired patients, and a lack of reliable multicenter evidence; reported anesthetic effects are not definitive proof of monitoring performance.

The practical spinal-monitoring overview is an older narrative review describing its authors’ approach; its warning criteria are not a universal consensus standard. Basic and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring and recovery, not SSEP-specific management.

The supplied sources do not specify the actual operation, so a procedure-specific airway, position, access, or surgical-phase plan cannot be derived. Case-specific targets and treatment decisions require the operative context and team judgment.

sources.label: Pharmacologic and Physiologic Influences Affecting Sensory Evoked Potentials: Implications for Perioperative Monitoring
Current approach on spinal cord monitoring: the point of view of the neurologist, the anesthesiologist and the spine surgeon
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Evacuation is undertaken urgently when an intracranial hematoma is a mass lesion requiring surgical treatment. The available sources do not establish a single operative approach or patient position.

Prioritize cerebral perfusion and prevention of secondary brain injury: avoid hypotension and hypoxemia, maintain appropriate ventilation, and use hyperventilation only judiciously for short-term ICP control or surgical exposure.
Anticipate evolving coagulopathy, blood loss, and associated injuries; continue resuscitation while avoiding hypotension and delays to evacuation for invasive monitoring.

Plan recovery around serial neurological assessment and intensive monitoring; extubation decisions and postoperative destination depend on the clinical course, as the available review gives no specific emergence protocol.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The anesthesia context is urgent evacuation of an intracranial mass lesion, including traumatic hematomas. The clinical decision to proceed and the operative approach are determined by the treating neurosurgical team; the review does not specify access selection.

Do not treat endoscopic-assisted small-craniotomy evacuation as routine practice on this evidence. A single reported case notes that brain swelling can make endoscopic manipulation difficult and time-consuming; it cannot establish comparative safety or usual technique.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury
Endoscopic-Assisted Hematoma Evacuation Through a Small ...

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: On arrival, rapidly reassess airway, breathing, circulation, neurological status, associated injuries, and secondary-insult risks. Record a brief neurological baseline, including GCS and pupillary responses, and review the injury timeline and mechanism.
Look for evolving extracranial injury or uncorrected volume loss when assessing hypotension, anemia, or hypoxemia; these may coexist with head trauma and affect cerebral perfusion.

Consider coagulopathy in severe TBI and review relevant medication and laboratory information with the clinical team. The available review describes TBI-associated coagulopathy but does not establish a hematoma-specific reversal regimen.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring and, for craniotomy, consider arterial catheterization for beat-to-beat pressure assessment and arterial blood-gas and glucose measurements. Do not delay evacuation of an expanding hematoma to place invasive monitors.

Use ICP monitoring when clinically indicated in severe TBI; the review summarizes BTF criteria involving GCS, CT findings, and specified risk features. These criteria should not be read as a requirement to place a monitor before urgent decompression.
Positioning is procedure- and access-dependent. The supplied TBI review provides no specific positioning recommendation; coordinate with the surgeon and protect access to the airway and monitors.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Patients requiring hematoma surgery need a secured airway, although some patients with extradural hematoma may arrive conscious and breathing spontaneously. Assess tube position on arrival if already intubated; account for full-stomach risk and possible cervical-spine injury during urgent airway management.

Intubation technique depends on urgency, clinician expertise, and available resources; it generally incorporates rapid-sequence intubation with cricoid pressure and manual in-line stabilization. Have a backup plan because hypoxemia and hypercarbia can increase cerebral blood volume and worsen intracranial hypertension.

Choose induction agents in light of hemodynamics and cerebral physiology. The review cautions that ketamine has been associated with increased CBF and ICP in this setting; this is not a source for a universal drug regimen.

Adjust ventilation using arterial gas assessment when needed; end-tidal CO₂ may not reliably represent arterial PCO₂ in TBI. Avoid indiscriminate hypocapnia and restore normocarbia before dural closure.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain cerebral perfusion and avoid secondary insults. The review summarizes BTF guidance to avoid systolic hypotension and maintain CPP within its stated range; individual targets require clinical context and are not interchangeable with a fixed MAP target.
Use hyperventilation only as a short-term measure for raised ICP or exposure, recognizing that excessive hypocarbia can reduce cerebral blood flow and cause ischemia.

Low concentrations of volatile anesthetic or TIVA may be used judiciously; the review reports no demonstrated TBI-outcome advantage of one over the other. Avoid nitrous oxide in this context because it may increase CBF and ICP.

Treat signs of transtentorial herniation or progressive neurological deterioration as a critical escalation point. Mannitol is described as a standard hyperosmolar agent, but the review reserves it for these clinical circumstances because osmotic diuresis may cause hypovolemia and hypotension.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: If new hypotension, anemia, or hypoxemia develops, assess for extracranial injury as well as anesthetic or surgical causes; maintain resuscitative care while identifying the source.

Coagulopathy is associated with worse TBI outcomes, but these sources do not provide a procedure-specific reversal pathway. Escalate suspected coagulopathy for prompt multidisciplinary assessment rather than applying an unsupported agent or threshold.

Rebleeding and brain swelling are recognized concerns in the discussion of open evacuation approaches. This case-report discussion supports awareness of the hazards, not a prediction of their incidence or a routine technique recommendation.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury
Endoscopic-Assisted Hematoma Evacuation Through a Small ...

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use glucose-free isotonic crystalloid as the review's preferred fluid approach and avoid hypotonic solutions. Preserve intravascular volume, particularly when treating raised ICP, because hypotension can worsen secondary brain injury.

Blood products and coagulopathy management should be guided by the patient's bleeding, laboratory findings, and clinical context. The review reports uncertainty about optimal transfusion thresholds and does not support a universal transfusion trigger.

Hypertonic saline is discussed as an option for ICP reduction and, in refractory severe TBI, as second-tier therapy; reported outcome evidence is mixed. The source does not establish a universal administration protocol.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Provide adequate analgesia and amnesia while preserving the ability to assess neurological status. With controlled ventilation, the review reports no direct cerebral-hemodynamic effect from opioids.
A scalp block may be considered as an adjunct for craniotomy analgesia and reduced anesthetic or opioid requirements; the cited review does not establish it as necessary for hematoma evacuation.
The supplied evidence does not provide a hematoma-specific PONV prevention or treatment regimen.

sources.label: Perioperative management of traumatic brain injury
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The available TBI review provides no specific extubation protocol. Base emergence and airway decisions on neurological status, physiological stability, and the anticipated need for ongoing support; do not assume immediate extubation is appropriate in every case.
Arrange postoperative intensive monitoring and continued physiological optimization, including neurological and ICP assessment when indicated.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Use a PACU or equivalent area, such as an ICU, for postanesthesia care unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise; transport and handoff should include ongoing evaluation and appropriate monitoring.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal source is a narrative review of perioperative TBI care, not a procedure-specific guideline. It states that research addressing intraoperative and immediate perioperative management is limited; use its physiological principles with clinical judgment.

The neuroanesthesia manual is educational and provides no evidence grading or supporting study details; its recommendations should not override more applicable contemporary guidance or patient-specific judgment.

The endoscopic evacuation report is a single case with explicit limits on generalization. The ASA monitoring standards and neuromuscular-blockade guidance inform monitoring and recovery, but do not supply hematoma-specific operative or reversal protocols.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lumbar interbody fusion is used for lumbar degenerative disease; the supplied procedure-specific material describes tubular and endoscopic MIS-TLIF, including use in degenerative disease and spondylolisthesis. It does not establish anesthetic practice for OLIF or ALIF.

For tubular MIS-TLIF, the described approach is prone surgery under general anesthesia with motor- and sensory-evoked-potential and electromyographic monitoring. Positioning and the anesthetic technique should be coordinated with the planned approach and monitoring.

Prone positioning can impair venous return and increase epidural venous pressure if the abdomen is compressed; positioning should preserve abdominal freedom and avoid pressure on the eyes. The supplied sources do not establish procedure-specific hemodynamic targets.

Recovery should include timely assessment of neurologic status and effective pain control while avoiding techniques that could impede neurologic assessment. This is a priority, not a source-defined recovery protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The procedure-specific sources describe tubular MIS-TLIF and uniportal endoscopic TLIF. TLIF includes neural decompression, disc and endplate work, interbody implant placement, and percutaneous pedicle-screw fixation.
The supplied evidence does not describe OLIF or ALIF technique, selection, or anesthetic management. Do not transfer TLIF-specific details to those approaches.
MIS-TLIF modality selection is described as depending on patient characteristics and surgeon expertise; ability to tolerate prone surgery is one cited consideration.

sources.label: Nuances of the Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Technical Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify levels, planned approach, positioning, use of neuromonitoring, and the surgeon’s operative plan; the sources do not provide a procedure-specific assessment template.

Assess cardiopulmonary comorbidity and tolerance of prone positioning. The regional-anesthesia review notes that prone positioning and procedure magnitude may present additional concerns in patients with cardiopulmonary disease.

Review neurologic baseline and the intended neuromonitoring plan with the surgical team. The source describes monitoring during tubular MIS-TLIF but does not define anesthetic targets or a response protocol.

The materials do not supply approach-specific anticoagulation, blood-preparation, or risk-stratification criteria; determine these from the individual case and applicable local guidance rather than importing unsupported fixed requirements.

sources.label: Nuances of the Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Technical Review
REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For the described tubular MIS-TLIF, the patient is prone; the senior author prefers a Jackson table, while positioning may vary with surgeon preference and procedural goals. The review describes a Wilson frame for the endoscopic approach.
Protect pressure points, maintain head venous return, avoid ocular pressure, and leave the abdomen free of compression. Reassess airway access and lines after turning.
Fluoroscopy is used for level localization and positioning checks; the MIS-TLIF review emphasizes clear AP and lateral views. Radiation precautions are relevant to the operating team.
For tubular MIS-TLIF, the source describes MEP, SSEP, and EMG monitoring. Use standard anesthetic monitoring; no supplied source supports a universal arterial-line requirement for these procedures.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is described for tubular MIS-TLIF, but the procedure-specific review does not specify airway device or ventilation settings. Plan airway access for prone surgery and reassess after positioning.

A technical note describes selected awake endoscopic TLIF under light-to-moderate conscious sedation, with spontaneous ventilation and no advanced airway. This is a reported technique, not a default approach; it requires experienced personnel and discussion of possible conversion.

For any anesthetic technique in the prone position, consider how airway obstruction or urgent conversion would be managed; the review specifically advises anticipating difficult-airway management when conversion may be needed.

REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain communication between anesthesia and surgery during neural decompression, disc preparation, implant placement, and screw placement. The supplied review does not establish a specific blood-pressure or anesthetic target for these phases.
For monitored tubular MIS-TLIF, coordinate anesthetic management with the neuromonitoring team. The sources do not specify a universal anesthetic regimen or neuromuscular-blockade policy.

Use fluoroscopic confirmation and surgical judgment during implant work. The review warns that endplate violation and inappropriate implant sizing can contribute to subsidence, fracture, or migration.

Be alert to unintended anterior longitudinal ligament violation during TLIF work; the review identifies potential entry into the abdominal cavity or injury to major vessels. It does not quantify risk or define a management algorithm.

sources.label: Nuances of the Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Technical Review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Endoscopic TLIF risks include DRG injury and postoperative dysesthesia; possible nerve-root irritation is also described.

Consider major-vessel injury if anterior ligament violation or unexplained instability is suspected, and escalate urgently with the surgical team. The supplied evidence identifies the hazard but provides no operation-specific response protocol.

After prone positioning, investigate airway obstruction, tube displacement, pressure injury, or hemodynamic deterioration. Prone physiology and airway movement during repositioning are identified concerns in the general spine sources.
Implant migration, endplate fracture, subsidence, and infection are reported procedural complications; the source does not support using these reports to estimate an individual patient’s risk.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Avoid abdominal compression in the prone position because it can impair venous return and increase epidural venous pressure and bleeding risk. Individualize fluid and hemodynamic management to the patient and operative course.

The MIS-TLIF review reports that cohort comparisons favored MIS over open TLIF for blood loss, drainage, and transfusion outcomes, but provides no numerical estimates or fluid regimen. Do not infer a fixed blood-loss expectation or transfusion plan.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal blood-product preparation, antifibrinolytic regimen, fluid total, or perfusion target for TLIF, OLIF, or ALIF.

Nuances of the Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Technical Review

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan postoperative analgesia while preserving the ability to assess neurologic function. Regional or neuraxial adjuncts may help pain control, but technique and suitability require case-specific discussion.
The review cites supplementary local and regional techniques as an enhanced-recovery recommendation for lumbar fusion, but does not establish an optimal technique or regimen.
The available procedure-specific material does not support a standard PONV prophylaxis regimen for these approaches.

sources.label: REGIONAL ANESTHESIA FOR NEUROSURGERY
Nuances of the Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Technical Review

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After prone surgery, plan safe repositioning and reassess ventilation, airway security, and hemodynamics. The supplied procedure-specific sources do not define an extubation sequence.
Assess neurologic status and communicate new deficits promptly. Consider analgesic choices that may interfere with motor assessment in coordination with the surgical team.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm recovery before extubation; this applies when blockade is used, not to every anesthetic technique.
Postanesthesia care should include appropriate evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with handoff and monitoring suited to the patient’s condition.

The awake endoscopic technique and its outcomes come from a technical note describing one surgeon’s initial institutional experience; this does not establish routine anesthetic practice.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Transsphenoidal surgery reaches sellar tumours through the nasal passage and sphenoidal sinus, usually endoscopically; microscopy is used less often. The airway and surgical access are shared constraints, so oral tracheal intubation is preferred.

Priorities include assessing pituitary hormone function and comorbidities, anticipating difficult airway management—particularly with acromegaly—and maintaining haemodynamic stability near the internal carotid arteries and cavernous sinus.

Plan a controlled emergence that limits coughing, retching and positive-pressure mask ventilation where possible; these may threaten haemostasis or a skull-base repair. Remove any pharyngeal pack and clear blood and secretions before extubation.

Recovery priorities include neurological and visual assessment, airway observation where risk is elevated, and monitoring fluid balance, urine output and electrolytes for postoperative diabetes insipidus (DI).

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The transnasal route is the commonest surgical approach for pituitary tumours and the standard approach for adenomas. The objective is safe tumour resection, relief of optic-apparatus mass effect and reduction of regrowth risk.

Endoscopy is described as the gold-standard technique; navigation may assist, particularly in revision surgery or anatomical mapping. Transcranial surgery is reserved for selected large or invasive tumours or inadequate transsphenoidal resection.

ENT and neurosurgical collaboration is common. A skull-base CSF leak may require repair with autologous tissue or other material; the possibility of grafting affects emergence and postoperative precautions.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess hormonal function, visual fields and acuity, cardiovascular and respiratory disease, metabolic status, and airway. The cited review lists hormone profiling and baseline blood count, electrolytes, renal function, glucose and blood type/screen; tailor additional investigations to the clinical picture.

Assess and manage coexisting adrenal or thyroid deficiency before surgery. Clarify perioperative steroid replacement with endocrinology and local protocol; stress-dose replacement is generally recommended except in ACTH-secreting Cushing’s disease.

Acromegaly may involve difficult airway anatomy, OSA and cardiac disease; Cushing’s disease may involve obesity, hypertension, diabetes and prothrombotic risk. Assess and optimise relevant comorbidities rather than assuming a single airway or monitoring plan.
Pituitary apoplexy is described as a life-threatening presentation with reduced consciousness, headache and visual defects; urgent specialist assessment is important.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery
Anesthesia for Pituitary Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Position supine with head-up tilt; the review describes 20–30° to improve venous drainage. Head support may be a horseshoe rest, pillow or Mayfield clamp. Expect restricted access because of the surgical team and equipment arrangement.

Use standard monitoring and consider invasive arterial pressure monitoring, particularly given haemodynamic changes and proximity to major vessels. Wide-bore peripheral access is recommended; central access is rarely needed unless cardiovascular compromise is present.

Consider urinary catheterisation for complex cases where DI is anticipated. If TIVA is used, the review recommends depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring; consider an arterial-line site carefully in acromegaly because wrist compression may affect ulnar arterial flow.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery
Anesthesia for Pituitary Surgery

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan airway management with the surgical route in mind: oral intubation with a reinforced tube positioned away from the field is preferred. Have difficult-intubation equipment available; videolaryngoscopy is increasingly used first-line in acromegaly.

For high-risk patients, particularly with laryngeal involvement, discuss planned awake tracheal intubation before surgery. Airway assessment may include flexible nasal endoscopy when symptoms such as hoarseness, dyspnoea or snoring warrant it.
A mouth and pharyngeal pack may reduce blood entering the glottis and stomach. If used, clearly communicate its placement and removal; the source specifically advises checking that it is removed.

The review favours TIVA with short-acting agents for controlled emergence and haemodynamic titration; it reports improved surgical visualisation and reduced blood loss versus inhalational anaesthesia in a cited meta-analysis, but no demonstrated superiority in postoperative recovery quality.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Limit cardiovascular disturbance during induction and maintain haemodynamic control. Intranasal vasoconstrictors and endonasal surgical stimulation can cause unexpected haemodynamic changes; use caution in patients with cardiovascular disease.

Monitor urine output and fluid balance, particularly with hormone-secreting or large tumours. The surgical team may request Valsalva to improve visualisation, check for a CSF leak, or ensure haemostasis. Alert the anaesthesia team to a CSF leak because it limits maintenance of a 30° head-up tilt after surgery.
A lumbar drain may be used selectively for large, invasive adenomas, but the review notes limited evidence and infrequent use in the UK; this is not a routine requirement.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery
Anesthesia for Pituitary Surgery

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Internal carotid artery injury is rare but potentially fatal. Rapid resuscitation, urgent angiographic assessment and multidisciplinary management are described; skull-base teams should have an established vascular-injury protocol.

CSF leak occurs in 2–12% of transsphenoidal resections and is more common with revision surgery and large adenomas. Prompt repair is essential because of risks including meningitis and pneumocephalus.
Monitor symptoms, fluid balance, urine and serum osmolalities, and electrolytes for postoperative DI. Desmopressin may be required; consider endocrinology consultation for DI management.

Airway compromise after extubation requires prompt assessment; early reintubation or supraglottic-device insertion may be considered. Avoid excessive mask positive pressure where possible because of potential CSF leak, pneumocephalus or bleeding.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery
Anesthesia for Pituitary Surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Anticipate bleeding because major blood vessels are close to the pituitary; consider large-bore peripheral IV access.

Venous bleeding is generally managed surgically with pressure, haemostatic agents or additional reverse Trendelenburg. Major arterial injury is a separate emergency requiring rapid escalation and the institution’s vascular-injury pathway.
Replace fluid losses as clinically appropriate, including in persistent DI; individualise fluid management to haemodynamics, losses and endocrine status rather than applying a fixed regimen.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Pituitary Surgery
Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Surgery is not typically painful; use simple analgesics and short-acting opioids for breakthrough pain. NSAIDs are generally avoided because of bleeding concerns.

Prevent nausea and vomiting: retching can raise venous and intracranial pressure, increasing bleeding risk and potentially revealing an unrecognised CSF leak. The sources support prophylaxis but do not specify a universal drug regimen.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Plan smooth emergence to avoid coughing, bleeding, graft displacement and CSF leak while enabling early neurological assessment. Remove any throat pack and clear blood and secretions under direct vision before extubation.
Awake extubation is described as ideal, with the patient sitting where feasible; consider additional airway precautions in patients with difficult airways, acromegaly, severe obesity or sleep apnoea.

Perform regular immediate postoperative visual and neurological observations; deterioration warrants urgent imaging and neurosurgical review. Closely monitor DI risk with symptoms, fluid balance, urine and serum osmolarities, and electrolytes.

Avoid nose-blowing and straining during recovery as directed by the surgical team. Postoperative CPAP practice is unresolved; the review describes avoidance where possible but reports no clear guideline or consensus.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The main procedure-specific sources are educational summaries/reviews, not formal guidelines or trials. They do not report a formal review methodology; apply their recommendations with local protocols and specialist input.
The supplied material does not establish a uniform perioperative steroid regimen; the review explicitly notes variation and recommends local protocol and endocrinology involvement.
The supplied evidence does not define a postoperative surveillance or treatment protocol for SIADH/hyponatraemia after pituitary surgery; this remains an important case-specific evidence gap.
The source describes no routine fluid regimen or transfusion threshold. This draft therefore does not prescribe a universal fluid volume, blood preparation, or transfusion target.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for pituitary surgery

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A VP shunt drains cerebrospinal fluid from the cerebral ventricles into the peritoneal cavity; the procedural source describes placement under general anesthesia.
Key procedural hazards include intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage, catheter malposition, infection, abdominal perforation, and overdrainage with subdural hematoma.

Preoperative imaging and neurologic context matter: suspected malfunction can present with headache, lethargy, nausea or vomiting, seizure, or altered responsiveness; CT or MRI is used to assess ventricular size.

For anesthetic recovery, maintain appropriate monitoring and reassess consciousness and neurologic status; VP-shunt-specific emergence and recovery protocols are not established by the available sources.

sources.label: Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The shunt comprises a ventricular catheter, a valve, and a distal catheter; the usual distal destination is the peritoneal cavity.
The proximal catheter may be introduced through a frontal or parieto-occipital route. The choice and target are surgical decisions informed by imaging and ventricular anatomy.
Placement involves ventricular access and abdominal access, with a passer carrying the distal catheter between incisions. The source does not establish a single required abdominal approach.

sources.label: Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review brain CT or MRI for ventricular size and planned proximal catheter placement. The source identifies imaging review as part of preoperative planning.

Establish the neurologic baseline and consider whether symptoms may reflect acute shunt malfunction or infection. Reported features include headache, lethargy, diplopia, nausea and vomiting, seizure, fever, and neck rigidity.

The procedural source lists infection over the entry site or infection of the CSF as absolute contraindications to shunt placement, and altered coagulation as a relative contraindication. It does not provide an adult anesthetic risk-stratification protocol.

sources.label: Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The procedural source describes supine positioning. For a parieto-occipital approach, the head is tilted contralateral to the shunt side.
Image-guided navigation is listed for small ventricles, not as a universal requirement. Confirm the planned approach and required equipment with the surgical team.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards require continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes are specified.

sources.label: Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The VP-shunt procedural source specifies general anesthesia but does not define an airway device, anesthetic agents, or a procedure-specific ventilation strategy. Select these according to the patient, operation, and responsible anesthesiologist’s plan.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify correct positioning clinically and by identifying carbon dioxide in expired gas. Continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis from placement until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location.

sources.label: Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Ventricular catheter placement carries a recognized hemorrhage risk. Maintain awareness of the neurologic and hemodynamic context during ventricular access; the available sources do not establish VP-shunt-specific targets or a management algorithm.

For patients with raised ICP, the general neuroanesthesia manual describes head-up tilt and mild-to-moderate hypocapnia as measures used in that context. It does not establish these as mandatory targets for every VP-shunt case.
The neuroanesthesia manual advises avoiding nitrous oxide when pneumocephalus is present. This is a conditional, general neuroanesthesia statement—not evidence for a blanket VP-shunt prohibition.

bullets: Recognized procedural complications include malposition, intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage, abdominal perforation, shunt infection, and obstruction or disconnection.
Overdrainage is associated with subdural hematoma; the source also lists abdominal CSF collections and visceral perforation among complications.

In a patient with a known shunt and new symptoms concerning for malfunction, assess the clinical course and obtain appropriate imaging with the neurosurgical team; the source identifies shunt radiographs for system integrity and CT or MRI for ventricular size.

bullets: The VP-shunt source provides no fluid-management or blood-loss guidance. It identifies intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage as a complication, but does not support a routine fluid total, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold.

bullets: The VP-shunt procedural source does not give an analgesic regimen or PONV plan. The neuroanesthesia review describes scalp block as an adjunct for craniotomy, but does not establish its role or a regimen for VP-shunt placement.

bullets: The VP-shunt source does not specify emergence or extubation instructions. Manage emergence according to the patient’s neurologic and respiratory status; do not treat a craniotomy emergence recommendation as a VP-shunt protocol.

In PACU or an equivalent setting, continually evaluate the patient and monitor oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; communicate the perioperative course during handoff.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, apply quantitative monitoring and confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

bullets: The VP-shunt source is a procedural overview, not an anesthesia reference; it states that airway, anesthetic technique, monitoring, physiologic targets, and critical anesthesia phases are unspecified.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ECT induces a generalized tonic-clonic seizure using scalp electrodes under general anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade. Ventilation is generally assisted by face mask; tracheal intubation is not routine.

The key physiologic pattern is early parasympathetic bradycardia or, rarely, asystole, followed by seizure-associated sympathetic tachycardia and hypertension. Monitor closely and be prepared to manage clinically important instability.
Select and titrate anesthesia to the patient: anesthetic dose and choice can affect seizure generation, hemodynamics, and recovery. The available review does not establish one universal regimen.
After stimulation, assess oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and level of consciousness. Headache and nausea are common post-ECT complaints; postictal delirium or agitation may occur.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ECT delivers an electrical stimulus through scalp electrodes under general anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade to induce a therapeutic generalized seizure. Electrode placement and stimulus properties affect seizure threshold and treatment effects.
Common electrode placements are bitemporal, bifrontal, and right unilateral; selection is part of the ECT treatment approach rather than an anesthetic positioning instruction.

Assess seizure duration using EEG, electromyography, or observed muscle movement. The review reports an appropriate motor duration range, but this should not be conflated with a universal anesthetic target or an EEG duration.
Treatment is commonly delivered in repeated sessions, but course length and frequency vary with response and urgency; do not infer a fixed course from the anesthetic sources.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess psychiatric and medication history, physical status, airway, and relevant investigations. The review describes evaluation comparable to other general anesthesia and notes that difficult mask ventilation, aspiration risk, or prolonged ventilation may require unplanned intubation.

Review ongoing medicines with the treating team. The review says usual medications are generally continued through the morning, with specified exceptions; it does not support blanket benzodiazepine or antihypertensive holding rules.

Consider cardiovascular and respiratory comorbidity carefully. The review identifies several conditions associated with relatively high risk during ECT, so individualized assessment and preparation are important.

Fasting guidance in the review allows clear liquids, including oral antihypertensive medication, up to the stated interval; apply relevant institutional policy and patient-specific aspiration assessment.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For ECT delivered in a NORA setting, account for potential limitations in equipment, patient monitoring, and access to emergency support; conduct careful risk assessment and preparation.

Recommended ECT intra-procedure monitoring includes non-invasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, ECG, and capnography; continue observation for motor seizure activity and coordinate EEG assessment with the ECT team.
Protect teeth and soft tissues: the stimulus can activate jaw muscles despite relaxation, so place the bite block carefully before stimulation.

sources.label: Safety of nonoperating room anesthesia: a narrative review
Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Face-mask ventilation with a simple bag-valve-mask system is generally used. Routine tracheal intubation is not recommended, but airway difficulty, aspiration risk, prolonged ventilation, or special circumstances may change the approach.

Provide oxygenation and assess ventilation throughout anesthesia. The ECT review recommends capnography; it does not establish a universal end-tidal carbon dioxide target or endorse a fixed hyperventilation protocol.
A bite block is important because forceful jaw clenching can occur despite neuromuscular relaxation. Check placement before the electrical stimulus and remain alert to dental or oral injury.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring where available and confirm adequate recovery before extubation if an airway device is used; these are general NMB recommendations, not a mandate for intubation in ECT.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Between stimulus and seizure onset, parasympathetic predominance can produce hypotension, bradycardia, or asystole; during the seizure, rebound sympathetic activity produces tachycardia and hypertension.

The cardiovascular response can be substantial, particularly for patients with cardiovascular disease. Track hemodynamics and respond to clinically significant instability in the context of the individual patient.

Antihypertensives may blunt seizure generation, while anesthetic agents also differ in anticonvulsant and hemodynamic effects. Select and adjust agents to balance seizure quality and patient risk; no single drug is appropriate for every patient.
Seizures also increase cerebral blood flow, intracranial pressure, and cerebral oxygen demand; account for relevant neurologic and cardiovascular comorbidity in anesthetic planning.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Watch for significant hypertension, tachycardia, bradycardia, or hypotension, especially in patients at risk of ischemia or other cardiovascular complications. Escalate and manage according to observed severity and local emergency processes.

Potential complications include pulmonary edema, ventricular tachycardia, myocardial infarction, aspiration, respiratory failure, cerebral hemorrhage, dental injury, and tongue or gingival laceration. Serious events are not the expected course, but require recognition and escalation.

Transient postictal agitation or delirium may occur. Assess for reversible contributors and maintain patient and staff safety; the review describes behavioral measures and medication options without establishing a single required treatment.
An implanted cardiac device is not by itself a reason to assume ECT cannot proceed; device function and interference risk require case-specific planning.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The ECT review does not provide a fluid-management or bleeding-management protocol. No routine fluid total, blood preparation, or access gauge is established by the available ECT-specific evidence.
Monitor circulation during the procedure and recovery; prioritize recognition of hemodynamic instability rather than assuming a particular fluid intervention.
Oral and dental trauma, including tongue laceration, is a reported complication; inspect and address clinically apparent injury rather than anticipating routine hemorrhage.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Headache is a common post-ECT complaint; the OpenAnesthesia review reports prophylactic ketorolac and/or acetaminophen as usual options. Individualize for contraindications and patient context.
Nausea is reported after ECT, and ondansetron is described as a prophylactic option. The source gives a regimen, but this reference omits dosing and does not treat it as mandatory.
Myalgia can follow succinylcholine; the review describes NSAIDs, including ketorolac, as options for prevention or treatment. Consider patient-specific risks when selecting analgesia.
Post-ECT nausea and vomiting are reported complications; consider prophylaxis in context, particularly when patient or anesthetic factors increase risk.

sources.label: Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations
Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Continue appropriate assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness through recovery. The ECT review recommends monitoring standard non-invasive hemodynamic variables and oxygen saturation for a post-treatment observation period.
Expect possible transient confusion or agitation, headache, nausea, and muscle pain; reassess the patient and escalate if recovery is not consistent with the observed course.
If neuromuscular blockade has been used, assess recovery appropriately; general ASA guidance recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.
The ECT-specific source does not establish a universal discharge time or discharge protocol. Discharge readiness should follow applicable local postanesthesia standards and physician assessment.

bullets: The ECT-specific evidence is educational review material and a narrative review, not a single standardized protocol or formal evidence-graded guideline. Individual anesthetic choices and doses therefore require clinical judgment.
The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general anesthesia standards, not ECT-specific protocols; use them for the aspects within their stated scope.
The NORA safety review is available here only as an abstract and provides no ECT-specific recommendations.
The review gives no specific patient positioning or vascular-access recommendations.

title: ICU Bedside Procedures Under Anesthesia / Sedation
aliases: ICU Bedside Procedures Under Anesthesia / Sedation

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ICU bedside procedural anesthesia covers a varied set of procedures; the anesthetic approach ranges from sedation and analgesia to monitored anesthesia care or TIVA, selected for the patient and procedure.
Prioritize cardiopulmonary stability: critically ill patients may tolerate transient hypoxemia or hypercarbia poorly, and anesthesia can increase respiratory and hemodynamic support needs.
Anticipate remote-location constraints—limited workspace, equipment, personnel, and emergency support—and coordinate the procedural and ICU teams before starting.
Plan recovery in the ICU or equivalent postanesthesia-care area, with condition-appropriate monitoring, reassessment, and a clear handoff.

sources.label: Procedural anesthesia at the bedside
Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Bedside care may be appropriate when transport could cause decompensation or interrupt critical care. It avoids transport but does not remove the need to assess whether the location can support the procedure and rescue needs.

The supplied evidence includes ICU bedside GI endoscopy and interventional pulmonology procedures such as bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage. It does not establish an anesthetic protocol for every procedure listed in the case description.
Anesthetic depth is procedure- and patient-dependent. The review describes a spectrum from sedation and analgesia through monitored anesthesia care to TIVA; it does not supply a universal regimen.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Non-Operating Room Anesthesia: Patient Selection and Special Considerations
Procedural anesthesia at the bedside

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess current organ dysfunction and support needs, including hemodynamic instability, shock, arrhythmias, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, bleeding, electrolytes, ventilation status, and vascular access.

Consider procedure urgency, comorbidities, and whether the ICU environment can support the planned care. Critically ill patients may be more susceptible to anesthetic adverse effects in the setting of multiorgan dysfunction.

Discuss the plan and consent with the patient or family as appropriate, and coordinate with ICU staff and relevant procedural and surgical teams, including anticipated complications and escalation options.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Before a bedside procedure, account for limited space, fewer available personnel and tools, and potentially limited ability to escalate care if complications arise.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; during moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the circumstances invalidate it.

Maintain continuous ECG display and determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes during anesthesia. The available sources do not specify a universal bedside position or monitoring package for all procedures.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For an already ventilated patient, protect the existing airway and avoid accidental extubation during the procedure. The ICU endoscopy review specifically identifies this risk for patients with an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy receiving ventilation.

For endoscopy, consider airway compression, positioning-related respiratory limitation, and aspiration risk. The NORA review describes a secure endotracheal airway for patients not appropriately nil per os or with specified GI pathology; this is not a universal intubation instruction for bedside procedures.

During general anesthesia, verify airway-device placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide. With mechanical ventilation, use a device that detects breathing-system disconnection and provides an audible alarm.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Non-Operating Room Anesthesia: Patient Selection and Special Considerations
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Titrate anesthetic and analgesic effects cautiously in the context of limited physiologic reserve and existing respiratory or hemodynamic support. The available review does not define drug doses or targets for this case.

Watch for transient hypoxemia or hypercarbia and worsening hemodynamics; these may be poorly tolerated in critically ill patients. Escalation should be guided by the patient’s condition and local critical-care resources, rather than an unsupported universal algorithm.

Preserve coordination with the proceduralist and ICU team through critical portions of the procedure; the sources do not establish procedure-specific anesthetic phases or physiologic targets for the full range of bedside procedures.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Remote-location anesthesia has recognized hazards including oversedation and inadequate respiratory management, associated in cited claims analysis with workspace, staffing, and unfamiliar-equipment limitations. This is a general safety signal, not an ICU-specific risk estimate.

Maintain awareness of respiratory compromise, arrhythmia, and hemodynamic deterioration, and ensure the team knows how to access available emergency support. The supplied evidence does not provide a single rescue algorithm for this heterogeneous case.
For ventilated patients, treat circuit-disconnection detection and audible alarm availability as part of the setup, rather than relying on recognition after deterioration.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Safety of nonoperating room anesthesia: a narrative review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use the existing ICU assessment and support plan as context for perfusion management; anticipate that anesthesia may increase hemodynamic support needs. The sources do not specify a universal fluid strategy or vasopressor regimen.

Review anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy with the procedural team when relevant. The review notes that interruption may not be possible before an emergency procedure and that endoscopic interventions can have increased bleeding risk in treated patients.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Anesthesia or sedation may reduce anxiety, discomfort, and pain and improve cooperation. Select the approach according to patient condition and procedural requirements.
The source set does not establish an ICU bedside analgesic regimen or PONV-prevention strategy. Avoid treating the case-field drug list as a supported recipe.

sources.label: Procedural anesthesia at the bedside
Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After anesthesia care, use the ICU or another area providing equivalent postanesthesia care. Recovery observation should reflect the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Reassess on arrival, provide a verbal handoff, and transmit the preoperative condition and anesthetic/procedural course to the receiving nurse. Continue appropriate monitoring during transport if transport is required.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The general bedside procedural-anesthesia source is a review whose supplied abstract does not describe individual procedures, drug regimens, doses, monitoring parameters, or outcomes. It supports planning and risk assessment, not a detailed procedure protocol.

The ICU GI endoscopy source is a mini review and explicitly lacks standardized anesthesia protocols and procedure-specific anesthetic regimens; its scope cannot establish management for tracheostomy, chest tubes, feeding tubes, or debridement.

Basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards supply general safety requirements, not procedure-specific selection, airway, fluid, or complication protocols. Case-specific targets are not established in the available sources.
The supplied sources do not establish a case-wide blood-product threshold, crossmatch policy, fluid total, or procedure-specific bleeding plan.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal return-to-prior-sedation or ventilator-setting protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult MRI is nonpainful; minimal or light sedation may be sufficient, while some patients need deeper sedation or general anesthesia to remain still. The sources do not establish one preferred drug regimen.
Prioritize MRI-device screening, MRI-appropriate equipment, and monitoring that remains observable despite restricted access and possible signal artifacts.

Key hazards include airway or ventilation compromise that is difficult to detect, projectile injury, burns, and monitoring interference. Plan how to summon help and move the patient out of zone IV for emergencies.
Recovery should follow the facility’s postanesthesia-care standards, with appropriate monitoring and discharge assessment; the sources do not define an MRI-specific emergence protocol.

sources.label: Non-Operating Room Anesthesia: Patient Selection and Special Considerations
Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Anesthetic care may range from moderate sedation to general anesthesia, depending on patient factors, scan needs, and the ability to remain still. MRI itself is generally nonpainful; avoid assuming that every adult requires general anesthesia.
Select depth and airway strategy for the individual and the scan. Lighter anesthesia can still be complicated by airway compromise and may require interruption of imaging and treatment.
Coordinate the plan with radiology and support staff, including scan duration, patient position, monitoring and equipment needs, and emergency roles.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Identify implants, embedded foreign bodies, and patient-attached metal before entry into the controlled MRI areas. Establish the status of each relevant device with the responsible MRI team; do not infer compatibility from the device category alone.

For a pacemaker or defibrillator, the advisory describes substantial hazard but also recognizes MRI-conditional devices and exceptional MRI circumstances. If MRI is considered essential, it calls for a device-specific management plan with the appropriate clinicians and device expertise.

Assess respiratory function, hemodynamic stability, comorbidities, and the need for special monitoring or airway equipment. For acute or severe renal insufficiency, the advisory cautions against gadolinium administration because of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use equipment identified as MRI safe or conditional for its intended location. Work with MRI personnel to establish equipment locations and ensure equipment does not compromise image acquisition.

Maintain observation of the patient and physiologic monitors directly or by video, and make vital signs viewable from zone III when the provider is not in zone IV. Position leads carefully because heating and burns can occur even with nonferromagnetic leads.

Apply basic anesthesia monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and patient. MRI can distort signals; ECG interpretation may be limited, and pulse-oximetry or temperature-probe readings may be affected.
Account for acoustic noise and extended distance from the patient; use communication and tubing arrangements appropriate to the scanner and local setup.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan airway management before imaging because access and direct assessment of ventilation can be difficult in the scanner. If the patient is at risk of airway compromise, the advisory supports more aggressive airway management, including a tracheal tube or laryngeal mask airway.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment invalidates that monitoring. Pulse oximetry alone does not assess ventilation.
Have MRI-appropriate alternative airway devices and immediately accessible suction available. Perform complex airway management in a controlled environment outside zone IV.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain vigilance during scanning: noise, limited line of sight, equipment interference, and distance from the patient can delay recognition of deterioration. Ensure that monitoring remains visible and that a means of rapid intervention is available.

Consider airway obstruction, apnea, hypoventilation, and hemodynamic instability during the scan. MRI-related ECG artifacts can make interpretation unreliable; suspected cardiac events warrant assessment outside the scanner zone.

Be alert to heating and temperature changes, especially during longer scans and in patients with relevant risk factors. The available sources do not establish a universal MRI temperature-management regimen.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Projectile injury is a life-threatening environmental hazard. Restrict entry to screened personnel and objects, and follow local MRI emergency procedures if a projectile event occurs.

A quench can release cryogen gas and displace oxygen if venting fails; escaping gas may also raise pressure and impede opening the zone-IV door. Follow institutional protocol and remove the patient from zone IV if possible; magnetic-field hazards may persist afterward.

For a medical emergency, summon help and move the patient out of zone IV to the designated safe area; emergency equipment and resuscitation should be available there. Do not assume non-MRI-safe equipment can be brought into zone IV.

Burns can result from heated or looped monitoring cables and probes. Investigate discrepant monitor readings with awareness of MRI artifact and remove the patient from the scanner zone when needed for accurate assessment.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The MRI advisory does not provide procedure-specific fluid, bleeding, or perfusion regimens. Manage these according to the patient’s condition and the requirements of the planned anesthetic rather than applying an MRI-specific total.
Plan access and infusion delivery around the MRI environment; use MRI-appropriate equipment or an arrangement approved for its location.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: MRI is generally nonpainful, but the advisory does not establish an analgesic regimen or an MRI-specific PONV prevention strategy. Avoid importing a routine analgesic prescription from this evidence.
Assess and manage recovery symptoms according to the patient’s clinical needs and local postanesthesia care practice; these sources do not provide MRI-specific PONV guidance.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The MRI advisory does not specify emergence technique or timing. Coordinate recovery location and handoff with radiology and receiving staff, with monitoring, oxygen, suction, and resuscitation capability appropriate to the patient.
Use applicable postanesthesia standards: transport with a knowledgeable anesthesia team member, reassess on arrival, hand off the course and current status, and continue monitoring through recovery.
If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, apply the cited quantitative monitoring recommendations before extubation; they are conditional on blocker use and do not imply routine paralysis for MRI.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The ASA MRI advisory is consensus-based practice advice, not an absolute requirement; it states that evidence is limited and that local policy and clinical circumstances matter.
The MRI safety review is an educational summary rather than a procedure-specific anesthetic protocol. The general NORA review also notes limited outcome data and varied practices.
The basic monitoring and postanesthesia sources provide general standards, not MRI-specific drug selection, airway choices, fluid plans, or emergence timing.
Adult MRI-specific drug selection and device-specific clearance protocols are not resolved by the supplied material; apply institutional MRI safety processes and individualized anesthetic judgment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adults receiving cranial SRS, treatment commonly proceeds with the patient awake or lightly sedated; MAC is often sufficient. General anesthesia is reserved for selected patients who cannot tolerate or remain still for treatment.

The defining anesthetic challenge is reliable immobility in a remote treatment environment with restricted access during irradiation. Plan observation, communication, and a safe route for team access before treatment begins.

Prioritize standard oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment; remote observation does not remove the need to reconcile radiation-room access with applicable anesthesia monitoring standards.

After treatment, assess recovery in an appropriate postanesthesia-care setting. For cranial frame-based SRS, frame removal and pin-site care precede discharge or further observation; the source describes most patients as outpatients.

sources.label: Stereotactic Radiosurgery
16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cranial SRS uses imaging and computer planning to direct focused radiation at an intracranial target; it is not conventional surgery. Adults generally do not require general anesthesia and may remain awake with light sedation.

For frame-based Gamma Knife, local anesthetic is administered before a stereotactic frame is secured to the skull with pins. The team analyzes images and formulates a radiation plan; for treatment, the frame is secured to an apparatus. Some devices, such as CyberKnife, use masks rather than frames to hold the head in place.

SBRT and proton therapy are within the requested case scope, but the supplied adult-specific evidence chiefly describes conventional radiation therapy and cranial SRS. Do not assume its SRS workflow or anesthetic approach applies unchanged to those modalities.

sources.label: Stereotactic Radiosurgery
16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish whether the patient can tolerate the immobilization device and remain still, and discuss the planned level of sedation or anesthesia with the procedural team. Claustrophobia, anxiety, movement disorders, and painful treatment-planning procedures are described as factors that may make anesthetic support necessary.

For frame-based SRS, clarify the sequence and tolerance of frame placement under local anesthesia before proceeding with the treatment plan. The AANS source notes possible pin-site bleeding or infection, but does not provide an anticoagulant-management protocol.
When MRI is part of the workflow, screen for metallic implants and foreign bodies and arrange MRI-compatible equipment and monitoring; follow the site's MRI safety process.

sources.label: 16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition
Stereotactic Radiosurgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan the equipment layout and patient observation with the radiation team before treatment. The radiation-oncology chapter describes closed-circuit cameras directed at the patient and monitors, and notes that circuit extensions may be needed when equipment placement is constrained.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and setting, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment. The XRT chapter lists ECG, noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and qualitative end-tidal CO₂ monitoring in its remote-monitoring description.

Resolve room-evacuation procedures against applicable anesthesia standards before treatment. The chapter describes evacuation during irradiation, while ASA monitoring standards require continuous presence of qualified anesthesia personnel, with a specific provision for hazards that may require intermittent remote observation. The sources do not establish a universal compliant workflow for every radiation vault.

Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For a cooperative adult undergoing SRS, awake or lightly sedated management is described; the supplied sources do not establish a single airway device or anesthetic drug regimen for adults.

If general anesthesia is selected, account for limited airway access from immobilization and the remote setting. For frame-based treatment, the chapter specifically notes that the frame restricts airway access and calls for a means to remove it quickly if access becomes necessary.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment invalidates that monitoring. The ASA standards also require exhaled carbon dioxide confirmation after placement of an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask.

sources.label: Stereotactic Radiosurgery
