sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Do not impose a fixed pre-spinal fluid volume or delay urgent neuraxial anesthesia to administer one. Fluid preloading or coloading may be used to reduce hypotension, with management individualized to the patient.

Maintain perfusion by promptly recognizing and addressing neuraxial hypotension; the obstetric guideline identifies vasopressors as treatment options and notes the importance of maternal heart rate when considering agent selection.
Prepare blood-product access according to hemorrhage risk and institutional practice. The sources do not provide a universal fluid total, transfusion threshold, or emergency-case blood-loss target.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia, consider neuraxial opioid analgesia rather than relying on intermittent parenteral opioids. Select the regimen according to the patient, technique, and applicable institutional guidance.

Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia according to ERAC protocols. Scheduled acetaminophen and NSAIDs with systemic opioids reserved for as-needed use are described in the low-risk example regimen; account for contraindications and disease-related organ dysfunction.
Use prophylactic measures to reduce intraoperative nausea and vomiting, including prevention and treatment of spinal-associated hypotension. Avoid treating pain with anxiolytics or hypnotics alone.

Discuss intraoperative pain and patient experience, and arrange appropriate follow-up for significant pain or distress. The supplied ASA statement does not give a follow-up schedule or a complete medication algorithm.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Use a PACU or equivalent recovery area after anesthesia unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Continue evaluation and monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Transport the patient with an anesthesia-care-team member who can communicate the anesthetic and surgical course to the receiving nurse; the team member remains until nursing responsibility is accepted.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are recommended. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The obstetric anesthesia guideline is a professional practice guideline, not an absolute requirement or outcome guarantee; its literature searches covered an earlier evidence period. Apply its recommendations with current institutional policy and clinical judgment.

The SOAP enhanced-recovery consensus concerns scheduled cesarean delivery, although it notes that many pathway elements may also apply to nonscheduled cases. Its example medication regimens should not be treated as emergency-specific prescriptions.
The supplied ASA pain statements describe relevant issues but their provided best-practice sections are blank; they do not establish a complete intervention, dosing, or follow-up pathway.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Blepharoplasty removes upper-lid skin, sometimes with muscle or fat; lower-lid surgery may remove skin or fat, reposition fat, or tighten the lid. Simple procedures may be done with local anesthesia; more extensive plans may need sedation or general anesthesia.

The dominant vision-threatening concern is postseptal bleeding causing retrobulbar hematoma. Meticulous hemostasis and prompt recognition of severe eye pain, proptosis, or visual symptoms are priorities.

Assess ocular surface and lid function before surgery; postoperative dry eye, lagophthalmos, and corneal exposure are relevant risks. Recovery assessment should include attention to vision and symptoms suggesting orbital compression.

Choose the anesthetic and recovery setting to the procedure and patient. If anesthesia or sedation is provided, follow applicable basic monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards; the available sources do not establish a single blepharoplasty-specific regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Upper-lid surgery commonly excises excess skin; orbicularis muscle or postseptal fat may also be addressed. Avoid assuming every operation includes these additional steps.
Lower-lid procedures vary: they may include skin or fat resection, fat repositioning, lid-cheek treatment, or lid tightening. The intended components affect surgical extent and anesthetic selection.

Simple skin-or-fat excision can be performed under local anesthesia. More extensive or combined surgery may require intravenous sedation or general anesthesia; selection is individualized rather than dictated by a single technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review ophthalmic and medical history, including baseline vision, dry-eye symptoms, visual obstruction, thyroid disease, diabetes, hypertension, steroid-treated inflammatory disease, and bleeding or clotting disorders. The procedure review recommends a full eye examination, including retinal examination.

Assess tear production and eyelid position/function when clinically relevant. Pre-existing dry-eye symptoms are important because they correlate with postoperative complications; visual-field testing can document obstruction from ptosis or dermatochalasis.

Reconcile antithrombotic therapy with the surgeon and relevant prescriber; do not infer a routine stop plan from these sources. One block review advises physician consultation before stopping anticoagulants, but that is not a blepharoplasty-specific medication-management protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The reviewed blepharoplasty sources do not establish an intraoperative patient position or a procedure-specific room layout. Preoperative markings are described with the patient sitting upright in neutral gaze; this does not establish operative positioning.

For monitored anesthesia care, general anesthesia, or regional anesthesia, apply the applicable basic monitoring standards: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.
With moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes or invalidates it.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Local anesthesia, often with sedation, is an option for many oculoplastic procedures; the available evidence does not establish a natural-airway plan or a specific sedative regimen for blepharoplasty. If IV sedation is used, the procedure source calls for an anesthesia provider familiar with airway management.

General anesthesia is an option for complex or prolonged procedures and for patients unable to follow instructions or remain still. Airway-device selection remains individualized; the broad ophthalmic review describes supraglottic devices as widely used but does not make that a blepharoplasty-specific requirement.

When an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify its position by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas. From placement until extubation or removal, or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location, perform continual end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis using a quantitative method.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Injection may be an uncomfortable phase; local anesthetic is used to permit surgery under local anesthesia, and the procedure review notes sedation during injection may be helpful. No drug or dose regimen is established by the blepharoplasty sources.

During postseptal fat resection, meticulous hemostasis is emphasized because bleeding in that compartment can cause retrobulbar hemorrhage and severe visual injury. Maintain clear communication with the surgeon about concerning bleeding or ocular symptoms.

Oculocardiac reflex is a possible response to ocular surgery or manipulation. The ophthalmic regional-anesthesia review advises that atropine or glycopyrrolate be available; it does not establish a blepharoplasty-specific prophylaxis or treatment sequence.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Consider retrobulbar hematoma after blepharoplasty when severe ocular pain, proptosis, or visual complaints arise; all features need not be present. This is a time-critical surgical emergency.

The described emergency treatment is orbital decompression with lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. Escalate immediately to the ophthalmic surgeon/emergency team; the source emphasizes urgency but does not specify an anesthesia-led algorithm.

Other relevant complications include dry eye, lagophthalmos with corneal exposure, and lower-lid ectropion. Corneal lubrication is described for lagophthalmos and dry-eye management; persistent symptoms may require ophthalmology follow-up.

bullets: The procedure review provides no fluid-management guidance. Fluid choice and amount should therefore be individualized to the patient and anesthetic course; no fixed volume is supported here.
Meticulous hemostasis is emphasized, particularly during postseptal fat resection; bleeding in the postseptal compartment may cause retrobulbar hemorrhage and, in severe cases, blindness.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Surgeon-administered local anesthetic is part of the described approach. The procedure sources do not establish a postoperative analgesic regimen; avoid assuming routine opioids or a particular adjunct.

Ice packs are described as postoperative care to reduce swelling. The cited overview specifies application to the surgical site for three days; this is a surgical-care detail, not an anesthesia analgesia protocol.

No blepharoplasty-specific PONV regimen is provided. The adult ophthalmic review describes less postoperative nausea and vomiting with total intravenous anesthesia in general, but does not establish a case-specific anesthetic or prophylaxis prescription.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For general anesthesia in ophthalmic surgery, avoid coughing, straining, and retching at emergence where feasible because these can increase intraocular pressure. This is broad ophthalmic guidance, not a blepharoplasty-specific emergence protocol.

After anesthesia, use an appropriate PACU or equivalent setting, continue evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, and document the recovery period. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard, subject to its stated exceptions.

Include assessment for visual complaints and orbital hematoma symptoms in postoperative surveillance. Severe pain, proptosis, or visual complaints warrant urgent ophthalmic evaluation because decompression is emergent when orbital compartment syndrome is suspected.

The 2009 overview gives brief anesthesia options and surgical details but lacks airway-management guidance, monitoring recommendations, and an anesthetic regimen. Its local/general choices should be interpreted as options, not a decision rule.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult cataract extraction is usually a short, day-case procedure using topical or other locoregional anesthesia; topical anesthesia is the most commonly used technique. The approach should reflect patient cooperation, comfort, and the procedure.

The dominant anesthetic concern is maintaining a still, communicative patient when awake techniques are used. Coughing, straining, or movement may complicate delicate eye surgery; general anesthesia is an option when the patient cannot cooperate or remain still.

Oculocardiac reflex and complications of ophthalmic blocks are relevant hazards. Have appropriate monitoring and expertise available for the selected technique, and recognize that no block is risk-free.

Recovery priorities are assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and procedure, eye-drop instructions, and vigilance for concerning visual symptoms, pain, or redness. Avoid assuming a specific recovery protocol from the available evidence.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The standard operation for a functionally significant cataract is removal of the crystalline lens and replacement with an artificial intraocular lens. The provided sources describe modern phacoemulsification, but do not establish detailed surgical steps.

Topical anesthesia, sometimes supplemented by intracameral local anesthetic, is a common approach. Selection should be collaborative and account for patient-specific comfort and the surgeon’s experience; other locoregional approaches are available.
Use an awake technique only when the patient can safely cooperate with the procedure. GA may be considered when cooperation or stillness is not achievable, or for complex or prolonged surgery.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess medical history, anxiety, comfort, and ability to communicate and cooperate with the proposed technique. Dementia, deafness, anxiety, or language barriers may affect whether an awake approach is feasible; age alone is not a reason to exclude GA.

Consider relevant systemic and ocular comorbidity and optimize when clinically indicated. Ocular conditions and anatomy may affect surgical or postoperative risk; these sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific risk score.

Routine preoperative tests are not supported for low-risk ophthalmic surgery absent a clinical indication. Testing should be directed by the history, examination, and whether the result could change management.

Fasting practice depends on the planned anesthetic and local policy: the review describes fasting for GA or deep sedation, while noting that many centers have removed fasting for routine locoregional procedures with minimal sedation. Do not apply a single fasting approach to every case.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Choose a regional anaesthetic technique according to the operation’s requirements for anaesthesia, ocular akinesia and, occasionally, paralysis of orbicularis oculi; regional anaesthesia is suitable only if the patient can lie flat and still.

For monitored anesthesia care or regional anesthesia, qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present and continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes are specified by the basic monitoring standard.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation by observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the method is precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. The cited standard does not prescribe a cataract-specific sampling setup.

When administering an ophthalmic block, the regional-anesthesia review calls for baseline monitoring, IV access, trained assistance, and availability of an anesthetist and airway/resuscitation equipment. This block-specific preparation should not be generalized into mandatory access for every topical-only case.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Topical and locoregional techniques are established approaches; the cited sources do not require an airway device for these techniques. Choose anesthetic depth to preserve cooperation when the procedure relies on an awake patient.

If GA is chosen, airway-device selection should reflect the patient and operation. The review describes supraglottic devices as widely used and reports fewer emergence problems, including coughing and straining, compared with tracheal intubation; it does not establish one device as universally preferred for cataract surgery.

During general anaesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. From endotracheal-tube or laryngeal-mask placement until removal or initiation of transfer, perform continual quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis. During moderate or deep sedation, continually observe qualitative clinical signs and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure or equipment.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Awake surgery depends on safe communication and cooperation. Discuss the patient’s ability to follow instructions and remain still before selecting the technique; the sources do not define a universal sedation target or a cataract-specific movement threshold.

Coughing, straining, and retching can increase intraocular pressure, including at emergence. Aim to avoid these responses through an individualized anesthetic approach; no single airway or anesthetic technique is established for all patients.

Oculocardiac reflex can occur during eye surgery and may cause marked bradycardia or hypotension. Keep the possibility in mind during ocular manipulation; the regional-anesthesia review says atropine or glycopyrrolate should be available, but provides no universal prophylaxis strategy.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize surgical complications described in the guideline, including anterior or posterior capsule rupture, dropped nucleus, zonular dialysis, iris or IOL damage, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage. The executive summary does not provide an anesthesia-specific management algorithm.

Ophthalmic blocks carry technique-specific risks. Sharp-needle blocks can cause rare serious injury, while sub-Tenon’s block avoids a sharp instrument but still has reported complications; select and perform a block only with appropriate expertise.

With suspected local-anesthetic toxicity or central spread after a block, recognize that severe neurologic and cardiovascular manifestations are possible and escalate for airway and cardiovascular support. The cited review describes the hazard but does not establish a cataract-specific response protocol.

bullets: The sources describe cataract surgery as minimally stressful with minimal blood loss, but give no cataract-specific fluid regimen or bleeding-management protocol. Individualize fluid and access decisions to patient factors and the anesthetic actually planned.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Topical anesthesia is commonly used; intracameral lidocaine may be added to reduce intraoperative pain. The guideline does not provide a dose or a broader systemic analgesic regimen.

The guideline recommends an intracameral cefuroxime injection at the end of surgery to reduce postoperative endophthalmitis, within its stated European regulatory context. This is a surgical infection-prevention recommendation, not an anesthetic analgesic regimen.

The review describes less postoperative nausea and vomiting with total intravenous anesthesia than with some alternatives, but this does not justify selecting TIVA routinely for cataract surgery. bullets: For GA, avoid coughing, straining, and retching where possible because these can increase IOP. The review describes this as an emergence concern but does not prescribe a specific emergence regimen.

After anesthesia, use postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient’s condition. The ASA standard calls for continual evaluation, attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase.

Provide eye-drop and eye-protection instructions, including avoiding eye rubbing. Advise patients to seek assessment for decreased vision after improvement, new flashes or floaters, increased pain, or redness.

bullets: The cataract guideline is an executive summary of selected recommendations, not an anesthesia reference. It explicitly leaves airway management, positioning, monitoring requirements, physiologic targets, and anesthesia-specific postoperative monitoring unspecified.

The ophthalmic anesthesia review covers adults and multiple eye procedures, but some technique advice is preference-based or theoretical, and practice varies internationally. Apply its general airway and block discussion in scope rather than treating it as a cataract-specific standard.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open-globe repair closes a full-thickness ocular wound. General anesthesia is preferred for repair when possible, but the supplied procedure sources do not establish a specific anesthetic or airway regimen.

The immediate ocular hazard is expulsion of intraocular contents. Minimize pressure on the eye and avoid manipulating prolapsed contents; surgical choices such as anterior-chamber reformation also have pressure and wound-leak trade-offs.

Stillness and avoidance of coughing, straining, or retching are important considerations: a general ophthalmic anesthesia review links these events at emergence with increased intraocular pressure, but does not define an open-globe-specific airway strategy.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia observation and attention to nausea or vomiting that could provoke pressure increases. The provided sources do not specify an open-globe-specific emergence, analgesia, or PONV regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open-globe injury (OGI) repair addresses a full-thickness corneal or scleral wound. The surgical review covers corneal-wound closure, anterior-chamber reformation, and scleral exploration and visualization.

For corneal wounds, the surgeon may reform the anterior chamber with filtered air or ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD). Air may deflate through a wound; OVD can maintain the chamber but may elevate IOP and obscure wound edges.
Scleral exploration may require conjunctival peritomy; posterior exploration and extraocular-muscle handling are surgical considerations rather than a basis for a universal anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess overall fitness for general anesthesia and obtain consent when circumstances permit. Ocular or orbital trauma may accompany head, neck, or other bodily injuries; life-threatening injuries take priority.
A suspected open globe warrants a rigid shield. Avoid preoperative retrobulbar block in an open globe; eye movement assessment may also be limited for posterior wounds when movement risks expulsion.
Consider pre- and intraoperative antibiotics as part of the surgical infection-prevention plan. The supplied sources do not establish a single regimen for every OGI.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Retinal-detachment repair may use vitrectomy, scleral buckling, or other vitreoretinal approaches. Adult vitrectomy is often performed with monitored anesthesia and a regional block; general anesthesia is selected when cooperation or procedural factors require it.
If intraocular gas is present, nitrous oxide must not be administered: diffusion into the gas can rapidly raise intraocular pressure and cause ocular morbidity.
Globe manipulation can provoke the oculocardiac reflex, including bradycardia and hypotension. Recognize a change promptly and communicate with the surgeon.

Recovery priorities include avoiding coughing, straining, and retching that can increase intraocular pressure, assessing for pressure elevation, and following the surgeon-prescribed postoperative position.

bullets: Retinal-detachment surgery encompasses different surgical approaches, including pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and scleral buckling. The operation and tamponade choice are surgical decisions; the supplied sources do not establish a single approach for this combined-procedure label.

For adult vitrectomy, monitored anesthesia with a retrobulbar block is a common approach in the procedure-specific review; general anesthesia is used selectively, including when the patient cannot cooperate. bullets: Establish whether the patient can maintain the anticipated postoperative position. Neck, back, rheumatological, or cardiopulmonary limitations may affect the feasibility of face-down or specified head-tilt positioning.

Discuss anticipated air travel and high-altitude exposure when the surgical team is choosing tamponade. Patients with intraocular gas should avoid air travel and other activities involving atmospheric-pressure shifts while gas remains.

Assess medical comorbidity and ability to cooperate, and select preoperative testing based on clinical indication rather than routine testing for all patients. Diabetes is relevant to perioperative assessment, but the sources do not establish a retinal-surgery-specific glucose target.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult strabismus surgery aims to realign the eyes by weakening, strengthening, or repositioning extraocular muscles. General anaesthesia is commonly used; selected cooperative adults may have topical or other limited techniques for suitable procedures.

Key intraoperative concerns are the oculocardiac reflex (OCR) during muscle traction and airway/ventilation factors that can increase its likelihood. Coordinate with the surgeon; stop traction if the reflex occurs and escalate treatment if it persists or is severe.

PONV is a relevant adult recovery issue, but the available evidence does not support describing it as uniformly the highest-risk procedure or prescribing one regimen for every adult. Use individualized prophylaxis and opioid-sparing analgesia.

Plan recovery around assessment of pain, nausea/vomiting, and alignment-related symptoms such as diplopia; diplopia is common early and often improves. Apply standard postanaesthesia monitoring and handoff requirements.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Surgery changes extraocular muscle force or position: recession weakens, resection strengthens, and transposition changes muscle position. Procedure complexity, laterality, prior surgery, and whether adjustable sutures are planned inform anaesthetic selection.

General anaesthesia is suitable across ages and commonly used, particularly for complex, repeated, or bilateral surgery. Topical anaesthesia is an option only for selected cooperative adults and suitable procedures; muscle traction and detachment can be uncomfortable.

Adjustable-suture cases may involve a later awake alignment assessment and adjustment under topical anaesthesia after anaesthetic effects resolve. Avoid assuming that a long-acting block is neutral for this pathway, as it may delay the second stage.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify adult-onset symptoms and assess for underlying causes. The anaesthesia review specifically identifies thyroid function, bleeding disorders, and anticoagulant use as areas for assessment; thyroid eye disease should be stable and the patient euthyroid before surgery.

Review prior strabismus or other ocular surgery, relevant comorbidity, patient cooperation, and the planned technique. These factors may affect suitability for topical/regional techniques and the potential for difficult access or block spread.

Do not treat strabismus itself as an established malignant-hyperthermia risk factor or infer that volatile anaesthesia must be avoided. The review reports no association and describes volatile agents as commonly used in children; adult-specific comparative MH evidence is not established here.

bullets: Use standard anaesthesia monitoring appropriate to the technique. During anaesthesia, ECG is continuously displayed and blood pressure and heart rate are determined and evaluated at least every five minutes; use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

For general anaesthesia, follow standard monitoring requirements for ventilation and airway-device placement, including expired carbon-dioxide monitoring. Keep the patient and surgical field observable as required by the selected approach.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Either a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) or endotracheal tube may be used for general anaesthesia. If LMA patency is in doubt, address the airway before surgery begins; mid-case exchange may contaminate the surgical field.

The review favours assisted or controlled ventilation over spontaneous breathing because hypercarbia can increase OCR risk. Maintain attention to oxygenation and ventilation and avoid factors that promote hypercarbia or hypoxaemia.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: OCR is triggered by pressure on the globe or traction on extraocular muscles and may present as bradycardia or arrhythmia. Adult reported incidence in the review is lower than in children, but the reflex remains clinically relevant.

Coordinate muscle traction with the surgeon. If OCR occurs, ask for immediate release of traction; this often restores rhythm. If it persists or recurs, anticholinergic treatment may be considered, with escalation guided by the clinical state.

OCR generally diminishes with repeated stimulation, but do not rely on this to prevent an event. The review reports that acute traction is more reflexogenic than gradual traction and that opioid and dexmedetomidine use can potentiate OCR.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For marked bradycardia, arrhythmia, or failure to recover promptly after traction stops, communicate with the surgeon and escalate anaesthetic management. The available sources describe possible severe rhythm disturbances but do not establish a single treatment sequence for every event.

Recognize that globe perforation, slipped or lost muscle, retinal detachment, and infection are reported surgical complications. Suspected globe injury or muscle loss requires prompt communication with the ophthalmic surgeon and reassessment of the anaesthetic approach if further exploration or repair is needed.
After surgery, diplopia is common in the first week and often resolves. Persistent or concerning visual symptoms warrant ophthalmic assessment rather than an assumption that symptoms are expected.

bullets: Use an individualized multimodal, opioid-sparing approach. The review supports paracetamol, intravenous NSAIDs, topical local anaesthetic, and limited opioid use; supplementary regional block is a team decision, not a required component.
The review reports adult PONV at 30%, independent of general anaesthetic technique, and notes that ondansetron plus dexamethasone is often given prophylactically to adults.

Inferior oblique surgery tends to be more uncomfortable and often induces more postoperative nausea. Short-acting narcotics in the recovery room are a possible cause of nausea and vomiting in some patients.

bullets: ACL reconstruction is usually arthroscopic and often outpatient; the available evidence describes general, regional, and combined anesthetic approaches but does not establish one as routine for every patient.
Postoperative pain is a major recovery concern. Graft-related pain may differ, and available comparisons do not establish a single analgesic regimen as superior.

Regional analgesia can be part of a multimodal plan. Adductor canal and femoral blocks have broadly similar pain outcomes in most cited comparisons, but femoral block is associated with greater quadriceps weakness.

Prioritize functional recovery and safe mobilization while monitoring for pain, nausea, and residual motor impairment; PACU observation and discharge decisions should follow applicable local standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adults with an unstable ankle mortise and suitable soft tissues, ankle ORIF restores alignment and stability; fixation is fracture-specific and may involve plates, screws, or syndesmotic stabilization.

Neuraxial techniques may provide surgical anesthesia for foot/ankle surgery. Peripheral nerve blocks may be used for postoperative analgesia or as adjuncts to general or neuraxial anesthesia; a popliteal sciatic block is commonly combined with a saphenous block for foot/ankle surgery. Choose an approach based on patient and procedural factors; the supplied review does not establish a preferred approach for ankle ORIF.

The dominant case-specific concerns are soft-tissue condition and wound healing, neurovascular integrity, and comorbidities such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy. Timing should reflect the soft-tissue envelope rather than a fixed interval.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and reassessment of the operated foot’s neurovascular status, swelling, and splint. Regional analgesia may support postoperative pain control, but motor block and safe mobility require attention.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ORIF is generally selected for an unstable mortise in a patient fit for surgery when the soft tissues are favorable. The operative aim is anatomical restoration with stable fixation; fracture pattern determines the construct.

Fixation options described include plates and screws for fibular fractures, fracture-specific medial or posterior malleolar fixation, and screws or tightropes for syndesmotic diastasis. These are surgical options, not a universal construct.

Intraoperative imaging is used to assess alignment and syndesmotic stability; the described options include the Hook (Cotton) test and external-rotation stress views. Posterior malleolar anatomy may require preoperative CT for operative planning.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess fracture pattern, mortise stability, syndesmotic involvement, skin and swelling, and relevant comorbidities. Diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy can adversely affect healing; assess vascular status and baseline neurologic function.

Fracture blisters and substantial swelling signal soft-tissue risk. Definitive fixation may be delayed while swelling subsides; the evidence supports judging timing by tissue condition, not applying a fixed wait.

Complete individualized VTE risk assessment, including prior DVT, immobilization or nonweight bearing, and other relevant patient risk factors; sources do not support a universal prophylaxis regimen for all ankle-fracture patients.

bullets: No ankle-ORIF source specifies an airway plan or establishes general anesthesia, a supraglottic airway, or tracheal intubation as routine. Choose anesthesia and airway management for the patient, procedure, and intended sedation depth.

Regional options include neuraxial anesthesia and peripheral blocks. The review describes popliteal sciatic block as commonly combined with saphenous block for foot/ankle surgery; it does not establish this combination as complete or preferred anesthesia for every ORIF.
Regional technique selection should account for block coverage, duration, comorbidities, anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, and potential motor effects on recovery and mobility.

bullets: Soft-tissue preservation and stable anatomical reduction are central operative priorities. For syndesmotic injury, imaging and the described stress tests assess reduction and stability.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Important operative complications include infection, wound dehiscence, nerve or vascular injury, delayed union, nonunion, and hardware problems. Soft-tissue compromise and diabetes increase concern for wound complications.

Reassess neurovascular status when clinically indicated, including pulses, color, temperature, sensation, and motor function. A threatened limb or concerning change requires prompt escalation to the surgical team.

Regional anesthesia can be complicated by block failure, nerve injury, hematoma, infection, or local-anesthetic systemic toxicity. Use the source’s general safety principles, including ultrasound where applicable and incremental injection; no ankle-ORIF-specific rescue regimen is established here.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Peripheral regional analgesia is an option for postoperative pain. The regional-anesthesia review describes popliteal sciatic block, commonly combined with saphenous block, for foot/ankle surgery; discuss coverage, duration, motor effects, and alternatives with the patient and care team.
Regional techniques may reduce postoperative opioid consumption, but block-related weakness can increase fall risk; plan mobility support until function and balance are adequate.

Peripheral nerve blocks are often used for postoperative analgesia. Select a technique based on factors including block coverage and duration and the effect of postoperative motor blockade on physical therapy and recovery.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Provide postanesthesia care with monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. The receiving team should get a handoff and documented arrival status.

Reassess distal neurovascular status, swelling, and splint condition in recovery. The source requires documented neurovascular assessment around manipulation; the specific frequency after ORIF is not established in the supplied evidence.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported. These recommendations do not apply to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade or general anesthesia.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Carpal tunnel release divides the transverse carpal ligament to decompress the median nerve. Strong guideline support favors local anesthesia alone; the available sources do not establish WALANT as the required technique.

The anesthetic priorities are to provide adequate local anesthesia while avoiding unnecessary sedation; if sedation is used, monitor for respiratory compromise and other sedation-related adverse effects.

Mini-open and endoscopic release have similar patient-reported outcomes in the guideline evidence; discuss technique and anesthetic options with the patient rather than treating one approach as mandatory.

Postoperative priorities supported here are multimodal non-opioid pain treatment and appropriate postanesthesia observation. Procedure-specific sensory, motor, and wound-assessment instructions are not established in these sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The operation is open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a distal radius fracture. The available sources identify the procedure but do not establish a specific surgical approach or routine anesthetic technique.

General anesthesia and regional anesthesia are both described in a large registry comparison; upper-extremity regional techniques are options when their coverage and patient-specific risks are appropriate.

Key anesthesia priorities supported here are selecting a technique with the patient and team, monitoring for block-related complications, and anticipating pain after a peripheral block resolves. The sources do not define a distal-radius-specific physiologic risk profile.
Recovery should include appropriate postanesthesia evaluation and monitoring. A specific distal radius neurovascular-check protocol is not provided by these fetched sources.

bullets: The evidence identifies ORIF for distal radius fractures but does not describe the operative exposure, fixation sequence, imaging workflow, or fracture-specific surgical decision-making. Do not infer these from the anesthesia studies.

A small retrospective series describes wide-awake local anesthesia with no tourniquet (WALANT) during volar or dorsal plating. It is a reported alternative, not evidence that WALANT is routine or suitable for every patient or fracture.

The WALANT report used active wrist and finger movement to assess fixation stability and possible implant impingement. This finding describes that series; it does not establish a required intraoperative assessment for other anesthetic or surgical approaches.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Discuss general and regional options with the patient and surgical team, considering cooperation, anxiety, planned manipulation, block coverage and duration, comorbidities, and the potential effect of motor block on recovery.

Before a peripheral block, assess relevant neurologic, pulmonary, cardiovascular, and hematologic history and examination. Consider pulmonary reserve when choosing an upper-extremity approach because some approaches can impair diaphragmatic function.

For an awake local-anesthetic approach, assess whether the patient is willing and able to tolerate an awake procedure. The reported series identified substantial anxiety or inability to tolerate the procedure as reasons WALANT might not be appropriate.

Review anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy in relation to the proposed block site and bleeding consequences; the regional-anesthesia review describes superficial-block decisions as case-by-case. Follow applicable current guidance rather than importing a timing regimen from this summary.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: In matched registry cohorts, reported complications did not differ significantly between regional and general anesthesia. This observational result does not rule out individual complications or establish that either approach is risk-free.

Regional techniques can fail or cause nerve injury, hematoma, infection, or local-anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Recognize concerning neurologic or cardiovascular changes promptly and escalate to the institution’s applicable block-complication/LAST response resources; the review is not a distal-radius-specific response protocol.

A broad review reports that rebound pain can follow peripheral nerve blocks, and that one cited quality-improvement analysis found more unplanned physician-office visits for postoperative pain with regional anesthesia. These findings support planning for pain after block resolution, not a fixed drug regimen.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: External fixation uses percutaneous pins and an external frame to stabilize a fracture provisionally or definitively. In damage-control care, stabilization may precede later definitive fixation after the patient’s physiology improves.

Anesthesia is context-dependent: the review describes general or regional anesthesia for external fixation, while a selected ED technique may use local anesthesia with or without conscious sedation. The available sources do not establish a single technique or airway plan.

Priorities include maintaining physiologic stability and protecting soft tissues while obtaining stable fixation. Watch for compartment syndrome, neurovascular injury, pin-related problems and skin pressure injury.

Recovery destination and surveillance should reflect injury severity and the anesthetic: postanesthesia care or equivalent care is required, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: External fixation stabilizes bone and soft tissues while leaving access for wound assessment and subsequent procedures. Uses described include provisional stabilization of complex fractures, including open fractures or fractures with substantial soft-tissue involvement, and temporary stabilization pending soft-tissue recovery or definitive surgery.

The construct and setting depend on injury and patient circumstances. The review reserves ED fixation for critically ill patients as a life-saving measure and describes other external-fixation methods as appropriate for an operating room with a sterile environment.

Plan pin locations with the anticipated definitive approach in mind; pin placement should not interfere with later fixation. Fluoroscopy usually assists placement and alignment assessment, but availability and use vary by setting.

Regional anesthesia may provide surgical anesthesia or postoperative analgesia. Choice requires weighing block coverage and duration, patient factors, and possible motor effects against recovery needs.

bullets: Hip fracture repair may use general or neuraxial anesthesia; select the approach for the patient, fracture, comorbidities, and expected procedure rather than treating spinal anesthesia as universally superior.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The available procedure-specific material covers elective lumbar surgery that includes laminectomy. It does not establish a distinct anesthetic pathway for cervical versus lumbar decompression, or define how extent, levels, or associated procedures change the plan; coordinate these details with the surgical team.

General anesthesia is usually preferred for spine surgery in the broad review. Spinal anesthesia is discussed as an alternative for selected elective lumbar cases, not as a default for all laminectomies or for cervical surgery.

The lumbar spinal-anesthesia review describes selection constraints and the need to anticipate airway rescue when a patient is prone. Those observations support careful case selection and contingency planning, not routine use of spinal anesthesia.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Record pre-existing motor and sensory deficits before surgery so that postoperative findings can be compared with baseline. Assess the relevant neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and airway risks, with assessment proportionate to the planned operation and comorbidity.

Cervical and upper-thoracic surgery can complicate airway management; rheumatoid arthritis and other musculoskeletal disorders are among factors the review associates with difficulty selecting an intubation technique. The supplied sources do not establish awake fiberoptic intubation as mandatory, or specify a cervical intubation technique.

For a regional technique, consider airway rescue feasibility, patient cooperation, expected duration, and the intended number of levels. The lumbar review describes these as selection considerations for elective lumbar surgery, not as criteria for general anesthesia.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For minor spine procedures classified by the review as up to two-level decompression without instrumentation, it describes an 18–20G IV and an arterial line only when medically indicated. Do not generalize access recommendations for major or complex operations to every decompression.

When prone, use team communication, appropriate equipment, padding, and positioning checks; reassess positioning as the case proceeds. The review describes risks ranging from soft-tissue injury to visual loss and peripheral nerve injury.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards. Add invasive pressure monitoring or evoked-potential monitoring according to patient, procedural extent, and the monitoring plan; the sources do not establish either as universal for laminectomy.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: With general anesthesia, plan a secured airway suitable for prone surgery and verify its position after placement. Cervical or upper-thoracic surgery may make airway management challenging, but the supplied sources do not compare specific airway techniques for this operation.

Maintain required ventilation monitoring during general anesthesia, including quantitative expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring from airway placement through extubation or transfer. For moderate or deep sedation, monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment makes it invalid or impractical.

Spinal anesthesia with sedation is described only for selected elective lumbar surgery. The review emphasizes airway contingency planning because airway loss in the prone position can be life-threatening; it does not make that technique appropriate for every patient or procedure.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid treating deliberate hypotension as a routine blood-conservation measure. The spine review found no adult evidence demonstrating its effectiveness and notes potential organ-ischemia and visual-loss risks; another supplied review discusses pressure support to preserve cord perfusion. Individualize hemodynamic goals to the patient, operation, and neuromonitoring.

For cases using evoked potentials, coordinate anesthetic technique and changes in anesthetic or hemodynamic conditions with the monitoring team. The source favors TIVA for spinal fusion monitoring; this does not establish that TIVA is required for every decompression.

Prone positioning can alter cardiovascular physiology and may contribute to bleeding if abdominal or thoracic pressure is increased. Check positioning and abdominal decompression rather than relying on a fixed positioning prescription.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Position-related visual loss and peripheral nerve injury are recognized hazards of prone spine surgery. Maintain attention to pressure points, head and eye positioning, hemodynamics, anemia, and volume status; the cited review does not provide a laminectomy-specific risk estimate.

Dural tear is recognized in the lumbar anesthesia review. It reports no significant difference in durotomy risk between spinal and general anesthesia in comparative studies, but the supplied evidence does not establish a specific intraoperative response or postoperative protocol.

If a new postoperative neurologic finding is detected, promptly compare it with the documented baseline and communicate with the surgical and anesthesia teams. The supplied sources support baseline documentation and postoperative examination, but do not specify an imaging or reoperation algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The supplied sources do not support a fixed fluid total, routine cell salvage, or universal transfusion preparation for laminectomy. Base fluid and blood-product planning on the actual extent, patient factors, and anticipated bleeding rather than importing recommendations for complex reconstruction.

TXA and cell salvage are discussed in the broad spine review as blood-conservation options, particularly in larger procedures; the evidence supplied does not establish routine use for a limited decompression or provide a procedure-specific regimen here.

Preserve perfusion while avoiding unsupported pressure targets. One review describes possible spinal-cord perfusion effects of prone positioning and cerebrospinal-fluid pressure; another cautions that deliberate hypotension may increase ischemic risk.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Multimodal analgesia may combine neuraxial or peripheral nerve blocks with NSAIDs, acetaminophen, gabapentinoids, and patient-controlled analgesia. Bilateral ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block has been reported to reduce postoperative opioid requirements and improve patient satisfaction in lumbar surgery.

Do not infer that NSAIDs are universally appropriate or inappropriate after decompression from fusion-related evidence. The supplied spine review says selective COX-2 effects were reported while non-union and bleeding concerns remained debatable; it does not resolve drug choice for this individual procedure.

The lumbar anesthesia review reports higher postoperative nausea and vomiting with general anesthesia in one cited comparison, but provides no procedure-specific PONV prevention protocol. Assess risk and select prophylaxis clinically rather than adopting an unsupported universal regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general anesthesia, facilitate an early neurologic examination where clinically feasible. Compare motor and sensory findings with the preoperative record; the supplied sources do not establish a specific extubation sequence for lumbar or cervical laminectomy.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF recovery of at least 0.9 before extubation. This applies when blockade is used, not to local-anesthetic or neuraxial cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; use quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase. Escalation and discharge decisions remain subject to clinical assessment and facility policy.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-relevant source is a narrative review of spinal anesthesia in elective lumbar surgery, combining literature and institutional experience; it is not a guideline and does not establish routine practice for cervical surgery. The broader spine review is also narrative and notes limited evidence and variation across operations.

The blood-pressure review is a broad orthopedic clinical review, not a laminectomy-specific guideline. Its spinal-surgery suggestions should be reconciled with the spine review's caution about deliberate hypotension, rather than converted into universal targets.

The monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade sources provide general standards rather than a procedure-specific anesthetic plan. They support basic monitoring, recovery observation, and quantitative reversal assessment when neuromuscular blockade is used.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Long-bone fracture fixation may use open reduction and internal fixation with plates or an intramedullary nail; the sources do not establish one approach as usual across tibia, femur, and humerus fractures.

For intramedullary fixation, prioritize recognition of evolving respiratory or neurologic changes consistent with fat embolism syndrome (FES); the cited review describes supportive care rather than a procedure-specific intraoperative rescue algorithm.

Choose general, neuraxial, or combined anesthetic techniques according to the patient, fracture, and procedure; the available evidence does not justify a universal airway or anesthetic technique for all long-bone ORIF.

Recovery priorities include ongoing oxygenation and mental-status assessment when FES is a concern, appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, and confirmation of adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when a neuromuscular blocking drug was used.

bullets: The operation addresses a diaphyseal fracture by reduction and fixation. The supplied evidence discusses plate-and-screw ORIF and intramedullary nailing, but does not compare fixation choices across tibial, femoral, and humeral shaft fractures.

The fracture pattern, operative approach, and planned fixation determine positioning and the need for imaging or traction. The available procedure-focused study does not provide positioning or setup instructions applicable across these operations.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish injury context and assess for concurrent hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability. The orthopedic blood-pressure review describes hemorrhage as a source of reduced circulating volume and blood-pressure instability in trauma; it does not give a fracture-specific blood-loss estimate.

Consider FES in the setting of a long-bone fracture or intramedullary instrumentation. Assess for respiratory distress, altered mental status, petechiae, and—where present—abrupt hypotension or fever; onset may be delayed after injury or instrumentation.

Review cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, and antithrombotic comorbidities as part of individualized assessment. The available fracture cohort was an older, isolated periprosthetic distal-femur population and cannot define risk for all long-bone trauma patients.

bullets: Select positioning and room equipment for the fracture, approach, and fixation plan. The supplied procedure cohort does not establish a standard table, traction arrangement, fluoroscopy setup, or access plan for long-bone ORIF.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and assess blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Select general, neuraxial, or combined anesthesia based on patient factors, positioning, surgical requirements, and anticipated duration. In a cohort of isolated periprosthetic distal-femur ORIF, most patients received general endotracheal anesthesia; that observation does not establish a universal technique for shaft fractures.

Regional techniques may serve as surgical anesthesia or postoperative analgesia. The review notes that lower-extremity peripheral blocks are typically adjuncts for surgical anesthesia because of anatomical limitations; technique and coverage require individualized selection.

When a neuromuscular blocking drug is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This guidance applies to neuromuscular blockade, not to every regional or local-anesthetic case.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Remain alert to changes in oxygenation, ventilation, mental status, and circulation during fracture instrumentation. The available review identifies long-bone fracture and intramedullary nailing as contexts for FES but does not establish a specific intraoperative monitoring threshold or reaming intervention.

Avoid both hypertensive spikes and hypotension where FES is a concern; the review describes a relationship between blood-pressure variation, intramedullary pressure, and fat entry, without defining a universal long-bone anesthesia target.

Maintain standard continual assessment of ventilation and circulation throughout anesthesia; with general anesthesia, use the required expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the nature of the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates it.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Suspect FES when respiratory distress, altered mental status, or petechiae develop after long-bone injury or instrumentation; hypotension and fever may also occur. Escalate promptly for respiratory or hemodynamic support rather than relying on an unsupported case-specific algorithm.

The review describes supportive management of established FES, including oxygen or mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure and correction of coagulopathy or acidosis. It does not provide a procedure-specific resuscitation sequence.

Pulmonary embolism can also cause sudden unexplained hypotension or refractory tachycardia, but the supplied discussion focuses on hip and pelvic surgery and should not be treated as a long-bone ORIF-specific incidence or protocol.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: In a retrospective cohort of isolated periprosthetic distal femur fractures, median estimated blood loss was 200 mL (IQR 137.5–250 mL; range 10–1,000 mL). This cohort does not establish expected blood loss or transfusion practice for tibial, femoral-shaft, or humeral ORIF; it reports no fluid administration, transfusions, or specific blood-management measures.

In active hemorrhagic trauma, resuscitation and operative priorities depend on the clinical context; the review discusses damage-control surgery and restrictive volume resuscitation for hemorrhagic injury, not a routine fluid prescription for fracture fixation.

The fracture cohort provides no fluid-administration, transfusion, or blood-management protocol; selection of fluids, blood products, and adjuncts should not be inferred from its reported blood-loss distribution.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Consider peripheral regional analgesia as part of an individualized multimodal plan. The review describes femoral and adductor-canal techniques, among others, but does not establish a single preferred block for all fracture sites or approaches.

Weigh analgesic coverage against motor impairment and fall risk. Femoral block can weaken quadriceps; adductor-canal techniques are described as relatively motor-sparing but may still affect strength.

bullets: Base extubation on the patient's clinical status and adequate recovery from any neuromuscular blockade used; quantitative TOF confirmation of at least 0.9 is recommended before extubation when applicable.

Provide postanesthesia care with continual assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry during the initial recovery phase.

title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Orthopedic) — Toe / Ray / Transmetatarsal
aliases: Lower Extremity Amputation (Orthopedic) — Toe / Ray / Transmetatarsal

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Toe, ray, and transmetatarsal amputation removes diseased tissue while aiming to preserve functional limb length when possible. The available amputation review does not establish a specific operative or anesthetic approach for these exact levels.

General or regional anesthesia are described options; selection is individualized. A popliteal sciatic block combined with saphenous coverage is described for foot/ankle surgery, but the sources do not establish it as a reliable sole anesthetic for every amputation at these levels.

Healing potential, infection, and perfusion at the chosen level are central concerns. In patients with diabetes, the review emphasizes glycemic control and early antibiotics; it cautions that perfusion measures do not capture all factors relevant to healing.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring and plan recovery around the patient’s condition, pain, wound, and perfusion assessment. The supplied sources do not support a universal glucose target, fluid volume, block recipe, or discharge plan for this operation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative level and extent depend on diseased tissue, soft-tissue viability, and the ability to obtain bone coverage. Preserving functional limb length is a stated priority when feasible.

The amputation chapter describes major lower-extremity and selected foot-level procedures, but does not detail toe, ray, or transmetatarsal operative technique. Do not infer a particular incision, tourniquet requirement, or wound-closure method for these levels from it.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess whether viable tissue and perfusion are likely to support healing at the proposed level, alongside infection and soft-tissue status. TcPO₂ is discussed as an estimate of healing potential, not a stand-alone decision rule.
For diabetes, the review identifies glycemic control and early antibiotic treatment as optimization priorities. It does not provide a target glucose value or a procedure-specific insulin regimen.

Before regional anesthesia, assess cooperation, relevant neurologic and cardiopulmonary status, infection, and antithrombotic or coagulation issues. A local or systemic infection may preclude regional anesthesia; decisions for superficial blocks in anticoagulated patients depend on site and bleeding consequences.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The amputation review describes supine positioning. Use a tourniquet only when appropriate; it notes that some patients lack vascular inflow and do not require one. Protect skin beneath an applied tourniquet.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. The ASA standards require continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes; temperature monitoring is indicated when clinically significant change is intended, anticipated, or suspected.
For diabetic foot wounds or gangrene, the amputation review describes keeping the wound under a dry dressing and isolating it from the incision site during preparation.

bullets: The available amputation evidence supports GA or regional anesthesia as options, with case-by-case selection; it supplies no specific airway plan. Popliteal sciatic and saphenous blocks are described in the regional-anesthesia review for lower-limb and foot/ankle coverage. If moderate or deep sedation is used, ventilation assessment includes continual clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless precluded or invalidated. An airway device or general anesthesia is not imposed by the procedure description.

bullets: Infection and tissue viability shape the operative level and approach. For septic shock, the review describes open amputation with staged reconstruction as a possible source-control strategy; it does not establish that approach for routine foot-level amputation.

Tourniquet inflation and release can affect blood pressure. A general orthopedic review describes potential hypertension with inflation and hypotension with deflation; this is not a procedure-specific protocol, so observe hemodynamics and respond to the individual course.

Reassess the healing potential of the planned level with the surgical team; the source identifies wound breakdown and possible higher-level revision as concerns but does not provide a foot-level rescue algorithm.

Regional anesthesia can fail or cause nerve injury, bleeding, infection, or local-anesthetic systemic toxicity. Use appropriate monitoring and be prepared to address block failure or convert the anesthetic approach; the review provides no amputation-specific incidence estimates.

bullets: The selected amputation level must have adequate healing potential. The review discusses TcPO₂ as one assessment aid but stresses that clinical condition, soft tissues, neuropathy, and function also matter.

The amputation review gives no fluid, blood-loss, or transfusion protocol for this operation. Individualize fluid and blood management to the patient’s status, observed losses, and comorbidities rather than applying a fixed volume.

Regional anesthesia is associated with reduced blood loss and transfusion need in cited major-amputation literature, but another cited analysis found no difference in several postoperative outcomes. These data do not establish a blood-management prescription for minor foot-level procedures.

After anesthesia, use PACU or equivalent care, with monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition and attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A verbal handoff and documentation of arrival status are required by the cited postanesthesia standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lumbar discectomy includes different surgical approaches. In an adult observational study of elective microdiscectomy, general anesthesia (GA) involved tracheal intubation and prone positioning; spinal anesthesia was also studied. The evidence does not establish one technique as universal.

Select anesthesia case by case, considering patient preference and cooperation, comorbidities, and surgical complexity. For endoscopic procedures, local anesthesia with or without sedation, epidural anesthesia, and GA are described; these findings should not be assumed to define practice for every discectomy approach.

Prioritize safe positioning and appropriate anesthetic monitoring. Awake feedback may help identify possible nerve irritation during some endoscopic procedures; GA removes that immediate feedback, and the review describes neuromonitoring as a possible aid while noting limited procedure-specific evidence.

Recovery priorities include evaluating pain and the patient's condition after anesthesia, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. When neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

bullets: Avoid assuming a single anesthetic technique fits all cases. For endoscopic discectomy, preserving patient feedback may help with nerve identification; complex or lengthy surgery is among the circumstances in which the review says GA may be selected.

The endoscopic review lists EMG, SSEPs, and MEPs as possible means of detecting nerve or spinal-cord injury under GA, but states that procedure-specific IONM studies are lacking. Neuromonitoring use should not be presumed routine for a single-level discectomy.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Pain during endoscopic manipulation can be inadequately controlled with local anesthesia; severe uncontrolled pain may cause hemodynamic fluctuation and may require changing anesthesia or terminating surgery. This concern is specific to the described endoscopic context.

Recognize that GA is associated in the endoscopic review with airway or breathing complications, vomiting, and longer recovery; opioids also carry respiratory and other adverse-effect risks. The review does not give a discectomy-specific rescue algorithm.

During local anesthesia, patient feedback about sensation and movement may help identify nerves and detect possible neurological injury; under general anesthesia, neuromonitoring may assist in detecting nerve or spinal-cord injury.

bullets: No supplied discectomy-specific source establishes a fluid volume, expected blood loss, or hemorrhage-management protocol. Individualize fluid and blood management to the patient and operative course.

bullets: For endoscopic procedures, options described include local anesthetic, responsive sedation, epidural anesthesia, and GA. Inadequate analgesia and intolerable pain are recognized limitations of local anesthesia in some procedural phases.

A broad orthopedic review describes multimodal analgesia as combining regional techniques with non-opioid and opioid options. This is general orthopedic context, not a validated discectomy-specific regimen.

In the adult observational study, PONV was associated with submaximal satisfaction, and GA patients reported more throat irritation and mouth dryness. These findings inform counseling and recovery observation but do not establish comparative risk for all discectomy populations.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The adult microdiscectomy study reports patients awakened in the operating room and transferred to PACU with stable vital signs. This is a study protocol, not a universal extubation or emergence requirement.

PACU care should include continual assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; a quantitative oxygenation method is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

When a neuromuscular blocker has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited ASA guideline overview. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

After anesthesia, admit the patient to a PACU or equivalent unless the responsible anesthesiologist orders otherwise. Continually evaluate and monitor the patient as appropriate, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature; use pulse oximetry during the initial phase of recovery.

bullets: The most procedure-specific anesthesia review concerns full-endoscopic discectomy and cautions that its underlying studies provide limited evidence. Its conclusions should not be generalized without qualification to all open or microscopic discectomy.

The adult microdiscectomy comparison is a single-center, non-randomized observational study with limited follow-up; it informs reported patient experience but does not establish a universal preferred anesthetic.
The blood-pressure and regional-anesthesia reviews are broad orthopedic sources, not discectomy-specific guidelines. Their general findings are used only with explicit scope limits.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pelvic fracture fixation is a spectrum: provisional external fixation and staged damage-control orthopedics are described for hemodynamically unstable patients; early definitive fixation is described for stable or adequately resuscitated patients.
The dominant immediate physiologic threat is major retroperitoneal hemorrhage with hemodynamic collapse; rapid mechanical stabilization and coordinated hemorrhage control are central priorities.

In unstable polytrauma, damage-control strategy aims to limit physiologic deterioration, including hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy; timing and extent of fixation depend on injury and response to resuscitation.

Recovery priorities include reassessment for ongoing bleeding and associated complications, appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, and coordination of thromboprophylaxis and mobilization when clinically appropriate. The available sources do not establish a routine extubation or ICU pathway for every patient.

sources.label: Advances in Managing Pelvic Fractures in Polytrauma: A Comprehensive Review
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Stabilization may be provisional or definitive. External fixation is described as a rapid means of provisional pelvic stabilization and hemorrhage control in damage-control orthopedics; the choice of fixation is based on the clinical situation and injury pattern.

For stable or adequately resuscitated patients, early total care with definitive fixation is described as an option. The review characterizes this approach, including its timing, for selected patients; it does not establish a universal schedule for an individual case.

Percutaneous fixation and open reduction and internal fixation have different trade-offs in exposure, reduction, and potential complications. The supplied review discusses these comparatively but does not provide a patient-specific selection rule.

sources.label: Advances in Managing Pelvic Fractures in Polytrauma: A Comprehensive Review

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish current physiologic stability, injury burden, and response to initial resuscitation when framing the damage-control versus definitive-fixation strategy. Lactate clearance and base deficit are identified as markers used to assess perfusion and resuscitation adequacy.

Review available imaging and the clinical trajectory for injury pattern and ongoing hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT is described as providing information on these issues; the source does not define an anesthesia-specific imaging or testing protocol.
Maintain a high index of concern for associated urogenital injury as part of the polytrauma assessment. The review reports these injuries but does not set out a screening algorithm.

The sources do not establish a universal preoperative risk score, airway evaluation pathway, or laboratory schedule specific to pelvic fixation; assess and coordinate according to the patient’s injuries and local trauma process.

sources.label: Advances in Managing Pelvic Fractures in Polytrauma: A Comprehensive Review

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The provided evidence does not prescribe a pelvic-fixation room layout, vascular-access configuration, or positioning. These depend on the planned approach, imaging needs, and the patient’s condition; the cited review supplies no procedure-specific setup standard.

During anesthesia, maintain continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ECG is continuously displayed and blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the ASA basic monitoring standards.

Additional invasive or advanced monitoring is not established as routine for this procedure by the supplied sources; select it for the clinical context rather than treating it as a universal requirement.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The available pelvic-fracture review does not specify an airway device, intubation technique, or ventilation strategy for fixation. No universal airway approach can be derived from these sources; select a technique for the patient's physiology, injuries, and planned procedure.

For general anesthesia, verify airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, and continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis until extubation or transfer begins, consistent with ASA basic monitoring standards.
The sources do not establish that general anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, or tracheal intubation is mandatory for every pelvic fracture procedure.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Major pelvic-ring bleeding can arise from the posterior pelvic venous plexus and may cause rapid hemodynamic collapse. Treat deterioration as a potential hemorrhage emergency and coordinate promptly with the surgical and trauma teams for control and stabilization.

In damage-control orthopedics, rapid mechanical stabilization is described as reducing mortality and helping prevent progression of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. The review does not specify an anesthetic sequence or physiologic target for achieving this.
Fixation timing and extent should remain linked to physiologic status and response to resuscitation; instability is not a reason to extrapolate a fixed anesthetic or operative recipe from the review.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Severe retroperitoneal bleeding can cause hemodynamic collapse.

The review identifies hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, and postoperative infection among early complications. Prophylaxis and mobilization require coordination with bleeding risk, fixation, and the overall injury plan.

Percutaneous techniques may reduce soft-tissue disruption but are associated in the review with risks including malunion, screw malposition, and neurovascular injury. These are procedural hazards for the team to account for, not anesthesia-specific management instructions.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The review describes hemorrhage control and mechanical stabilization as key elements in pelvic trauma, but provides no transfusion ratio, fluid regimen, or blood-product threshold. Do not treat a fixed resuscitation recipe as established by this evidence.
Lactate clearance and base deficit are identified as measures for assessing perfusion and resuscitation adequacy. The source does not define thresholds or a target-directed protocol for their use.
Near-infrared spectroscopy and continuous cardiac-output analysis are mentioned as possible assessment technologies in the review, not as required monitoring or validated pelvic-fixation targets.

bullets: The supplied pelvic-fracture review does not provide a surgical anesthetic analgesia regimen. Analgesic selection should be individualized to injury, coagulation status, and the intended recovery pathway rather than inferred from the review’s discussion of conservative care.

Neuraxial or regional techniques require individualized assessment of bleeding risk and neurologic context. The broad regional-anesthesia review identifies coagulopathy as a concern for neuraxial procedures because bleeding may cause spinal hematoma and neurologic injury.
