sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: When liposuction is combined, account for tumescent-fluid absorption and possible intravascular volume change; avoid assuming that infiltrated volume is equivalent to blood loss or that a fixed crystalloid total is appropriate.

Prioritize surgical hemostasis and evaluate blood loss and perfusion in clinical context. The procedure-specific source does not provide a fluid regimen, transfusion trigger, expected blood-loss value, or universal blood-availability requirement.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthetic infiltration and TAP and/or rectus sheath blocks are described options for abdominal-wall analgesia. Select technique and local anesthetic according to patient factors, planned procedures, and cumulative exposure; the abdominoplasty review supplies no drug dose or regimen.

Multimodal analgesia can combine regional/field techniques and systemic nonopioid agents, with opioids used sparingly where appropriate. Evidence in the plastic-surgery review supports multimodal strategies generally but notes that NSAIDs may not suit every procedure, including abdominoplasty.

Plan PONV prevention and treatment according to individual risk and applicable guidance. The available plastic-surgery source describes PONV-reduction as an ERAS goal but does not provide an abdominoplasty-specific prophylaxis regimen.

bullets: The abdominoplasty review does not specify an emergence or extubation protocol. If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative recovery before extubation; tailor other emergence decisions to the clinical situation rather than applying an unsupported procedure-specific recipe.

Provide postanesthesia care with continual evaluation appropriate to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Use quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase and communicate the operative and anesthetic course to the receiving nurse.
Postoperative surveillance should include wound drainage, hematoma or seroma, flap compromise, pain, and VTE; support mobilization and drain education as directed by the surgical team.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Implant-based reconstruction restores the breast mound after mastectomy using an implant/prosthesis approach; the available breast-reconstruction guidance also covers autologous reconstruction, so not every recommendation is implant-specific.

For cases using general anesthesia, the breast-reconstruction consensus recommends TIVA; it reports less PONV with TIVA than with volatile anesthesia. Use multimodal PONV prevention and opioid-sparing analgesia, individualized to the patient and procedure.

Prioritize temperature above 36°C and balanced fluid management that avoids both over- and under-resuscitation. The sources do not establish a case-specific fluid total or a universal role for invasive monitoring.

Recovery priorities include active assessment and treatment of PONV and pain, appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, and confirmation of adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when a neuromuscular blocker has been used.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The reconstructive objective is restoration of the breast mound following mastectomy. The available consensus covers both implant/prosthesis and autologous reconstruction; it does not provide a comparative selection rule for expander versus direct-to-implant techniques.

For anesthetic planning, distinguish implant-based surgery from free-flap reconstruction. Free-flap-specific monitoring, thrombosis, and donor-site recommendations should not be applied automatically to an implant-only case.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess smoking, obesity, and diabetes as potential modifiers of reconstructive surgical risk. The consensus recommends smoking abstinence before surgery and weight reduction for patients with obesity; individual feasibility and timing require clinical judgment.

Review medical status and develop an anesthesia-care plan. The supplied sources do not establish implant-specific eligibility criteria or validate the case-file claims about oncology clearance, prior chemotherapy, or radiation as anesthesia decision rules.

bullets: The breast-reconstruction consensus does not specify positioning, arm placement, vascular access, or routine invasive monitoring for this procedure. Select setup based on the planned operation and patient; do not treat the case-file positioning or arterial-line suggestions as established requirements.
Maintain standard anesthetic monitoring and monitor temperature when clinically indicated; breast-reconstruction guidance recommends active warming and maintaining temperature above 36°C.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The reconstruction consensus recommends general anesthesia with TIVA, but does not specify an airway device, airway-selection thresholds, or a ventilation strategy for implant-based cases. Choose these according to individual assessment rather than the unsupported case-file LMA/ETT thresholds.
When general anesthesia is given, continually evaluate ventilation and expired carbon dioxide; verify endotracheal tube or laryngeal-mask placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Use active warming and temperature monitoring. The consensus supports forced-air warming and prewarming as part of preventing hypothermia; it does not establish an implant-specific temperature-management protocol beyond its stated temperature recommendation.

TIVA is favored in the breast-reconstruction consensus partly for PONV reduction. Ensure prophylaxis is multimodal; the supplied evidence does not justify copying a fixed drug combination or dose from the case file.

bullets: Reduce infection risk with chlorhexidine skin preparation and intravenous antibiotics covering common skin organisms within one hour of incision. Prolonged antibiotics beyond 24 hours have not been proved beneficial.

bullets: Avoid both over-resuscitation and under-resuscitation; maintain water and electrolyte balance. The consensus recommends balanced crystalloids rather than saline and describes goal-directed therapy as useful.

bullets: Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia. The consensus lists NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, gabapentin, and local-anesthetic infiltration among options; selection should account for patient factors and operative considerations.

Treat PONV as an important recovery concern: use preoperative and intraoperative prophylaxis, with combined antiemetic classes supported over a single class in the consensus evidence. Neurokinin-1 antagonists, when selected, must be administered preoperatively; no doses are specified here.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The supplied evidence does not establish a usual technique for adult burn-scar reconstruction. It covers acute burn excision and coverage, and separately head-and-neck free-tissue transfer; these are related but not interchangeable procedures.

For extensive burn excision, substantial blood loss and hypothermia are important concerns. Free-flap evidence adds the need to avoid hypotension while also avoiding fluid overload; applicability depends on the operation performed.

Airway assessment should account for mouth opening, mandibular mobility, airway patency, and mask-ventilation feasibility. The acute-burn review supports considering fiberoptic intubation with spontaneous ventilation when these features are concerning; it does not establish a preferred device for reconstruction.

Recovery priorities include reassessing airway and respiratory status, temperature, circulation, and pain. If a free flap is performed, its postoperative monitoring is time-sensitive; ICU admission is not established as routine by the supplied evidence.

bullets: Assess airway patency, mouth opening, mandibular mobility, facial or glottic edema, and the feasibility of mask ventilation. Ask about inhalation injury and respiratory function where relevant; the acute-burn review notes that airway manifestations may be delayed.

Review nutrition, anemia, comorbidities, and prior treatment as potential modifiers if major reconstruction or free-tissue transfer is planned. The cited malnutrition and anemia risk discussion is from head-and-neck cancer reconstruction and should not be treated as a burn-specific risk estimate.
Anticipate that vascular access and monitoring sites may be limited by burn wounds or edema; establish feasible sites and a backup approach based on examination and operative needs.

Monitor temperature and use active warming strategies appropriate to exposure and procedure. Burn patients are described as vulnerable to, and intolerant of, hypothermia; free-flap evidence also emphasizes temperature maintenance.

For general anesthesia, apply basic monitoring standards, including continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

bullets: Choose airway management from the patient’s airway examination and the planned operation. Facial injury can make endotracheal-tube fixation difficult. Securement should avoid wound irritation or graft injury, and tube position should be reassessed when fixation or operative conditions could have changed.

bullets: Airway edema can evolve after initial assessment in acute burns, particularly during fluid resuscitation. Reassess airway status when clinical circumstances change; the source cautions against intubation without clear indications while emphasizing the risk of a later difficult airway.

If free-tissue transfer is performed, flap compromise is time-sensitive. Use the surgical team’s established monitoring pathway and escalate promptly for concerning clinical or Doppler findings; the source does not establish one monitoring device as superior.

Burn excision blood loss can be difficult to estimate because blood may be concealed or obscured by irrigation and dressings. Continue to reassess for bleeding rather than relying on a single estimate.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Complex wound care ranges from local-anesthetic laceration repair to major reconstructive free-flap surgery; the available evidence does not establish one usual anesthetic technique for all cases. Match the approach to wound extent, site, contamination, and reconstructive requirements.

For wound repair, assess and clean the wound, identify structural injury and bleeding, remove devitalized tissue when indicated, and restore deeper anatomy without undue tension. These principles are supported mainly for acute lacerations, not every operative debridement.

For free-flap reconstruction specifically, priorities include perfusion, avoidance of hypotension and hypothermia, and avoiding excessive fluid administration. Do not generalize these procedure-specific concerns into a fixed target or regimen for other wound procedures.

Recovery requires monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and patient, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Wound-specific dressing and hemodynamic review may also be relevant; no universal recovery protocol for complex wound closure is established here.

Review abdominal and chest scars, prior operations, hernia history, radiation or chemotherapy, and donor- and recipient-site anatomy. Imaging methods may be used to map perforators and plan the flap.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Coordinate access and workflow for chest and abdominal operative sites with the surgical team. The available case-specific reviews do not establish a standard patient position, arm position, vascular-access configuration, or room layout.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards require ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; arterial pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

Agree on a flap-monitoring method and communication/escalation pathway with the microsurgical team. Clinical assessment and Doppler or tissue-oxygen technologies are described; no particular system is established as superior.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is used in reported practice, sometimes combined with regional techniques. The supplied DIEP-specific evidence does not specify an airway device, airway approach, or ventilation protocol; determine these from patient, procedure, and team needs.

During general anesthesia, follow basic ventilation monitoring standards, including continual evaluation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to cases without NMB.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid hypothermia with temperature monitoring and active warming. The DIEP review reports varying temperature recommendations, so do not convert an isolated numerical target into a universal threshold without considering its source and context.

Maintain perfusion while avoiding fluid overload. Hypotension management should account for volume status and the possibility of impaired flap flow; communicate planned interventions and their effects with the surgical team.

Do not categorically avoid vasopressors or assume one anesthetic agent is required for flap success. The DIEP-specific review describes vasopressor use as controversial and reports no consensus on the optimal anesthetic combination.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Microvascular compromise, including venous thrombosis or pedicle kinking, is time-sensitive. A change in clinical or device monitoring findings warrants prompt communication with the surgical team and urgent evaluation for possible re-exploration.

Anticipate donor-site bleeding, seroma, wound problems, and abdominal-wall morbidity; bilateral reconstruction and donor-site technique may affect morbidity. Escalate suspected bleeding or perfusion compromise rather than relying on an assumed expected blood loss.

VTE and PONV are relevant postoperative hazards. Recognize and escalate suspected thromboembolism or significant respiratory/hemodynamic deterioration; the sources do not establish a single prevention or rescue protocol for every patient.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize fluid therapy to support circulating volume and flap perfusion while limiting edema and overload. Both under-resuscitation and excess fluid may be harmful; available sources do not justify a universal total volume or rate.
Use hemodynamic and clinical context to guide fluid decisions; goal-directed approaches are reported in some settings, not established as obligatory or uniformly superior.

Assess blood loss and anemia clinically and individualize transfusion decisions. The supplied DIEP review reports clinical-indication-based transfusion and cautions that transfusion associations vary with operative duration and extent; no threshold is prescribed here.

Plan VTE prophylaxis according to individual risk and the surgical team’s assessment of thrombosis and bleeding. Evidence summarized for intraoperative and postoperative antithrombotic strategies is mixed; do not infer a universal heparin regimen.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Consider general anesthesia with regional analgesia as part of multimodal, opioid-sparing care. Described options include TAP, pectoral, epidural, and paravertebral techniques; choice should reflect patient factors, anticoagulation considerations, and local expertise.

A reported ERAS pathway used scheduled nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, and gabapentin, with muscle relaxants and tramadol as needed and narcotics as a fifth-line pain-control option. For patients requiring anticoagulants, a review describes patient-controlled IV analgesia (PCIA) to avoid potential epidural hematoma.

Provide risk-appropriate PONV prevention and rescue planning. PONV may increase abdominal pressure and contribute to donor-site complications; no single drug regimen is established by these sources for all patients.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied procedure-specific sources do not establish an extubation method or timing. If NMB was used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation; otherwise base emergence and disposition on the patient’s clinical status.

After anesthesia, provide PACU or equivalent care with monitoring appropriate to the patient, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; use pulse oximetry during the initial recovery phase.

Continue flap assessment and promptly escalate concerning changes. Ward, step-down, or ICU disposition should be determined by clinical needs and the ability to provide reliable monitoring; selected series outcomes do not establish universal eligibility for early discharge.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The facelift review describes general anesthesia as preferred and an endotracheal tube placed in the midline and monitored closely. A separate retrospective cohort studied selected patients undergoing face and neck lifts to correct PMMA filler-related deformities under local anesthesia; it does not establish routine anesthetic practice.

Hematoma is the dominant procedure-specific concern. Hypertension is a controllable risk factor, so perioperative blood-pressure management and prompt recognition of expanding neck or facial swelling matter; a large hematoma can threaten the airway.

Manage blood pressure, pain, anxiety, nausea, and vomiting across the perioperative course. The source supports strict multimodal control but does not establish a universal numeric blood-pressure target or a particular emergence drug regimen.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring and appropriate postanesthesia observation. The reviewed surgical practice kept patients overnight, but this is an author-reported practice rather than a universal disposition requirement.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The reviewed operation involves facial skin flaps and work around the SMAS. Surgical extent and technique vary; the available sources do not support one universal facelift approach or a specific operative plan for every patient.

A short-scar rhytidectomy with SMAS plication is described in a cohort treated for deformities after permanent filler. That cohort excluded general anesthesia and should not be used to define the usual anesthetic or operative approach for routine rhytidectomy.

In the filler-revision cohort, the stated objective was filler and inflammatory-lesion removal with facial shaping to restore symmetry and contour; this is a subgroup-specific indication, not a general description of all facelifts.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review medical history, examination, medications, and supplements, with attention to blood thinners, hypertension, and nicotine-product use. The surgical review calls for medical optimization of hypertension and necessary medical clearance; it does not specify an anticoagulant interruption interval.

Nicotine exposure is a skin-flap risk modifier. The review recommends cessation before surgery and describes urine nicotine testing in smokers as the authors’ practice; assess applicability rather than treating this as a society standard.

The article recommends EKG and laboratory testing for patients older than 50. This is a recommendation within a surgical review, not a universal anesthesia-testing rule; testing should be based on the individual’s clinical assessment and applicable policy.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Blood pressure and heart rate are determined and evaluated at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standard.

Positioning is not established by the general facelift review. One local-anesthetic filler-revision cohort used supine positioning with a neutral head and eye protection; do not generalize that setup as a required position for all rhytidectomies.
Plan access and equipment around the chosen technique and the surgical field. Available facelift sources do not establish a routine arterial line, vascular-access configuration, or room layout.

bullets: General anesthesia is preferred in the surgical review, which describes a midline endotracheal tube with close intraoperative monitoring. This is an author-described technique; the sources do not establish an LMA preference or a universal airway device.

The ASA monitoring standard requires confirmation of airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, with continual quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis from placement until removal or transfer begins.

bullets: Prioritize blood-pressure control throughout surgery because hypertension is a controllable hematoma risk factor. The source supports strict multimodal management but provides no validated numeric target for this procedure.

Address anxiety, pain, nausea, and vomiting proactively as part of the source-described approach to reducing perioperative symptoms and complications. Specific drug choices and doses are not established here as universal regimens.
The authors avoid nitrous oxide because of postoperative nausea concerns and inhalational anesthetics because of vasodilation concerns.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: The review identifies hematoma as the most common reported complication after rhytidectomy, with an incidence of 0.9%–9%; it identifies hypertension as a controllable risk factor. Prompt recognition is emphasized because large hematomas can compromise the airway, and large hematomas require return to the operating room.

Other complications identified include seroma, nerve injury, and skin-flap necrosis. The review describes risk-reduction measures as part of the surgical approach, but does not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue algorithm for these events.

Escalate urgently when expanding hematoma or airway compromise is suspected; the source specifies return to the operating room for large hematomas. It describes aspiration for selected small hematomas after liquefaction, rather than as an immediate substitute for managing a threatening collection.

bullets: The review does not report blood-loss estimates, transfusion criteria, or an IV-fluid regimen.

A closed-suction neck drain is described in the review’s surgical technique; drain placement and management are operative decisions, not a universal anesthesia requirement.

bullets: The source emphasizes preemptive management of pain and nausea/vomiting, given their relevance to perioperative blood-pressure and hematoma management. It does not establish a universal analgesic regimen.

The review describes antiemetic use, including dexamethasone and ondansetron, as part of its authors’ practice. It notes conflicting evidence regarding dexamethasone and does not support treating that regimen as mandatory or universally optimal.
The reviewed source does not give a general postoperative analgesic plan. Tailor analgesia to the patient and procedure while maintaining attention to nausea, pain, and blood pressure.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The facelift review supports strict postoperative blood-pressure, pain, and nausea management but does not specify an emergence technique or establish a cough-suppression drug regimen. Avoid presenting a specific emergence recipe as evidence-based standard care.

In postanesthesia care, continually evaluate the patient and monitor according to clinical condition, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

The facelift review reports overnight admission in the authors’ practice. It does not establish a universal recovery location or duration; disposition should follow the clinical assessment and institutional requirements.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Gender-affirming operations span chest, facial, reproductive-organ and genital procedures; anesthetic approaches vary by operation and patient, from local anesthesia with sedation or regional techniques to general anesthesia.

Assess current and prior hormone therapy, comorbidities, medications, and individual VTE risk. Available evidence does not support routine preoperative cessation of estrogen for patients without specific risk factors; decisions require individualized discussion.

Plan for procedure-specific airway challenges, especially after facial or voice procedures. For microsurgical free-flap cases, prioritize maintaining perfusion and normothermia while avoiding fluid overload; the available flap evidence is not specific to gender-affirming surgery.
Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia observation, multimodal pain and PONV management, dignity-centered communication, and coordinated surveillance when a free flap is present.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The procedural range includes chest reconstruction, facial procedures, reproductive-organ removal, vaginoplasty, metoidioplasty, phalloplasty and related reconstruction. Anatomy and operative extent must be established for the planned procedure rather than inferred from gender identity.

Anesthetic options differ by procedure: the review lists general, regional, and local-anesthetic-with-sedation approaches across breast, genital, facial and pitch-altering procedures. These are options, not a universal technique hierarchy.
Some phalloplasty procedures use a microsurgical free flap. The supplied gender-affirming review does not establish a procedure-specific anesthetic protocol for these cases.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the hormone regimen and duration, prior gender-affirming procedures, medical conditions and medication interactions. Consider the patient’s psychosocial needs and readiness without treating a particular clearance process as established by these sources.

Estrogen-associated VTE risk is a relevant modifier, but risk evidence in transgender people is mixed. Assess individual risk factors and discuss any hormone change with the patient and prescribing clinician; do not apply a routine cessation rule.

Testosterone is not routinely required to be stopped before elective surgery according to the review; assess relevant hematologic, hepatic and cardiovascular context rather than assuming a uniform effect.

Ask about chest binding and prior facial or voice procedures, and review psychotropic and antiretroviral medications for potential interactions. Laboratory interpretation during hormone therapy has limitations.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use respectful, privacy-conscious communication: confirm and consistently use the patient’s preferred name and pronouns, limit unnecessary room traffic, and avoid unnecessary questions.

Positioning and access should be planned for the actual operation and duration. The gender-affirming review does not provide specific positioning or vascular-access recommendations; do not infer a universal lithotomy setup or repositioning schedule.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the chosen technique. ASA standards require ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment during anesthesia.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Assess airway history and anatomy, including prior facial reconstruction and voice-pitch procedures. These can complicate mask ventilation or be associated with tracheal stenosis, vocal-cord injury or other airway changes.

A difficult-airway plan is particularly relevant when prior laryngeal or facial procedures may alter airway access or assessment. Case reports of unexpected difficult airway after vocal feminization qualify a hazard; they do not establish a routine airway device or technique.

Do not impose endotracheal intubation or general anesthesia for every gender-affirming procedure: the review lists local anesthesia with sedation and regional techniques for selected procedure categories as well as general anesthesia.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For procedures involving urethral reconstruction, anticipate that urinary catheterization may be difficult; coordinate with the surgical team and seek appropriate urologic assistance when needed.

Review possible hormone-related drug interactions and altered pharmacokinetics. The literature does not provide validated anesthesia-delivery adjustments for transgender patients receiving hormone therapy.

When a microsurgical free flap is used, preserve perfusion and normothermia and avoid fluid overload. These principles are supported by free-flap literature from other surgical populations and are not validated as a gender-surgery-specific protocol.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Remain alert to VTE and pulmonary embolism in the context of individual risk, estrogen exposure, immobility and extensive surgery. Available evidence does not establish a universal prophylaxis regimen for these procedures.
Reported surgical complications include rectal injury, rectovaginal fistula, urethral stricture, fistula, and incontinence.

For flap compromise, prompt recognition and coordination with the microsurgical team are central. Free-flap review evidence describes thrombosis as time-sensitive, but its rates and salvage estimates come from head-and-neck reconstruction, not gender-affirming phalloplasty.

sources.label: Perioperative considerations for person-centered gender affirming surgery

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use case-specific assessment to maintain perfusion without excessive fluid administration in free-flap surgery. Available reviews describe risks at both extremes but do not establish a gender-affirming-surgery fluid volume or rate.

Anticipate blood loss according to the operation and coordinate blood-management planning with the surgical team. The gender-affirming review provides no procedure-specific blood-loss data or transfusion protocol.

Vasopressor use in free-flap surgery is debated; the broader review reports studies without a demonstrated increase in flap complications, while emphasizing adequate volume status and individualized use. Do not treat this as a universal drug or target recommendation.

bullets: Use an individualized multimodal analgesic approach that accounts for prior pain, psychological contributors and the procedure. Regional or neuraxial techniques are options for selected cases, not requirements.
Evidence cited for epidural supplementation after penile-inversion vaginoplasty reports lower opioid consumption, but the review supplies neither a specific regimen nor an effect size.
Use evidence-based PONV prophylaxis based on the clinical context. Transgender-specific PONV risk has not been empirically established, so do not infer risk from gender identity alone.

bullets: Provide monitored postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature. Recovery location and disposition depend on clinical needs; no gender-surgery-specific rule is established here.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are supported by ASA guidance. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.
For a free flap, coordinate postoperative surveillance with the reconstructive team. The gender-affirming source does not establish a monitoring schedule or disposition protocol.

bullets: The supplied hand-specific sources describe local infiltration and peripheral nerve blocks for hand and wrist procedures, but do not establish a usual anesthetic technique for flap coverage. They do not support a default general anesthetic or regional-only plan for this operation.

The evidence-supported priorities are to avoid preventable local-anesthetic injury and recognize systemic toxicity; hand-specific tourniquet strategy and flap-perfusion targets are not established by the supplied sources.

If a free flap is used, clinical examination and Doppler assessment are described for free-flap monitoring in other reconstructive populations; applying those recommendations to hand flaps requires case-specific judgment.

Use applicable basic anesthetic and postanesthesia standards; if neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative recovery assessment at the adductor pollicis is recommended before extubation. These standards do not determine the anesthetic technique for hand flap surgery.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The case concerns coverage of hand or digit defects with a flap. The supplied sources discuss bedside hand/wrist procedures and several common hand operations, but do not describe operative selection, design, or anesthetic management specifically for flap coverage.

Local infiltration and regional nerve blocks are described options for hand and wrist procedures; the hand review does not prescribe one technique for each operation. Do not treat these descriptions as a recommendation for flap coverage or as evidence that sedation or general anesthesia is unnecessary.

WALANT is described for selected common hand procedures and minor trauma, typically using locally infiltrated lidocaine with epinephrine without tourniquet, sedation, brachial plexus block, or general anesthesia. That evidence does not establish this approach for flap coverage.

bullets: Confirm the patient can communicate symptoms during any nerve block. The hand review advises against nerve blockade when the patient cannot report possible intraneural injection, including when intubated or sedated; distorted landmarks may also make a block inappropriate.

Consider whether circulation is compromised before using epinephrine-containing local anesthetic in a digit or distal extremity. The review describes support for standard concentrations in the literature but specifically advises caution with compromised circulation; it does not provide a patient-selection protocol for flap surgery.
Consider local-anesthetic systemic toxicity risk: LAST is dose-dependent and can follow excessive tissue administration or direct intravascular delivery.

bullets: No supplied hand-specific source establishes an airway device, induction technique, or default need for general anesthesia for flap coverage. The hand local-anesthesia review explicitly does not provide airway management or general-anesthetic regimens.

bullets: When performing a nerve block, use real-time patient feedback and withdraw the needle immediately if the patient reports an electric-shock sensation or nerve-distribution paresthesia. The source cautions against blocks when the patient cannot provide this feedback.

WALANT literature describes epinephrine-containing local anesthetic as a means of hemostasis instead of a tourniquet for the procedures reviewed. It does not establish a tourniquet policy for flap coverage or support assuming that tourniquet use is required or avoided.

If epinephrine is considered for a digit, account for the source's stated caution in patients with compromised circulation; its review-level reassurance for otherwise healthy patients is not a guarantee of safety in an individual flap.

bullets: Consider local-anesthetic systemic toxicity after excessive tissue administration or inadvertent intravascular delivery. Reported early manifestations include muscle twitching, tinnitus, headache, confusion, and metallic taste; more severe toxicity can include loss of consciousness, convulsions, coma, respiratory depression, and death.
If LAST is suspected, stop injection, call for help, stabilize vital signs, treat seizures (for example, with benzodiazepines), and initiate 20% intravenous lipid emulsion therapy.

The source notes that epinephrine vasoconstriction in a finger can be reversed with phentolamine, but describes reversal as almost never clinically required. This review statement is not a substitute for local emergency protocols or individualized assessment.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The hand anesthesia review is a clinical and literature review, not a guideline or trial; its primary focus is bedside hand and wrist procedures and it does not prescribe technique for each operation. It is the most directly relevant supplied source, but does not resolve flap-coverage anesthesia.

The WALANT review covers selected common hand operations and minor trauma; it is not a comprehensive perioperative anesthesia reference and does not supply airway, positioning, monitoring, fluid, or postoperative protocols.

The two free-flap reviews concern head-and-neck reconstruction and abdominal-based breast reconstruction, respectively. Their procedure-specific fluid, monitoring, analgesic, and recovery recommendations cannot be assumed to establish care for hand flaps.

ASA basic monitoring, preanesthesia, and postanesthesia standards support general anesthesia-care processes, not a case-specific anesthetic plan. The supplied basic preanesthesia page is brief and does not provide detailed assessment or management recommendations.
Unresolved, case-relevant evidence needs include flap-type-specific anesthesia selection and hand-flap surveillance and rescue pathways. The provided sources do not establish these points.
The hand-anesthesia review does not specify patient-selection criteria, contraindications, or a preoperative assessment protocol.
The supplied hand-anesthesia review provides no fluid-management guidance or fluid volumes.
The supplied hand-anesthesia review does not provide an emergence protocol or detailed postoperative surveillance instructions.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Local flap reconstruction moves adjacent, vascularized tissue into a defect; the advancement-flap chapter describes movement directly into the defect, while the case series includes several local and regional flap types.

For advancement flaps, local anesthesia is usual; general anesthesia may be needed for more complex or extensive reconstruction. The available sources do not establish one anesthetic technique for every local flap.
The central flap-specific concern is preserving perfusion: avoid overstretching or narrowing the flap, and assess color and turgor for early signs of vascular compromise.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and attention to flap appearance. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative confirmation of recovery applies before extubation; it is not a requirement for cases without blockade.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Advancement flaps move adjacent tissue directly into a defect; the chapter groups advancement and rotation flaps as “sliding” flaps. It also describes transposition and other named techniques, but does not provide a single operative method applicable to all defects.

Local-flap reconstruction is described when a wound is too large for primary suturing and grafting or local wound care is not feasible. If adjacent tissue cannot advance adequately, the chapter identifies alternative vascularized tissue transfer or grafting as options to explore.
The sources include local and regional soft-tissue flap procedures, but do not establish that a particular flap type, anesthetic, or operative setting is appropriate for every defect.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess whether surrounding tissue can be advanced and whether scarring, infection, inflammation, or prior radiation may impede movement of healthy adjacent tissue; the chapter identifies these as reasons to explore alternatives.

Recent smoking history is identified as a relative contraindication in the advancement-flap chapter. This is a risk modifier, not a universal prohibition; the source also cautions about habitual tobacco users.

For WALANT flap surgery, the case-series authors identify vascular disease and allergy to lidocaine or epinephrine as reasons patients at their center were not considered suitable. This is a report of that series’ selection practice, not a universal eligibility rule for local-flap surgery.

Successful Use of WALANT in Local and Regional Soft Tissue Flaps: A Case Series

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: No procedure-specific operative positioning or vascular-access plan is established in these sources. Position should therefore be determined by the defect and surgical approach rather than inferred from this reference.

For general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or monitored anesthesia care, the ASA standards call for continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every five minutes.

When local anesthesia is administered without sedation, ventilation is assessed by continual observation of qualitative clinical signs under the ASA standard. Monitoring during the WALANT series’ holding-area injections was not reported as a general monitoring protocol.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The sources do not establish a routine airway device or airway technique for local-flap surgery. The advancement-flap chapter states that general anesthesia may be necessary for more complex or extensive reconstruction; airway planning remains dependent on the selected anesthetic and operation.

If general anesthesia is used, the ASA standard requires continual ventilation assessment and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the nature of the patient, procedure, or equipment invalidates it. If an LMA or endotracheal tube is inserted, verify position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Protect flap perfusion by avoiding excessive stretch or narrowing. The chapter notes that excessive thinning can disrupt the subdermal plexus and that pressure from hematoma or edema can contribute to vascular compromise.

In the WALANT case series, authors caution that epinephrine should be injected adjacent to the flap-harvest incision, not over or deep to the vascular pedicle. This is a reported technique-specific precaution and does not establish a universal local-anesthetic regimen.

The case series allowed time for anesthetic effect before incision in two more involved flap types to obtain a hemostatic field; it does not establish a general timing requirement for other flap procedures.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Monitor for changes in flap color and turgor. The chapter describes a swollen, firm, dusky flap as suggestive of venous insufficiency and a pale, cool flap as suggestive of arterial insufficiency.
Vascular compromise is identified as the most common cause of partial or total flap necrosis in the chapter; venous congestion is described as more common than arterial inflow obstruction.

The chapter describes reducing closure tension, draining an underlying hematoma, and treating infection as measures that may address identified contributors to compromised circulation. Suspected compromise warrants prompt surgical assessment; the available sources do not establish a single troubleshooting pathway for all cases.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No case-specific fluid, blood-loss, transfusion, or hemodynamic target is established for local-flap surgery in the available sources. Individualize management to the patient and operation rather than applying a fixed volume or target.
The advancement-flap chapter discusses bleeding and hematoma as complications and notes that appropriate intraoperative hemostasis is relevant; it does not provide a blood-management protocol.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local anesthesia is usual for advancement flaps in the educational chapter; more extensive reconstruction may require general anesthesia. The sources do not establish a postoperative analgesic regimen for local-flap surgery.

The WALANT series reports that no patients were prescribed postoperative opioids, but its small, single-surgeon case series does not establish that opioid-free care is suitable for every patient or flap procedure.
A PONV-prophylaxis regimen specific to local-flap surgery is not provided in these sources.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After anesthesia, the patient should receive postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent location unless specifically ordered otherwise by the responsible anesthesiologist. Continually evaluate the patient and monitor as appropriate, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Evaluate flap appearance and wound status during recovery. The advancement-flap chapter identifies color and turgor changes as early signs of vascular compromise; detailed recovery-room intervals are not established for local flaps.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis apply before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to procedures performed without neuromuscular blockade.

bullets: The WALANT flap evidence is a retrospective series of 21 patients from one surgeon, with no comparison group; it does not report adult-specific outcomes, airway management, or comparative anesthesia outcomes. It cannot establish a general anesthetic standard.

Free-flap reviews concern microvascular free-tissue transfer and breast reconstruction, not routine local-flap coverage; their procedure-specific recommendations should not be imported as local-flap standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Panniculectomy removes excess abdominal skin and subcutaneous tissue to relieve functional symptoms; it is not cosmetic abdominoplasty. General anesthesia is typical, but the available procedure sources do not establish a specific anesthetic technique.

The major procedure-specific concerns are compromised abdominal tissue perfusion, wound-healing problems, seroma, and bleeding. Preserve tissue vascularity and anticipate that large resections can involve significant bleeding.

VTE prevention and early mobilization are important perioperative priorities. The procedure-specific review recommends risk stratification and mechanical prophylaxis; pharmacologic prophylaxis is part of the authors’ described practice, not a universal patient-specific prescription.

Recovery should include the procedure-specific bent-at-the-waist, semi-Fowler positioning and postanesthesia observation. When neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm quantitative recovery to a TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation excises excess abdominal skin and subcutaneous tissue en bloc to address a large overhanging panniculus and improve function. It is distinguished from abdominoplasty: panniculectomy does not tighten or plicate the abdominal wall muscle.

The source describes limited undermining because tissue vascularity may be compromised, particularly after massive weight loss. Incision and resection extent depend on anatomy and surgical planning; the source discusses possible removal of the umbilicus when excision extends above it.

Large-volume cases may require specialized exposure equipment. The practical review describes suspension systems to improve visualization; this is a surgical setup option, not a required anesthetic technique.

sources.label: Panniculectomy — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Panniculectomy: Practical Pearls and Pitfalls

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess comorbidities, prior abdominal operations and scars, diabetes, smoking or nicotine exposure, weight stability, nutritional status, and possible hernia. The procedure is elective; the source advises deferral when important medical problems are uncontrolled.

Post-bariatric patients may have micronutrient or protein deficiencies relevant to wound healing. Review nutritional history and available evaluation; the source does not establish a universal laboratory panel or correction regimen for anesthesia.

Discuss expectations, wound risks, and the practical demands of postoperative care. Procedure sources emphasize stable weight and readiness for potential complications, but do not provide an anesthesia-specific risk score or selection algorithm.

sources.label: Panniculectomy — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Panniculectomy: Practical Pearls and Pitfalls

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan equipment and table capacity for the anticipated panniculus and resection. A bariatric bed and, in selected large cases, a suspension system are described; individual equipment needs depend on the operative plan.

The supplied procedure sources do not specify a routine intraoperative patient position. The practical review describes placing the patient supine to confirm markings, which does not establish the operative position.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, including ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is typical in the procedure description, but the panniculectomy sources specify no airway device, airway technique, or airway risk. They therefore do not support a universal intubation or induction plan.

When general anesthesia with an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is used, verify placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide; continue quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis through the stated anesthetic period.
No panniculectomy-specific ventilation strategy or airway management recommendation is established in the supplied procedure literature.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The central abdominal skin’s blood supply can be interrupted during flap elevation; prior scars may also compromise vascular territories. Surgical sources emphasize conservative dissection and preservation of perfusion.

Large superficial vessels may cause substantial bleeding and impair visualization. The practical review describes ligation as the senior author’s approach; it should not be represented as a universal anesthetic or surgical standard.

Thermal injury to skin edges is identified as a potential contributor to necrosis and breakdown; the review describes sharp skin incision before electrocautery for subsequent dissection and selected hemostasis.

sources.label: Panniculectomy — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Wound complications include cellulitis, dehiscence, and tissue necrosis; the source associates these with relative hypoperfusion and poor adipose-tissue blood supply. Recognize evolving wound compromise and coordinate surgical assessment and wound care.

Seroma is a common complication, particularly after larger dissection. Drains are used in the described surgical care; the source emphasizes preserving Scarpa fascia and minimizing dissection as preventive measures.

Hematoma may require surgical exploration if it expands, bleeding persists, or drain blood is bright red. These are surgical-source warning features; no anesthesia-specific intervention algorithm is supplied.

VTE risk reflects operative duration, extensive dissection, and postoperative inactivity. The practical review describes preoperative risk stratification, compression devices, and mobilization; prophylaxis choices require individualized assessment.

sources.label: Panniculectomy — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Panniculectomy: Practical Pearls and Pitfalls

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Bleeding can be clinically important in large-volume resections, but the supplied panniculectomy sources do not establish a fluid protocol, transfusion threshold, or hemodynamic target. Base management on the observed clinical course and applicable institutional practice.
Avoid treating a fixed fluid volume as a procedure standard. A separate panniculectomy review similarly states that it provides no fluid-management or transfusion protocol.
Perfusion of the abdominal flap is a central surgical concern; dissection and closure planning should account for the potentially limited blood supply of elevated tissue.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The practical review describes multimodal postoperative analgesia with limited breakthrough opioid use, but this is the authors’ practice rather than a universal regimen. Select an approach appropriate to the patient and local protocols.
Panniculectomy-specific sources do not establish a single analgesic technique or drug regimen. One source explicitly states that analgesic medications and techniques are not specified.
PONV prophylaxis is included in the practical review’s broader perioperative analgesia approach, but no panniculectomy-specific prophylaxis regimen is established by the supplied sources.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation. This recommendation applies to blockade management, not to cases without neuromuscular blockers.

Postanesthesia care should include continuous evaluation appropriate to the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.
For wound protection, patients are instructed to remain bent at the waist 30 degrees in a semi-Fowler position for one week, then slowly return to fully upright.
The procedure literature does not establish extubation criteria or a procedure-specific postoperative respiratory protocol.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The panniculectomy sources are procedural reviews, not anesthesia guidelines. They describe general anesthesia as typical but do not specify airway management, anesthetic drugs, monitoring protocols, or an anesthetic regimen.

The practical-pearls article is a narrative review reflecting the senior author’s experience and literature review, not a comprehensive guideline or comparative trial. Its institution- or author-specific practices should not be generalized automatically.

General ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards, and the neuromuscular-blockade guideline, support only the domains within their stated scope; they do not fill procedure-specific anesthetic planning gaps.

Available sources do not establish a case-specific anesthetic technique, airway or ventilation strategy for patients with obesity or sleep-disordered breathing, or an individualized fluid and bleeding-management protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Reconstruction follows excision and debridement of a deep pressure sore; coverage may use primary closure or a local flap, selected according to wound site, size, and the operative team’s approach.

The central perioperative concerns supported by these sources are wound infection control, adequate debridement and nutrition, and postoperative wound complications including dehiscence, necrosis, or flap failure.

Anesthetic technique and positioning should be determined for the individual patient and operation; the pressure-ulcer sources do not establish a usual anesthetic, airway, monitoring, or fluid regimen.

Recovery priorities described for this operation are wound care, nutrition, regular turning to avoid sustained pressure, and control of underlying medical problems; anesthetic recovery should meet general postanesthesia standards.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative principle is to excise devitalized tissue and cover the resulting wound with durable, well-perfused tissue. Local flaps may be musculocutaneous, fasciocutaneous, or perforator flaps, with rotation, advancement, or island designs.

The reported team’s site- and size-based examples include V–Y or SGAP flaps for sacral wounds and tensor fascia lata or pedicled anterolateral thigh flaps for trochanteric wounds. These are reported choices, not universal selection rules.

Primary closure is another option in selected wounds. In one retrospective cohort, eligibility for primary closure with closed-incision negative-pressure therapy required no residual necrotic tissue after debridement, good infection control and nutritional support, and wound edges that could be approximated.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess wound extent and condition, infection control, debridement needs, nutritional support, and whether the proposed reconstruction and postoperative care are feasible for the patient’s circumstances.
The clinical series excluded patients considered unfit for anesthesia, but did not specify how fitness was assessed. It therefore does not supply an anesthesia-specific risk-stratification method.
Plan care in context of the patient’s support and wound-care needs; the source describes multidisciplinary input and emphasizes family education, rehabilitation, and social support.

bullets: Position is not established as a standard by the pressure-ulcer sources. They report lateral decubitus positioning in one case and prone positioning in another; the procedure article gives no general positioning recommendation.
Use the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards: qualified anesthesia personnel remain present, and oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature are continually evaluated.
Basic standards also require continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

bullets: The available sources do not establish an airway device or anesthetic technique for pressure-ulcer reconstruction. One discussion notes intubation for prone sacral flap reconstruction, but does not provide airway-management details or make it a universal approach.

When general anesthesia is used, follow basic ventilation monitoring standards, including continual assessment of ventilation and expired carbon dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

bullets: The supported surgical priorities are complete excision of devitalized tissue and coverage with well-perfused tissue. The sources do not define anesthetic physiologic targets or procedure-specific critical anesthesia phases.

Temperature monitoring is part of basic anesthesia standards when clinically significant temperature change is intended, anticipated, or suspected; the pressure-ulcer series provides no procedure-specific temperature target.

For selected SGAP and pedicled anterolateral thigh flaps, the reported team used intraoperative fluorescence imaging to identify compromised areas; this is a described surgical adjunct, not a general anesthesia requirement.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: In a single-surgeon series of 117 patients with stage III or IV pressure sores, reported minor complications included partial dehiscence and necrosis (20.3%; 28 patients), while major complications included flap failure and dehiscence (7.2%; 10 patients). These are cohort findings, not individualized predictions.
The same series found complications associated with larger flap area; interpret this as an observational association rather than a causal estimate or a rule for flap selection.

The sources do not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue algorithm for flap compromise or wound complications. Escalate concerns through the operative and surgical teams; do not infer a treatment protocol from these cohort reports.

bullets: The pressure-ulcer studies do not specify emergence or extubation management. Apply the anesthetic plan and general postanesthesia standards to the individual patient rather than assuming a particular airway or disposition.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Rhinoplasty may address cosmetic and functional goals, often with septoplasty or other nasal procedures. The described operating-room approach uses general anesthesia with orotracheal intubation; TIVA with propofol and remifentanil is commonly preferred by clinicians described in the source.

Prior nasal surgery, bleeding risks, hypertension, and intranasal drug use can alter preoperative planning. Active cocaine use is a reason to avoid elective nasal surgery; the source does not establish a cocaine-specific anesthetic treatment protocol.

The principal intraoperative priorities supported here are access to the nasal field, limiting bleeding, and smooth emergence. TIVA is described as providing permissive hypotension to decrease bleeding and reducing coughing, agitation, and nausea on emergence; no numeric blood-pressure target is established.

Recovery should include attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with procedure-specific follow-up for bleeding, edema, and nasal obstruction. The available sources do not establish a rhinoplasty-specific throat-pack or extubation protocol.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Open Rhinoplasty
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Rhinoplasty may be undertaken for functional, aesthetic, gender-affirming, oncologic, or traumatic-reconstruction goals; patients may have both functional and aesthetic aims. Establish the planned components because the source describes a range of possible procedures rather than one uniform operation.

Open, endonasal, and tip-delivery approaches are described. Open exposure is commonly used for tip modification and may be used in primary or revision surgery; endonasal approaches can address dorsal and selected lower-third structures.

Revision surgery may be more difficult because of scar tissue and previous cartilage manipulation. The anesthetic plan should reflect the actual operative extent and access requirements; the sources do not establish a single anesthetic for every approach.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Open Rhinoplasty

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify functional symptoms, patient goals, expectations, prior nasal procedures, and airway history. Assess relevant comorbidities, including OSA, hypertension, sinus disease, bleeding disorders, and recreational drug use.

Review anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs, supplements, and bleeding history; poorly controlled hypertension is also identified as a bleeding or septal-hematoma risk modifier. Medication changes require individualized clinical assessment rather than a universal stop interval.

Active cocaine use is a reason to avoid elective nasal surgery. For prior use, the source recommends individualized consideration because impaired healing may persist; it does not specify a time interval that resolves this risk.

Identify body dysmorphic disorder and poorly controlled depression when assessing expectations; referral or deferral may be appropriate. OSA-related postoperative oxygenation difficulty may affect disposition planning.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Open Rhinoplasty

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The described setup is supine with arms tucked and the head of the bed slightly elevated for access and to decrease bleeding. Protect the eyes before local anesthetic injection.

With the described orotracheal technique, the tube is taped at the midline of the lower lip to keep it out of the operative field and avoid distorting the lower nose. Expose the midface; additional access may be needed if graft harvest is planned.

Apply applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes during anesthesia.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The rhinoplasty review describes general anesthesia with orotracheal intubation. It does not specify a particular tube design or provide a procedure-specific airway rescue plan.

TIVA with propofol and remifentanil is preferred by many clinicians described in the source; the article associates it with permissive hypotension and less coughing, agitation, and nausea on emergence. This is a reported preference, not a universal requirement or a dose regimen.

For every patient receiving general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation. After endotracheal-tube or laryngeal-mask placement, verify correct positioning by clinical assessment and identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas; continue quantitative end-tidal CO₂ analysis until extubation/removal or initiation of transfer to a postoperative care location.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: TIVA is described as an approach that can provide permissive hypotension to decrease bleeding. The sources provide no rhinoplasty-specific numeric blood-pressure target; avoid converting this reported technique into a fixed target.

Local infiltration and nasal decongestant pledgets are part of the described surgical preparation. The review lists lidocaine with epinephrine and pledgets soaked in oxymetazoline or cocaine; the choice and use are described in the surgical source, not as an anesthesia drug protocol.

The source advises allowing time for local vasoconstriction and describes tranexamic acid as a possible measure to reduce bleeding and postoperative ecchymosis or edema. It does not establish either as mandatory for every case.

sources.label: Rhinoplasty — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Epistaxis, ecchymosis, edema, and persistent or new functional or cosmetic deficits are recognized postoperative concerns. Assess bleeding clinically; the source notes hypertension and coagulopathy should be evaluated when postoperative bleeding persists.

Persistent nasal bleeding may require further evaluation and, rarely, packing; the source describes packing as generally reserved for persistent bleeding. It does not provide an intraoperative blood-loss expectation or a universal intervention threshold.

A septal hematoma requires prompt recognition and drainage in the source’s procedure-specific discussion. If abscess is suspected, the source advises immediate antibiotics; these are surgical complication-management statements, not an anesthetic rescue algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The source describes permissive hypotension with TIVA as a means of decreasing bleeding, but gives no numeric target. Blood-pressure management should therefore be individualized; the available material does not support a fixed MAP range for rhinoplasty.

Postoperative bleeding is often mild; head elevation and nasal decongestant sprays are described as measures that may help. Compression is usually discouraged because of pain and risk of compromising the operative result.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The procedure review describes multimodal postoperative pain options, including long-acting local anesthetic, COX-2 inhibitors, acetaminophen, and gabapentin, but provides no comparative regimen or doses. Select an approach considering the individual bleeding and medication risks.

The source reports that liposomal bupivacaine nerve blocks may improve pain control during the first few postoperative days and reduce opioid requirements; this is a described option, not a required technique.

Nausea and emesis are concerns on emergence, and the rhinoplasty source describes an intravenous corticosteroid as potentially helping postoperative nausea. The evidence provided does not specify a universal antiemetic combination or support the case-field claim that a particular regimen is mandatory.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Smooth emergence is a stated goal; coughing, agitation, nausea or emesis, and hemodynamic instability are concerns. TIVA is associated in the source with reduced coughing, agitation, and nausea on emergence.

The source describes an optional orogastric tube for evacuation of stomach contents at the end of the procedure, while cautioning that late passage immediately before emergence may be stimulating. It does not describe a mandatory throat pack or a throat-pack removal workflow.

Provide postanesthesia care with continual evaluation and monitoring appropriate to the patient, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Recovery disposition should reflect the clinical course and OSA-related oxygenation concerns.
Procedure-specific recovery attention includes epistaxis, nasal obstruction, pain, and swelling; the source describes head elevation and gentle icing as postoperative nursing guidance.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Scar revision is a set of surgical and nonsurgical options; selected candidates may undergo office-based treatment under local anesthesia. The approach depends on scar type and anatomy, with techniques including excision, Z-plasty, W-plasty, and dermabrasion.
Counsel that revision aims to improve a scar, not remove it. Assess functional effects, scar maturity, prior treatment, and whether the expected result is acceptable to the patient.

Do not assume general anesthesia or an airway intervention is needed: selected scar procedures may be done under local anesthesia. The supplied sources do not establish an anesthetic regimen for more extensive procedures.
For recovery, prioritize wound assessment and communication of bleeding or infection concerns. The sources do not establish a specific postoperative analgesic regimen.

sources.label: Insights on in-office scar revision and resurfacing procedures
Scar Revision (StatPearls)

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Select treatment according to scar type, location, tissue loss, tension, and functional limitation. The purpose may be cosmetic or functional; restoration of function is the primary goal when range of motion is limited.

Surgical options described include elliptical excision, Z-plasty, W-plasty, flaps, and grafts. Z-plasty can lengthen an incision and reorient a scar; the choice and design depend on the site and tissue available.

Nonsurgical or adjunct options include intralesional corticosteroids, 5-fluorouracil, laser resurfacing, fillers, and dermabrasion. Raised scars and depressed scars have different treatment options; avoid treating these methods as interchangeable.

sources.label: Scar Revision (StatPearls)
Insights on in-office scar revision and resurfacing procedures

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess whether the scar is mature and whether surgery is appropriate now. The overview describes maturation over about 12–18 months; immature scars may have poor surgical results, so maturity assessment should inform timing rather than relying on a single calendar cutoff.

Establish the patient’s functional and cosmetic goals, prior treatments, and expectations. Explain that the goal is improvement, not elimination, and that complications can produce a less desirable scar.

Review healing risks and medication context, including tobacco use, diabetes, nutrition, immunosuppression, and anticoagulants. For elective revision, the source advises against proceeding when anticoagulation cannot be stopped; the supplied evidence gives no stop interval.

sources.label: Scar Revision (StatPearls)

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The literature supports clinic-based treatment under local anesthesia in selected candidates and identifies a staffed operating room with basic general-surgery equipment for surgical revision. It does not define a universal room or equipment configuration for every technique.

Positioning is determined by scar location; no source provides procedure-specific positioning guidance. Plan monitoring according to the anesthetic actually provided rather than imposing a general-anesthesia setup on local-only treatment.

When MAC or another anesthetic within the ASA standard’s scope is used, follow applicable basic monitoring standards, including continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not establish airway devices, airway technique, ventilation strategy, or criteria for choosing local anesthesia versus sedation or general anesthesia. Do not infer a routine airway intervention from the operation name.
For an anesthetic that includes moderate or deep sedation, apply the relevant ventilation monitoring standard; this is a general anesthesia standard, not a scar-revision-specific protocol.

sources.label: Scar Revision (StatPearls)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For excision and closure, source-described surgical principles include atraumatic technique, anatomic alignment, and tension-free repair; these are surgical considerations, not an anesthetic protocol.

Local anesthetic is commonly used for selected office procedures. The review notes that epinephrine-containing infiltrative anesthetic can prolong effect and provide hemostasis, but it does not provide a scar-revision dosing protocol.

Avoid assuming that topical anesthetic application is risk-free: the review describes cardiotoxicity and central nervous system injury with inappropriate concentration or application over large areas. The sources do not provide a universal local-anesthetic ceiling for this procedure.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Local-anesthetic systemic toxicity is a relevant hazard, particularly with inappropriate topical application. The supplied sources establish the potential for serious toxicity but do not give a procedure-specific recognition or treatment algorithm.

Early surgical complications include bleeding, pain, infection, suture reaction, and flap necrosis. Postoperative concerns should be communicated promptly to the surgeon; the source does not specify anesthetic troubleshooting steps.
Delayed issues include recurrent contracture, hypertrophic scarring, pigment change, nerve injury, atrophy, and trap-door deformity. Counsel that revision may not produce the desired result.

bullets: The scar-revision sources provide no procedure-specific fluid, blood-loss, transfusion, or vascular-access protocol. Do not import fluid or blood-management recommendations from free-flap reconstruction reviews, which address different operations and populations.
Bleeding from the surgical site is identified as an early complication; the supplied sources do not establish expected blood loss or a scar-revision-specific management threshold.

bullets: The procedure review describes local anesthetic options for selected scar procedures, but the supplied sources do not establish a postoperative analgesic regimen or a scar-revision-specific PONV strategy.

bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not describe emergence or a structured postanesthesia recovery protocol. Recovery arrangements should reflect the anesthetic delivered and the patient’s condition.

After anesthesia care, use the applicable postanesthesia standards for observation, handoff, documentation, and disposition. The ASA standard calls for attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.
Monitor for signs of bleeding or infection and promptly inform the surgeon of concerns.

bullets: The office-procedure article is a narrative review, not an anesthesia reference or primary outcome study. It supports selected local-anesthetic procedures and treatment options, but not a complete perioperative anesthetic plan.
